properties.text: Identity type per row (human_employee / human_contractor / service / shared / system_account) — drives policy variant applied

guidance: Record the date and time each identity last accessed any system in a dedicated "last-used" column for every row in the register.
Assign responsibility to a named individual for updating and verifying the "last-used" timestamp data at least monthly.
Cross-reference each "last-used" timestamp with system access logs to confirm accuracy and completeness.
Name the owner of each identity as a specific person, not a generic role or department, to avoid ambiguity in orphan detection.
Document the automated process or schedule that checks for identities idle beyond the defined threshold and triggers suspension or review.
properties.text: Last-used timestamp per row (drives auto-suspend at N days idle; orphan detection)

guidance: Name a specific individual as the owner for each identity in the register, including service accounts, avoiding group or team names.
Record the full name and contact details of each owner directly in the register for every identity entry.
Date each entry to show when the owner was assigned responsibility for the identity.
Review the register regularly and update owner assignments if individuals change roles or leave the organization.
properties.text: Named owner per row (human owner accountable for THIS identity — even for service accounts, must be a human)

guidance: Add a "Risk Tag" column to your identity register to flag identities with elevated privileges or sensitive access.
Mark each relevant row with a clear risk tag such as "Elevated Privilege" or "Sensitive Scope" based on documented access rights.
Name the risk assessor for each tagged identity as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Record the date when each risk tag was last reviewed or updated for traceability.
Avoid leaving any risk tag column blank for identities with privileged or sensitive access—auditors will flag missing tags as a gap.
properties.text: Risk tag per row where the identity has elevated privileges or sensitive scope (drives faster-cadence review)

guidance: Record an explicit expiry date for every service, shared, and temporary identity in the identity register.
Name the owner responsible for each identity, using a specific individual’s name rather than a team or department.
Document the date when each identity was last reviewed or renewed, alongside the expiry date, in the register.
Cross-reference each identity entry with supporting documentation that explains the business justification for its continued use.
Avoid leaving any expiry date field blank or marked as "indefinite"—update all entries to have a concrete, reviewable date.
properties.text: Expiry date per row for service / shared / temporary identities (forces deliberate renewal rather than indefinite drift)

guidance: Record each identity's current status as a separate column in the register, using clear values like "active", "suspended", "disabled", or "pending_termination".
Update the status field immediately when a lifecycle event occurs, and log the date and person making the change in the same row.
Name the owner of the register as a specific individual, not a team or department, in a dedicated column.
Retain a history of status changes for each identity, including previous status, change date, and reason, as a separate audit log or tab.
properties.text: Status per row (active / suspended / disabled / pending_termination) updated as lifecycle events fire

guidance: Record each action item from the identity-management program review in a dated meeting minutes document, listing the specific adjustment discussed.
Assign a named individual as the responsible owner for each action item, avoiding generic roles like "IT team" or "management."
Document the rationale for each action item, linking it to the relevant program review finding or risk identified during the session.
Capture the agreed target completion date for every action item in the same record, ensuring deadlines are explicit and trackable.
properties.text: Action items captured (e.g. tighten auto-suspend threshold, expand HR-cascade automation, retire shared accounts)

guidance: Record the exact date and time when each user’s access is revoked in the revocation log for every identity.
Name the individual who performed the revocation for each entry, avoiding generic labels like "IT" or "admin team".
Cross-reference each revocation entry with the corresponding access removal request or trigger event for traceability.
Retain the revocation record alongside supporting evidence, such as screenshots or system logs, showing the access was removed at the recorded time.
properties.text: Actual revocation timestamp per record (drives SLA-met calculation)

guidance: Assign a named individual to run periodic checks that all contractor accounts with expired end dates are fully disabled in the identity system.
Document the date, scope, and results of each review in a register, listing every expired contractor account and its current status.
Cross-reference each disabled account with supporting system logs or screenshots showing the actual disablement action and timestamp.
Record any exceptions or failures found, along with the responsible person's name and the corrective action taken.
Name the reviewer as a specific person on each review record — do not use generic labels like "IT" or "Security Team".
properties.text: Contractor-expiry verification (audit that expired contractor identities are actually disabled, not just flagged)

guidance: Cross-reference the per-identity revocation record to the specific credential-revocation record by unique identifier or ticket number.
Record the date and time when both the identity and credential revocation actions are completed.
Name the individual responsible for verifying that both records are present and matched before closing the revocation event.
Attach evidence of the completed credential-revocation record; do not rely on verbal confirmation or unchecked status fields.
Document any discrepancies or delays between identity and credential revocation, including actions taken to resolve them.
properties.text: Cross-reference to A.5.17 credential-revocation record (paired event; both must complete to close the loop)

guidance: Record the date of each identity-management program review in a central log, showing that intervals do not exceed 180 days.
Assign a named individual responsible for scheduling and conducting each review, listing their name in the review documentation.
Attach the signed review report or meeting minutes, clearly dated, as evidence of the completed review.
Cross-reference the review schedule with actual review dates to confirm no review was missed or delayed beyond the 180-day limit.
Name the review owner as a specific person, not a team or department, to avoid ambiguity in responsibility.
properties.text: Review date within the planned 180-day interval

guidance: Record the identity being revoked, including full name, unique identifier, and date of revocation, in a dedicated revocation log entry.
Name the IT identity-owner responsible for initiating the revocation and require their physical or digital signature on the record.
Require a second signature from either the HR representative or the hiring manager, confirming the revocation, even if the handover was not in person.
State the reason for revocation and the method used, ensuring details are specific to the individual and not generic or templated.
Avoid listing groups or departments as signatories; ensure both signoff fields contain named individuals with dates.
properties.text: Dual signoff per record (IT identity-owner + HR or hiring manager — captures even when in-person handover impossible)

guidance: Record the exact effective date of each identity revocation in the revocation log, specifying last working day, contract end, or incident decision time.
Name the individual who authorized the revocation and include their signature or approval in the record.
Document the reason for revocation alongside the effective date to provide clear context for the timing decision.
Avoid using vague dates such as "immediate" or "ASAP"; specify the actual calendar date for each revocation.
properties.text: Effective date per record (last working day OR contract expiry OR incident decision time)

guidance: Assign a named individual to lead the periodic review of your identity and access management (IAM) tooling and record their name and review date.
Document the current IAM tool version, recent vendor releases, and any newly available features in a dated review log.
List and describe any new IAM capabilities evaluated, such as just-in-time access, and note whether they have been adopted or deferred.
Identify and record any gaps between current IAM tool capabilities and your organization’s needs, including planned actions or mitigation steps.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual—do not use generic roles like "IT team" or "security group"—to avoid audit findings about unclear accountability.
properties.text: IAM tooling check (vendor releases, new capabilities like just-in-time access; capability gaps to consider)

guidance: Record the unique identifier of each revoked identity in the revocation record, matching the format used in your identity register.
Cross-reference each revocation entry with the corresponding identity register entry to confirm the link is accurate and current.
Name the revoked identity’s owner as a specific individual, not a generic label or group, in the revocation record.
Date each revocation record to show when the identity was revoked.
properties.text: Identity identifier per record (links to identity register entry)

guidance: State the exact date of the next planned identity-management program review in the review report, ensuring it is within 180 days of the current review.
Record the name of the individual responsible for scheduling the next review, not just a team or department.
Document the method used to calculate the next review date, referencing the current review's completion date.
Retain a signed copy of the review report showing the next review date and responsible person.
properties.text: Next planned review date stated (within 180d of this review)

guidance: Name a specific individual responsible for conducting orphan identity analysis, listing their full name and job title in the review documentation.
Document the date of each periodic review, including a summary of the method used to identify orphan accounts across all relevant systems.
Record each orphan identity found, noting the system, user identifier, and the absence of an active HR record or business justification.
State the remediation action taken for every orphan identity, such as account disablement or deletion, and include the date and responsible person.
Attach evidence of completed remediation, such as system logs or screenshots, to the review record for each orphan identity addressed.
properties.text: Orphan analysis (identities without active HR record / business reason; remediation per orphan)

guidance: Record the date and time when each user identity is disabled in a revocation log, including the responsible administrator’s name.
Document the scheduled verification window, such as a 30-day post-disable check, in the same revocation record for each identity.
Assign a specific individual to perform and sign off on the verification that no access has reappeared for the disabled identity after the set window.
Attach evidence of the verification check, such as screenshots or audit logs, to the revocation record for each identity.
Name the verifier as a specific person—do not use generic labels like "IT team" or "admin group."
properties.text: Post-disable verification window noted (e.g. 30-day check that no stale access reappears via service-account chains)

guidance: Record the status of mailbox forwarding for each departing user, including the date forwarding was configured or explicitly not required.
Document whether all file-share access for the individual has been transferred to another user or revoked, listing specific shares and actions taken.
List all group memberships held by the user and confirm the date each was removed or reassigned, referencing supporting system logs.
Name the responsible person who verified and signed off on the completion of all residual-cleanup actions for each identity.
Avoid leaving any cleanup status fields blank or marked as "N/A" without explanation, as auditors will flag incomplete records.
properties.text: Residual-cleanup status per record (mailbox forwarding configured, file-share access transferred or revoked, group memberships cleared)

guidance: Name the IT identity-lead, HR partner, and InfoSec lead as individual reviewers in the review record, not as roles or teams.
Record the date each reviewer completed their portion of the periodic identity-management program review in the official review log.
Require each named reviewer to sign or electronically acknowledge their participation and agreement with the review findings.
Retain the completed review document with all reviewer names and signatures in a central, access-controlled repository.
properties.text: Reviewer identity (IT identity-lead + HR partner + InfoSec lead jointly)

guidance: Select a sample of active service accounts from your identity-management system and record their unique identifiers in a dated review log.
Name the owner of each service account as a specific individual, not a team or department, in the review documentation.
Confirm and document that each listed owner is still employed by the organisation as of the review date.
Review and record whether the assigned permissions and scope for each service account remain appropriate for its current use.
Check and note the expiry date for each service account, flagging any that have lapsed or are missing expiry information.
properties.text: Service-account hygiene audit (sample of service accounts re-validated: owner still employed, scope still appropriate, expiry not lapsed)

guidance: Record the date and time each identity revocation was requested and when it was actually completed in the revocation record.
State the specific SLA for revocation timing in the record, referencing the documented policy or contract where the SLA is defined.
Assign the SLA-met flag as "yes" if the revocation was completed within the stated SLA, or "no_with_reason" if not, with a clear explanation.
Name the individual who reviewed and confirmed the SLA-met status for each record, avoiding generic roles like "IT" or "the team."
Attach any approved exception or deviation documentation if the SLA was not met, including the date and approver’s name.
properties.text: SLA-met flag per record (yes / no_with_reason — gap between effective and actual must be within stated SLA, or exception logged)

guidance: Extract a list of all terminated users from HR records, including both their termination effective date and identity revocation date, for the review period.
Calculate and document the time gap between each user's termination date and the date their access was revoked, highlighting any cases exceeding your defined SLA.
Investigate and record explanations for any outlier cases where revocation exceeded the SLA, attaching supporting evidence such as email threads or incident tickets.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual who conducted the analysis, not a group or department, and date the completed review.
Retain the signed review report and supporting evidence for auditor inspection.
properties.text: Termination-SLA analysis (gap between leaver effective_date and identity_revocation date; outliers investigated)

guidance: Record the trigger type for each identity revocation event, selecting from the approved list: termination, contract_end, suspension_to_disable, incident_revocation, or orphan_cleanup.
Document the date and time when the revocation was actioned for each identity in the revocation record.
Name the individual who authorized the revocation, ensuring a specific person is listed rather than a team or department.
Cross-reference each revocation record with the relevant supporting documentation, such as termination notice or incident report.
Avoid using generic or undefined trigger types; only use the specified categories to prevent auditor rejection of the record.
properties.text: Trigger type per record (termination / contract_end / suspension_to_disable / incident_revocation / orphan_cleanup)

guidance: Name a specific individual as the owner for each service, shared, or non-human account in the identity register, avoiding generic roles or teams.
Record the intended scope and permitted activities for each account in a dated entry within the identity lifecycle management procedure.
Document an explicit expiry or review date for every service, shared, or non-human account, and update the register when extensions are granted.
Log evidence of periodic monitoring for unusual activity on these accounts, including the date reviewed and the reviewer’s name.
Retain approval records for the creation, renewal, or decommissioning of each account, signed and dated by the designated owner.
properties.text: Service / shared / non-human account governance (named human owner, expiry, scope, monitoring) — promoted from SHOULD because this is the weakest spot in most identity hygiene programs

guidance: Document the suspension process in your procedure, including triggers for leave of absence, risk investigations, and auto-suspend after a defined inactivity period.
State the exact inactivity threshold in days that triggers automatic suspension, and record the date this threshold was approved by management.
Name the individual responsible for reviewing and actioning suspension requests, avoiding generic titles like "IT team" or "HR department".
Record each suspension event with the user’s name, reason for suspension, date initiated, and who approved the action.
Retain evidence of periodic reviews of suspended accounts, including review dates and the reviewer’s name.
properties.text: Suspension steps for leave of absence, risk events (under investigation), or extended inactivity (auto-suspend at N days idle)

guidance: State the maximum allowed time between employment termination and deactivation of all access, such as "within 24 hours of the last working day."
Document the step-by-step process for disabling accounts, including who is responsible and how deactivation is confirmed.
Name the individual role responsible for access removal decisions, avoiding generic titles like "IT team" or "HR department."
Record the date and time when each terminated user's access was actually disabled, and retain these records for auditor review.
properties.text: Termination steps with stated deactivation timeline (e.g. within 24h of last day; immediate on involuntary termination)

guidance: Document a procedure that states each individual is assigned a unique user identity for all systems and services.
Name the person responsible for approving creation of new user identities, listing their full name and job title.
Record evidence that shared user accounts are prohibited, such as a clear statement in the procedure and removal of any existing shared accounts.
List all current user identities in a register, showing each identity mapped to a specific, named individual.
Specify that generic or group names are not used for individual accounts—each account must be traceable to one person.
properties.text: Unique identity per person (no shared user accounts for individuals; named accountability)

guidance: Document the initial allocation method for each credential type, specifying whether it uses in-person verification, secure channel, ephemeral link, or hardware-token enrolment.
Name the individual responsible for approving each allocation method, listing their full name and job title in the procedure.
Record the date the allocation procedure was last reviewed and updated, attaching the signed approval from the designated authority.
Cross-reference each allocation method to supporting evidence, such as enrolment logs or secure channel configuration records, for every credential type.
Specify allocation steps for each credential type separately—do not use generic language that could apply to any system or credential.
properties.text: Initial allocation method for authentication information per credential type (in-person, secure channel, ephemeral link, hardware-token enrolment)

guidance: Document all break-glass credentials in a separate, access-controlled file or vault, listing account names, purpose, and creation dates.
Assign a named individual as the custodian responsible for maintaining and updating the break-glass credential documentation.
Record each instance of break-glass credential access in an audit log, including the date, time, reason, and person accessing.
State the storage method for break-glass credentials, such as sealed envelope or digital vault, and include evidence of periodic integrity checks.
Name the custodian as a specific person, not a group or department, to avoid ambiguity in responsibility.
properties.text: Break-glass credentials documented separately (emergency-only accounts with sealed-envelope or vault-with-audit access)

guidance: State password and credential complexity requirements, including minimum length, character types, and history, in a dated and version-controlled procedure document.
Define maximum password age and rotation frequency for each risk tier or user group, with clear mapping in the procedure.
Assign a named individual as the procedure owner—do not use generic titles like "IT" or "the team".
Record the date of last procedure review and approval, with the approver's name and signature captured in the document.
Cross-reference the procedure to supporting technical controls or system configurations that enforce the stated requirements.
properties.text: Password / credential complexity and rotation requirements (length, character classes, history, max-age — risk-tiered per scope)

guidance: Document the step-by-step process to follow when a credential compromise is reported or detected, including notification, investigation, and forced credential rotation.
Assign a named individual or role responsible for overseeing the compromise response and ensure their contact details are listed in the procedure.
Record each credential compromise incident in an incident log, including date detected, actions taken, and investigation results.
State the requirement to check for related or expanded compromise by reviewing access logs and linked accounts after any incident.
Specify that all actions and decisions must be documented with names and timestamps—avoid relying on verbal or undocumented responses.
properties.text: Compromise-response path (when a credential is reported or detected compromised — forced rotation, identity-level investigation, scope expansion check)

guidance: List each authentication factor class used (knowledge, possession, inherence) in your procedure, with examples of methods for each class.
Map and document which combinations of authentication factors are required for each access tier, referencing specific systems or data types.
State how multi-factor authentication requirements change based on risk level or sensitivity, with clear criteria for each tier.
Name the individual responsible for maintaining and updating the authentication mapping—avoid using a team or department as the owner.
Attach a dated approval record for the procedure, signed by a designated authority.
properties.text: Authentication factor classes documented (knowledge / possession / inherence) and which combinations satisfy MFA per access tier

guidance: Cross-reference the Authentication Information Management Procedure to the Identity Lifecycle Procedure by name and document location, explicitly linking credential issuance and revocation steps.
State in the procedure that credentials are only issued after identity creation and are revoked immediately upon identity termination, with process steps mapped to A.5.16.
Name the owner of the procedure as a specific individual, not a generic role or team, to avoid ambiguity in responsibility.
Record the date of the latest review and approval of both procedures, showing alignment and current cross-referencing.
properties.text: Cross-reference to A.5.16 identity lifecycle (credential issuance follows identity creation; credential revocation follows identity termination; pairing enforced not optional)

guidance: State in the procedure that multi-factor authentication is required for all admin accounts, remote access, and access to sensitive data systems.
List the specific systems and applications where multi-factor authentication is enforced, including screenshots or configuration records as evidence.
Name the individual responsible for maintaining and updating the multi-factor authentication settings, not just a team or department.
Record the date the procedure was last reviewed and updated to reflect the mandatory multi-factor authentication requirement.
Attach a sample access log or authentication report showing successful use of multi-factor authentication for an in-scope account.
properties.text: Multi-factor authentication mandated for in-scope access (admin accounts, remote access, sensitive data access) — promoted from SHOULD because MFA is no longer optional baseline

guidance: State in the procedure where passwordless or phishing-resistant authentication methods like FIDO2 or passkeys are currently deployed, including system names and deployment dates.
Document the organization's intention to expand passwordless or phishing-resistant authentication, specifying planned systems and estimated timelines.
Name a specific individual responsible for overseeing the implementation and tracking of passwordless authentication initiatives.
Avoid using generic statements such as "passwordless authentication is encouraged"; instead, provide concrete examples and deployment details.
properties.text: Passwordless / phishing-resistant authentication noted where deployed (FIDO2, passkeys) — direction-of-travel statement

guidance: List each credential type in the register with a clear, unique identifier such as "user_password" or "api_key" next to each entry.
Assign a specific individual as the register owner; avoid generic labels like "IT team" or "security group".
Record the date each credential type was added or updated in the register to show current and historical visibility.
Cross-reference each credential entry with its related system or application to demonstrate complete coverage and traceability.
properties.text: Each credential type captured with a unique identifier (user_password / admin_password / api_key / service_token / cert / mfa_factor / break_glass)

guidance: List each credential type in the register with a unique, descriptive name that clearly distinguishes it from other credential types.
Link every credential type entry to the specific identity types that are authorized to use it, referencing the corresponding identity register row.
Record the date each linkage was established or last reviewed, and name the individual who confirmed the linkage.
Cross-reference each credential type to the relevant identity register entry, using a unique identifier or row number for traceability.
Name the identity types precisely; avoid vague labels like "users" or "staff" that do not match explicit entries in the identity register.
properties.text: Identity-register linkage per row (which identity types use this credential type — closes the loop with A.5.16)

guidance: Record the exact date and time each credential was last rotated in a dedicated column for every entry in the credential register.
Name the person responsible for updating the last-rotated timestamp for each credential, ensuring individual accountability is clear.
Review the register to confirm there are no missing or default timestamps such as "N/A" or "unknown" for any credential row.
Cross-reference the last-rotated timestamps with change logs or ticketing records to verify accuracy and completeness.
properties.text: Last-rotated timestamp per row where applicable (drives drift detection — stale-rotation alert)

guidance: Record the required multi-factor authentication (MFA) factor classes for each credential entry in the register, matching the access tier assigned.
Cross-reference each credential’s access tier with your documented MFA policy to confirm alignment with your organisation’s MFA requirements.
Name the owner responsible for maintaining and updating the credential register as a specific individual, not a group or department.
Date each entry or update in the credential register to show when MFA requirements were last reviewed or changed.
Avoid leaving MFA requirement fields blank or using generic terms like "as needed"; specify the exact factor classes required for each credential.
properties.text: MFA factor requirement per row where applicable (which factor classes; tied to access tier)

guidance: Name a specific individual as the owner for each credential type listed in the register, avoiding group or department names.
Record the full name and current job title of each owner next to the corresponding credential entry in the register.
Document the date each owner was assigned responsibility for their credential type in the register.
Review the register quarterly and update owner assignments if there have been role or personnel changes.
properties.text: Named owner per row (human owner accountable for this credential type — covers governance, escalation, retirement decisions)

guidance: Add a "Phishing-Resistant" column to your credential register, labeling each credential as either "Yes" or "No" based on its authentication method.
List the specific authentication technology for each credential entry, such as "FIDO2," "passkey," "hardware token," "SMS," or "password."
Cross-reference each credential entry with supporting documentation or system logs that confirm the authentication method in use.
Name the person responsible for maintaining the accuracy of the phishing-resistant status for each credential, using a specific individual's name, not a team or department.
Record the date of the last review or update for each credential entry to show ongoing maintenance and accuracy.
properties.text: Phishing-resistant flag per row where the credential is phishing-resistant (FIDO2, passkeys, hardware-token) vs phishable (SMS, password)

guidance: Record the rotation cadence for each credential in the register, stating the exact number of days, automation status, or specific event triggers.
Name the person or system responsible for rotating each credential, listing a specific individual or system name, not a team or generic role.
Document the date of the last rotation and the next scheduled rotation for each credential entry.
State the trigger types for any on-event-only rotations, describing the qualifying events in clear, specific terms.
Review the register to confirm no entries have missing or vague cadence details such as "as needed" or "periodically".
properties.text: Rotation cadence per row (manual N-days / automated / on-event-only with stated trigger types)

guidance: List each credential type in the register with a unique row for clear identification.
Specify for each row which systems and identities use the credential type, naming systems and identity groups explicitly.
Record the date each entry was last updated to show the register is actively maintained.
Name the register owner as a specific individual responsible for updates, not just a team or department.
Attach supporting documentation that cross-references system access lists or identity inventories for each credential type.
properties.text: Scope per row (which systems/identities use this credential type)

guidance: List each production credential in the register with its exact storage vault name, such as 'AWS Secrets Manager' or 'Azure Key Vault'.
Specify the storage location for every credential as a managed vault or secrets manager, never as a spreadsheet, config file, or generic location.
Name the owner responsible for each credential's storage as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Record the date when each credential was last verified in its storage vault, including the verifier's name.
Attach evidence of vault access controls for each credential, such as a screenshot or export of permissions settings.
properties.text: Storage vault per row (named secrets manager / KMS / cert store — never 'spreadsheet' or 'config file' for production credentials)

guidance: Document the step-by-step reset and recovery process, including how users are prompted for identity re-verification using a separate communication channel.
State the method used for identity re-verification, ensuring it does not rely on static security questions or information easily guessed or found.
Record the rate-limiting controls in place for reset and recovery attempts, including thresholds and lockout procedures, in the procedure.
Name the owner as a specific individual responsible for maintaining and updating the reset and recovery procedure, not a team or department.
Retain logs showing recent reset or recovery events, including timestamps and the method of identity re-verification used.
properties.text: Reset / recovery process with identity re-verification (out-of-band; no static security questions; rate-limited)

guidance: Record all action items from each periodic authentication-information program review in a dated meeting minutes document or an action tracker.
Assign each action item to a named individual with a target completion date, avoiding generic owners like "IT" or "the team".
Document the specific adjustment or improvement required for each action item, such as expanding multi-factor authentication or automating token rotation.
Attach supporting evidence for each action item, such as screenshots, updated procedures, or communications confirming implementation steps.
Review and update the action tracker after each review cycle to show progress, completion, or carry-over of outstanding items.
properties.text: Action items captured (e.g. expand MFA to remaining identity types, automate rotation for service tokens, retire phishable factors)

guidance: Record the exact date and time each credential is revoked in the revocation log for every individual credential event.
State the reason for revocation in each record, clearly distinguishing between compromise and routine revocations.
Name the person who authorized each revocation, listing their full name rather than a team or department.
Cross-reference each revocation entry with the related incident or request ticket to show the trigger for the action.
Avoid leaving any revocation record undated or with only a general time range, as auditors will flag missing or vague timestamps.
properties.text: Actual revocation timestamp per record (drives the SLA-met calculation analogous to A.5.16; compromise revocations have tighter SLA)

guidance: Record details of recent authentication-information compromise events in a dated incident log, including the date of detection and affected systems or accounts.
Document the actions taken after each compromise, specifically noting if forced rotation of authentication information was performed and when.
Confirm that the scope of the compromise was reassessed after detection, with evidence of expanded checks or investigations if new risks were identified.
Name the individual responsible for reviewing each compromise response, ensuring a specific person is listed rather than a team or department.
Attach supporting evidence, such as screenshots or logs, showing both the rotation action and scope assessment were completed for each incident.
properties.text: Compromise-response sample (recent compromise events re-examined: was rotation forced? was scope expansion checked?)

guidance: Record the unique identifier of each credential being revoked or reissued in the revocation/reissue log, matching the entry in the credential register.
Cross-reference the credential identifier in the revocation/reissue record with the corresponding credential register entry to confirm traceability.
Name the individual who authorized the revocation or reissue, ensuring the record does not list only a team or department.
Date each revocation or reissue action in the record to provide a clear timeline of credential changes.
properties.text: Credential identifier per record (links to credential register entry; specific instance, not just type)

guidance: Record the date of each authentication-information program review in a central log, showing the actual review date and the previous review date.
Assign a named individual responsible for scheduling and conducting the review, listing their name and role in the review log.
Cross-reference the review log with the planned 180-day interval to confirm no review exceeds the required timeframe.
Attach the signed review summary or meeting minutes as evidence for each review entry in the log.
Name the review owner as a specific person, not a group or department, to avoid auditor concerns about unclear accountability.
properties.text: Review date within the planned 180-day interval

guidance: Record the exact date and time when each credential revocation or reissue is initiated in the revocation log.
State the required effective time for each revocation or reissue, specifying if it is immediate or scheduled for a later point.
Name the individual authorizing the effective time decision for each entry, avoiding generic roles like "IT team" or "admin".
Retain supporting evidence, such as incident reports or rotation schedules, that justify the chosen effective time for each action.
Confirm that the effective time recorded matches the actual system change timestamp by cross-referencing system logs for each event.
properties.text: Effective time per record (when the revocation needed to take effect — immediate for compromise, end-of-day for rotation)

guidance: Record the date, time, and unique identifier for each credential revocation or reissue in a dedicated register.
Cross-reference each credential revocation entry to the corresponding identity revocation record from A.5.16 when the action was identity-triggered.
Name the individual who authorized the credential revocation, ensuring a specific person is listed rather than a group or department.
Attach supporting documentation, such as email or ticket, confirming the identity revocation event that led to the credential action.
Review the register regularly to confirm all identity-triggered credential revocations have a valid, linked A.5.16 record.
properties.text: Cross-reference to paired A.5.16 identity revocation record where this credential revocation was identity-triggered (closes the loop)

guidance: Extract a list of all in-scope user identities from your identity management system and save it as a dated report.
Generate a separate report showing which of these identities have multi-factor authentication (MFA) currently enabled.
Calculate the percentage of in-scope identities with MFA enrolled and document this figure in a dated summary.
Identify and list each identity type not covered by MFA, providing a brief explanation for each gap in a gap analysis document.
Name the person responsible for the MFA coverage audit as a specific individual, not a team or department.
properties.text: MFA enrolment coverage audit (% of in-scope identities with MFA enrolled; gap analysis per uncovered identity type)

guidance: Record the date of the current authentication-information program review in a dated meeting note or review log entry.
State the next planned review date, ensuring it is no more than 180 days after the current review, in the same record.
Name the individual responsible for scheduling the next review, listing their full name rather than a team or department.
Attach the review schedule or calendar invite showing the next review date to the review documentation.
properties.text: Next planned review date stated (within 180d of this review)

guidance: Record the current percentage of user accounts protected by phishing-resistant authentication methods in a dated review document.
Compare and document the change in phishing-resistant credential coverage since the previous review, referencing both dates and percentages.
Name a specific individual responsible for tracking and reporting progress, avoiding generic titles like "IT team" or "security group".
Outline and date a clear roadmap with milestones for increasing phishing-resistant authentication coverage, attaching supporting plans or project timelines.
Retain evidence of management review or approval of the documented roadmap, such as a signed meeting minute or approval email.
properties.text: Phishing-resistance progression review (delta in phishing-resistant credential ratio since last review; roadmap to higher coverage)

guidance: Record the exact date and time when each credential is revoked in a central log, including the responsible person's name.
State the length of the verification window after revocation (e.g. "7 days") in the revocation record for each credential.
Document the results of post-revocation checks, showing whether any authentication attempts using the revoked credential occurred during the verification window.
Name the individual who performed the post-revocation verification, ensuring this is a specific person and not a team or generic role.
Retain evidence of any follow-up actions taken if stale authentication attempts were detected within the verification window.
properties.text: Post-revocation verification window noted (e.g. 7-day check that no stale auth attempts using the revoked credential succeed)

guidance: Record the status of each credential as "revoked," "reissued," or "active" in your credential management log, including the date of status change.
State the reason for revocation or reissue for each affected credential, such as routine rotation or suspected compromise, in the same record.
Name the individual who authorized the revocation or reissue for each credential entry, avoiding generic roles or team names.
Attach supporting evidence, such as incident reports or re-enrolment confirmations, to each record where compromise or forced re-enrolment occurred.
Review records regularly to confirm that no credential shows both "active" and "revoked" status simultaneously for the same period.
properties.text: Replacement-issued status per record where applicable (rotation replaces credential; compromise may force forced re-enrolment, not just rotation)

guidance: Record the date, time, and method used to invalidate all active sessions linked to the revoked credential in the revocation record.
Document the specific actions taken to revoke or delete all refresh tokens and cached credentials associated with the user or service.
Name the person responsible for performing and verifying the residual-access check for each revocation event, not just the system or a generic team.
Attach evidence, such as system logs or screenshots, showing successful completion of session invalidation and token revocation steps for each case.
Confirm that no residual access remains by performing and recording a test login attempt or access check after revocation is complete.
properties.text: Residual-access check per record (sessions invalidated, refresh tokens revoked, cached credentials purged — not just the credential record disabled)

guidance: Name both the IT identity lead and the Information Security lead as joint reviewers in the review record for each periodic authentication-information program review.
Record the vault custodian as an additional reviewer in the review log when vault-related authentication information is included in the program scope.
Document the full names and job titles of all reviewers—do not use generic labels like "the team" or "IT department."
Capture the date each reviewer completed their review and include their electronic or physical signature in the review artefact.
properties.text: Reviewer identity (IT identity-lead + InfoSec lead jointly; vault custodian where vault discipline is in scope)

guidance: Select a sample of user and system credentials that have exceeded the defined rotation period, recording usernames, credential types, and last rotation dates.
Document the root cause for each stale credential, including missed notifications, process gaps, or technical failures, in a dated review log.
Assign a named individual to investigate and resolve each stale credential, recording their name and the date responsibility was accepted.
Confirm that all sampled credentials have been rotated or deactivated, and record the completion date for each action in the review log.
Name the credential owner as a specific person for each entry—do not use generic labels like "IT team" or "system administrator".
properties.text: Rotation-compliance audit (sample of credentials past their rotation cadence; root cause per stale credential)

guidance: Record the date, time, and unique identifier of each compromised credential in a dedicated revocation or reissue log entry.
Name the individual responsible for investigating each credential compromise, ensuring a specific person is listed rather than a team or department.
Document the systems, data, and accounts reviewed for potential access by the actor using the compromised credential, referencing each by name.
State the findings of the scope-expansion check, including any evidence of lateral movement or related incidents, in the same record.
Cross-reference the revocation record with incident response or access review reports from controls A.5.25 and A.5.26, noting the relevant document locations.
properties.text: Scope-expansion check per compromise record (if a credential was compromised, what else might the actor have accessed? — surfaces lateral-movement concerns to A.5.25/A.5.26)

guidance: Record the trigger type for each credential revocation or reissue event using the approved list: identity_termination, rotation_due, compromise_detected, lost_token, factor_change, or decommission.
Document the date and time when the revocation or reissue action was performed for each credential event.
Name the individual who authorized the revocation or reissue, ensuring a specific person is listed rather than a team or department.
Cross-reference each record with supporting evidence, such as incident reports or termination notices, that justify the selected trigger type.
Review records regularly to confirm no trigger type is left blank or described with free-text outside the approved taxonomy.
properties.text: Trigger type per record (identity_termination / rotation_due / compromise_detected / lost_token / factor_change / decommission)

guidance: Name a specific individual as the owner responsible for conducting the periodic authentication-information program review, not a team or department.
Document the date, scope, and sample selection criteria for each vault-discipline audit in a review log.
Record the findings for each sampled production system, noting whether credentials were found in the vault, configuration files, spreadsheets, or chat history.
Assign and document remediation actions for any credentials discovered outside the approved vault, including the responsible person and target completion date.
Retain signed evidence of management review and approval of the audit results and remediation plans.
properties.text: Vault-discipline audit (sample of production systems re-checked: are credentials in the vault, or in config files / spreadsheets / chat history?)

guidance: State the specific hashing algorithm used for authentication information, such as argon2, scrypt, or bcrypt, in the documented procedure.
Document that all authentication information is salted before hashing, with details on salt generation and storage method.
Record the location and configuration of the secrets manager or vault where authentication information is stored.
Confirm that no authentication information is stored or transmitted in plaintext by providing dated technical evidence or configuration screenshots.
Name the procedure owner as a specific individual, not a team or department, in the procedure document.
properties.text: Storage requirements (hashed + salted with modern algorithm — argon2/scrypt/bcrypt; vaulted in secrets manager; never plaintext anywhere)

guidance: Document the approved methods for transmitting authentication information, specifying encryption and out-of-band requirements in a formally version-controlled procedure.
State that authentication information must never be sent via plain email or on the same channel as the user’s identity.
Name a specific individual as the procedure owner—do not list a team or department as responsible.
Record the date of the last review and approval of the procedure, including the approver’s name and signature.
Cross-reference the procedure with technical controls or system logs that demonstrate compliance with the documented transmission methods.
properties.text: Transmission method requirements (out-of-band, encrypted, never on the same channel as the identity itself; never via plain email)

guidance: Document the procedure for protecting authentication information, including rules against sharing, re-use, and use of password managers, in a dated written policy.
Name the reporting path for suspected compromise by specifying a current, individual contact person and their contact details in the procedure.
Publish the advisory guidance to all personnel and record the date and method of distribution, such as email or intranet post.
Retain evidence of personnel acknowledgment, such as signed forms or electronic receipts, confirming they have read and understood the guidance.
State password-manager recommendations clearly, referencing approved solutions and prohibiting generic statements like "use a secure tool."
properties.text: Advisory guidance to personnel on protecting their authentication information (no sharing, no re-use, password-manager guidance, compromise reporting path)

guidance: State the exact retention period for access approval evidence in the Access Rights Management Procedure, specifying the number of years or months.
Name the person or role responsible for enforcing the retention period, using a specific individual or job title rather than a generic group.
Document the location where approval evidence will be stored, such as a named system, folder, or database.
Record the procedure version and date of last update to show when the retention period was last reviewed or changed.
Avoid using vague terms like "retain as needed" or "keep for a reasonable time"—specify a clear, measurable retention timeframe.
properties.text: Retention period for approval evidence stated (drives the audit trail for who-approved-what-when)

guidance: Name the authoriser for each asset class as a specific individual in the procedure, not as a generic role like "IT manager".
Document the date and method of each asset owner's authorisation before granting access, attaching the record to the access request.
Cross-reference each access approval to the relevant asset register entry, showing the asset class and named owner.
Retain signed or digitally approved authorisation records for all access requests, ensuring they are available for auditor review.
properties.text: Asset owner authorization required before access is granted (named authoriser per asset class, not generic 'IT manager')

guidance: State the emergency-access procedure in a separate, clearly labeled section within the Access Rights Management Procedure document.
Name all pre-approved emergency-access accounts, including unique identifiers and assigned individuals, in a dated and version-controlled list.
Require mandatory written justification for each use of emergency access, recorded in an auditable log with user, date, and reason.
Document the process for immediate post-use review of emergency access events, including the name of the reviewer and the review date.
Avoid grouping emergency access with standard access procedures; auditors will flag if the process is not distinctly separated.
properties.text: Emergency-access ('break-glass') procedure stated separately (pre-approved accounts with mandatory post-use justification + audit)

guidance: Cross-reference each access right in the procedure to a unique, registered user identity listed in your current identity register.
Document the process for immediately revoking access when a user identity is deleted or disabled in the identity management system.
Name the person responsible for reconciling access rights with registered identities at least quarterly, and record the date of each reconciliation.
State that generic, shared, or orphan accounts are prohibited, and require all access rights to be linked to a named individual.
properties.text: Explicit linkage to A.5.16 identity management (every access right attaches to a registered identity; no orphan access)

guidance: Document the process for granting access, showing how least privilege is enforced for each role or user type in the procedure.
Cross-reference your access provisioning steps to the segregation-of-duties matrix, highlighting how flagged combinations are identified and managed.
Record examples of blocked or compensated access requests, including the date, requester, and decision, to demonstrate segregation-of-duties controls in action.
Name the person responsible for reviewing and updating the segregation-of-duties rules—avoid listing a team or department as the owner.
properties.text: Provisioning applies least privilege and segregation-of-duties checks (cross-link to A.5.3 segregation of duties — flagged combinations are blocked or compensated)

guidance: Document a clear process for modifying user access when an employee changes roles or responsibilities, including required approvals and timeframes.
Name the individual responsible for updating access rights during role changes, specifying their job title and contact details.
Record each access modification request and its completion date in an access log, referencing the specific user and new role.
Include a step for promptly reviewing and removing old access permissions that are no longer needed after a role change.
Specify the mover process distinctly—do not combine it with joiner or leaver steps, as auditors flag missing or unclear mover procedures.
properties.text: Path for modification of access on role or responsibility change (joiner-mover-leaver flows; mover is the typically-missed leg)

guidance: Cross-reference the access rights management procedure to the current version of the topic-specific access control policy by title and document number.
State the date when the access control policy was last reviewed to show alignment with the procedure’s effective date.
Name the individual responsible for maintaining both the access rights management procedure and the access control policy.
Avoid referencing a generic or outdated policy; cite the specific, current policy relevant to your organisation.
properties.text: References the topic-specific access control policy (A.5.15) — drives consistency between policy and operational practice

guidance: Name the owner of the privileged access management process as a specific individual, not a generic team or department.
Document each privileged access request using the dedicated A.8.2 intake form, including requester, date, and requested access details.
Record separate approval for privileged access by a designated approver, distinct from standard access approvals, with date and signature.
Log all privileged access grants in a register that is separate from standard access logs, showing user, approver, and activation date.
Cross-reference each privileged access entry in the procedure to the A.8.2 process documentation to demonstrate the separation of intake and approval.
properties.text: Privileged access requests route through the A.8.2 privileged-access process (separate intake, separate approval, separate logging)

guidance: Record the full name of the individual who approved each access grant in the Access Rights Register entry for that user.
Capture the date when each access grant was authorised, linking it to the named approver for traceability.
Name the authoriser as a specific person, not a generic role or group, to avoid ambiguity in accountability.
Cross-reference each access grant with the supporting approval request or ticket to provide evidence of the decision process.
properties.text: Authoriser captured per grant (named individual, not generic role; drives accountability)

guidance: Record the specific business reason for each access grant in the Access Rights Register, using clear language that matches the user's job responsibilities.
Name the person who approved the access and include the approval date alongside the business justification entry.
Cross-reference each access entry with the supporting request or ticket that documents the original business need.
Avoid using generic justifications like "needed for work"—state the actual task, project, or system purpose for each access grant.
properties.text: Business justification stated per grant (why this access is needed — informs review decisions later)

guidance: Record the exact date access was granted for each user or account entry in the Access Rights Register.
Cross-reference each grant date with the corresponding authorisation record to confirm access was not given before approval.
Name the person who granted access for each entry, using a specific individual rather than a generic title or team.
Retain the original authorisation document or ticket linked to each grant date for future verification.
properties.text: Grant date captured per row (proves the grant happened in the right order — authorisation → grant, not reverse)

guidance: Cross-reference each access right entry to a unique identity in the identity-management register by including the corresponding identity record ID in every row.
Confirm that no access right is assigned to an identity marked as disabled or deleted in the identity-management register by checking status fields.
Record the date and name of the person who last verified the linkage between the access rights register and the identity-management register.
Name the owner of the access rights register as a specific individual, not a team or department, to avoid ambiguity in responsibility.
Flag and resolve any access right entries that do not have a valid, active identity reference, documenting actions taken for each orphaned entry.
properties.rationale: A.5.16 coherence — was SHOULD, promoted to MUST
properties.text: Linkage to A.5.16 identity-management register per row — every access right attaches to a registered identity (no orphan rights pointing to disabled or deleted identities)

guidance: Add a "Last Verified" date column to your Access Rights Register to record when each individual access entry was most recently reviewed.
Record the actual date of last verification for every access entry, not just the date of the most recent overall review.
Name the verifier as a specific individual for each row, avoiding generic entries like "IT" or "the team".
Update the "Last Verified" date immediately after each access check, ensuring no row is left blank or with outdated information.
properties.text: Last-verified date per row (when this access was last confirmed still needed — drives staleness detection between formal reviews)

guidance: Flag each privileged-access entry in the Access Rights Register with a clear marker indicating it requires separate oversight under control A.8.2.
Cross-reference each flagged privileged-access entry to the corresponding A.8.2 review schedule and reviewer in the register.
Name the reviewer for each privileged-access entry as a specific individual, not a generic role or team.
Record the date of the most recent A.8.2 review for each privileged-access entry in the register.
properties.text: Privileged-access rows flagged for A.8.2 oversight (drives separate-tier review and tighter cadence for privileged subset)

guidance: Record the next review-due date for each access right entry in the register, using a clear and consistent date format.
Name the person responsible for each access right’s review, listing a specific individual rather than a team or department.
Cross-reference each review-due date with the last completed review to confirm the interval aligns with your documented schedule.
Retain evidence of any changes to review-due dates, including who made the change and when, in an audit trail.
properties.text: Next review-due date per row (drives the schedule for the periodic review leaf)

guidance: Add a "Status" field to each row in the Access Rights Register, using only "active", "suspended", or "revoked" as values.
Record the current status for every user or account entry, updating the field immediately when access changes.
Name the person responsible for updating status fields as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Retain a dated record of each status change, including who made the update and the reason for the change.
Cross-reference each "revoked" status with the corresponding revocation record to confirm lifecycle closure.
properties.text: Status field per row (active / suspended / revoked) — drives the review's orphan check and the revocation_record lifecycle close-out

guidance: List each user or account by full name or unique identifier, mapping them directly to the specific systems, applications, or data assets they can access.
Record the date each access right was granted, the reason for access, and the name of the authorising person for each entry.
Cross-reference each access entry with the corresponding employment or contract status to identify and flag orphaned or outdated accounts.
Name the register owner as a specific individual responsible for updates—not as "IT", "the team", or a department.
Review and update the register at least quarterly, recording the review date and the reviewer’s name for each cycle.
properties.text: Subject-to-asset rights mapping (who has access to what — drives review and the orphan-access check)

guidance: Record each temporary access grant in the Access Rights Register with the user's name, access scope, and the specific expiry date.
Flag every temporary-access row with a clear "temporary" status and the associated expiry date field completed.
Assign responsibility to a named individual for reviewing expired temporary access entries and confirming timely removal.
Avoid leaving expiry date fields blank or using generic terms like "as needed"—enter a concrete, calendar-based expiry date for each temporary access.
properties.text: Temporary-access rows flagged with expiry date (drives automated cleanup; complements the procedure's temporary_access SHOULD)

guidance: Record each access rights modification or revocation in the access register, including the date, the specific change, and the person making the update.
Attach a revocation record for every access removal, such as a ticket or signed confirmation, and link it to the corresponding register row.
Update the register row with a reference to the action item or ticket that triggered the change, ensuring traceability for each adjustment.
Name the individual who approved the rights change in the register entry—do not leave this field blank or list only a department.
Confirm all action items related to access changes are marked as closed, with closure dates and supporting evidence attached to each register entry.
properties.text: Action items closed where rights were amended or revoked (each modification or revocation traceable to a register row update + revocation_record where applicable)

guidance: List specific ad-hoc triggers for access rights reviews, such as organisational restructure, mergers, major access policy changes, or security incidents, in your access review procedure.
Document the date and details of each ad-hoc access rights review, including the trigger event, in an access review log.
Name the person responsible for initiating ad-hoc access reviews in response to each listed trigger, ensuring a specific individual is identified.
Attach supporting evidence, such as meeting minutes or incident reports, that confirm the occurrence of the trigger event prompting the review.
Avoid using vague or generic triggers like "as needed" or "when necessary"; specify concrete events that require an ad-hoc review.
properties.text: Ad-hoc review triggers listed (org restructure, M&A, major access policy change, security incident affecting access controls)

guidance: Record the full name of the individual who authorised each access revocation in the access revocation log, alongside the date of authorisation.
Capture both IT and HR or the relevant manager’s names and signatures for access revocations related to employment termination, confirming dual approval.
Attach supporting documentation, such as termination notices or revocation requests, to each record to show the context and basis for the action.
Avoid listing authorisers as generic roles or teams; always specify identifiable individuals for each approval.
properties.text: Authoriser of the revocation (named individual; for terminations the dual-signoff pattern of IT + HR/manager applies)

guidance: Cross-reference each access revocation record with the central access rights register to identify all systems and permissions assigned to the individual.
Record the revocation status for every listed access right, including secondary and non-primary accounts, with a date and responsible person's name.
Attach supporting evidence for each revoked right, such as screenshots or system logs, directly to the corresponding row in the revocation record.
Name the individual who verified that no access rights remain, avoiding generic entries like "IT team" or "administrator".
Document any exceptions or delays in revocation with a clear explanation and follow-up action, signed and dated by the responsible manager.
properties.text: Completeness check per record — all access rights for the subject (from the register) accounted for (each row statused 'revoked' with its own evidence), not just the primary identity rights

guidance: State whether the entire access register or a risk-based sample was reviewed, and record this decision in the review summary document.
Document the method used to select any sample, including risk criteria and rationale, in the review plan or meeting minutes.
Name the reviewer(s) as specific individuals in the review record, avoiding generic labels like "IT team" or "security group".
Record any areas or systems not covered in this cycle as identified gaps, and flag them for inclusion in the next scheduled review.
Retain a dated copy of the completed review checklist or report showing which accounts, systems, or roles were examined.
properties.text: Coverage stated — full register reviewed OR risk-tiered sampling with documented selection method; gaps flagged for next cycle

guidance: Record the date of the most recent access rights review in an access review log, including the name of the reviewer.
Cross-reference the review date against the planned 180-day interval to confirm it falls within the required timeframe.
Document any overdue reviews with a corrective action entry, including the reason for delay and the planned completion date.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual, not a group or department, to avoid ambiguity in accountability.
Retain evidence of the completed review, such as a signed checklist or annotated user access report, for the current and previous review cycles.
properties.text: Review date within the planned interval (typically within 6 months of last review under the 180d cadence)

guidance: Record the exact effective date of access revocation on each access removal record, matching the last working day, contract end, or role-change date.
Document the source event that triggered revocation, such as resignation letter, contract termination notice, or role-change approval, and link it to the record.
Name the individual who authorized the revocation, ensuring the record is not left unsigned or attributed to a generic group.
Attach supporting evidence, such as HR notifications or decision emails, to each revocation record to verify the timeliness of the action.
Avoid using vague or default dates like "immediate" or "as soon as possible"—enter a specific calendar date for each revocation.
properties.text: Effective date per record (last working day OR contract expiry OR role-change effective date OR explicit revocation decision time)

guidance: Record the date and time when access was revoked for each user in a system-generated log or access management tool.
Attach a screenshot or export of the updated user permissions list showing the individual’s access has been removed from each relevant system.
Obtain a confirmation email or signed statement from the system owner verifying that access was disabled, not just requested.
Name the person who performed the revocation as a specific individual, avoiding generic references like "IT" or "the team".
Cross-reference the revocation record with the original access removal request to confirm all listed systems were addressed.
properties.text: Evidence access was actually disabled (system log entry, RBAC change attestation, confirmation from each affected system) — not just 'we asked'

guidance: Document the process that links HR off-boarding events in your HR system directly to access revocation actions in your IT systems.
Record each access revocation with the corresponding HR termination event ID, date, and the name of the person who completed the action.
Name the process owner as a specific individual responsible for monitoring the HR-to-IT access revocation workflow, not a generic team or department.
Cross-reference each access revocation record with the HR system log to show the revocation was triggered by the HR event, not a manual IT request.
Retain evidence of periodic checks confirming that no access revocation occurs without a matching HR off-boarding trigger.
properties.text: Tied to HR off-boarding workflow (A.6.5 linkage) — termination trigger fires from HR system, not from manual IT request

guidance: Cross-reference each access revocation record with the corresponding identity record to confirm the same person’s access was revoked as documented in A.5.16.
Record the trigger for each revocation—termination, contract end, role change, or explicit revoke—alongside the identity in the revocation log.
Confirm that, for terminations or contract ends, the identity is fully deactivated and no active accounts remain for that person.
Verify that, for role changes or explicit revokes, the identity remains active only with updated permissions, and document this status in the record.
Name the reviewer who performed the identity-pair check for each record, avoiding generic entries like "IT" or "team".
properties.text: Identity-pair check per record — confirms A.5.16 identity revocation_record exists for the same identity (where the trigger is termination/contract-end) OR identity remains active (where trigger is role-change/explicit-revoke); closes the bidirectional lifecycle loop

guidance: State the next planned access rights review date in the access review log or tracking document.
Name the person responsible for scheduling and conducting the next review, listing them as a specific individual.
Record the method used to determine the review frequency, such as referencing a policy or risk assessment.
Retain evidence of communication informing relevant staff of the upcoming review date, such as an email or meeting note.
properties.text: Next planned review date stated

guidance: Cross-reference each entry in the access rights register against the current identity register to confirm all access is linked to an active identity.
Record the date and outcome of each reconciliation, including any orphaned access rights identified during the review.
Document the removal or revocation of any access rights found to be attached to disabled or deleted identities, noting the responsible individual and completion date.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual, not a team or department, to avoid ambiguity in accountability for the reconciliation process.
properties.text: Orphan-access check — every register row reconciled against A.5.16 identity register; any rights attaching to disabled/deleted identities surfaced and revoked

guidance: Record the outcome for each user or account reviewed, stating clearly if access was unchanged, amended, or revoked.
Document the rationale for every access that was amended or revoked, specifying the reason for the change in a dated entry.
Name the reviewer responsible for each access decision, ensuring a specific individual is listed rather than a team or department.
Retain the review log with all outcomes and rationales in a format that can be traced back to the original review date.
properties.text: Outcome per reviewed subject (no change / amended / revoked) with rationale where amended or revoked

guidance: Record the date and time when each user or service account is disabled, capturing this in an access revocation log.
Assign a named individual to perform a follow-up review of all related accounts and group memberships within 30 days of revocation.
Document the results of the 30-day review, noting any reactivated or lingering access, and include the reviewer's name and date.
Name the reviewer as a specific person — do not use generic labels like "IT team" or "administrator" in the review record.
Retain evidence of any corrective actions taken if stale access is discovered, including who approved and completed the remediation.
properties.text: Post-disable verification window noted (30-day check that no stale access reappears via service-account chains or forgotten group memberships)

guidance: Identify all users with privileged access and list them in a separate, dated register distinct from general user access records.
Cross-reference each privileged user's access rights review with the oversight controls documented under A.8.2, noting the review date and reviewer.
Schedule privileged access reviews at a more frequent interval than standard users, and record each review's completion date and responsible reviewer.
Name the reviewer for privileged access as a specific individual, not as a group or department, to avoid ambiguity in accountability.
Document any changes or removals of privileged access immediately, including the date, reason, and authorising individual.
properties.text: Privileged-access subset reviewed with extra scrutiny (cross-link to A.8.2 privileged-access oversight; tighter cadence may apply for this slice)

guidance: Record the date and time when each user's primary access is revoked, including the name of the person who performed the action.
Document the removal or transfer of shared mailbox memberships, file-share access, and distribution-list memberships for each user in the revocation record.
List all OAuth tokens and API keys associated with the user, and confirm their revocation or rotation with supporting evidence for each.
Name the responsible individual who verified and signed off on the full closure of access, avoiding generic roles such as "IT" or "the team".
Attach a final checklist or closure statement to each record, confirming all residual access points have been addressed and no open items remain.
properties.text: Residual cleanup status per record (shared mailbox memberships removed or transferred, file-share access reassigned, distribution-list memberships cleared, OAuth tokens revoked, API keys rotated) — full lifecycle closure, not just primary RBAC revocation

guidance: Name both the asset owner and the Information Security lead as joint reviewers in the access rights review record, listing their full names and job titles.
Record the date and time when each reviewer completed their part of the access rights review, creating a clear audit trail.
Confirm in the review record that neither reviewer is the same person who originally authorised the access, noting the authoriser’s name for cross-checking.
Require both reviewers to sign or electronically acknowledge the completed review, attaching evidence of their independent review actions.
Avoid using generic titles like "the team" or "IT department" for reviewers; always specify individuals by name.
properties.text: Reviewer identity and role recorded (asset owner + InfoSec lead jointly; reviewer must not be the same person who authorised the access)

guidance: State whether the access rights review covers all users or a sample, and record this decision in the review plan with the date.
Document the method used to select the sample, such as risk-based, random, or by role, in the review procedure.
Name the individual responsible for defining and approving the sampling approach, listing them in the review documentation.
Avoid describing the sample as "representative" or "random" without detailing the actual selection process used.
properties.text: Sampling approach declared if not full coverage of the register (selection method documented — risk-stratified, random, role-targeted)

guidance: Record the effective date and time of each user's role change or termination in the access revocation log.
Document the actual date and time when access was revoked for each user, referencing system logs or access management tools.
State the SLA for access revocation, such as "within 24 hours of role change," in your documented procedure and reference it in each record.
Assign a clear SLA-met flag for each revocation record as "yes" or "no_with_reason," including a justification if not met.
Name the responsible individual for each access revocation action—avoid using group names or generic titles like "IT team."
properties.text: SLA-met flag per record (yes / no_with_reason) — gap between effective and actual revocation timestamp must be within the procedure's stated SLA, or exception logged; auditor-critical proof of 'within 24h of role change' timeliness

guidance: State the required access revocation timeframes for each trigger type—termination, role-change, and incident—in a dated access control policy document.
Cross-reference each access revocation record with the specific trigger type and the corresponding timeliness target stated in the policy.
Record the actual revocation date and time for each access removal, alongside the trigger event date and type, in an access log.
Name the policy owner as a specific individual responsible for maintaining and updating timeliness targets—not a generic team or department.
properties.text: Timeliness target stated explicitly per trigger type (24h for termination, 5 days for role-change, immediate for incident-driven)

guidance: Record the specific trigger for each access revocation, using one of the approved categories such as termination, role change, or incident-driven.
Document the date and time the revocation was initiated, along with the name of the person who requested the action.
Name the individual who approved the revocation, ensuring this is a specific person and not a generic role or team.
