Cross-reference each revocation entry with supporting evidence, such as a termination letter, contract end notice, or incident report.
Avoid using vague or catch-all reasons like "other" or "N/A" as the trigger; always select or describe a clear, auditable cause.
properties.text: Revocation trigger captured (termination / role change / contract end / explicit revoke / incident-driven / temporary-expiry / orphan-cleanup)

guidance: State in the procedure how service accounts are created, including approval steps and required documentation for each new account.
Name a specific individual as the owner for each service account—do not use generic roles like "IT team" or "system administrator".
Document the process for periodic review and re-attestation of all service accounts, including frequency and responsible person.
Record how deprovisioning of unused or obsolete service accounts is handled, with a log of actions taken and dates.
properties.text: Service account / non-human identity handling stated (provisioning, owner attribution, periodic re-attestation — service accounts are the weakest spot in most access programs)

guidance: State the specific timeframes for granting, modifying, and revoking access rights in the procedure, referencing days or hours for each operation.
Name the person or role responsible for meeting each SLA target, listing them individually rather than as a group or department.
Record the date the procedure was last updated to show when SLA targets were most recently reviewed or changed.
Cross-reference the SLA targets in the procedure with the rev_sla_met flag logic in the revocation record system to confirm alignment.
properties.text: SLA targets stated per operation (grant within X days, modification within Y days, revocation within Z hours of trigger — drives the rev_sla_met flag on revocation_record)

guidance: Document each temporary access request with a named requester, purpose, start date, and mandatory expiry date in an access log.
Assign responsibility to a specific individual to approve and record each temporary access grant, avoiding generic roles or group approvals.
Configure the access management system to automatically revoke temporary access at the recorded expiry date, and retain system logs showing revocation events.
Review the access log monthly to confirm all expired temporary accesses have been revoked, and record the review date and reviewer’s name.
properties.text: Temporary access provisions for time-bound tasks or third parties (expiry date mandatory; automated revocation at expiry)

guidance: Document the specific conditions that trigger inclusion of security requirements in supplier agreements, referencing risk assessment outcomes and supplier criticality.
Name the individual responsible for deciding when security requirements are added to supplier contracts, ensuring this is not a generic team or department.
Record each decision to include or exclude security requirements in a dated log, cross-referencing the related supplier risk assessment.
State how and when the handoff to the supplier agreement process under A.5.20 occurs, with a clear reference in the procedure.
properties.text: Conditions under which security requirements get into the supplier agreement (handoff to A.5.20)

guidance: Document the due diligence process steps in the Supplier Information Security Risk Management Procedure, including use of questionnaires, attestation reviews, and audits.
Assign responsibility for conducting supplier due diligence to a named individual, not a generic role or team.
Retain completed supplier questionnaires, attestation documents, and audit reports with supplier names and dates in a central, accessible location.
Record the final due diligence decision, including approval or rejection, with the approver’s name and date on a formal record.
properties.text: Due diligence steps before engagement (questionnaire, attestation review, audit)

guidance: Document a written procedure describing how your organisation and the supplier will jointly handle security incidents and contingency situations, including clear escalation steps.
Name a specific individual in your organisation responsible for coordinating incident and contingency actions with the supplier, not just a generic team or department.
Record evidence of joint incident response exercises or tabletop tests with the supplier, including dates, participants, and outcomes.
Retain signed acknowledgement from the supplier confirming their agreement to the joint incident and contingency handling procedure.
properties.text: Incident and contingency handling jointly with the supplier

guidance: Record the date and time when each supplier’s logical and physical access was removed in a dedicated offboarding log.
Name the specific individual responsible for confirming access removal for each supplier, not just a team or department.
Cross-reference each access removal entry with supporting evidence, such as screenshots of revoked accounts or badge deactivation records.
Document the completion of access removal by obtaining a signed confirmation from the responsible individual for each offboarded supplier.
properties.text: Logical and physical access removal evidence (link to A.5.18 / A.7.2)

guidance: Name the individual who authorised the supplier offboarding decision in the offboarding record, using their full name and job title.
Record the date the authorisation was given, ensuring it matches the documented offboarding decision.
Obtain a signature or written confirmation from the authoriser, either digitally or on a physical document.
Avoid listing the authoriser as a group or department; specify a single accountable person for clear traceability.
properties.text: Authoriser of the offboarding decision

guidance: Document the date and method of data return or destruction in a supplier offboarding record, referencing the specific contract or agreement.
Obtain a signed attestation from the supplier confirming all data has been returned or securely destroyed, including the date and responsible individual.
Retain supporting evidence such as certificates of destruction, data transfer logs, or email confirmations as attachments to the offboarding record.
Name the responsible internal staff member overseeing supplier data return or destruction, avoiding generic titles like "IT team" or "Procurement."
properties.text: Data return or destruction evidence (with attestation from supplier where applicable)

guidance: Document a summary of lessons learned from each supplier offboarding in a dated record, including any issues or successes encountered during the process.
Update the supplier offboarding procedure or selection criteria to reflect relevant lessons learned, referencing the specific offboarding record and date.
Name the individual responsible for reviewing and incorporating lessons learned, ensuring a specific person is listed rather than a team or department.
Retain evidence of the procedure or criteria change, such as a version-controlled document showing the update and the date of revision.
Cross-reference the updated procedure or criteria with the original lessons-learned record to demonstrate the feedback loop is complete.
properties.text: Lessons-learned link feeding back into the procedure or selection criteria

guidance: State the maximum number of days allowed for supplier access removal in your supplier offboarding procedure, referencing the specific timeliness target.
Record the actual access removal date for each offboarded supplier in a dated log, alongside the contract end date.
Name the person responsible for confirming access removal as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Retain evidence of completed access removal, such as screenshots or system logs, attached to each supplier's offboarding record.
Review a sample of recent offboarding records to confirm the timeliness target was consistently met and document any exceptions.
properties.text: Timeliness target stated (e.g., access removed within 5 business days of contract end)

guidance: Document the date and details of the operational handover from the outgoing supplier, including named recipients and specific transferred responsibilities.
Record the name and contract start date of any replacement supplier engaged, attaching the signed agreement or onboarding confirmation.
Retain written confirmation from relevant business owners that all critical services and data have been transitioned or secured before final supplier disengagement.
Name the responsible individual overseeing the offboarding process—do not list a team or department as the owner.
properties.text: Transition completion evidence (operational handover, replacement supplier engaged where applicable)

guidance: Record the specific offboarding trigger for each supplier, such as contract termination, non-renewal, supplier failure, or re-tendering, in the offboarding log.
Document the date the offboarding trigger was identified and the person who confirmed it in the supplier offboarding record.
Attach supporting evidence, such as termination notices or non-renewal correspondence, to the supplier’s offboarding file.
Name the individual responsible for verifying the offboarding trigger, avoiding generic titles like "the team" or "procurement."
properties.text: Offboarding trigger captured (termination / non-renewal / supplier failure / re-tendering)

guidance: Describe the frequency and method for periodic reassessment of supplier information security risks in the documented procedure, including a named responsible individual.
Specify clear triggers for event-driven reviews, such as incidents, contract changes, or new threats, and record these in the procedure.
Reference how and when third-party security reports or attestations from suppliers are obtained and reviewed, with evidence of the latest review date.
Name the owner as a specific individual — not a team or department — responsible for ensuring ongoing supplier risk monitoring activities are completed.
Attach a sample completed monitoring log or review record, showing dates, findings, and actions taken for at least one supplier.
properties.text: Ongoing monitoring approach (periodic reassessment, event-triggered review, third-party reports)

guidance: State in the procedure that all new suppliers must complete the standard supplier security questionnaire before onboarding.
Reference the exact title and current version number of the standard supplier security questionnaire within the procedure.
Cross-reference the location of the questionnaire in your document management system or supplier onboarding portal.
Name the person or role responsible for maintaining and updating the standard supplier security questionnaire in the procedure.
Avoid using a generic reference such as "see supplier questionnaire"—specify the unique document name and version to prevent ambiguity.
properties.text: Reference to standard supplier security questionnaire

guidance: List each supplier in the register with a separate row, including the full legal name and a unique identifier.
Specify the type of access granted to each supplier per row, choosing from logical, physical, network, application, or app-to-app.
Record the date when the access type was last reviewed or updated for each supplier entry.
Name the person responsible for approving each supplier’s access type, using a specific individual’s name rather than a generic title or team.
Attach supporting documentation or a cross-reference to the contract or agreement that describes the access type for each supplier.
properties.text: Access type per row (logical / physical / network / application / app-to-app)

guidance: Assign a risk classification to each supplier in the register, using a clear tier or category that matches your documented risk methodology.
Record the name of the person who determined each supplier’s risk classification, along with the date of the assessment.
Cross-reference each supplier’s risk classification to supporting documentation, such as a completed risk assessment or due diligence checklist.
Name the risk classification for each supplier as a specific tier or category — do not leave this field blank or use generic terms like "varies".
properties.text: Risk classification (tier or category) per row

guidance: List all suppliers in the Supplier Register, including full legal names and a primary contact for each entry.
Mark each supplier with a clear "critical" or "non-critical" flag based on documented business impact criteria.
Cross-reference every supplier flagged as "critical" with related audit and continuity controls in A.5.29 and A.5.30, noting specific links.
Name the owner of the Supplier Register as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Record the date of the last review or update for each supplier entry to show current status.
properties.text: Critical-supplier flag (drives audit + continuity scrutiny — link to A.5.29 / A.5.30)

guidance: Record each supplier’s full legal name and primary business address in the supplier register.
List the specific products or services each supplier provides, using clear descriptions rather than generic categories.
Assign a criticality rating to each supplier, with a named individual responsible for the assessment and the date it was completed.
Name the owner of each supplier entry as a specific person, not a team or department.
properties.text: Each supplier captured: identity, products/services, criticality

guidance: Name a specific individual as the relationship owner for each supplier entry in the Supplier Register, listing their full name and job title.
Record a designated information security contact for each supplier, including their full name and direct contact details.
Document the date each owner and InfoSec contact was last reviewed or updated in the register.
Avoid using generic terms like "IT team" or "Procurement" as owners; always list a named person for accountability.
properties.text: Named internal owner accountable per supplier (relationship owner + InfoSec contact)

guidance: List each supplier in the register as a separate row, including their full legal name and primary contact details.
Record all disclosed sub-suppliers or fourth parties for each supplier in dedicated columns or linked rows, clearly identifying their relationship.
State the date each sub-supplier or fourth party was last confirmed as disclosed by the primary supplier.
Name the person responsible for maintaining and updating each supplier entry, avoiding generic titles like "the team" or "Procurement".
Attach supporting documentation or correspondence where suppliers have disclosed their sub-suppliers, referencing the file location or communication date.
properties.text: Disclosed sub-suppliers / fourth parties tracked per row

guidance: List each supplier in the register with a separate row, including their full legal name and a unique identifier.
Assign a supplier type to every row, selecting from defined categories such as ICT service, ICT infrastructure component, logistics, or utilities.
Document the criteria used to classify supplier types in a reference column or linked procedure, with the latest review date and approver's name.
Name the person responsible for maintaining supplier type accuracy in the register, using a specific individual rather than a team or department.
Review the register for any rows with missing or generic supplier type entries, and update them to reflect the correct, specific category.
properties.text: Supplier type per row (ICT service / ICT infra component / logistics / utilities / etc.)

guidance: Document the process for identifying backup or alternative suppliers when a critical supplier is disrupted, including clear decision criteria and responsible roles.
Name the individual responsible for activating backup supplier arrangements, listing their full name and job title in the procedure.
Record the date when the backup or alternative supplier process was last tested or reviewed, attaching supporting evidence such as test reports or meeting minutes.
State the specific steps to follow if no backup supplier exists, including escalation paths and risk acceptance documentation signed by a senior manager.
Avoid using generic statements like "alternative suppliers will be used"—specify named suppliers or detailed sourcing procedures tailored to your organisation.
properties.text: Backup or alternative supplier processes / treatment of supplier disruption

guidance: Record all action items from each supplier portfolio review in a dated log, including those related to monitoring or training adjustments.
Assign each action item to a named individual with a target completion date documented in the review log.
Document the specific monitoring or training arrangement that requires adjustment, referencing the relevant supplier and rationale discussed in the review.
Attach evidence of follow-up, such as updated training materials or revised monitoring procedures, to the action item record.
Name responsible individuals for each action item—avoid listing only teams or departments as owners.
properties.text: Action items captured where monitoring or training arrangements need adjustment

guidance: Record the date of the most recent supplier portfolio review in a central register, clearly linked to the responsible owner.
Name the individual who conducted the review, avoiding generic entries like "Procurement Team" or "IT Department".
Document the planned review interval in months or years, and cross-reference it with the actual review date.
Retain a signed or approved record of the review decision, including any actions or follow-ups identified during the review.
properties.text: Review date within the planned interval

guidance: State the next planned review date for the supplier portfolio in your supplier management register or tracking document.
Record the name of the individual responsible for conducting the next review alongside the planned date.
Document the date this review schedule was last updated to show the information is current.
Name the owner as a specific individual — not a team or department — to avoid ambiguity about accountability.
properties.text: Next planned review date stated

guidance: List all suppliers in the current portfolio, including their assigned tier, in a dated review document.
Record the outcome for each supplier or tier as "no change," "re-tiered," "added," or "removed," with supporting rationale.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual, not a group or department, and capture their signature or approval on the review record.
Attach evidence of any changes, such as updated contracts or exit documentation, to the review file.
State the review date clearly; avoid undated or draft versions that could cause confusion about the review period.
properties.text: Outcome per supplier or per tier (no change / re-tiered / added / removed)

guidance: Name the reviewer by full name and job title in the supplier portfolio review record for each review cycle.
Record the date the review was completed and link it to the documented reviewer identity.
Specify the reviewer’s role as procurement lead or information security lead, avoiding generic titles like "the team" or "IT department".
Retain evidence of the review, such as a signed or digitally acknowledged review summary, showing the named reviewer’s approval.
properties.text: Reviewer identity and role (typically procurement + InfoSec lead)

guidance: List specific ad-hoc events—such as mergers, acquisitions, new business lines, or supplier incidents—in your supplier review procedure document.
Record each unscheduled supplier portfolio review in a dated log, including the triggering event and the decision to initiate the review.
Assign a named individual to approve the initiation of each ad-hoc review, avoiding generic roles like "the team" or "procurement."
Attach supporting evidence of the triggering event, such as incident reports or business case documents, to the review record.
properties.text: Ad-hoc triggers (M&A, market events, new business line, supplier incident) prompting unscheduled review

guidance: List each supplier type and access type in your procedure, describing how they interact with your information or systems.
Define minimum information security requirements for each supplier and access type, referencing specific controls or standards where applicable.
Assign a named individual to approve and update these minimum requirements, recording their name and the approval date in the procedure.
Specify rules that are tailored to your organisation — do not use generic or boilerplate requirements that could apply to any company.
properties.text: InfoSec rules per supplier type / access type with minimum requirements

guidance: Document the criteria used to select and evaluate suppliers, including how information sensitivity and service criticality are factored into the process.
Record the results of a risk analysis for each supplier, showing how risks related to information security were identified and assessed.
Attach references or attestations from suppliers that demonstrate their information security capabilities and relevant certifications.
Name the individual responsible for approving supplier selection decisions, ensuring a specific person is listed rather than a team or department.
Retain dated records of each supplier evaluation, including the criteria applied and the outcome of the assessment.
properties.text: Selection and evaluation criteria based on sensitivity of information and services (risk analysis, references, attestations)

guidance: List all supplier types relevant to your organisation, such as ICT services, infrastructure, logistics, utilities, and financial providers, in your risk management procedure.
Document clear definitions and examples for each supplier type to avoid ambiguity or overlap between categories.
Name the person responsible for maintaining and updating the supplier type list, ensuring a specific individual is identified rather than a team or department.
Record the date of the most recent review or update to the supplier type documentation within the procedure.
properties.text: Supplier types identified and documented (ICT services, ICT infrastructure components, logistics, utilities, financial, etc.)

guidance: Define concrete tiering criteria such as data sensitivity, operational dependency, and financial exposure in a documented section of your Supplier Information Security Risk Management Procedure.
Assign each supplier to a specific risk tier based on the documented criteria, and record the assignment with the supplier’s name and assessment date.
Name the person responsible for tiering decisions as a specific individual, not a group or department, in the procedure document.
Attach a completed example of a supplier tiering assessment that references the actual criteria used, not generic or boilerplate language.
properties.text: Tiering model with concrete criteria (data sensitivity, dependency, financial exposure)

guidance: Document the training curriculum that covers secure engagement and information exchange practices with suppliers, including the date it was last updated.
Record attendance lists showing named employees who completed the supplier information security training, including training dates.
Assign responsibility for delivering and updating the training to a specific individual, not a team or department.
Retain copies of training materials and completion certificates for each employee as evidence of participation.
Review and update training content annually, and keep a dated record of each review and revision.
properties.text: Training of own personnel on appropriate engagement and information exchange with suppliers

guidance: Name the individual who approved the information security policy, specifying their full name and job title on the approval document.
Document the date the policy was formally approved, ensuring it appears on the signed approval page.
State the signatory’s authority to approve the policy, referencing the delegation chain if the signatory is not the CEO.
Attach or cross-reference the formal delegation document or board resolution that grants approval authority to the signatory.
Avoid using generic titles or groups as approvers; always identify a specific person with documented authority.
properties.text: Statement of the signatory's authority to approve (delegation chain if not CEO)

guidance: Name the approving top management individual by full name and job title on the policy approval page.
Record the exact approval date next to the signature or approval statement on the policy document.
Sign the policy document physically or electronically to confirm explicit approval by top management.
Avoid using undated or pre-signed templates; ensure each policy version shows a unique approval date.
properties.text: Approval date recorded

guidance: Name the signatory as a specific top management individual, such as the CEO or board chair, on the policy approval page.
Record the approval date next to the signature to show when top management formally endorsed the information security policy.
Retain a signed copy of the approved policy in a central repository accessible for audit and reference.
Document any delegation of approval authority in meeting minutes or a formal memo, including the name and title of the delegate.
properties.text: Signatory at top-management level (CEO, board chair, or delegated equivalent)

guidance: Name the specific policy version, including version number and date, in the approval document to clearly identify what is being approved.
Record the approval date alongside the policy version reference in the approval record.
Assign the approval to a named individual in top management, not a group or generic title.
Retain a copy of the signed approval document that explicitly references the approved policy version.
properties.text: Reference to the specific policy version being approved

guidance: Distribute the current information security policy to all personnel using a trackable method such as email with read receipt or an e-learning platform.
Collect individual acknowledgments of receipt and understanding, such as signed registers or digital confirmations, for each staff member.
Record the date of acknowledgment and the name of each person in a central register or learning management system report.
Name the policy version and date in the acknowledgment record to avoid confusion with previous or draft versions.
Retain completed acknowledgment records for all current personnel and ensure records are updated when new staff join or policies change.
properties.text: Acknowledgment of receipt and understanding by personnel (e.g. signed register, e-learning completion)

guidance: List all staff, scoped subsets, or named groups who must receive the information security policy, specifying names or roles as appropriate.
Record the date and method used to communicate the policy to each identified audience, such as email, intranet post, or in-person meeting.
Confirm receipt or acknowledgment from each recipient group, capturing signatures, read receipts, or completed acknowledgment forms.
Name the audience as specific individuals or defined groups—do not use vague terms like "everyone" or "all staff" without clear definition.
properties.text: Audience reached (all staff, scoped subset, or named groups)

guidance: Record the exact channel used to communicate the information security policy, such as intranet, email, training session, or town hall, in a dated log.
Name the person responsible for sending or presenting the policy, listing their full name and job title in the communication record.
Attach or link supporting evidence, such as a screenshot of the intranet post, a copy of the email, or an attendance list from a training session.
Specify the date the policy was communicated using the chosen channel, ensuring the record shows when staff received the information.
Avoid using vague descriptions like "shared with staff"—state the specific channel and method used for each communication event.
properties.text: Channel used (intranet publication, email, training session, town hall)

guidance: Record the exact date the information security policy was published and communicated in a dated register or communication log.
Name the person responsible for sending or posting the policy, specifying a real individual rather than a generic role or team.
Retain a copy of the communication, such as an email, intranet post, or announcement, showing the date and recipients.
Cross-reference the policy version communicated with the date in your register to confirm alignment between the document and the communication record.
properties.text: Date of publication/communication

guidance: Identify all relevant external parties, such as contractors and suppliers, who require awareness of the information security policy.
Document the date, recipient name, and method used each time the information security policy is communicated externally.
Retain copies of the actual communication sent, such as emails or signed acknowledgements, to each external party.
Name the responsible individual who approves and oversees external policy communications, avoiding generic titles like "the team" or "IT department".
Review and update the communication record annually, noting the review date and any changes in external parties or policy content.
properties.text: Communication to relevant interested parties (contractors, suppliers) where appropriate

guidance: State in the policy that the organisation is committed to meeting all relevant legal, regulatory, and contractual information security obligations.
Name the person or role responsible for monitoring changes in applicable laws, regulations, and contracts within the policy document.
Record the approval of the policy by a named senior manager, including their signature and the date of approval.
Specify the date of the latest policy review and ensure it is not older than one year from today.
Name the owner as a specific individual, not a generic group or department, to avoid ambiguity in accountability.
properties.text: Commitment to legal, regulatory and contractual compliance

guidance: Name the policy owner as a specific individual, such as the CISO or equivalent, in the policy document’s header section.
Record the owner’s full name, job title, and contact details directly within the policy document.
Sign and date the policy to confirm the owner’s acceptance of responsibility for its content and maintenance.
Avoid listing the owner as a group, team, or department—use only a named individual to meet accountability requirements.
properties.text: Policy owner named (typically CISO or equivalent)

guidance: State the organisation’s information security principles and objectives clearly within the policy document, using language specific to your business context.
Name the individual responsible for approving the policy, and include their signature and approval date on the document.
Document a version number and review date on the policy to show it is current and regularly maintained.
Avoid using generic or boilerplate principles; tailor statements to reflect your organisation’s actual security priorities and goals.
properties.text: Information security principles and objectives stated

guidance: Record the date of the most recent information security policy review in a central log or register.
Document the planned review interval for the policy, specifying the exact timeframe (e.g., every 12 months) in a dated record.
Confirm the actual review date falls within the documented interval since the previous review, and note any exceptions with reasons.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual, not a group or department, in the review record.
Retain the signed or approved review record showing both the review date and the reviewer’s name.
properties.text: Review date within the planned review interval (typically within 12 months of last review)

guidance: State the next planned review date in the policy review record, using a clear and specific calendar date.
Record the name of the individual responsible for scheduling the next review, not just a team or department.
Confirm that the stated review date aligns with your organisation’s defined policy review cycle or schedule.
Retain the dated review record in a location accessible to relevant stakeholders for reference during audits.
properties.text: Next planned review date stated

guidance: Record the date the information security policy review was completed in a dated entry on the review record.
State the outcome of the review as "no change," "amended to vN," or "retired," and include the version number if amended.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual responsible for the review, not a group or department.
Sign or otherwise formally approve the review outcome to show it was authorized by the appropriate person.
properties.text: Outcome of the review (no change / amended to vN / retired)

guidance: Record the full name of the person who conducted the policy review in the review record.
State the reviewer’s official job title or role next to their name in the review documentation.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual — do not use group names, generic titles, or departments.
Date the review entry to show when the individual completed their assessment.
properties.text: Reviewer identity and role

guidance: List specific events that would trigger an ad-hoc policy review, such as major system upgrades, regulatory changes, or security incidents.
Document each trigger with a clear description and date added in the policy review record.
Name the person responsible for monitoring and identifying these triggers, ensuring a specific individual is listed rather than a group or department.
Review the triggers annually and update the record with the review date and the name of the reviewer.
properties.text: List of significant-change triggers that should prompt an ad-hoc review

guidance: Name a specific individual as the owner of the information security policy, avoiding generic titles like "the team" or "IT department".
Document each key information security role and its responsibilities in the policy, listing job titles and a summary of duties.
Record the date the policy was last reviewed and approved by senior management, including the approver’s full name and signature.
Cross-reference the policy with an up-to-date organisational chart to show alignment between named roles and actual staff positions.
properties.text: Roles and responsibilities for information security

guidance: State the exact types of information assets, locations, and personnel covered by the policy in a dedicated “Scope” section of the document.
Name the owner of the policy as a specific individual, including their job title and contact details, not just a department or team.
Record the date the scope statement was last reviewed and updated, showing it reflects current operations and boundaries.
Cross-reference the scope section with your asset register and organizational chart to confirm all relevant areas and roles are included.
properties.text: Scope of the policy defined (which assets, locations, personnel)

guidance: List all topic-specific policies by title and version number within the main Information Security Policy document.
Cross-reference each listed policy to its relevant ISO27001 control, such as A.5.10 for Acceptable Use or A.5.12 for Classification.
State the location or repository where each referenced policy can be accessed, using a direct link or file path.
Name the policy owner as a specific individual, not a team or department, for each topic-specific policy referenced.
Date the Information Security Policy and all referenced policies to show current and aligned versions.
properties.text: References to topic-specific policies that flow from this one (e.g. A.5.10 AUP, A.5.12 classification, A.6.4 disciplinary)

guidance: State the current version number clearly on the front page of the Information Security Policy document.
Record the effective date of the policy in a visible location, such as the document header or title page.
Name the policy owner as a specific individual, not a group or department, to avoid ambiguity in responsibility.
Retain previous versions and their effective dates in a version history table within the document or as an appendix.
properties.text: Version number and effective date

guidance: State acceptable uses of the supplier’s services or systems in a dedicated section, using clear examples relevant to your organisation.
List specific unacceptable uses, such as sharing credentials or using data for non-contracted purposes, in the agreement template.
Reference the internal policy or standard that defines acceptable and unacceptable use, including the policy’s title and version.
Name the person responsible for maintaining the template as a specific individual, not a team or department.
properties.text: Acceptable + unacceptable use rules stated

guidance: State in the supplier agreement that your organisation has the right to audit the supplier’s security controls at reasonable intervals.
Specify in the template that independent security certifications, such as ISO 27001 or SOC 2, may be accepted as alternatives to on-site audits.
Name the person or role responsible for reviewing and approving supplier-provided attestations or certifications in each agreement.
Record the date and version of the template used for each supplier agreement to show the inclusion of audit rights language.
Name the owner as a specific individual — not a team or department — responsible for maintaining and updating the template.
properties.text: Audit rights (right to audit; accept attestations like ISO 27001 / SOC 2 in lieu)

guidance: Name the authorized personnel or roles permitted access in the agreement, specifying individuals or job titles rather than generic terms like "staff."
Document the exact conditions under which access is granted, such as purpose, duration, and required approvals, within the agreement template.
Record the date and version of the template to demonstrate when the security requirements were last updated.
Assign responsibility for maintaining and updating the template to a specific named individual, not a group or department.
properties.text: Named or role-defined authorized personnel + conditions for access

guidance: Name the person responsible for mapping your organisation’s information classification scheme to each supplier’s scheme in the agreement template.
Document your organisation’s classification levels and each supplier’s equivalent levels side-by-side in a table within the agreement template.
State any differences or gaps between your classification scheme and the supplier’s, and describe how these will be addressed in the agreement.
Attach a dated record of the most recent review or update of the classification mapping for each supplier agreement template.
Specify the mapping for each supplier, not just a generic mapping — avoid using boilerplate language that could apply to any supplier.
properties.text: Information classification mapping (org scheme → supplier scheme where they differ)

guidance: Record the governing jurisdiction for each supplier agreement in the Supplier Agreement Coverage Register, using the exact wording from the signed contract.
Cross-reference each jurisdiction entry to the relevant section or clause number in the corresponding supplier agreement.
Name the person responsible for verifying jurisdiction entries as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Date each jurisdiction entry to show when it was last reviewed or updated in the register.
properties.text: Governing jurisdiction per agreement

guidance: Name a specific individual as the owner accountable for each supplier agreement, avoiding generic titles like "the team" or "procurement department".
Record the owner's full name and job title next to each supplier agreement entry in the Supplier Agreement Coverage Register.
Document the date when the owner was assigned responsibility for each agreement in the register.
Review and update the register at least annually to confirm the named owner is still current and accurate.
properties.text: Named owner accountable for the agreement (typically procurement or legal partner)

guidance: List each supplier in the Supplier Agreement Coverage Register with their full legal name and unique identifier.
Record the signed date of the current, active agreement next to each supplier entry in the register.
Attach a copy of the signed agreement showing the signature and date for each supplier listed.
Name the individual responsible for maintaining and updating the register, not a generic team or department.
Review the register quarterly and update any expired or replaced agreements with new signed dates.
properties.text: Signed-date of the active agreement per supplier

guidance: List all approved sub-processors for each supplier in the Supplier Agreement Coverage Register, including full legal names and approval dates.
Cross-reference each supplier entry with the corresponding record in the Supplier Register required by control A.5.19.
Record the name and signature of the individual who approved each sub-processor, along with the date of approval.
Avoid using generic terms like "various" or "TBD" for sub-processor names; specify each entity clearly.
properties.text: Approved sub-processors per supplier tracked (link to A.5.19 supplier register)

guidance: Record the template version number and date used for each supplier agreement in the Supplier Agreement Coverage Register.
Cross-reference each supplier entry in the register with the actual signed agreement to confirm the template version applied.
Name the person responsible for updating the register with template version details for each new or renewed supplier agreement.
Avoid leaving the template version field blank or marked as "current"—enter the specific version identifier for each supplier.
properties.text: Template version applied per supplier

guidance: Record the start date, end date, and renewal terms for each supplier agreement in a dedicated column for every row in the register.
Name the responsible individual who maintains and updates the register, listing their full name rather than a team or department.
Review each row to confirm no agreement is missing a renewal or expiry date, and update any incomplete entries immediately.
Retain a copy of the signed agreement or renewal notice linked to each register entry for verification of dates.
properties.text: Agreement term and renewal/expiry date per row

guidance: List each supplier in the register with a unique row, including their full legal name and a clear description of the service provided.
Assign a specific supplier tier to every row, using a defined tiering scheme documented elsewhere in your supplier management process.
Cross-reference each supplier’s tier to the relevant agreement clause variant required, ensuring the clause matches the assigned tier.
Record the date and name of the person who last updated the supplier tier, so changes are traceable to a specific individual.
Name the supplier tier owner as a specific person, not a team or department, to avoid ambiguity in responsibility.
properties.text: Supplier tier per row (drives which clause variant is required)

guidance: State in the template that all supplier-handled data must be encrypted both at rest and during transmission, referencing specific encryption standards.
Specify in the template the permitted geographic locations or countries where supplier data may be stored or processed.
Name the individual or role responsible for reviewing and updating the data handling requirements section in the template, not just "the team."
Record the date of the most recent update to the data handling requirements within the template document.
properties.text: Data handling requirements (encryption at rest and in transit, location/sovereignty)

guidance: State the step-by-step process for identifying, reporting, and resolving defects in the supplier agreement, including responsible roles and response timelines.
Document the escalation path and decision-makers for conflicts between your organisation and the supplier, with named contacts and clear resolution stages.
Name the owner as a specific individual responsible for managing defect and conflict resolution, not a generic team or department.
Record the date the defect and conflict resolution processes were last reviewed and approved by a senior manager.
properties.text: Defect resolution and conflict resolution processes

guidance: Name the approver for each supplier agreement deviation as a specific individual, not a group or department.
Record the date and outcome of each deviation approval in the register, linking to the relevant risk assessment.
State the residual risk level for each deviation and cross-reference the justification for the chosen approver’s authority.
Retain evidence of the approver’s formal decision, such as a signed approval or documented email confirmation.
properties.text: Approver of the deviation, at level proportional to residual risk

guidance: Record the exact ISO27001 clause number and title deviated from for each entry in the Supplier Agreement Deviation Register.
Reference the specific section or template paragraph in the supplier agreement where the deviation occurs for every row.
Name the individual who approved each deviation, avoiding generic entries like "management" or "procurement team".
Date each deviation entry to show when the deviation was identified and approved.
Attach or link supporting documentation, such as the approved deviation request or related correspondence, to each register entry.
properties.text: Clause deviated from per row (identified by template section)

guidance: Record each supplier agreement deviation with a unique entry, including the date, supplier name, and the specific requirement not met.
State the compensating control applied for each deviation, such as increased monitoring, contractual remedies, or an alternative security requirement.
Name the person responsible for approving each compensating control as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Attach evidence of risk assessment justifying the compensating control, including the date and the assessor’s name.
Review and update the register regularly, documenting the date of each review and the reviewer’s name.
properties.text: Compensating control stated (monitoring, contractual remedy, alternative requirement)

guidance: Record a clear expiry or re-papering target date for each supplier agreement deviation entry in the register.
Name the responsible individual for tracking and actioning each deviation’s expiry or re-papering, not just a team or department.
Document the date each deviation was last reviewed to confirm ongoing relevance and update the register accordingly.
Attach supporting evidence, such as approval emails or meeting minutes, showing agreement to the target date for each deviation.
properties.text: Expiry / re-papering target date for each deviation (so deviations age out rather than persist indefinitely)

guidance: Record the specific reason for each supplier agreement deviation in the register, referencing commercial necessity, market constraint, or supplier capability.
Name the individual who approved each deviation, ensuring the register lists a specific person rather than a team or department.
Date each entry in the deviation register to show when the reason was documented and the deviation approved.
Attach supporting evidence, such as correspondence or meeting notes, that substantiates the stated reason for the deviation.
properties.text: Reason for the deviation captured (commercial necessity, market constraint, supplier capability)

guidance: State in the Supplier Agreement Deviation Register the specific triggers that require reassessment, such as supplier ownership changes or new risk findings.
Record the date and details of each reassessment trigger event in the register, linking to supporting evidence like incident reports or supplier notifications.
Assign a named individual responsible for monitoring supplier and risk changes, avoiding generic entries like "procurement team" or "management".
Document each reassessment decision with the date, outcome, and the name of the person who approved the action taken.
Cross-reference each reassessment entry to the relevant supplier agreement or risk assessment document to show clear linkage.
properties.text: Trigger for reassessment when supplier or risk circumstances change

guidance: Cross-reference each supplier in the deviation register to the unique identifier used in your supplier register under control A.5.19.
Record the supplier’s full legal name and identifier for every deviation entry, ensuring it matches exactly with the supplier register.
Name the person responsible for maintaining the deviation register as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Document the date each deviation entry is added or updated to maintain a clear audit trail.
properties.text: Supplier identifier per row (link to A.5.19 supplier register)

guidance: Name a specific individual as the security incident contact for your organization in the agreement, including their full name, title, and contact details.
Record the supplier’s designated security incident contact by full name, title, and direct contact information within the agreement template.
Confirm that both contacts are listed as individuals, not generic roles like "IT team" or "Security Department," to avoid ambiguity.
Retain the date when the contact information was last updated to demonstrate the information is current.
properties.text: Security incident contacts named on each side

guidance: Insert a clause in the template requiring suppliers to notify your organisation of security incidents within a specific timeframe, such as 24 hours of detection.
Specify in writing that suppliers must actively collaborate with your organisation during incident investigation and remediation efforts.
Name the responsible contact person or role at your organisation for suppliers to notify in the event of an incident.
State the notification timeline as a clear, concrete number of hours or days—avoid vague terms like "promptly" or "as soon as possible."
Record the template version number and approval date to show the clause was reviewed and formally adopted.
properties.text: Incident notification clause with timeline (e.g. within 24h of detection) + collaboration during remediation

guidance: List all relevant legal, statutory, regulatory, and contractual obligations that apply to supplier relationships in a dedicated section of the template.
Reference specific data protection, intellectual property, and copyright requirements by name and applicable law or regulation within the agreement template.
Assign a named individual responsible for updating the template when relevant laws or contractual obligations change.
Specify obligations using clear, supplier-specific language — avoid generic or boilerplate clauses that could apply to any organisation.
Record the date and version number on each template update to show when legal requirements were last reviewed.
properties.text: Legal, statutory, regulatory, contractual obligations (data protection, IP, copyright)

guidance: List the minimum security controls required for all suppliers in the template, referencing specific standards, certifications, or technical measures.
Specify expected certifications, such as ISO 27001 or SOC 2, and include them as mandatory fields to be completed in each agreement.
Name the person responsible for approving supplier security requirements in each template version, using a full name and job title.
State the date the template was last reviewed and updated, ensuring it is not left blank or marked as "N/A".
Avoid using generic language like "appropriate controls" without examples; provide concrete, checkable requirements for suppliers to meet.
properties.text: Minimum security requirements (controls baseline, certifications expected)

guidance: Record the planned review interval for supplier agreement templates in a dated schedule approved by a named responsible individual.
Document the most recent review date and the reviewer’s name in a version-controlled log or register.
Confirm the next scheduled review date is within the documented interval from the last review in the same log.
Name the review owner as a specific individual, not a team or department, in the review documentation.
Retain evidence of the completed review, such as a signed checklist or meeting minutes, with the review date clearly shown.
properties.text: Review date within the planned interval

guidance: Assign a named individual to coordinate the supplier agreement template review and record their name and review period in a tracking log.
Document the date and source of external counsel or industry-benchmark input consulted during the review in the review report.
Attach or reference the specific external advice or benchmark documentation used, ensuring it is relevant to your sector and agreement type.
Record the decision and any changes made to the template based on the external input, including who approved them and when.
Name the external input source specifically—avoid vague references like "industry feedback" or "legal team" without clear attribution.
properties.text: External counsel or industry-benchmark input considered

guidance: State the next planned review date clearly on the supplier agreement template, using a specific day, month, and year.
Record the name of the individual responsible for the next review, avoiding generic titles like "team" or "department".
Document the date this next review date was last updated, ensuring it is not left blank or undated.
Retain a copy of the supplier agreement template showing the current next review date for auditor inspection.
properties.text: Next planned review date stated

guidance: Assign a named individual to conduct the periodic review of the supplier agreement template and record their name in the review log.
Document the review date, outcome (no change or amended), and any version increment in a tracked change log or version history table.
State the rationale for any amendments made, referencing relevant changes in requirements or risks, in the review documentation.
Avoid using undated or generic review entries—each review must specify the date, reviewer, and clear outcome.
properties.text: Outcome (no change / amended; version increment if amended)

guidance: Assign a named individual to monitor relevant regulatory updates affecting supplier agreements, recording their name and the date responsibility was accepted.
Document each regulatory change identified, including the source, date, and a summary of its impact on supplier agreements.
Update the supplier agreement template to reflect new or amended regulatory requirements, noting the specific clauses changed and the date of revision.
Record the review meeting where regulatory changes were discussed, listing attendees, date, and decisions made regarding template updates.
Name the person who approved the revised template, ensuring the approval is signed and dated—do not leave this section blank or unsigned.
properties.text: Regulatory changes considered (data protection, sector-specific obligations)

guidance: Name the individual responsible for managing the re-papering plan in a dated document.
List all existing supplier agreements that do not match the new template version in a tracked register.
Document the timeline and milestones for updating each agreement, including target completion dates.
Attach evidence of communication sent to suppliers about required agreement updates, such as dated emails or letters.
Record approvals of the re-papering plan by a named decision-maker, with signature and date.
properties.text: Re-papering plan for existing supplier agreements that need to catch up to a new template version

guidance: Name both the legal lead and the information security lead as joint reviewers in the supplier agreement review record for each review cycle.
Record the date of each periodic review and link it to the specific supplier agreement template version reviewed.
Obtain signatures or written confirmation from both named reviewers to evidence their joint participation in the review.
Avoid listing a group or department as reviewer; specify individual names for both legal and information security leads.
properties.text: Reviewer identity (legal + InfoSec lead jointly)

guidance: Assign a named individual to lead the supplier agreement template review and record their name and review date in the review log.
Document recent changes in the threat landscape, such as new incident-notification requirements, in the review meeting minutes.
Cross-reference updated agreement clauses with current regulatory or industry guidance to show alignment with new threats.
State explicitly in the review record which new or emerging threats were considered and how the template was updated in response.
Name the reviewer as a specific person, not a generic role or team, to avoid ambiguity in accountability.
properties.text: Threat-landscape changes considered (e.g. emergent incident-notification expectations)

guidance: State the specific screening or vetting checks required for supplier personnel in the agreement template, such as background checks or reference verification.
Document the roles or situations where screening is mandatory, making clear which supplier personnel are in scope.
Name the individual or job title responsible for confirming supplier compliance with screening requirements in each agreement.
Specify that screening requirements must be tailored to your organisation’s risk profile, not copied generically from another template.
properties.text: Screening / vetting requirements for supplier personnel (where applicable)

guidance: List all security-specific service level agreements, such as patching timelines, multi-factor authentication, and vulnerability remediation, directly in the supplier agreement template.
Specify measurable targets for each security requirement, including exact timeframes and performance metrics, within the agreement template.
Name the individual responsible for monitoring supplier compliance with these SLAs, not just a team or department.
Attach a dated approval record showing that the template, including security SLAs, was reviewed and accepted by a designated authority.
properties.text: Security-specific SLAs (e.g. patching cadence, MFA requirements, vulnerability remediation timelines)

guidance: State in the template that suppliers must obtain written approval before engaging any sub-processors or fourth parties.
Document the process for suppliers to request and receive approval for sub-processor use, including named approvers and required documentation.
Specify in the template that all security requirements in your agreement must be flowed down to any approved sub-processors.
Name the individual responsible for reviewing and updating sub-processor clauses in the template—do not list a team or department.
Include a section requiring suppliers to provide a list of all sub-processors used, with names and dates of engagement.
properties.text: Sub-processor / fourth-party restrictions, approval process and propagation of requirements

guidance: State in the template that, upon contract termination, the supplier must return or securely destroy all data belonging to your organisation.
Specify transition arrangements in the template, including timelines and responsibilities for data handover and service continuity during the exit process.
Name the individual responsible for overseeing supplier offboarding and data handover, rather than using a generic role or department.
Include a requirement for the supplier to provide a signed certificate confirming data destruction or return at contract end.
Record the date of the latest template review and approval by a named authority to demonstrate it is current and in use.
properties.text: Termination obligations: data return/destruction, transition arrangements, handover of records

guidance: Document the criteria used to assign suppliers to each risk or tier category, including thresholds and examples, in a dated reference table.
List the variant security clauses for each supplier tier in the template, clearly labelling which clauses apply to which tier.
Cross-reference each clause set in the template to the corresponding supplier tier definition, so auditors can trace requirements to risk levels.
Name the person responsible for maintaining and updating the tiering criteria and clause sets, specifying their full name and role.
Avoid using generic or identical clause sets for all tiers; tailor requirements to demonstrate proportionality and record the rationale for differences.
properties.text: Variant clause sets per supplier tier

guidance: State the specific training and awareness topics related to information security and access that suppliers must cover in their staff programs within the agreement template.
Name the individual at your organisation responsible for verifying supplier training and awareness compliance, listing their full name and job title.
Document the frequency at which suppliers must provide evidence of completed training, specifying a clear interval such as "annually" or "upon onboarding."
Require suppliers to provide dated records or certificates of completed training for all staff with access to your information or systems.
Specify that generic or boilerplate training requirements will not be accepted; tailor requirements to the risks and access levels relevant to your organisation.
properties.text: Training and awareness requirements specific to information and access

guidance: List all ICT components and services used by your organisation, including those provided by third parties, in a dated inventory document.
Identify and record which components or services are critical to your operations, specifying why each is considered critical in the inventory.
Name the person responsible for reviewing and updating the critical components list, ensuring the owner is a specific individual, not a team or department.
Document the criteria used to determine criticality, referencing any business impact analysis or risk assessment that supports your decisions.
Attach evidence of your most recent review of the critical components list, such as meeting minutes or a signed approval form.
properties.text: Identification of critical components needing special scrutiny (especially when outsourced)

guidance: Name the authoriser for each ICT component replacement or delay as a specific individual, not a generic role or team.
Record the date when the authorisation decision was made for each replacement or delay.
Document the risk acceptance statement if a replacement is delayed, including the reason and any mitigating actions.
Retain a signed or digitally approved record of the authorisation decision in your asset management or change control system.
properties.text: Authoriser of the replacement (or of the delay + risk acceptance)

guidance: Record the actual cutover date for each ICT component replaced, listing the unique asset identifier and the person responsible for the change.
Document any delays in replacement by describing the reason, the affected asset, and the date the delay was identified.
State any compensating controls applied during the delay period, including start and end dates, and reference the risk assessment supporting these controls.
Obtain a signed risk acceptance statement from a named, accountable manager if replacement was delayed and risks were accepted.
Name the owner of each record as a specific individual, not a team or department, to avoid ambiguity in accountability.
properties.text: Cutover date executed (or compensating controls + risk acceptance where replacement was delayed)

guidance: Cross-reference each ICT component in your register with its manufacturer’s published end-of-life date, recording the source and date checked.
Document a rolling 12-month forecast listing all components scheduled for end-of-life, including planned replacement or mitigation actions and responsible individuals.
Update the forecast quarterly, saving each version with a revision date and the name of the person who made the update.
Name the forecast owner as a specific individual, not a team or department, to avoid ambiguity in responsibility.
Retain evidence of completed replacements or mitigations, such as signed-off work orders or change records, linked to the forecast entry.
properties.text: Rolling 12-month EOL forecast linked back to the component register

guidance: Document each ICT component replacement by recording the date, reason for replacement, and any issues encountered in a lessons-learned log.
Assign a named individual to review each lessons-learned entry and identify any sourcing or control gaps revealed during the replacement process.
Update the end-of-life replacement procedure with specific improvements based on documented lessons learned, citing the date and person responsible for the update.
Name the procedure owner as a specific individual—do not use a team or department as the owner.
Retain evidence of periodic reviews of the lessons-learned log and procedure updates, including reviewer names and review dates.
properties.text: Lessons-learned from the replacement feeding back to the procedure (e.g. sourcing-control gaps)

guidance: Record the date the end-of-life ICT component was identified and the decision to replace it in a change management log.
Name the person responsible for selecting the replacement component and document their selection decision in a dated record.
Document how sourcing controls, such as supplier evaluation and approval steps, were re-applied for the new component, including references to supporting evidence.
Attach or link to purchase orders or contracts showing the approved supplier and the specific replacement component chosen.
State the version or model of the replacement component to avoid generic descriptions that could apply to any device.
properties.text: Replacement component selected and sourcing controls re-applied

guidance: Record the specific end-of-life trigger for each ICT component, such as vendor announcement, contract end date, or identified vulnerability, in the replacement log.
Attach supporting evidence for the trigger, such as a vendor notice, contract excerpt, or vulnerability report, to each component’s end-of-life record.
Name the person who confirmed and documented the end-of-life trigger for each component, ensuring it is not left blank or attributed to a group.
Date each entry to show when the end-of-life trigger was identified and recorded for the component.
Review records to confirm no generic or copy-paste triggers are used; each trigger must be specific to the component and its context.
properties.text: EOL trigger per record (vendor announcement / contract end / vulnerability-driven decommission)

guidance: Assign a named individual to perform post-replacement checks and record their name and date on the verification log.
Document the specific integrity-verification steps completed for each replaced ICT component, including test results and any issues found.
Record the outcome of functional acceptance testing, listing the date, tester’s name, and confirmation that the component meets operational requirements.
Attach supporting evidence such as screenshots, test logs, or signed checklists to each replacement record.
Specify the actual person responsible for verification — do not use generic roles or team names.
properties.text: Post-replacement verification (integrity-verification, functional acceptance)

guidance: Document the procedure for notifying suppliers and internal teams about supply chain security incidents, including required timelines and communication channels, in a dated policy.
Name the person or role responsible for initiating and overseeing information sharing about supply chain issues in the procedure.
Record each supply chain incident notification with the date, recipient, summary of information shared, and method of communication in an incident log.
Specify in the procedure that notifications must be written and traceable—do not rely on verbal-only or undocumented communications.
properties.text: Rules for sharing information about supply chain issues or compromises with suppliers and within own group

guidance: Document the procedure for verifying the integrity of delivered components, including steps for checking digital signatures or hashes, in your ICT Supply Chain Information Security Procedure.
Record the results of each integrity check, including the date, method used (e.g., hash, signature), and the name of the person performing the check.
Retain evidence of the original supplier-provided hash or signature alongside your verification records for each delivery.
Name the responsible individual for performing and recording component integrity checks—do not list a team or department as the owner.
State the process for handling and reporting any failed integrity checks, including escalation steps and notification requirements, in the procedure document.
properties.text: Component integrity verification on delivery (signed firmware, signed packages, hash verification)

guidance: Describe the specific monitoring methods used to check supplier compliance with each stated security requirement in your ICT Supply Chain Information Security Procedure.
Record the frequency and responsible individual for each monitoring activity in a dated monitoring schedule.
Document the validation process, including how evidence of supplier conformance is collected, reviewed, and retained.
Name the owner of the monitoring and validation process as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Attach recent examples of completed monitoring or validation records that demonstrate the process in action.
properties.text: Monitoring and validation methods for conformance to stated security requirements

guidance: List each ICT product or service covered in the procedure, including its name, version, and supplier, in a dated inventory table.
State the required support and patching timelines for each product or service, referencing supplier documentation or contracts as evidence.
Assign a named individual responsible for monitoring and applying patches for each product or service, avoiding generic roles like "IT team."
Attach or link to supplier support lifecycle statements or patch release schedules for each product or service in the procedure document.
Record the date of the last review and update of support and patching expectations for each product or service in the procedure.
properties.text: Support and patching expectations stated for each ICT product/service

guidance: List each ICT component or service on a separate row in the register, including hardware, software, and cloud-based solutions.
Record the vendor name, product name, and specific version number for every entry to allow precise identification.
Assign a unique identifier to each component or service to avoid confusion between similar products or versions.
Name the owner of each register entry as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Update the register whenever a component is added, changed, or removed, and record the date of each change.
properties.text: Component / service identified per row (vendor, product, version)

guidance: Add a column to your ICT Component / Vendor Register that clearly labels each entry as "critical" or "non-critical" based on your risk assessment.
Document the criteria used to determine if a component or vendor is critical, and reference this criteria in the register.
Name the person responsible for assigning the criticality flag for each entry, ensuring a specific individual is listed, not a team or department.
Record the date when each criticality decision was made or last reviewed in the register.
Avoid leaving the criticality flag blank or using unclear terms like "TBD" or "unknown" for any entry.
properties.text: Critical-component flag per row (drives 27002:5.21e scrutiny)

guidance: Record the end-of-support and end-of-life dates for each ICT component or vendor entry as separate, clearly labeled columns in the register.
Cross-reference each date with official vendor documentation or public notices, and retain a copy or link alongside the register entry.
Name the person responsible for updating end-of-support and end-of-life information for each entry, using a specific individual rather than a team or department.
Update the register immediately when notified of changes to support or lifecycle dates, and log the date and source of each update.
properties.text: End-of-support / end-of-life date per row

guidance: Name a specific individual as the internal owner for each ICT component or vendor entry, avoiding generic labels like "team" or department names.
Record the owner's full name and current job title next to each component or vendor in the register, along with the date of assignment.
Document any changes in ownership by updating the register entry with the new owner's details and the effective date of the change.
Review the register quarterly to confirm all entries have a named owner and update any outdated information.
properties.text: Named internal owner per component (typically architecture or platform team)

guidance: Record the unique hash or version number from the software bill of materials (SBOM) for each ICT component listed in your register.
Cross-reference each ICT component entry with its corresponding SBOM file or repository location to allow traceability.
Name the responsible individual who verified the SBOM details for each component, including the date of verification.
Avoid listing only generic software names or vendors; specify exact product versions and SBOM references for each entry.
properties.text: SBOM hash / version reference per software component

guidance: List each ICT component or vendor in the register with a separate row for clarity and traceability.
Record all disclosed sub-suppliers or fourth parties associated with each vendor directly in the corresponding row.
Name the responsible individual maintaining the register, avoiding generic titles like "IT team" or "Procurement."
Date each entry or update to show when sub-supplier information was last verified or changed.
Retain supporting documentation from vendors confirming disclosure of their sub-suppliers for each listed relationship.
properties.text: Disclosed sub-suppliers / fourth parties per row

guidance: Document the approval status for each vendor and ICT component in the register, marking clearly as "approved" or "banned" with the decision date.
Name the individual who performed the vendor status check for each row, using their full name rather than a generic title or team.
Record the reference to supporting documentation, such as risk assessments or due diligence reports, for each approval or ban decision.
Confirm that each entry in the register includes a visible check stamp or digital equivalent showing the status was reviewed and verified.
properties.text: Approved-vendor / banned-vendor list check stamp per row

guidance: Document the specific information security requirements that must be passed to all sub-contractors or component suppliers in your ICT Supply Chain Information Security Procedure.
Name each primary supplier and require them in writing to cascade these requirements to their own sub-contractors or component suppliers.
Retain copies of signed agreements or attestations from suppliers confirming that they have communicated the requirements to all relevant sub-contractors.
Specify a named individual, not a department or team, responsible for verifying supplier compliance with this propagation requirement.
properties.text: ICT service / product suppliers required to propagate requirements through their sub-contractors / component suppliers

guidance: List each critical ICT supply chain component reviewed, referencing a unique identifier or asset tag for traceability.
Record specific action items for each component, such as monitoring improvements, upgrade requests, or replacement plans, with clear descriptions.
Assign a named individual responsible for each action item, avoiding generic roles like "IT team" or "management."
Date each action item entry and update to show when the action was captured or revised.
Retain meeting minutes or review logs that show discussion and decisions for each action item, signed or acknowledged by participants.
properties.text: Action items captured per critical component (e.g. tighten monitoring, push for upgrade, replan replacement)

guidance: Record the date of each ICT supply chain review in a central register, showing it falls within the organisation’s planned review interval.
Name the individual responsible for scheduling and conducting the review, listing them by full name rather than a team or department.
Retain a copy of the review report or meeting minutes, including the date, attendees, and summary of findings.
Cross-reference the review date with your documented review schedule to confirm the interval has not been exceeded.
properties.text: Review date within the planned interval

guidance: Identify all ICT components in use and record their expected end-of-life (EOL) dates in a dated inventory spreadsheet.
Document which components will reach EOL within the next planning horizon and note their current replacement status in the same inventory.
Assign a named individual as the owner responsible for tracking EOL status and updating the review record.
Record the date and outcome of each periodic supply chain review meeting, including decisions on replacements or mitigations.
Name the owner as a specific person, not a team or department, to avoid ambiguity in accountability.
