properties.text: Fallback path per row (which compensating measure activates; what residual risk it accepts)

guidance: Cross-reference each disruption scenario to specific security controls it impacts, listing relevant ISO27001 control numbers in a dedicated column.
Link each scenario to affected assets by referencing unique asset IDs from the A.5.9 asset register in the register row.
Name the responsible owner for each scenario as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Record the date each scenario entry was last reviewed or updated in the register.
Avoid generic or boilerplate control references; specify only those controls directly impacted by the scenario.
properties.text: In-scope controls per row (which security controls this scenario specifically impacts; cross-link to A.5.9 asset register for assets at risk)

guidance: Record the date each disruption scenario was last tested in a dedicated column within the Disruption Scenario Register.
Name the individual responsible for updating test dates, ensuring a specific person is listed rather than a team or department.
Cross-reference each scenario entry with supporting evidence of the test, such as a signed test report or meeting minutes.
Review the register quarterly to confirm that no scenario has a missing or undated last-tested entry.
properties.text: Last-tested date per row (drives stale-scenario detection — scenarios not exercised in N months flag for refresh)

guidance: Name a specific individual as the owner for each disruption scenario row, avoiding group names or roles like "IT" or "the team".
Record the owner's full name and job title directly in the register alongside each scenario entry.
Document the date when each owner was last assigned or confirmed for their scenario responsibility.
Review the register quarterly and update ownership details if there are any changes in personnel or responsibilities.
properties.text: Named owner per row (accountable for keeping this scenario's plan section current)

guidance: Record a recovery time objective (RTO) and recovery point objective (RPO) for each ICT disruption scenario in the register, using specific timeframes.
Cross-reference each ICT scenario entry to the corresponding backup and restoration procedure documented under control A.5.30.
Name the scenario owner as a specific individual, not a team or department, for each row in the register.
Date each entry and update when scenarios or recovery targets change, keeping a clear revision history.
properties.text: Recovery target per row where applicable (RTO/RPO for ICT scenarios — cross-link to A.5.30)

guidance: Assign a unique identifier to each disruption scenario in the register, using a consistent numbering or naming convention.
Record the full description of each scenario alongside its unique identifier in the register, ensuring no duplicate entries exist.
Name the person responsible for maintaining the register as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Cross-reference each scenario’s identifier with related risk assessments or business continuity plans to confirm full scenario coverage.
properties.text: Each in-scope scenario captured with a unique identifier

guidance: Assign a severity tier to each disruption scenario row using the defined categories: tier_1_full_disruption, tier_2_partial, or tier_3_localised.
Document the rationale for each severity tier assignment in a dedicated column, referencing impact or criteria used for classification.
Name the individual responsible for assigning and reviewing severity tiers in the register, avoiding generic roles like "the team" or "IT".
Record the date each severity tier was last reviewed or updated to show ongoing accuracy and relevance.
Cross-reference each scenario’s severity tier to the corresponding activation path or response procedure in your incident response documentation.
properties.text: Severity tier per row (tier_1_full_disruption / tier_2_partial / tier_3_localised) — drives the activation path

guidance: Add a column to the Disruption Scenario Register to indicate if the fallback for each scenario depends on a specific supplier.
Name the supplier explicitly in the register row where a dependency exists, rather than using generic terms like "third party" or "vendor."
Cross-reference each supplier-dependent fallback to the corresponding supplier entry in the Supplier Register maintained for control A.5.22.
Record the date and name of the person who last updated each supplier dependency flag in the register.
properties.text: Supplier dependency flag per row where the fallback relies on a specific supplier

guidance: List each disruption scenario in the register as a separate row with a unique identifier and a clear scenario description.
Assign one scenario type per row using only the approved categories: cyber_attack, natural_event, supplier_failure, regulatory_action, personnel_loss, or infrastructure_failure.
Record the name of the person responsible for classifying each scenario and the date the classification was made.
Avoid leaving the scenario type column blank or using custom categories not listed in the requirement.
properties.text: Scenario type per row (cyber_attack / natural_event / supplier_failure / regulatory_action / personnel_loss / infrastructure_failure)

guidance: Document each disruption scenario where service degradation leads to accepted risk exposure in a dedicated residual-risk register.
Assign a named individual as the risk owner for every scenario, avoiding generic labels like "the team" or "IT department".
Record the date each risk was reviewed and accepted, along with supporting evidence of management approval.
Cross-reference each scenario in the register to the corresponding section of the Information Security During Disruption Plan.
Retain evidence of periodic updates to the register, showing ongoing review and adjustment of risk ownership and acceptance.
properties.text: Residual-risk register for disruption scenarios where degradation creates accepted exposure (named risk owner per scenario)

guidance: Document a step-by-step restoration plan that lists the order for re-enabling each security control, including re-encryption, audit-log replay, and access-control reactivation.
Assign a named individual responsible for verifying that each control is restored and functioning as intended after disruption ends.
Record the date, time, and outcome of each restoration step in a log, including any issues encountered and how they were resolved.
Cross-reference the restoration plan with your business continuity and disaster recovery procedures, specifically linking to the process described in control A.5.30.
Name the owner as a specific person, not a team or department, to avoid ambiguity about who is accountable for restoration actions.
properties.text: Restoration of normal security controls after disruption ends (sequenced, verified — re-encryption, audit-log replay, access-control reactivation)

guidance: Record each action item from the continuity-security program review in a dated log, clearly describing the required adjustment or improvement.
Assign a named individual as the responsible owner for each action item, avoiding generic references such as "the team" or "IT".
Document the rationale for each action item, linking it to specific findings or scenarios discussed during the review.
Confirm that each action item includes a target completion date and update the log when the item is completed or status changes.
properties.text: Action items captured (e.g. add scenario, retire stale fallback, refresh communication paths, expand test scope)

guidance: Record the most recent program review date in a central log, clearly showing it falls within the last 180 days.
Name the individual responsible for scheduling and conducting the review, listing their full name and role.
Attach the signed review summary or meeting minutes, including the date and names of all participants.
Cross-reference the review log with the planned schedule to confirm no interval exceeds 180 days.
Specify the review owner as a named person, not a generic group or department.
properties.text: Review date within the planned 180-day interval

guidance: Select a representative sample of fallback procedures from your continuity-security program and list them by name and version in a dated review log.
Assign a named individual to re-validate each selected fallback, confirming in writing that dependencies, contacts, and technical steps are still current.
Record the results of each re-validation, noting any failures, outdated dependencies, or required updates, with the date and reviewer’s signature.
Name the fallback owner as a specific person for each procedure—avoid listing only a team or department as responsible.
Document any corrective actions taken for fallbacks that failed re-validation, including the date completed and the person who approved the fix.
properties.text: Fallback-validity check (sample of fallbacks re-validated: would they actually work? are dependencies still in place? are owners still in role?)

guidance: Assign a named individual to lead the industry-practice scan, recording their name and assignment date in the review documentation.
Document at least three recent, notable disruptions in your sector, including dates and sources for each event.
Summarize how peer organizations responded to these disruptions, citing specific public reports or industry publications.
State the lessons learned from these peer responses and explicitly link each lesson to a proposed update or confirmation of your own continuity-security plan.
Record the date and names of all participants who reviewed and approved the updated plan, avoiding unsigned or undated approval records.
properties.text: Industry-practice scan (notable disruptions in the sector; how peers handled; lessons applicable to our plan)

guidance: State the exact next planned review date in the program review record, making sure it is no more than 180 days from the current review.
Record the name of the individual responsible for scheduling the next review, rather than listing a team or department.
Document the date this review was completed, so the 180-day interval can be verified by counting from this entry.
Retain a copy of the signed or approved review record that includes both the current and next review dates.
properties.text: Next planned review date stated (within 180d of this review)

guidance: Document each real disruption event in the past review period, including date, impact, and how the response compared to the documented plan.
Record specific gaps where the continuity or security plan did not match the actual needs or actions taken during the disruption.
State any plan elements that were assumed necessary but proved unnecessary or irrelevant during real disruptions, with supporting examples.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual responsible for the analysis, not a group or department.
Retain meeting minutes or a signed report summarizing findings, lessons learned, and recommended plan updates based on divergence analysis.
properties.text: Real-disruption divergence analysis (where actual disruptions diverged from the plan — what was missing? what assumed? what proved unnecessary?)

guidance: Name each reviewer as a specific individual by full name and job title in the review record.
Record the date each reviewer completed their review and any comments or findings in the review documentation.
Document the involvement of Legal if regulatory communications are within the review scope, and the supplier-management lead if supplier dependencies are included.
Avoid listing groups or teams as reviewers; ensure only named individuals are recorded for each required role.
Retain a signed or digitally acknowledged statement from each reviewer confirming their participation in the periodic review.
properties.text: Reviewer identity (CISO + BCP-program owner + Legal where regulatory comms scope; supplier-management lead where supplier-dep scenarios in scope)

guidance: Name each scenario in the continuity register with a unique identifier and description, including the date it was last reviewed for relevance.
Document the outcome of a scenario-currency audit by listing which scenarios remain plausible, which are outdated, and any new scenarios identified.
Assign a named individual to sign and date the scenario-currency audit, confirming that each scenario was actively re-evaluated.
Record any scenarios removed or added, including the rationale for each change, in a dated change log attached to the register.
Avoid leaving scenario ownership or review responsibility to a group or department; specify a single accountable person for each scenario.
properties.text: Scenario-currency audit (each scenario in the register re-validated: still plausible? still relevant? new scenarios that should be added?)

guidance: Document the dates and outcomes of the last N continuity-security program tests in a table, including which scenarios were covered in each test.
Record each gap or issue identified during test-result analysis, referencing the specific test and scenario where it was found.
Assign a named individual to each remediation action for every gap, and include target and completion dates in the remediation log.
Calculate and state the ratio of tested scenarios to the total number of defined scenarios, providing both numbers and the resulting percentage.
Name the reviewer of the analysis as a specific person, not a generic group or department, and capture their dated sign-off on the review summary.
properties.text: Test-result analysis (last N tests reviewed; gaps surfaced; remediation per gap; ratio of scenarios tested vs total)

guidance: List each disruption scenario considered in the plan, including cyber attack, natural event, supplier failure, regulatory action, and key-personnel loss.
Cross-reference the cyber attack scenario to your threat intelligence documentation as required by control A.5.7.
Link the supplier failure scenario to your supplier management records as required by control A.5.21.
Name the person responsible for maintaining the disruption scenarios, avoiding generic roles like "the team" or "IT".
Date and version the disruption plan to show when scenarios were last reviewed or updated.
properties.text: Disruption scenarios considered (cyber attack [link to A.5.7 threat intel], natural event, supplier failure [link to A.5.21], regulatory action, key-personnel loss)

guidance: State the exact frequency for testing the Information Security During Disruption Plan in a dated document, such as "annually" or "every six months."
Assign a named individual responsible for coordinating and overseeing each scheduled test, listing their name and role in the plan.
Record the scheduled test dates for the next 12 months in a calendar or register accessible to relevant stakeholders.
Document management approval of the test schedule with a dated signature or email confirmation from a named decision-maker.
Specify the cadence as a clear interval, not vague terms like "regularly" or "as needed," to avoid auditor rejection.
properties.text: Test schedule for the plan (cadence stated; promoted from SHOULD because untested continuity plans fail when actually needed)

guidance: Identify all plan sections that rely on supplier or third-party actions to maintain or restore information security during disruptions.
Cross-reference each third-party-dependent control in the disruption plan with the corresponding supplier risk assessment or review record from A.5.22.
Name the specific supplier or third party responsible for each control, avoiding generic labels like "vendor" or "external partner."
Record the date and outcome of the most recent review of these third-party dependencies, including any follow-up actions required.
Attach supporting documentation, such as supplier agreements or communications, that confirm the third party’s commitment to the required actions.
properties.text: Third-party-dependent controls flagged (where the plan relies on supplier action — cross-link to A.5.22 review)

guidance: Name each information security responsibility in the matrix and assign it to a specific individual or a clearly defined job title.
Document the full name or unique job title for each responsibility, avoiding generic terms like "the team" or "IT department".
Record the date when each assignment was last reviewed or updated to show the matrix is current.
Obtain sign-off from a senior manager confirming the accuracy and completeness of the assignments in the matrix.
properties.text: Allocation to named individuals or positions, not just abstract role labels

guidance: Name the approving individual by full name and job title, ensuring they are a specific person rather than a group or department.
Document the signatory’s authority to approve by referencing the relevant delegation letter, board resolution, or organisational chart.
State the date of approval clearly on the document to establish when the roles and responsibilities allocation was authorised.
Attach or cross-reference the delegation chain if the signatory is not the CEO, showing the flow of authority from the top level.
properties.text: Statement of the signatory's authority to approve (delegation chain if not CEO)

guidance: Name the approving top management individual by full name and job title in the roles and responsibilities allocation document.
Record the approval date clearly next to the signature or approval statement within the document.
Sign the allocation document physically or electronically to confirm formal approval by top management.
Avoid leaving the approval date field blank or using undated templates, as auditors will flag missing or unclear approval dates.
properties.text: Approval date recorded

guidance: Name the individual at top management level (such as CEO, board chair, or delegated equivalent) as the signatory for roles and responsibilities allocation.
Document the approved roles and responsibilities in a dated record that clearly lists all relevant positions and their assigned duties.
Sign the allocation document with a handwritten or secure digital signature from the named top management signatory.
Retain the signed and dated approval in a central location where it can be easily retrieved for audit purposes.
Avoid listing the signatory as a generic group or department; specify an actual person holding a top management position.
properties.text: Signatory at top-management level (CEO, board chair, or delegated equivalent)

guidance: Name the specific version number and date of the responsibility matrix in the approval document.
Record the full name and job title of the top management individual granting approval.
Sign and date the approval document to confirm when the roles and responsibilities allocation was authorized.
Attach or cross-reference the exact responsibility matrix version being approved, not a generic or draft version.
Avoid using vague references such as “latest matrix”; always specify the unique identifier of the approved version.
properties.text: Reference to the specific version of the responsibility matrix being approved

guidance: Assign a named individual as the accountable owner for each information asset listed in the matrix, avoiding generic titles like "IT" or "the team".
Document the specific protection and risk management responsibilities for each asset owner directly in the matrix.
Record the date of assignment and the name of the person making the assignment for each asset entry.
Review and update the matrix at least annually, capturing the date of review and the reviewer’s name.
properties.text: Accountability for protection and risk management of specific assets assigned

guidance: List all cloud and external services currently in use, including the provider name and a brief description of each service.
Document the specific information security responsibilities assigned to your organization and to each provider for every listed service.
Cross-reference each responsibility with a named individual or role within your organization, avoiding generic labels like "the team" or "IT department."
Attach the relevant sections of provider contracts or service agreements that define provider-side security responsibilities, including dates and signatures where available.
Review and update the matrix annually, recording the review date and the name of the person who completed the review.
properties.text: For cloud and external services, responsibilities split between the organization and the provider stated

guidance: List all staff or named role-holders who must receive information about roles and responsibilities in a dated communication log.
Record the date, method, and sender of each communication to provide a clear audit trail of dissemination.
Obtain confirmation of receipt from each recipient, such as a signed acknowledgement or email reply, and retain these records.
Name the audience as specific individuals or roles—do not use vague terms like "all staff" without supporting recipient details.
properties.text: Audience reached (all staff or named role-holders)

guidance: Document the exact channel used to communicate roles and responsibilities, such as "company intranet" or "onboarding pack," in a dated communication log.
Name the individual responsible for sending or publishing the communication, ensuring a specific person is listed rather than a generic team or department.
Retain a copy or screenshot of the actual communication as evidence, showing the content and the date it was shared with staff.
Record the list of recipients or audience, such as new hires or all employees, to demonstrate who received the information.
properties.text: Channel used (intranet publication, email, training session, onboarding pack)

guidance: Record the exact date when roles and responsibilities were communicated to staff in a dated communication log or announcement.
Name the individual responsible for sending or publishing the roles and responsibilities communication in the record.
Attach or link the actual communication document or message to the record for direct reference.
Avoid listing only the month or year; specify the full date to prevent auditor concerns about incomplete evidence.
properties.text: Date of publication/communication

guidance: Update the onboarding checklist to include a step for briefing new role-holders on their information security responsibilities, with the checklist owner named.
Record the date and name of each new joiner who receives the roles and responsibilities briefing in a central log.
Attach a signed or acknowledged copy of the briefing document to each new joiner’s personnel file as evidence of communication.
Name the individual responsible for delivering the briefing, avoiding generic titles like "HR" or "the team".
properties.text: Communication built into joiner onboarding so new role-holders are briefed on appointment

guidance: Name each individual assigned to a security role, such as CISO or asset owner, in a roles and responsibilities register with full name and job title.
Document the date and method of communication used to brief each role-holder on their specific responsibilities.
Obtain a signed or otherwise acknowledged statement from each role-holder confirming they have received and understood their responsibilities.
Store all acknowledgement records in a central location, referencing the specific role and date for each entry.
Avoid listing roles as groups or teams; always identify a specific person for each key responsibility.
properties.text: Role-specific briefing or acknowledgement from named role-holders (CISO, asset owners, etc.)

guidance: List each information security role in the matrix with the person's full name, not just a job title or department.
Document the specific competency or training required for each role, referencing relevant course names or certifications.
Cross-reference each competency or training requirement to the corresponding clause in your training policy or A.6.3 documentation.
Record the date each individual last completed the required training, using training records or certificates as evidence.
State any roles with missing or outdated training records, and document a remediation plan with assigned responsibilities and target dates.
properties.text: Notes competency/training requirements per role (cross-ref A.6.3)

guidance: Cross-reference each role and responsibility in the matrix to the relevant section of the Information Security Policy by section number or title.
Document the date and version of the Information Security Policy referenced in the matrix to show alignment with the current policy.
Name the matrix owner as a specific individual, not a group or department, to avoid ambiguity in accountability.
Attach or link the Information Security Policy directly within the matrix file to provide immediate access for verification.
properties.text: Links back to the Information Security Policy (A.5.1)

guidance: List each information security role in the matrix with the full name and job title of the person currently holding the role.
State the direct reporting line for each role by naming the specific individual or position to whom the role reports.
Document the escalation path for each role by specifying who issues must be escalated to, using named individuals or unique job titles.
Avoid using generic terms like "the team" or "management" for reporting or escalation; always specify a named person or unique position.
properties.text: Reporting and escalation lines stated (who each role reports to)

guidance: List each information security role in the matrix using the specific job title or named individual responsible.
Describe the decision rights, oversight duties, and execution tasks for each role in separate, clearly labeled columns.
Cross-reference each responsibility with the relevant policy or procedure document, including the document title and version date.
Assign a named owner to review and update the matrix at least annually, recording the review date and their signature.
Avoid using vague role descriptions like "the team" or "IT department"—specify individual titles or names for accountability.
properties.text: Responsibilities described per role (decision rights, oversight, execution)

guidance: Record the date of the most recent roles and responsibilities review in a dedicated register or tracking document.
Name the person responsible for conducting the review as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Confirm the review date falls within the planned interval by cross-referencing it with the previous review date and the documented schedule.
Sign and date the review record to provide clear evidence of when the review was completed.
properties.text: Review date within the planned review interval (typically within 12 months of last review)

guidance: State the next planned review date for roles and responsibilities in the review record, using a clear and specific calendar date.
Record the name of the person responsible for scheduling and conducting the next review alongside the planned date.
Update the review record immediately if the planned review date changes, keeping previous dates visible for audit history.
Avoid leaving the next review date field blank or using vague terms like "annually" or "TBD"—always enter a concrete date.
properties.text: Next planned review date stated

guidance: Name the reviewer as a specific individual responsible for conducting the roles and responsibilities review, not a generic title or team.
Record the date the review was completed in the review log or register.
State the outcome of the review clearly, specifying if there was no change, an amendment with the new version number, or a role added or removed.
Attach supporting evidence, such as updated role descriptions or approval emails, to the review record for any amendments or changes made.
Sign or formally approve the review record to confirm the accuracy and completion of the review process.
properties.text: Outcome of the review (no change / amended to vN / role added or removed)

guidance: Name the reviewer as a specific individual, including their full name and job title, on the roles and responsibilities review record.
Record the date the review was completed next to the reviewer’s details on the review record.
Document the reviewer’s role in the context of the review, specifying their authority or responsibility for this process.
Avoid listing a group, team, or department as the reviewer; always identify a single accountable person.
properties.text: Reviewer identity and role

guidance: List specific events that would trigger an ad-hoc review, such as mergers, major restructures, new business lines, or critical staff departures.
Document each trigger in the Roles and Responsibilities Review Record, including a brief description and the date it was added.
Name the person responsible for monitoring these triggers by full name and job title, not just a team or department.
Review the list annually and record the date and outcome of the review, even if no changes are made.
properties.text: List of significant-change triggers (reorg, new business line, key role departure) that should prompt an ad-hoc review

guidance: List all key information security roles, including CISO, ISMS Manager, Asset Owners, Risk Owners, Incident Manager, and DPO if required, in a table.
Name the owner of each role as a specific individual, not a team or department, and record their full name in the matrix.
Document the main responsibilities for each role in clear, specific terms within the matrix.
Date and approve the completed matrix with a signature from senior management to confirm accuracy and authority.
Review the matrix annually and record the review date and reviewer’s name to show it is kept up to date.
properties.text: Information security roles enumerated (CISO, ISMS Manager, Asset Owners, Risk Owners, Incident Manager, DPO where applicable)

guidance: List all information security roles and their assigned responsibilities in a matrix, including named individuals and their job titles.
Identify and document any roles where conflicting duties or potential conflicts of interest exist, referencing specific responsibilities.
Record the actions taken to resolve each identified conflict, such as segregating duties or introducing additional oversight, with dates and responsible persons.
Name the owner of the matrix as a specific individual, not a group or department, and include their contact details.
Review and update the matrix at least annually, recording the date of each review and the reviewer’s name.
properties.text: Notes conflicts to be resolved via segregation of duties (A.5.3)

guidance: List all information security tasks related to ISMS operation, asset ownership, risk management, audits, and security reviews in a single matrix.
Assign each task to a named individual, not a team or department, and include their current job title.
Record the date the matrix was last reviewed and updated, and keep a copy of the previous version for reference.
Cross-reference each task to relevant policy or procedure documents to show alignment with your ISMS framework.
properties.text: Allocation covers ISMS operation, asset ownership, risk management, audits and security review topics

guidance: Document the backup schedule, including frequency and retention periods, and cross-reference these with your Recovery Point Objective (RPO) in your business continuity plan.
Record the physical or cloud locations where backups are stored, specifying geographic separation from primary systems.
Name the individual responsible for managing and monitoring backup processes, not just a team or department.
Maintain dated records of backup restore tests, including verification results and any issues identified or resolved.
properties.text: Backup arrangements (frequency aligned to RPO, retention, geographic separation, restore tested and verified)

guidance: State in the ICT Readiness for Business Continuity Plan the specific reference to the disruption-security plan created under A.5.29, using the exact document title and version.
Cross-reference each ICT continuity control with its corresponding security requirement from the A.5.29 plan, listing both control identifiers side by side in a table.
Document any differences or gaps between the ICT plan and the A.5.29 disruption-security plan, including a dated action plan for resolving them.
Name the owner of the ICT Readiness for Business Continuity Plan as a specific individual, not a generic role or team.
Attach a signed approval page confirming that both the ICT and disruption-security plans have been reviewed together for alignment.
properties.text: Alignment with A.5.29 disruption-security plan stated explicitly (this is the ICT mechanical layer; A.5.29 is the security-annex layer; both must reconcile)

guidance: Cross-reference each system's RTO and RPO targets in the ICT Readiness Plan to the specific Business Impact Assessment section where they are justified.
Record the date and version of the Business Impact Assessment used to set each RTO and RPO, ensuring traceability to the latest approved assessment.
Link each scenario in the ICT Readiness Plan to the corresponding entry in the scenario register required by control A.5.29.
Name the person responsible for maintaining these cross-references as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Document any changes to RTO or RPO targets with a signed statement explaining the BIA-driven rationale for the adjustment.
properties.text: BIA-link explicit (RTO/RPO targets traceable to the Business Impact Assessment — not arbitrarily chosen numbers; cross-link to A.5.29 scenario register)

guidance: Document a communication tree that lists named individuals and their roles for each stage of ICT outage notification and escalation.
State clear escalation thresholds, including specific timeframes or incident severity levels that trigger each communication step.
Specify the cadence for status-page updates during outages, including who is responsible and the exact intervals for posting updates.
Name the communication tree owner as a specific person, not a generic group or department, to avoid ambiguity in responsibility.
Record the last review date and reviewer’s name on the communication tree to show it is current and actively maintained.
properties.text: Communication tree for ICT outages (who is informed, escalation thresholds, status-page update cadence)

guidance: Identify each critical service and document its failover or redundancy arrangement, specifying whether it is active-active, active-passive, or cold-standby.
Name the responsible individual for maintaining and testing each failover arrangement, avoiding generic titles like "IT team" or "Operations".
Record the most recent test date and outcome for each failover or redundancy setup, including any issues found and actions taken.
Attach supporting diagrams or configuration records that clearly show how failover or redundancy is implemented for each critical service.
Review and update the documented arrangements at least annually, capturing the reviewer's name and the date of each review.
properties.text: Failover / redundancy arrangements for critical services (active-active / active-passive / cold-standby per service tier)

guidance: Record the actual recovery time for each recovery event in a dated entry, referencing the specific system or service restored.
State the target recovery time objective (RTO) for each event alongside the actual recovery time in the same record.
Document any gap between actual recovery time and the target RTO, including a brief explanation if the target was missed.
Name the individual responsible for verifying and signing off on the recorded recovery times for each event.
Avoid leaving the recovery time field blank or using vague entries such as "as soon as possible"—always enter a specific duration.
properties.text: Actual recovery time per record (drives the RTO-met calculation; gap to target if missed)

guidance: Cross-reference the per-recovery event record to the specific plan_activation_record from A.5.29 when the recovery was triggered by a business continuity plan.
Record the date and time of the recovery event, matching these details to the corresponding activation record for traceability.
Name the individual who confirmed the recovery was BCP-driven, using their full name rather than a generic role or team.
Attach or link supporting documentation, such as incident reports or meeting minutes, that demonstrate the connection between the recovery and the BCP activation.
Review the event record to confirm no references are missing or ambiguous, especially where multiple activations occurred close together.
properties.text: Cross-reference to A.5.29 plan_activation_record where this recovery was BCP-driven (closes loop)

guidance: Record each recovery event with a unique identifier, date, and the names of all individuals directly involved in the process.
Document all gaps where the recovery process did not meet planned objectives, describing each gap clearly and specifically.
Assign a severity rating to each identified gap, using a defined scale that is referenced in your incident response documentation.
Name the person responsible for reviewing and confirming the accuracy of each gap and severity assessment, ensuring this is a specific individual.
Avoid leaving any gap description or severity field blank or marked as "N/A" without justification, as auditors will flag incomplete records.
properties.text: Gaps surfaced per record (where recovery fell short; severity per gap)

guidance: Record the date, time, and description of each recovery event in a dedicated log, including the individuals involved in the recovery process.
Document any lessons learned or patterns identified during the recovery event that may be relevant to future incidents or improvements.
Cross-reference each recovery event record with the A.5.27 lessons register if the event surfaces lessons or patterns worth retaining.
Name the person responsible for reviewing each recovery event and confirming whether new lessons should be added to the lessons register.
Avoid leaving the lessons field blank or copying generic statements—provide specific, event-driven insights for each record.
properties.text: Lessons feed per record to A.5.27 lessons register where recovery surfaced patterns worth retaining beyond this control

guidance: Assign a unique, sequential identifier to each recovery event record at the time the event is logged.
Record the assigned identifier prominently within the recovery event record, ensuring it appears on all related documentation.
Cross-reference the recovery event identifier in any follow-up reports or incident logs linked to the same event.
Avoid using generic or reused identifiers; confirm each identifier is specific to a single recovery event and not duplicated elsewhere.
properties.text: Recovery event identifier per record (unique, sequenced)

guidance: State the Recovery Time Objective (RTO) target for each recovery event in the event record, using a clear duration such as "4 hours".
Record the date and time the RTO target was set or confirmed for each event, referencing the relevant business continuity plan.
Name the individual who approved or confirmed the RTO target for the recovery event, using their full name and role.
Avoid copying generic RTO targets from templates; specify the RTO relevant to the specific system or process involved in the event.
properties.text: RTO target per record (what was committed)

guidance: List all services affected by each recovery event, using their exact names as shown in your official service register.
Cross-reference each listed service to its unique entry in the service register, including register ID or direct link.
Record the date and time of the recovery event alongside the service details in the event record.
Name the person responsible for entering and verifying the service information for each recovery event record.
Avoid using generic service descriptions or placeholders; specify only services formally documented in your service register.
properties.text: Services in scope per record (links to service register entries)

guidance: Record the details of each recovery event, including date, time, and actions taken, in a dedicated recovery event log.
Name the recovery owner and BCP-program owner as specific individuals for each event, avoiding generic titles or group names.
Obtain and retain signatures from both the recovery owner and BCP-program owner on each recovery event record.
Secure an additional signoff from the executive sponsor for any recovery event involving a critical service, with a clear date and name.
Store all signed recovery event records in a central, access-controlled location for future reference.
properties.text: Signoff per record (recovery owner + BCP-program owner; exec sponsor where critical-service real recovery)

guidance: Record the recovery event date, system affected, and the individual responsible for overseeing the recovery in each event record.
State the recovery outcome for each event using only the approved status options: rto_met, rto_missed_with_reason, partial_recovery_acceptable, or failed.
Document the reason for any missed or partial recovery, including supporting evidence such as logs or incident reports, in the event record.
Name the responsible individual for each event record — do not use generic labels like "IT team" or "operations".
Review each event record for completeness and accuracy, and sign off with the reviewer’s name and date.
properties.text: Success status per record (rto_met / rto_missed_with_reason / partial_recovery_acceptable / failed)

guidance: Record the recovery type for each recovery event, clearly marking it as real recovery, scheduled test, partial drill, or chaos engineering test.
Assign a unique identifier to each recovery event record to allow easy cross-referencing and traceability.
Name the person responsible for classifying the recovery type on each event record, using a specific individual rather than a team or department.
Date each recovery event record to show when the recovery activity took place and when the type was assigned.
Review all recovery event records quarterly to confirm that each has a clearly stated and accurate recovery type.
properties.text: Recovery type per record (real_recovery / scheduled_test / partial_drill / chaos_engineering_test)

guidance: Document step-by-step recovery procedures for each ICT service, using clear instructions that a technically competent person could follow without assumptions.
Name the responsible individual for each ICT service recovery procedure, avoiding generic titles like "IT team" or "Support staff".
Record the date each recovery procedure was last reviewed or tested, attaching evidence of the review or test outcome.
Cross-reference each recovery procedure to the relevant business continuity plan section, showing alignment with overall organizational priorities.
Attach any required scripts, configuration files, or checklists directly to the procedure, not just referenced as "available on request".
properties.text: Recovery procedures documented per ICT service (step-by-step, runbook-style — not 'restart the system' aspirational text)

guidance: Cross-reference each ICT service in the continuity register to its supporting asset entries in the A.5.9 asset register using unique asset IDs.
Record the date of the last cross-link review for each ICT service to show the register is kept current.
Name the person responsible for maintaining the cross-links, listing a specific individual rather than a team or department.
Document any changes to asset-service relationships with a dated entry and reference to the updated asset register row.
properties.text: Asset-link per row (cross-link to A.5.9 asset register entries that constitute this service)

guidance: List each ICT service in the register with a unique name and description to clearly identify what is being assessed.
Assign a criticality tier to each service using only the defined categories: tier_1_mission_critical, tier_2_business_critical, or tier_3_supporting.
Name the person responsible for assigning the tier for each service, ensuring it is a specific individual, not a team or department.
Record the date when each tier assignment was last reviewed or updated in the register.
Cross-reference each service’s tier with supporting business impact analysis documentation to show how the tier was determined.
properties.text: Criticality tier per row (tier_1_mission_critical / tier_2_business_critical / tier_3_supporting) — drives RTO/RPO selection

guidance: Document the physical location and country for each backup listed in the ICT Service Continuity Register, including any cross-border storage details.
Cross-reference each backup entry to the relevant section of your A.5.14 data transfer policy, using a direct link or policy reference number.
State any jurisdictional or legal implications for each backup location, such as local data residency laws or restrictions.
Name the responsible individual for verifying the accuracy of backup location and policy cross-links, avoiding generic roles like "IT team."
Record the date when each entry was last reviewed or updated to show current compliance with data residency requirements.
properties.text: Data residency note per row where backup geographic separation has jurisdictional implications (cross-link to A.5.14 transfer policy)

guidance: List each ICT service in the register with a unique name and owner, ensuring no duplicate or vague service descriptions.
Record both upstream and downstream dependencies for every service row, specifying exact systems or services by name.
State the required recovery order for each service, referencing dependencies to show which must be restored first.
Confirm all dependencies are reviewed and updated at least annually, recording the review date and responsible reviewer.
Name dependencies as specific systems or services, not as generic terms like "infrastructure" or "network".
properties.text: Service dependencies per row (upstream + downstream — recovery order matters; recover dependencies first)

guidance: Record the last-tested date for each ICT service in the continuity register, using a consistent date format for every entry.
Name the person responsible for updating each last-tested date, listing a specific individual rather than a team or department.
Cross-reference each last-tested date to supporting test evidence, such as a signed test report or meeting minutes.
Review the register quarterly to confirm no ICT service shows a last-tested date older than your defined maximum interval.
properties.text: Last-tested date per row (drives stale-test detection — services not tested in N months flag for refresh)

guidance: Name the recovery owner for each ICT service as a specific individual, listing their full name and job title in the register.
Record the date each recovery owner was assigned responsibility in a dedicated column of the ICT Service Continuity Register.
Cross-reference the recovery owner’s contact details with your staff directory to confirm accuracy and current employment status.
Avoid listing generic roles like "IT" or "the team" as recovery owners; update any such entries to a named person.
properties.text: Named recovery owner per row (technical lead accountable for the service's recovery, not just IT generally)

guidance: Record the Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO) as specific numeric values for each ICT service listed in the register.
Name the business owner responsible for setting each service’s RTO and RPO, ensuring a specific individual is listed, not a team or department.
Document the date each RTO and RPO value was last reviewed and approved, referencing the meeting minutes or approval record.
Cross-reference each RTO and RPO entry to the documented business continuity plan section that supports the chosen targets.
Avoid using vague terms like “best effort” or “TBD” for RTO/RPO; enter only concrete, measurable numbers in each field.
properties.text: RTO/RPO targets per row (specific numeric values, not 'best effort')

guidance: List each ICT service in the register with a clear, descriptive name that matches how it is referred to in operational documents.
Assign a unique identifier to every ICT service entry, avoiding duplicates or reused codes from retired services.
Record the date each ICT service was added to the register and the name of the person responsible for the entry.
Cross-reference each ICT service with related business processes or systems to demonstrate completeness and visibility.
Specify the owner of each ICT service as a named individual, not a team or department.
properties.text: Each in-scope ICT service captured with a unique identifier

guidance: Add a column to your ICT Service Continuity Register to flag each service where recovery depends on supplier action.
Cross-reference each flagged entry to the relevant supplier in your Supplier Register, including a link to the contract or agreement.
Record the date and name of the person who last reviewed and updated the supplier dependency flags.
Name the supplier dependency owner as a specific individual, not a team or department, for each flagged service.
Document any changes to supplier dependencies with a brief description and the date of the change in the register.
properties.text: Supplier dependency flag per row where recovery depends on supplier action (cross-link to A.5.21 / A.5.22)

guidance: Record all action items from each ICT readiness program review in a dated log, specifying the issue, required change, and responsible individual.
Assign each action item to a named person, not a team or department, and include their contact details in the action log.
Document the rationale for each action item, referencing the specific review findings or test results that triggered the adjustment.
Track the completion status and date for each action item in the same log, updating it as actions are resolved.
Retain meeting minutes or review notes that clearly show discussion and agreement on each action item, signed or acknowledged by participants.
properties.text: Action items captured (e.g. add new service, tighten RTO for service that consistently misses, retire stale scenario, refresh test schedule)

guidance: Identify all cloud providers whose features or service levels impact your ICT readiness, listing them by name and service type in your review document.
Document the specific hyperscaler features relied upon for ICT readiness, such as availability zone failover or region replication, in the periodic review record.
Record any recent or upcoming changes to the cloud provider's service level agreements that could affect your ICT readiness posture, including dates and details.
Cross-reference your ICT readiness review with your dependency register or risk register as required by control A.5.23, noting the relevant entry.
Name the responsible individual who reviewed and confirmed the cloud provider posture, avoiding generic roles like "the team" or "IT department."
properties.text: Cloud-provider posture noted (where ICT readiness depends on hyperscaler features — AZ failover, region replication; their SLA changes affect ours)

guidance: Record the most recent ICT Readiness Program review date in a central log, showing it falls within the planned 180-day interval.
Assign a named individual responsible for scheduling and conducting each review, listing them in the review documentation.
Attach a signed or approved summary of the review findings, including the date, to demonstrate completion within the required timeframe.
Cross-reference the review date against the planned review schedule to confirm no interval exceeds 180 days.
Specify the review owner by name, not by role or team, to avoid ambiguity in accountability.
properties.text: Review date within the planned 180-day interval

guidance: Identify a sample of critical ICT services and record their names and owners in a dated review log.
Cross-reference each service’s documented dependency map with current system architecture diagrams and vendor lists, noting any mismatches or outdated links.
Document any changes or shifts in dependencies since the last review, including new, removed, or altered connections, in the review log.
Assign responsibility for updating the readiness plan to a named individual, not a group or department, and record the assignment with a date.
Attach evidence of the review, such as meeting minutes or annotated diagrams, to show the dependency-currency check was completed for the sampled services.
properties.text: Dependency-currency check (sample of services where dependency map re-validated against current reality; shifts flagged for plan update)

guidance: State the next planned ICT Readiness Program review date in the review report, ensuring it is no more than 180 days from the current review.
Record the name of the individual responsible for scheduling the next review, not just a team or department.
Document the date the current review was completed and reference it alongside the next planned review date for clear audit tracing.
Retain a signed or approved copy of the review report that includes both the current and next review dates.
properties.text: Next planned review date stated (within 180d of this review)

guidance: Record the number of restore attempts made in the last review period, including dates and systems involved, in a dated report.
Calculate and document the percentage of successful versus failed restore attempts in the same report.
Investigate each failed restore attempt and attach a summary of root cause analysis and corrective actions taken.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual who signed off on the restore-success-rate analysis, not a generic role or team.
Retain the completed analysis report and supporting investigation records for auditor inspection.
properties.text: Restore-success-rate analysis (last N restores attempted; success rate; failed restores investigated)

guidance: Name each reviewer as a specific individual by title and full name, avoiding generic roles like "the team" or "IT department".
Record the date and outcome of the ICT Readiness Program review in a formal meeting minute or review log.
Obtain signatures or written confirmation from the CTO or IT-ops head, BCP-program owner, and InfoSec lead on the review record.
Secure CFO sign-off on the review record if any critical-service recovery time objective has a financial impact, attaching supporting analysis if applicable.
properties.text: Reviewer identity (CTO/IT-ops head + BCP-program owner + InfoSec lead jointly; CFO sign-off where critical-service RTO has financial impact)

guidance: Select a representative sample of critical ICT services and list them by name and owner in the review documentation.
Record the most recent Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO) test results for each sampled service, including test dates.
Compare actual test results to documented RTO and RPO targets for each service, noting any gaps in a dated summary table.
Document the root cause analysis for each identified gap, referencing specific incident reports or investigation records.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual and require their dated sign-off on the completed review report.
properties.text: RTO/RPO compliance audit (sample of services re-tested; gap to target per service; root cause per gap)

guidance: List each scenario from your A.5.29 register, showing which ones have been tested through actual ICT recovery exercises, with test dates.
Document any scenarios from the A.5.29 register that remain untested, including reasons for omission and risk impact.
Record a remediation plan for each untested scenario, assigning a named individual and target completion date for future testing.
Name the program review owner as a specific person, not a team or department, in the review documentation.
Attach evidence of the most recent review meeting, such as signed minutes or an attendance record with date and participant names.
properties.text: Scenario-coverage audit (which scenarios from A.5.29 register actually tested via real recovery; which still untested; remediation plan per gap)

guidance: Identify each critical ICT service in your Business Impact Analysis and list them by name in your Business Continuity Plan.
Document the Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO) for each ICT service, referencing the BIA date and source.
Name the responsible individual for approving each RTO and RPO, ensuring it is not a generic team or department.
Record the date when each RTO and RPO was last reviewed and approved, keeping this information visible in the plan.
Attach supporting BIA documentation that shows how each RTO and RPO was determined for traceability.
properties.text: Recovery Time and Recovery Point Objectives per ICT service (BIA-derived; RTO = how long can it be down; RPO = how much data loss is acceptable)

guidance: Document at least one test scenario simulating a full outage of critical ICT systems, including total loss of primary data center or cloud service.
Record a separate scenario simulating a partial failure, such as loss of a single application or network segment, with expected recovery steps.
Name the person responsible for designing and approving each scenario, listing them by full name and job title.
Attach dated evidence of completed tests for both partial and full outage scenarios, such as test reports or signed completion checklists.
Avoid using only partial-failure scenarios in your test documentation—include at least one full-outage case to meet auditor expectations.
properties.text: Test scenarios cover BOTH partial-failure AND full-outage cases (most orgs only test partial — auditor-tested concern)

guidance: Record the last test date for each critical ICT service in a dated log, clearly linking each entry to the specific service tested.
Document the test outcome for each service, including whether objectives were met and any disruptions or failures encountered.
List all gaps or weaknesses identified during each test, referencing the specific ICT service and test date.
Track the remediation status for each identified gap, noting the responsible individual and the completion date or current status.
Name the test owner as a specific individual for each service—do not use generic roles or teams as the owner.
properties.text: Test cadence and records (last test date per service, outcome, gaps identified, remediation status)

guidance: Identify all business processes in your continuity plan that depend on third-party suppliers for recovery, listing each supplier by name.
Document the specific recovery actions required from each supplier, including expected response times and contact details, in the plan.
Cross-reference each third-party dependency in your continuity plan to the corresponding supplier review record maintained under control A.5.22.
Name the responsible individual who will coordinate with each supplier during recovery, avoiding generic roles like "IT team" or "management."
Review and update the continuity plan annually, recording the date and approver’s name for each update.
properties.text: Third-party-dependent recovery noted (where recovery relies on supplier action — cross-link to A.5.22 supplier review)

guidance: List each legal, statutory, regulatory, or contractual requirement as a separate entry in the register with a clear, descriptive title.
Cross-reference each entry to the corresponding authority in the A.5.5 authority register using a unique identifier or hyperlink.
Name the responsible authority as a specific individual or role, not a group or department, to avoid ambiguity.
Record the date each entry was last reviewed or updated, along with the reviewer’s name.
Attach supporting documentation or source references for each requirement, such as legislation titles, contract numbers, or regulatory citations.
properties.text: Each entry tagged with the authority(ies) responsible — cross-link to A.5.5 authority register

guidance: Record the source used to monitor changes for each register entry, such as a named legal counsel, regulator alert, or specific industry feed.
Document the date each source was last checked for updates, linking this date directly to the relevant register entry.
Name the individual responsible for monitoring each entry’s source, avoiding generic roles like "the team" or "compliance department".
Attach or reference evidence of the latest update or alert received from each source, such as an email notification or newsletter copy.
properties.text: Source for change monitoring per entry (legal counsel, regulator alerts, industry feed)

guidance: List each legal, statutory, regulatory, and contractual requirement in the register with a clear, unique reference and effective date.
Describe the specific approach or method used to meet each requirement, referencing relevant controls, policies, or documented processes.
Cross-reference each requirement to supporting evidence, such as policy documents, process records, or control logs, with document titles and version numbers.
Name the responsible individual for each requirement, avoiding generic entries like "Compliance Team" or "Management".
Review and update the register at least annually, recording the review date and the reviewer’s name.
properties.text: Approach for compliance per item (how the obligation is met, which controls/policies/processes evidence it)

guidance: List each customer contract, regulator agreement, and sectoral code in the register with a unique reference and effective date.
Summarise the key contractual obligations for each entry, using plain language that is specific to your organisation.
Name the individual responsible for monitoring each obligation — do not use generic roles like "Legal" or "Compliance Team".
Attach or link to the full contract or agreement for each summarised obligation in the register.
Record the last review date and reviewer’s name for each entry to show obligations are kept up to date.
properties.text: Contractual obligations summarised (customer contracts, regulator agreements, sectoral codes)

guidance: List each legal, statutory, regulatory, and contractual requirement in the register with a unique reference number and a clear description.
Link each requirement entry to a specific, named document or record that demonstrates compliance, such as a policy, audit report, or certification.
Record the date each evidence document was last reviewed or updated, and name the person responsible for maintaining its accuracy.
Cross-reference the register entry to the exact section or page of the evidence document that addresses the requirement.
Name the owner of each requirement as a specific individual, not a team or department.
properties.text: Links to evidence of compliance per requirement (policies, audit reports, certifications)

guidance: List each legal, statutory, regulatory, or contractual requirement as a separate entry in your register, including a clear title and description.
Specify the exact jurisdiction(s) relevant to each entry, such as country, state, or region, and avoid using generic terms like "global" or "all locations."
Record the physical or operational locations impacted by each requirement, including headquarters, branch offices, customer sites, and data storage locations.
Name the responsible individual for each entry, ensuring the owner is a specific person rather than a team or department.
Date each entry and update the register whenever requirements or jurisdictions change, keeping a visible revision history.
properties.text: Jurisdictions covered explicitly per entry (HQ, places of operation, customer locations, data residency)

guidance: Record the last-verified or last-reviewed date for each requirement entry in the register, using a clear date format such as YYYY-MM-DD.
Name the person who performed the most recent review for each entry, listing a specific individual rather than a team or department.
Retain evidence of the review activity, such as a signed checklist or email confirmation, linked to each register entry.
Update the register immediately after any review or verification activity to avoid undated or outdated entries, which auditors will flag.
properties.text: Last-verified or last-reviewed date per entry

guidance: List each applicable law, regulation, and contractual obligation by full name and citation in the register, including GDPR and any sector-specific rules.
Record the jurisdiction and scope for each entry, specifying which business units, products, or data types are affected.
Assign a named individual as the owner for each requirement, avoiding generic labels like "Legal" or "Compliance Team".
Enter the date each requirement was last reviewed or updated, showing ongoing maintenance of the register.
Cross-reference each listed requirement to supporting documentation or contracts, such as data processing agreements or regulatory filings.
properties.text: Applicable laws and regulations enumerated (GDPR, sectoral, jurisdictional, transfer regimes)

guidance: List each obligation in the register with a clear tag: "statutory", "regulatory", "contractual", or "sectoral-code" based on its source.
Assign a specific review frequency to each obligation entry, referencing its tagged type to determine how often it must be checked.
Name the person responsible for reviewing each obligation, ensuring a named individual is listed rather than a team or department.
Record the date of the last review and the next scheduled review for each obligation entry in the register.
properties.text: Obligation type tag (statutory / regulatory / contractual / sectoral-code) to drive review cadence

guidance: Name a specific individual as the owner for each requirement in the register, avoiding generic titles like "the team" or "IT department".
Record the date the owner was assigned for each requirement to provide a clear timeline of accountability.
Document the owner's responsibility to track changes and monitor compliance for each listed requirement in the register.
Cross-reference each requirement entry with supporting evidence, such as meeting minutes or assignment emails, confirming the owner's acceptance.
properties.text: Owner named per requirement (who tracks change and compliance)

guidance: Document each new legal or regulatory obligation by recording the full name and contact details of the relevant authority in the register.
Cross-reference every new authority entry with the corresponding obligation and date of addition in the Legal/Regulatory Register.
Name the individual responsible for updating the register with new authority contacts, avoiding generic titles like "Compliance Team."
Retain evidence of communication confirming the authority’s contact information, such as an email or official notice, attached to the register entry.
Review the register after each update to confirm that all new authorities are listed and matched to their obligations.
properties.text: Authority-contact sync — adding an obligation that introduces a new regulator triggers A.5.5 register update

guidance: Document each change in legal or regulatory obligations in the register, including the date, source, and a summary of the change.
Identify and list all controls and policies impacted by the change, referencing their unique identifiers in the register entry.
Assign a named individual to assess the impact and record their findings, including any identified gaps or required actions.
Open and track specific gap actions in a dated action log, linking each action to the relevant obligation and impacted control or policy.
Name the owner for each action as a specific person, not a generic role or team, to avoid auditor concerns about accountability.
properties.text: Impact-assessment step when an obligation changes — affected controls and policies identified, gap actions opened

guidance: State the frequency for reviewing upcoming legal and regulatory changes in your procedure, specifying a clear interval such as "quarterly" or "monthly."
Assign a named individual, not a team or department, as responsible for monitoring proposed legislation and pending regulator decisions.
Document the sources to be checked for horizon-scanning, such as government websites, regulatory bulletins, or legal update services, in the procedure.
Record each horizon-scanning activity in a dated log, noting the sources reviewed and any relevant findings or actions required.
Review and update the procedure annually, capturing the review date and the name of the person who approved any changes.
properties.text: Horizon-scanning cadence for upcoming obligations (proposed legislation, pending regulator decisions)

guidance: Name the individual responsible for flagging new or changed legal and regulatory requirements, recording their name and role in the procedure.
Document the process for interpreting each flagged requirement, specifying who performs the interpretation and capturing their analysis in a dated record.
Assign a specific person to classify each requirement in the register, ensuring their name and the classification date are clearly recorded.
Record the decision on the compliance approach for each requirement, including the name and signature of the confirmer and the confirmation date.
Avoid using generic roles like "the team" or "compliance department" as owners; always list specific individuals by name.
properties.text: Intake path from trigger to register entry (who flags, who interprets, who classifies, who confirms compliance approach)

guidance: Assign a named individual or external counsel to review each proposed register entry for legal accuracy before it is finalized.
Document the review date and the name of the reviewer in the register entry’s approval section.
Require a written sign-off—such as an email or signed form—from the reviewer confirming the legal interpretation.
Avoid using generic approvals; specify the reviewer by name, not by role or department, for each entry.
properties.text: Legal review step before a new entry is finalised (internal or external counsel approval)

guidance: Name the register maintainer as a specific individual, such as the compliance lead or legal counsel, in the procedure document.
Document the maintainer’s responsibility for reviewing and updating the register for accuracy in a dated responsibilities section.
Record the maintainer’s acceptance of this responsibility with a signed and dated acknowledgement included in the procedure file.
Avoid listing a team or department as the maintainer; specify a single accountable person by name and role.
properties.text: Named maintainer (compliance lead, legal counsel, or designate) with documented responsibility for register accuracy

guidance: List all specific triggers that require an update to the legal/regulatory register, such as new laws, regulatory guidance, customer contracts, new jurisdictions, or sectoral code changes.
Document each trigger in the maintenance procedure with a clear description and an example to show how it applies to your organisation.
Assign a named individual responsible for monitoring these triggers, not a team or department, and record their name and role in the procedure.
Record the date when the update triggers were last reviewed and approved, and retain the signed approval from management.
properties.text: Update triggers enumerated (new law/regulation, regulator guidance, new customer contract, new jurisdiction, sectoral code change)

guidance: List all events that trigger an unscheduled review of the legal and regulatory register, such as regulator actions, court rulings, or major contract changes.
Document each ad-hoc review trigger in the register review procedure, including a clear description and examples for each type of event.
Name a specific individual responsible for monitoring and initiating register reviews when a trigger event occurs.
Record the date and details of each ad-hoc review, including the triggering event and any resulting changes to the register.
Avoid using vague triggers like "as necessary" or "when needed"—specify concrete events that require immediate review.
properties.text: Ad-hoc review triggers listed (major regulator action, court ruling, customer contract restructure)

guidance: Record the date of the most recent legal and regulatory register review in a dedicated column within the register.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual responsible for the last review, avoiding generic titles like "Compliance Team."
Document the planned next review date, ensuring it is no more than six months after the previous review date.
Retain a copy of the review sign-off or meeting minutes confirming the review took place on the recorded date.
properties.text: Review date within the planned interval (within 6 months of last review)

guidance: Assign a named individual to monitor upcoming legal and regulatory changes relevant to your business, recording their name and responsibility in the register.
Document each new or amended obligation entering force in the next 12-24 months, including the effective date and a summary of required actions.
Record the date of each periodic review, the reviewer’s name, and any decisions or actions planned to address upcoming obligations.
Attach evidence of proactive planning, such as meeting notes or action plans, showing how your organisation will prepare for these future requirements.
Name each obligation specifically; do not use generic phrases like “pending laws” or “future regulations” without clear identification and source.
properties.text: Forward-looking section — obligations entering force in the next 12-24 months that need preparation

guidance: Record the next planned review date for the legal and regulatory register in a dedicated column or field within the register.
Name the individual responsible for conducting the next review, using their full name rather than a role or department.
Document the date this next review date was last set or updated, ensuring it is clearly visible in the register.
Avoid leaving the next review date field blank or using vague terms like "TBA" or "ongoing"—always enter a specific future date.
properties.text: Next planned review date stated

guidance: Assign a named individual to lead the legal and regulatory register review, recording their name and the review start date in the register.
Record the outcome for each register entry as verified, amended, retired, or new added, including the date and reviewer’s initials.
State for each entry whether the current compliance approach remains adequate, documenting any changes or confirmations in the register.
Attach supporting evidence for any amendments or retirements, such as updated legal texts or correspondence with authorities.
Name the reviewer as a specific person for each entry — do not use generic labels like "Compliance Team" or "Legal Department".
properties.text: Per-entry outcome (verified / amended / retired / new added) with compliance-approach still-adequate confirmation

guidance: Name the reviewer who completed the periodic legal and regulatory register review, recording their full name and the review date.
Document each change identified during the review, listing the specific regulation or requirement and the nature of the update.
Cross-reference each change in the live register to the review record by including the review date and a summary of the change.
Retain evidence of the updated live register, showing the new version number or date and the initials of the person who made the changes.
Avoid using vague references like "reviewed by team" or undated entries—always specify individuals and dates for each update.
properties.text: Changes propagated back to the live register with reference to this review

guidance: Record the full name and job title of the person who conducted the legal/regulatory register review in the review log.
Document the date the review was completed and attach any supporting review notes or findings to the register.
Obtain a signed statement from legal counsel for any material changes, confirming their review and approval.
Name the compliance lead and legal counsel as specific individuals, not as generic roles or departments, in the review documentation.
properties.text: Reviewer identity and role recorded (compliance lead with legal-counsel sign-off where material)

guidance: Assign a named individual to lead the review of the legal and regulatory register, recording their name and the review date in the register.
Cross-reference the register entries against the latest documented list of applicable laws, regulations, and contractual obligations to identify any missing items.
Document any new or changed obligations that now apply, including the source, effective date, and responsible owner for each new entry.
State explicitly in the review record that all new applicability areas have been checked and either added or confirmed as not relevant.
Avoid using generic statements like "no changes" without showing evidence of the cross-check against the current obligations list.
properties.text: Cross-check against the applicable-obligations scope — any new applicability that should add entries

guidance: Cross-reference the list of applicable obligations in A.5.31 with the list of applicable authorities in A.5.5, showing clear links between each item.
Document the date and person responsible for updating both A.5.31 and A.5.5 scopes to confirm synchronized reviews.
State in the obligations scope record where shared drivers or requirements are addressed in both A.5.31 and A.5.5.
Name the owner for maintaining these cross-links as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Retain version history showing when updates in one scope triggered updates in the other, with timestamps.

properties.text: Legal/regulatory driver per retention period stated (statute, regulator guidance, contractual obligation, business need — never an arbitrary number)

guidance: List each record class in your register, using clear names that match your organisation’s actual records and business activities.
Specify a concrete retention period for each record class, stating the exact number of years or months to keep the records.
Define the event that triggers the start of the retention period for each class, such as "contract end date" or "employee departure."
State the action or event that marks the end of the retention period, such as "records destroyed" or "records archived."
Name the owner as a specific individual responsible for each record class, not just a team or department.
properties.text: Retention period per record class (concrete duration — years/months, with start-trigger and end-trigger defined)

guidance: List all specific ad-hoc review triggers in the Records Protection Program document, including new regulator actions, sector entry, mergers, acquisitions, and legal-hold pattern changes.
Document the date and details of the most recent ad-hoc review, including which trigger prompted the review and who conducted it.
Name the responsible individual for monitoring and initiating ad-hoc reviews, avoiding generic roles like "the team" or "IT department."
