Cross-reference each ad-hoc review event to supporting evidence, such as regulatory notifications, merger announcements, or legal-hold logs.
properties.text: Ad-hoc review triggers listed (new regulator action, new sector entry, M&A, legal-hold invocation pattern shift)

guidance: Record the date of the most recent Records Protection Program review in a central log or register.
Document the planned review interval, such as "every 12 months," in the program documentation or review schedule.
Confirm the next scheduled review date is no more than 12 months after the last completed review.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual responsible for the last review, not a group or department.
Retain a signed or approved record of the latest review, including the date and reviewer’s name.
properties.text: Review date within the planned interval (typically within 12 months of last review)

guidance: Select a sample of record classes whose retention periods have ended, using a documented list with retention end-dates and class descriptions.
Confirm each sampled record class has either a certificate of destruction on file or a documented legal hold with reference to applicable law or litigation.
Record any instances where records are retained past their retention end-date without valid legal hold, and flag these for remediation with assigned responsibility.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual, not a group or department, and record the review date on the audit documentation.
properties.text: Disposal audit — sample of classes past retention end-date confirmed disposed (certificate of destruction present) or held under documented legal hold; overruns flagged for remediation

guidance: List all records currently under legal hold, including the specific class or row, the responsible individual, the legal basis, and the expected release trigger, in a dated review log.
Name the legal hold owner as a specific individual for each record, avoiding generic labels like "Legal" or "Records Team".
Document the review of each legal hold's status, noting any that are overdue for release or lack a clear release trigger.
Record the remediation action taken for any stale or unreleased holds, including the date and the person authorizing the action.
Retain evidence of the periodic review meeting, such as a signed attendance sheet and a summary of decisions made.
properties.text: Active legal-hold status reviewed (which classes/rows currently held, by whom, on what basis, expected release trigger) — stale unreleased holds remediated

guidance: State the next planned review date for the Records Protection Program in the review documentation, using a clear and specific calendar date.
Name the individual responsible for scheduling and leading the next review, including their full name and job title.
Record the date the current review was completed to provide context for the next scheduled review.
Avoid using vague phrases like "next quarter" or "TBD"—enter an exact date to prevent auditor findings.
properties.text: Next planned review date stated

guidance: Record the date and outcome of the Records Protection Program review in a version-controlled document.
List all changes identified during the review, referencing the specific section or control affected.
Update the live Records Protection Program schedule to include each approved change, citing the review date and document as the source.
Name the individual responsible for updating the schedule, avoiding generic titles like "the team" or "Records Management."
Retain both the pre-review and post-review versions of the schedule to demonstrate that changes were properly propagated.
properties.text: Changes propagated back to the live schedule with reference to this review

guidance: Record the full name and job title of the person conducting the review in the review log for each Periodic Records Protection Program assessment.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual — do not use generic titles like "the team" or "IT department."
Document the date the review was completed and attach any supporting review notes or findings to the record.
Obtain a signed approval or email confirmation from legal counsel if the review identifies material changes or issues, and store this with the review record.
properties.text: Reviewer identity and role recorded (records manager / compliance lead with legal-counsel sign-off where material)

guidance: Name the person responsible for the records protection program review as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Document the outcome for each records class as verified, amended, retired, or new added in a dated review log.
State for each records class whether the retention period remains adequate, referencing the latest legal or business requirements.
Confirm for each records class that the assigned protection level is still appropriate, citing any changes in risk or sensitivity.
Sign and date the final review summary, listing all reviewed classes and outcomes, to provide a clear audit trail.
properties.text: Per-class outcome (verified / amended / retired / new added) with retention-still-adequate and protection-class-still-adequate confirmation

guidance: Cross-reference the current records protection program scope with the latest business activities, legal requirements, and data categories in your asset register.
Document any new business activity, legal driver, or data category identified since the last review in a dated update log.
Assign a named individual to review and approve additions or changes to records classes based on the cross-check findings.
Record the date and outcome of each periodic review, including confirmation that no relevant scope changes were missed.
Name the reviewer as a specific person—do not use generic labels like "Records Team" or "Compliance Department".
properties.text: Cross-check against the records-categories scope — any new business activity / legal driver / data category that should add classes

guidance: List all core business activities such as HR, finance, sales, operations, and regulated functions in a documented records categories scope.
Name a specific individual responsible for maintaining the records categories scope, avoiding generic titles like "the team" or "management".
Cross-reference each business activity to the distinct classes of records it generates, such as payroll, tax filings, contracts, or security logs.
Date and approve the records categories scope document to confirm it reflects current business operations and compliance obligations.
properties.text: Business activities considered (HR/employment, finance/tax, sales/customer, operations/security, regulated activities — each may generate distinct record classes)

guidance: List specific events that require a records categories scope review, such as new locations, new business lines, mergers, or new regulatory obligations.
Document the trigger list in the records management procedure, including the date of last update and the person responsible for maintaining it.
Assign a named individual, not a team or department, to monitor for these trigger events and initiate re-scoping when needed.
Record each time the trigger list is reviewed or updated, including the date and the name of the reviewer.
Cross-reference the trigger list in your records categories scope document to show it is actively used to maintain currency.
properties.text: Trigger list for re-scoping (new geography, new service line, M&A, new regulated activity — adding scope must trigger a schedule update)

guidance: List all categories of personal, sensitive, and regulated data your organisation handles in a dated document approved by a named data protection lead.
Cross-reference each data category to relevant laws or regulations, such as GDPR or sector-specific rules, in the same document.
State the business processes or systems where each data category is stored or processed, naming the responsible system owner.
Name the owner as a specific individual for each data category — do not use generic titles like "the team" or "IT department".
Retain a signed and dated review record showing this scope was checked and updated at least annually.
properties.text: Personal/sensitive/regulated data categories handled (drives PII overlay and special-category retention)

guidance: List all countries and regions where your organisation operates, stores, or processes records, including headquarters and any cloud or third-party data locations.
Document the specific legal or regulatory retention and erasure requirements for each jurisdiction identified, citing the relevant laws or regulations by name.
Assign a named individual responsible for monitoring changes in jurisdictional requirements and updating the records categories scope accordingly.
Record the date of your most recent review of jurisdictional coverage to demonstrate the information is current and actively maintained.
Specify each jurisdiction individually—do not use generic terms like "global" or "various regions" that lack clear scope.
properties.text: Jurisdictions covered (each may impose different minimum-retention or right-to-erasure constraints — HQ, places of business, data-residency destinations)

guidance: List each records category alongside the specific law, regulation, or contractual obligation that requires its retention, citing the statute or regulation by name.
Cross-reference each legal or regulatory driver to the corresponding entry in your A.5.31 records of processing register, using a unique identifier.
Record the date each legal driver was last reviewed for applicability and any changes, maintaining a dated log for auditor inspection.
Name the person responsible for verifying the legal basis for each records category, ensuring a specific individual is listed rather than a team or department.
properties.text: Legal/regulatory drivers enumerated (statutes mandating record-keeping: corporate law, tax law, employment law, sectoral regulations, GDPR Art.30, AML, etc.) — cross-link to A.5.31 register

guidance: Cross-reference each records category in your Records Categories Scope to the relevant obligation in your A.5.31 Applicable Obligations register, using unique identifiers.
Document the rationale for each cross-link, showing how the same driver or requirement informs both registers.
Review both registers together at least annually and record the date and names of reviewers to confirm ongoing alignment.
Name the owner of each register as a specific individual, not a team or department, to avoid ambiguity in responsibility.
properties.text: Cross-link to A.5.31 applicable-obligations scope — same drivers, separate registers; the two should stay aligned

guidance: List each privacy law and regulation by its full name and jurisdiction in the policy document, such as "General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) – European Union".
Reference the specific sections or articles of each law that apply to your organisation’s activities and types of personal data handled.
Name the person or role responsible for monitoring changes in privacy laws and updating the policy, using a named individual rather than a generic title.
Date the policy version and include a revision history showing when each law was last reviewed or added.
properties.text: Applicable privacy laws identified (GDPR, UK GDPR, regional equivalents, sectoral privacy laws — HIPAA, LGPD, PIPEDA, CCPA, etc.) — each named, not just 'privacy laws'

guidance: Cross-reference the organisation’s incident response procedures in the Privacy and PII Protection Policy, specifically citing sections that address personal data breaches.
State the requirement to notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of a personal data breach, as per GDPR Article 33.
Describe the process for assessing risk to individuals and, where high risk is identified, outline steps for notifying affected data subjects according to GDPR Article 34.
Name the policy owner as a specific individual with responsibility for breach handling and notification, not a generic team or department.
Record the date of the most recent policy review and update to show the inclusion of these cross-references and notification requirements.
properties.text: Breach handling reference (cross-link to A.5.24/A.5.26 incident family + GDPR Art.33 supervisory-authority notification within 72h + GDPR Art.34 data-subject notification where high risk)

guidance: Document the intake process for data subject requests, including contact channels and responsible roles, in the Privacy and PII Protection Policy.
List each data subject right enabled under GDPR Articles 12-22, with a clear cross-reference to your detailed DSAR procedure.
Specify response timeframes (SLAs) for each type of request, stating calendar days and escalation steps for missed deadlines.
Name the policy owner as a specific individual with authority, not a generic team or department.
Record the policy approval date and version number on the policy document.
properties.text: Data subject rights enabled (access, rectification, erasure, portability, restriction, objection where applicable; intake path + response SLAs documented — cross-link to GDPR Art.12-22 and DSAR procedure)

guidance: Cross-reference the Privacy and PII Protection Policy to the documented Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) process, including a direct link or appendix reference.
State the specific triggers for initiating a DPIA, citing GDPR Article 35 and summarizing EDPB Guidelines criteria within the policy.
Name the designated individual or role responsible for reviewing and signing off on DPIAs, avoiding vague terms like "the team" or "management."
Document the procedure for consulting with the supervisory authority, including contact details and required documentation, in the policy or as an attached process map.
Record the policy version and approval date on the document’s cover page to show it reflects current legal and regulatory requirements.
properties.text: PIA / DPIA process reference for high-risk processing (cross-link to GDPR Art.35 + EDPB Guidelines on DPIA — when to trigger, who reviews, supervisory-authority consultation path)

guidance: Name the Data Protection Officer (DPO) as a specific individual, including full name and job title, in the Privacy and PII Protection Policy.
Document the date the DPO was formally appointed and include a signed appointment letter or HR record as evidence.
State whether DPO designation is mandatory or voluntary for your organisation, referencing the relevant GDPR Article 37 criteria.
Record the DPO’s contact details in the policy, ensuring they are current and not a generic group email or phone number.
Retain evidence of regular DPO training or certification, such as dated certificates or training completion records.
properties.text: DPO designation note (mandatory under GDPR Art.37 for public authorities, large-scale special-category processing, large-scale systematic monitoring; voluntary otherwise — captured here regardless of mandate)

guidance: List each processing activity involving personal data in a table, including a brief description and the department responsible.
Identify and record the lawful basis for each processing activity, referencing the specific legal ground such as consent or contract.
Name the individual responsible for reviewing and updating lawful basis assignments, avoiding generic roles like "the team" or "IT."
Attach evidence of management approval for the lawful basis assignments, such as a dated and signed policy review document.
Cross-reference each lawful basis entry to the relevant section of applicable law or regulation, such as GDPR Article 6.
properties.text: Lawful basis discipline (lawful basis identified per processing activity — consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, legitimate interests; where law requires)

guidance: Name a specific individual as the owner of the privacy program in the policy, using their full name and job title.
Document the date when the policy owner was last assigned or updated, and keep this record with the policy document.
State in the policy whether a Data Protection Officer is required by law, and if not, specify the designated Privacy Officer or Information Security lead.
Avoid listing a group, team, or department as the owner; use only a single, named person for clear accountability.
Retain evidence of the owner's acceptance of responsibility, such as a signed or acknowledged statement within the policy.
properties.text: Named owner of the privacy program (DPO where law requires; Privacy Officer or InfoSec lead where DPO is not mandatory; named individual, not a generic 'Privacy Team')

guidance: List all categories of personal data processed for each activity in the PII Processing Register, using clear terms such as "contact data" or "health information".
Cross-reference each processing activity in the PII Processing Register to the corresponding entry in your GDPR Article 30 Record of Processing Activities.
Name the owner responsible for maintaining the PII Processing Register as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Record the date of the most recent review or update to each processing activity entry in the register.
Specify any special-category data processed, such as biometric or health data, and reference the relevant GDPR Article 9 or sectoral law.
properties.text: PII categories enumerated per processing activity (basic identifiers, contact data, financial, health, biometric, special-category — GDPR Art.9 / sectoral equivalents); links to GDPR Art.30 RoPA

guidance: State in the Privacy and PII Protection Policy whether ISO/IEC 27701 is in scope for your organisation, including the date this was determined.
Cross-reference specific ISO/IEC 27701 PII-controller and PII-processor controls applied, listing control numbers and their locations in your policy.
Document how the Privacy and PII Protection Policy extends or integrates with your existing Information Security Management System, citing relevant ISMS sections.
Name a specific individual responsible for maintaining the 27701 alignment note in the policy—do not use a team or department as the owner.
Retain a signed approval of the policy update by senior management, showing explicit acknowledgement of 27701 integration.
properties.text: ISO/IEC 27701 (PIMS) alignment note where applicable — extends the ISMS into a Privacy Information Management System; references the 27701 PII-controller / PII-processor controls applied

guidance: List each personal data processing activity in the PII Processing Register, including a clear description and the purpose for processing.
Record the specific security controls applied to each activity, such as encryption at rest, encryption in transit, and access control classification.
Cross-reference each listed control to the relevant ISO27001 A.8.x control and GDPR Article 32 requirement in the register entry.
Name the individual responsible for verifying the accuracy of each register entry — do not use a team or department as owner.
Document the date each register entry was last reviewed and updated, ensuring no undated or outdated entries remain.
properties.text: Security controls applied per activity (encryption at rest/in transit, access control class, pseudonymisation where used — cross-link to A.8.x and GDPR Art.32)

guidance: List each processing activity in your PII Processing Register with a unique reference and a clear, descriptive title.
Specify the exact categories of data subjects involved in each processing activity, such as customers, employees, minors, or vulnerable groups.
Name the owner of each processing activity as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Record the date each entry was last reviewed or updated to show the information is current.
Avoid using generic categories like "users" or "public" without further detail, as auditors will flag vague or incomplete classifications.
properties.text: Data subject categories per processing activity (customers, employees, prospects, minors, vulnerable groups — drives extra-safeguard decisions)

guidance: Record the DPIA status for each processing activity in the PII Processing Register as "required," "completed," or "not required with rationale."
State the rationale for any activity marked "not required," referencing the specific risk assessment or legal basis used in your determination.
Name the individual responsible for each DPIA decision, ensuring a specific person is listed rather than a team or department.
Date each DPIA status entry to show when the assessment or exemption decision was made.
Cross-reference completed DPIAs to their full reports or summaries, including document location or unique identifier.
properties.text: DPIA status per activity (required / completed / not required with rationale) — drives high-risk processing reviews

guidance: Record the date each personal data processing activity was last reviewed or verified directly in the PII Processing Register.
Assign responsibility for each activity’s review to a named individual, not a generic team or department.
Update the last-verified date immediately after each periodic review or change to the processing activity.
Cross-reference the last-verified date with meeting minutes or review logs to confirm the review actually took place.
properties.text: Last-verified date per activity (proves the entry is current; missing dates surface stale activities at review)

guidance: Record the lawful basis for each processing activity in the PII Processing Register, using the exact terms defined in your data protection policy.
Cross-reference each activity’s lawful basis entry to the relevant policy section or legal text supporting that basis.
Specify the Article 9 special-category basis for any processing of sensitive personal data, not just the general Article 6 basis.
Name the decision-maker who determined the lawful basis for each activity, avoiding generic references like "the team" or "compliance department."
Date each lawful basis entry to show when it was last reviewed or confirmed as accurate.
properties.text: Lawful basis recorded per activity (matches the policy's discipline — consent / contract / legal obligation / vital interests / public task / legitimate interests, with special-category Art.9 basis where applicable)

guidance: Name the owner for each processing activity as a specific role or individual, such as "HR Manager" or "Sales Director," not a generic team.
Record the date each owner assignment was made or last reviewed in the PII Processing Register.
Document the scope of responsibility for each owner, clearly linking them to the relevant processing activity in the register.
Cross-reference each processing activity with supporting documentation that describes the owner’s duties and authority.
properties.text: Owner per processing activity (named role responsible for the activity — HR for employee processing, Sales for prospect processing, etc.)

guidance: State the specific, explicit, and legitimate purpose for each PII processing activity in the register, avoiding vague terms like "business operations."
Cross-reference each stated purpose to GDPR Article 5.1.b in the register to demonstrate compliance with the purpose limitation principle.
Record the date each processing purpose was last reviewed or updated, along with the name of the reviewer.
Name the owner responsible for each processing activity as a specific individual, not a team or department.
properties.text: Processing purposes stated per activity (specific, explicit, legitimate — not 'business operations'; cross-link to GDPR Art.5.1.b purpose limitation)

guidance: Record the specific retention period for each PII processing activity, stating the exact duration and what triggers the start and end dates.
Cross-reference each retention period in the PII Processing Register to the corresponding entry in your A.5.33 records retention schedule.
Name the trigger events that start and end retention, such as "user account closure" or "contract termination," for each processing activity.
Avoid using arbitrary or generic durations like "as long as necessary" or "until further notice"—state concrete, justified timeframes.
properties.text: Retention period per activity (concrete duration with start/end triggers; cross-link to A.5.33 records schedule — no arbitrary numbers)

guidance: Cross-reference the PII Processing Register to the GDPR Article 30 Record of Processing Activities by including a direct hyperlink or document reference.
State in the PII Processing Register that it serves as both the ISO27001 and GDPR Art.30 register to clarify its dual purpose.
Name the register owner as a specific individual responsible for maintaining both compliance requirements, not just a team or department.
Record the date of the most recent update to the register and ensure it matches across both compliance frameworks.
properties.text: Direct link to GDPR Art.30 RoPA register where the two are kept as one artefact — saves duplication, prevents drift

guidance: List each processing activity involving personal data in the PII Processing Register, including a clear description of the activity and its purpose.
Record the destination country or countries for any cross-border transfer associated with each processing activity, specifying each jurisdiction by name.
State the legal mechanism used for each transfer, such as Standard Contractual Clauses, adequacy decision, Binding Corporate Rules, or derogation, and attach supporting documentation.
Enter 'none' explicitly in the register for activities where no cross-border transfer occurs, avoiding blank fields or ambiguous entries.
Name the responsible individual maintaining the register, ensuring this is a specific person rather than a team or department.
properties.text: Cross-border transfers per activity (destination jurisdictions + legal mechanism — SCCs / adequacy / BCRs / derogations; explicit 'none' where applicable)

guidance: State in the policy that personal data is collected only for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes, referencing GDPR Article 5.1.c.
Document retention periods for each personal data category, cross-referencing your records retention schedule from control A.5.33.
Name a specific individual as the policy owner responsible for enforcing data minimisation and retention, not a team or department.
Include a policy statement requiring regular review and deletion of personal data that exceeds retention periods, referencing GDPR Article 5.1.e.
Attach the latest approval date and signature of a senior manager to the policy document.
properties.text: Retention and data minimisation requirements (collect only what's necessary; retain only as long as needed; cross-link to A.5.33 records schedule and GDPR Art.5.1.c/e)

guidance: List all specific ad-hoc events that trigger a privacy and PII program review, such as regulatory changes, industry breaches, or mergers, in a dated policy document.
Name the individual responsible for monitoring and initiating reviews based on these triggers, recording their full name and role in the policy.
Document the process for identifying and responding to each trigger, including required actions and timeframes, in a written procedure approved by management.
Record each occurrence of a trigger and the resulting review in a change log, including the date, description, and outcome.
Avoid using vague trigger descriptions like "significant event"—specify concrete examples relevant to your organisation and sector.
properties.text: Ad-hoc review triggers listed (Schrems-style adequacy shift, new regulator enforcement action in scope sector, M&A, large-scale breach in industry)

guidance: Record each personal-data breach in a dated register, including a summary of the incident, detection date, and affected data subjects.
Confirm for every breach entry that notification to the supervisory authority was completed within 72 hours, with supporting evidence such as sent emails or submission receipts.
Document whether data subjects were notified for each breach, citing the rationale and attaching copies of notification messages where required.
Cross-reference each breach entry with the lessons-learned log, showing how outcomes were incorporated into the organisational improvement actions under A.5.27.
Name a specific individual responsible for breach management and notification decisions—do not list a team or department as the owner.
properties.text: Breach history for the period (every personal-data breach in scope confirmed handled per Art.33 72h notification + Art.34 data-subject notification where required; lessons fed into A.5.27)

guidance: Record the date of the most recent Privacy and PII Protection Program review in a central compliance log.
Name the individual responsible for scheduling and conducting the next review, specifying their full name and job title.
Confirm the planned review interval is documented and does not exceed 12 months from the previous review date.
Attach evidence of the completed review, such as meeting minutes or a signed summary, with the actual review date clearly shown.
Avoid listing the review owner as a group or department; assign a specific person to ensure clear accountability.
properties.text: Review date within the planned interval (typically within 12 months of last review)

guidance: Name a responsible individual to oversee the DPIA review process, listing their full name and role in the review record.
Document the completion status of all DPIAs in a dated register, clearly flagging any high-risk processing activities lacking a completed DPIA.
Record the last review date for each DPIA and note any that are older than 24 months or where processing activities have changed.
Update and retain evidence of refreshed DPIAs for any processing activities that have materially changed since the last assessment.
Avoid listing DPIA ownership as "the team" or "department"; always specify a single accountable person for each DPIA.
properties.text: DPIA completion status reviewed (any high-risk processing without a completed DPIA flagged; DPIAs older than 24 months refreshed where processing material to lifecycle changed)

guidance: Assign a named individual to lead the periodic review of Data Subject Access Request (DSAR) metrics, recording their name and review date.
Document DSAR volumes, average response times versus documented service level agreements, refusal rates, and extension rates in a dated summary report.
Record the number and nature of complaints received from supervisory authorities regarding DSAR handling in the same review report.
Cross-reference the review report with supporting evidence, such as DSAR logs and correspondence, to verify accuracy of reported metrics.
Name the reviewer as a specific person, not a team or department, to avoid auditor concerns about unclear accountability.
properties.text: DSAR metrics review (volumes, response times against SLA, refusal/extension rates, complaints to supervisory authority) — operational privacy health

guidance: State the next planned review date for the Privacy and PII Protection Program in a dated document, such as the review schedule or meeting minutes.
Name the individual responsible for scheduling and leading the next review, listing their full name and role in the same document.
Record the date this review schedule was last updated, ensuring it is clearly visible and not left blank or undated.
Avoid using vague terms like “annually” or “TBD”; specify an exact calendar date for the next planned review.
properties.text: Next planned review date stated

guidance: Assign a named individual to lead the privacy and PII protection program review, recording their name and the review period in a dated document.
List each privacy-related activity, and document the outcome for each as verified, amended, retired, or newly added, with supporting notes.
Confirm for every activity that the lawful basis for processing is still valid, recording the check date and the person who verified it.
State for each activity whether the data retention period remains adequate, including the review date and reviewer’s name.
Avoid using generic statements like “all activities reviewed”; record specific outcomes and checks for each individual activity.
properties.text: Per-activity outcome (verified / amended / retired / new added) with lawful-basis-still-valid and retention-still-adequate confirmation

guidance: Document the date and findings of each privacy and PII protection program review in a dedicated review log.
Update the live privacy and PII register to reflect all approved changes, citing the specific review log entry as the source.
Name the individual responsible for updating the register, avoiding generic labels like "the team" or "IT."
Retain evidence of the register update, such as a version history or change log entry with timestamps and references to the review.
properties.text: Changes propagated back to the live register with reference to this review

guidance: Record the full names and official roles of the Data Protection Officer or Privacy Officer and the Information Security lead on the review document.
Include the signature and date from legal counsel on the review document if privacy laws or regulations have changed since the last review.
Attach a copy of the meeting minutes or review log showing both required reviewers participated and agreed on the program assessment.
Name each reviewer as a specific individual—do not use group titles like "the team" or "management" in the documentation.
properties.text: Reviewer identity and role recorded (DPO or Privacy Officer + InfoSec lead jointly; legal-counsel sign-off where law has shifted materially)

guidance: Review the current privacy applicability scope document and highlight any new jurisdictions, regulated activities, or data subject categories since the last review date.
Cross-reference the updated scope against your privacy register to identify any missing entries related to new requirements.
Record the date of the review and the name of the reviewer in the privacy program review log.
Name any new or changed register entries with specific details, avoiding generic labels like "miscellaneous" or "other".
Retain supporting evidence, such as meeting minutes or correspondence, that confirm the review and any resulting register updates.
properties.text: Cross-check against the privacy applicability scope — any new jurisdiction, regulated activity, data subject category that should add register entries

guidance: List all current international data transfer mechanisms in use, including Standard Contractual Clauses, adequacy decisions, and Binding Corporate Rules, in a dated register.
Cross-reference each mechanism against the latest regulatory updates and guidance, noting any changes such as Schrems decisions or new SCC editions.
Document the date and outcome of the most recent validity check for each mechanism, including any identified risks or compliance gaps.
Flag any mechanisms found to be outdated or invalid for remediation, recording the assigned responsible individual and planned corrective actions.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual, not a group or department, and record their sign-off on the completed review.
properties.text: Transfer-mechanism validity check (SCCs current edition, adequacy decisions still standing — e.g. Schrems shifts, BCRs unchanged) — flag stale mechanisms for remediation

guidance: List specific events that require re-scoping, such as entering new countries, launching new services, or acquiring companies handling personal data.
Document the trigger list in the Privacy Applicability Scope record, including the date of the most recent update.
Assign a named individual responsible for monitoring business changes and initiating re-scoping when a trigger event occurs.
Avoid using vague triggers like "significant change"; describe each event in clear, concrete terms relevant to your organisation.
Retain evidence of periodic reviews of the trigger list, such as meeting minutes or review logs with dates and attendees.
properties.text: Trigger list for re-scoping (new geography, new service line entering a regulated sector, M&A bringing new data subject categories, new transfer destinations)

guidance: Name the data processing context and describe the specific activities, systems, and data types involved in each scenario.
Assign the status of controller, processor, or joint controller for each processing context, referencing GDPR definitions and relevant contracts.
Record the named individual responsible for determining and reviewing the status decision for each processing context.
Document the date of the most recent review or update to each context’s status and supporting rationale.
Specify the status owner as a named person, not a team, department, or generic role.
properties.text: Controller vs Processor vs Joint Controller status per processing context (drives different obligation sets — Art.24-31 for controllers, Art.28 for processors, Art.26 for joint controllers)

guidance: List all categories of individuals whose personal data your organisation processes, such as customers, employees, suppliers’ staff, minors, or patients, in a dated document.
Name the person responsible for maintaining and updating the data subject category list, identifying them by full name and job title.
Cross-reference each data subject category with relevant business processes or systems where their personal data is handled.
Avoid using generic terms like “users” or “staff” without further detail; specify each group clearly to prevent ambiguity.
Review and update the data subject category list at least annually, recording the date and the reviewer’s name for each update.
properties.text: Data subject categories the organisation touches (customers, employees, prospects, suppliers' staff, minors, healthcare patients, financial-services clients — drives extra-safeguard rules)

guidance: List all countries where your organisation has headquarters, branch offices, or conducts business operations in a dated scope document.
Record every location where personal data is processed, stored, or accessed, including cloud and third-party providers, with named contacts for each.
Identify and document the countries of residence for all data subjects whose personal data your organisation handles.
Specify all destinations to which personal data is transferred, whether routinely or occasionally, and include the legal basis for each transfer.
Name the scope owner as a specific individual, not a team or department, and include their contact details in the document.
properties.text: Jurisdictions covered (HQ + places of business + data subject residency + processing locations + transfer destinations — each may impose distinct privacy obligations)

guidance: Cross-reference the privacy applicability scope document to the applicable obligations register created for A.5.31, listing the relevant privacy laws and regulations.
Document the shared legal and regulatory drivers in both the privacy scope and the obligations register, using identical wording for the same requirements.
Name the individual responsible for maintaining alignment between the privacy scope and the obligations register, specifying their full name and role.
Record the date when the privacy scope was last reviewed for alignment with A.5.31, and keep a copy of the review decision.
Avoid using generic references like "see compliance register" without specifying document titles and sections; always provide direct cross-links.
properties.text: Cross-link to A.5.31 applicable-obligations scope — privacy laws are a subset; the two should share drivers and stay aligned

guidance: List each country or region where your organisation collects or processes personal data in a dated Privacy Applicability Scope document.
Enumerate the specific privacy laws and regulations that apply to each jurisdiction, such as GDPR for the EU or CCPA for California.
State the business activities or data types that trigger each law’s applicability, referencing supporting records or data maps where possible.
Name a specific individual as the owner of the Privacy Applicability Scope — do not use a team or department as the owner.
Review and update the document at least annually, recording the review date and the name of the reviewer.
properties.text: Applicable privacy laws enumerated per jurisdiction (GDPR for EU/EEA, UK GDPR for UK, CCPA for California residents, LGPD for Brazil, PIPEDA for Canada, sectoral laws — HIPAA, GLBA, FERPA where relevant)

guidance: List all business activities that process personal data, specifying the sector each activity falls under (e.g., healthcare, finance, telecom).
Identify and record the exact privacy laws or regulations that apply to each activity, citing the specific regime (e.g., HIPAA, GLBA, ePrivacy).
Name the owner as a specific individual responsible for maintaining the privacy applicability scope, not a team or department.
Date and approve the documented scope and mappings by a senior manager to confirm accuracy and accountability.
Cross-reference the privacy applicability scope in your risk register or compliance matrix, linking each regulated activity to its governing law.
properties.text: Regulated activities pulling in sectoral privacy regimes (healthcare → HIPAA, financial → GLBA/PSD2/DORA-privacy overlap, telco → ePrivacy, public sector → FERPA/government-records laws, advertising/profiling → ePrivacy)

guidance: Name a specific individual as the policy owner, listing their full name and job title in the policy document.
Document explicit references in the policy to technical controls protecting PII, including encryption, access control, logging, and pseudonymisation, with links to relevant procedures.
Cross-reference each mentioned technical control in the policy to its corresponding section in your security controls register, noting control numbers (e.g., A.8.24 for encryption).
State in the policy how these controls satisfy GDPR Article 32 and Article 5.1.f requirements, including a clear summary paragraph.
Record the policy approval date and the approver’s name and signature on the policy’s cover page.
properties.text: References security controls applied to PII (links to A.8.x technical controls — encryption A.8.24, access control A.5.15/A.8.3, logging A.8.15/A.8.16, pseudonymisation A.8.11; satisfies GDPR Art.32 integration with Art.5.1.f)

guidance: Cross-reference the Privacy and PII Protection Policy to the staff privacy training section in your training register, specifying where awareness content is covered.
Document the date and version of the Privacy and PII Protection Policy that includes the cross-link to A.6.3 awareness requirements.
Name the individual responsible for maintaining the cross-link between the policy and the privacy/PII training records.
Attach a sample training completion record for a staff member who processes personal data, showing the relevant privacy/PII training module.
properties.text: Cross-link to A.6.3 awareness — privacy/PII training for staff who process personal data (consent capture, DSAR handling, breach reporting)

guidance: List all countries where personal data is transferred, including both routine and occasional transfers, in a dated appendix to the Privacy and PII Protection Policy.
State the legal basis for each cross-border transfer, referencing specific mechanisms such as Standard Contractual Clauses, adequacy decisions, Binding Corporate Rules, or derogations.
Cross-reference the A.5.14 transfer policy and relevant GDPR Articles 44-49 within the Privacy and PII Protection Policy, using explicit section numbers or hyperlinks.
Name the policy owner as a specific individual with responsibility for cross-border transfer compliance, not as a team or department.
Review and update the policy at least annually, recording the review date and the reviewer’s name in the policy document.
properties.rationale: 27002:5.34 — preservation of privacy / GDPR Chap V
properties.text: Cross-border transfer discipline (which transfers happen, on what legal basis — SCCs / adequacy / BCRs / derogations; cross-link to A.5.14 transfer policy + GDPR Art.44-49)

guidance: Draft an executive summary section at the start of the review report that clearly addresses the organisation’s leadership by name or title.
Summarise the overall information security posture in plain language, highlighting key strengths and major risks identified during the review.
Reference the date of the review and the period covered, ensuring the summary reflects the current state at that point in time.
Assign authorship of the executive summary to a named individual or independent reviewer, not a generic team or department.
Attach evidence that the executive summary was formally shared with leadership, such as an email confirmation or meeting minutes with named recipients.
properties.text: Executive summary section addressed to leadership (audit-defensible communication of overall posture, not just the detailed findings list)

guidance: List each finding with a clear severity rating, such as "high," "medium," or "low," directly linked to the risk or impact described.
Reference the specific observation or evidence for each finding, such as log entries, interview notes, or document excerpts, within the report.
Assign a unique identifier to every finding so it can be traced back to supporting evidence and the relevant review date.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual, not a team or department, and include their signature and the date of the review.
Avoid using generic recommendations; describe each finding in concrete terms, showing how it was identified and why it matters.
properties.text: Findings listed with severity (concrete, evidenced, traceable to the underlying observation — not just generic recommendations)

guidance: Document the process for monitoring review findings and triggering alerts when target closure dates are missed in a written procedure.
Assign responsibility to a named individual for tracking overdue findings and initiating notifications, listing their name and contact details in the register.
Record the date and recipient of each overdue alert sent, maintaining a log that shows timely notification actions for all missed deadlines.
Name the escalation path for unresolved overdue items, specifying actual job titles or individuals rather than generic terms like "management" or "the team".
properties.text: Aged-overdue alerting (notification when target date passes without closure)

guidance: Record a unique closure evidence reference for each closed finding in the register, linking directly to the artefact that demonstrates the finding was addressed.
Cross-reference the closure evidence to a dated document, such as a revised policy, completed training record, or implemented control change.
Name the person who verified the closure evidence, ensuring the individual is identified by full name, not just a role or team.
Attach or link the actual closure artefact in the register entry, rather than describing it only in text or relying on verbal confirmation.
properties.text: Closure evidence reference per closed finding (link to the artefact that proves the finding was addressed — control change, policy update, training delivered)

guidance: Cross-reference the Independent Review Finding Response Register to the A.5.36 compliance-review nonconformity register using a clear section or column header.
State in the register documentation that both A.5.35 and A.5.36 requirements are addressed within this single artefact.
Name a specific individual as the register owner, avoiding generic titles like "Compliance Team" or "Management".
Record the date when the cross-linking and dual-purpose use of the register was last reviewed and approved.
properties.text: Cross-link to A.5.36 compliance-review nonconformity register where the two are kept as one artefact (common in mature programs)

guidance: Assign a unique identifier to each review finding, using a sequential or structured format that cannot be duplicated or reused.
Cross-reference each finding’s identifier with the original review report section or page number where the issue was documented.
Record the date and name of the person who entered each finding into the register for traceability.
Attach a copy or direct link to the source review report alongside each finding entry in the register.
Name the source review report explicitly for every finding entry—avoid vague references like "latest audit" or "external review".
properties.text: Per-finding unique identifier traceable back to the source review report

guidance: Record each review finding in the register with a unique identifier, date of discovery, and a short description of the issue.
Name a specific individual as the owner for each finding — do not use generic roles, teams, or departments.
Assign and document a clear target closure date for every finding, ensuring the date is realistic and agreed by the named owner.
Update the register with the owner's full name and the closure date, and have the owner acknowledge their responsibility with a dated signature or email confirmation.
properties.text: Named owner per finding (named individual, not generic team) with target closure date

guidance: Record the severity rating for each finding in the response register exactly as stated in the independent review report.
Cross-reference each severity entry in the register to the corresponding section or page in the original review report.
Name the person responsible for entering severity ratings, ensuring a specific individual is listed rather than a team or department.
Confirm that all findings in the register have a severity rating; do not leave any severity field blank or marked as "TBD".
Retain a copy of the independent review report alongside the register for direct comparison during audits.
properties.text: Severity recorded per finding (matches the report's severity classification)

guidance: Record the current status for each review finding as "open", "in-progress", "closed", or "aged-overdue" in the response register.
Enter the last-updated date for each finding, reflecting the most recent action or review.
Name the individual responsible for updating each finding’s status, not just a team or department.
Update the register promptly whenever a finding’s status changes or new information is received.
Cross-reference each finding with supporting evidence of actions taken, such as meeting notes or remediation tickets.
properties.text: Current status per finding (open / in-progress / closed / aged-overdue) with last-updated date

guidance: Record the agreed treatment for each review finding in the register, clearly stating whether it will be accepted, remediated, or transferred.
Document the rationale for the chosen treatment for each finding, referencing any supporting evidence or risk assessment used in the decision.
Cross-reference each treatment entry to the corresponding management response in the independent review report to confirm consistency.
Name the responsible individual for each finding’s treatment, avoiding generic roles like "the team" or "IT department".
Date each treatment decision and rationale entry to provide a clear timeline of actions taken.
properties.text: Agreed treatment per finding (accept / remediate / transfer with rationale; mirrors the management response committed in the report)

guidance: Name the reviewer as a specific individual or external firm, clearly stating their role and lack of operational responsibility for the reviewed areas.
Document the reporting line of the reviewer, showing separation from the management or teams responsible for the information security controls under review.
Attach a signed and dated statement from the reviewer confirming their independence for this review cycle.
Avoid listing the reviewer as a team, department, or anyone with day-to-day operational duties in the reviewed area; specify a unique, independent person or entity.
properties.text: Independence of the reviewer demonstrated (separate function, external auditor, or rotating internal reviewer with no operational ownership of the reviewed areas)

guidance: Record each finding’s management response directly in the review report, clearly stating whether it will be accepted, remediated, transferred, or risk-accepted.
Document the rationale for any risk acceptance decision, providing specific business or technical reasons rather than generic statements.
Name the responsible manager for each response as a specific individual, not as a team or department.
Date each management response entry to show when the decision was made.
Avoid referencing a separate action plan or follow-up document; ensure all responses are fully contained within the review report itself.
properties.text: Management response to findings (accept / remediate / transfer / risk-accept with rationale); response is documented IN the report, not deferred

guidance: Document the date and source of external benchmarking or industry-practice input reviewed during the meta-review cycle.
Name the individual responsible for sourcing and presenting external benchmarking data, specifying their role and contact details.
Attach copies or summaries of relevant external reports, frameworks, or benchmarking studies referenced in the meta-review.
Record the meta-review meeting minutes, explicitly noting discussion and consideration of external or industry-practice input.
Avoid referencing only internal sources or generic statements; cite at least one specific external benchmark or industry source.
properties.text: External benchmarking or industry-practice input considered

guidance: Record the total number of findings identified during each review cycle in a dated findings log maintained by the program coordinator.
Document the closure status of each finding as open, aged (with days outstanding), or closed, including closure dates and responsible individuals.
Calculate and update the findings-closure rate for the program at least quarterly, showing open, aged, and closed findings in a summary report.
Name a specific individual responsible for tracking and reporting findings status—do not list a team or department as the owner.
Retain evidence of management review and sign-off on the findings-closure summary for each reporting period.
properties.text: Findings-closure rate across the program (open / aged / closed)

guidance: Document the actual review dates for each scheduled independent review in a dated log maintained by the program coordinator.
Cross-reference each completed review to the planned schedule, marking any missed or rescheduled scope areas with reasons.
Name the reviewer for each scope area as a specific individual, not a group or department.
Record a summary statement confirming that all planned scope areas were reviewed, signed and dated by the program owner.
Attach evidence of any corrective actions taken for missed reviews, including approval from the program owner.
properties.text: Coverage check — did the schedule actually run? all planned scope areas reviewed?

guidance: Record the date of the most recent meta-review in a central register, clearly referencing the specific review cycle it covers.
State the planned interval for meta-reviews in your documented review program, including start and end dates for each cycle.
Confirm the meta-review occurred within the planned interval by cross-referencing the actual review date with the scheduled timeline.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual, not a group or department, in the meta-review documentation.
Retain evidence of the meta-review decision, such as a signed or digitally approved summary report with the review date clearly shown.
properties.text: Meta-review date within the planned interval

guidance: List each reviewer's name and role for every periodic review, linking them to the specific area they assessed.
Cross-reference each reviewer’s assigned area with their regular job responsibilities to confirm no one reviewed their own area.
Document the rotation schedule showing reviewer assignments changed between review periods, with dates and names.
State the independence criteria reviewers must meet, and record how each reviewer satisfied these criteria for the relevant review period.
Name the reviewer for each area as a specific individual, not as a team or department.
properties.text: Independence-discipline check — did the actual reviewers meet the criteria? rotation worked? any reviewer reviewing their own area?

guidance: State the next planned meta-review date in the Periodic Independent Review Program Meta-Review document.
Record the date in a calendar or tracking system used for compliance activities, with a reference to the meta-review document.
Name the person responsible for scheduling and conducting the next meta-review, using their full name and job title.
Avoid leaving the next review date as "TBD" or blank, as this would be flagged by an auditor.
properties.text: Next planned meta-review date stated

guidance: Document each decision to adjust the review cadence or scope in a dated record, specifying whether the change is to tighten, loosen, re-tier, or alter the reviewer pool.
Name the individual who approved the adjustment, ensuring the record lists a specific person and not a group or department.
State the rationale for each adjustment, referencing the relevant risk assessment, incident, or business change that prompted the decision.
Retain evidence of communication to all affected reviewers or stakeholders, such as an email or meeting minutes, confirming awareness of the new cadence or scope.
Cross-reference the adjustment record with the latest version of the Periodic Independent Review Program to show the change has been implemented.
properties.text: Cadence-adjustment or scope-adjustment decisions (tighten / loosen / re-tier / change reviewer pool)

guidance: Name the program owner, InfoSec lead, and audit committee chair (if applicable) as individual reviewers in the meta-review record.
Document the date each reviewer completed their section of the meta-review, using a dated signature or electronic confirmation.
Attach evidence of each reviewer’s input, such as comments, approvals, or meeting minutes, to the meta-review file.
Avoid listing groups or roles as reviewers; specify named individuals to satisfy accountability requirements.
properties.text: Reviewer identity (program owner + InfoSec lead jointly + audit committee chair where applicable)

guidance: Cross-reference each current finding with the previous review’s findings, clearly marking items as new, open, closed, or aged.
Record the date each finding was first identified and, if closed, the date of closure, in the review report.
Name the responsible individual for tracking and updating the status of each finding, not just a team or department.
Document a summary section that highlights overall movement since the last review, including the number of findings resolved or still outstanding.
Attach supporting evidence, such as action plans or closure confirmations, for each finding marked as closed.
properties.text: Comparison or movement from prior review's findings (open / closed / aged) — proves the program returns value across cycles

guidance: State each recommendation clearly in the review report, describing a specific action to address the identified issue.
Assign a named individual as the suggested owner for each recommendation, avoiding generic roles like "IT" or "the team".
Indicate the priority of each recommendation using a defined scale, such as high, medium, or low, with justification.
Date and sign the report to confirm when the recommendations were made and by whom.
properties.text: Recommendations stated (with priority and owner suggestion — actionable, not abstract)

guidance: State the exact start and end dates of the review activity in the report, referencing the calendar dates when the review work was performed.
Specify the observation window by clearly recording the period under examination, including both the beginning and ending dates.
Confirm the report includes the date it was finalized and issued, not just the review dates.
Name the review period using precise dates — avoid vague phrases like "recent months" or "quarterly review."
properties.text: Review date and period covered (start/end of the review activity + observation window)

guidance: State the full name and professional accreditation or qualification of each reviewer in the report, such as CISA or ISO 27001 Lead Auditor.
Attach a copy of the reviewer’s relevant certification or provide a link to a verifiable credential directory.
Record the date of the most recent certification renewal or qualification update for each reviewer.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual, not a team, department, or external firm without listing the responsible person.
properties.text: External auditor accreditation or internal reviewer qualifications stated (CISA, ISO 27001 LA/LI, sector-specific credentials)

guidance: State the planned review frequency for each scope area in the register, specifying intervals such as annual or more frequent for higher-risk domains.
Record the date when the review schedule was last approved, along with the name of the approver.
Name the owner responsible for maintaining the schedule as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Cross-reference any risk assessments or business justifications that require tighter review cadences for certain domains.
Avoid leaving any scope area with an undefined or "as needed" review interval; each must have a concrete, scheduled cadence.
properties.text: Planned cadence stated (annual is the doctrine baseline; risk-tier or scope-area may drive tighter cadences for hot domains)

guidance: List specific ad-hoc change triggers in the Independent Review Schedule Register, such as mergers, major system changes, regulatory updates, or significant breaches.
Record the date each ad-hoc trigger was identified and the corresponding decision to initiate an out-of-cycle review.
Name the individual responsible for recognizing and documenting each trigger, avoiding generic roles like "the team" or "IT department".
Attach supporting evidence, such as board minutes or incident reports, that confirm the occurrence of each listed trigger.
properties.text: Ad-hoc change triggers documented (M&A, major architectural shift, regulatory upheaval, major breach) — fires reviews outside the planned cadence

guidance: Record each scheduled independent review in the register, including the planned date and the assigned reviewer’s full name.
Log the actual completion date for every review, leaving the field blank if the review has not yet occurred.
Calculate and update a column showing the difference between scheduled and completed dates, highlighting any missed or overdue reviews.
Name the owner of the register as a specific individual, not a team or department, to ensure clear accountability.
Retain evidence of follow-up actions for any missed reviews, such as emails or meeting notes, attached to the relevant register entry.
properties.text: Scheduled-vs-completed delta tracked (so missed reviews surface)

guidance: Record the most recent independent review date in the schedule register, using a specific calendar date, not just a month or year.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual, avoiding generic roles or team names.
Cross-reference the review entry with supporting evidence, such as a signed review report or meeting minutes.
Confirm that the recorded date matches the date on the supporting review documentation.
properties.text: Last review date recorded (proves the schedule is anchored in reality, not aspirational)

guidance: List each scope area separately in the register, ensuring each has its own row or entry.
State the next scheduled review date for every scope area, using a clear and unambiguous date format.
Name the responsible individual for each scope area's review, avoiding generic titles like "team" or "department".
Record the date when the register was last updated to show information is current.
Cross-check that no scope area is missing a next review date, as missing dates are a common audit finding.
properties.text: Next review date stated (per scope area where sliced)

guidance: Name a specific individual as the owner responsible for executing the Independent Review Schedule Register; do not use a team or department name.
Record the owner's full name and job title in the register, along with the date they were assigned accountability.
Document the management sponsor’s name and their formal approval of the owner’s accountability, including the date of approval.
Retain a signed or digitally approved record confirming the owner’s acceptance of their responsibility for the register.
properties.text: Named owner accountable for executing the schedule (typically CISO / InfoSec lead with management sponsor)

guidance: Document the process used to select independent reviewers, specifying whether external rotation, internal independence criteria, or an audit-firm agreement is applied.
Name the reviewer for each scheduled review as a specific individual, not as a team or department.
Record the date and outcome of each reviewer selection decision in the Independent Review Schedule Register.
Attach supporting evidence, such as signed agreements or documented independence checks, to each entry in the register.
properties.text: Reviewer selection mechanism (external rotation, internal independence criteria, audit-firm framework agreement) — drives the independence guarantee

guidance: List all ISMS scope areas, including people, processes, and technologies, in the Independent Review Schedule Register with clear, specific names.
Document the planned review cycle for each scope area, stating whether it is reviewed annually end-to-end or in defined slices.
Describe the rationale for any sliced review approach, specifying which areas are covered in each cycle and the schedule for full coverage.
Name the owner of the review schedule as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Record the date the schedule was last updated and approved, with the approver’s name clearly shown.
properties.text: Scope areas planned (the ISMS may be reviewed end-to-end annually OR sliced across cycles — both acceptable; the slicing is documented)

guidance: Name the individuals, processes, and technologies reviewed in a dedicated section of the report, listing each element separately and specifically.
Document the review methods used for each dimension—such as interviews for people, walkthroughs for processes, and technical assessments for technologies—with corresponding dates.
State the evidence examined for each area, such as training records for people, documented procedures for processes, and configuration logs for technologies.
Confirm the reviewer is independent by including their name, role, and relationship to the organisation, avoiding vague terms like "external party" or "consultant".
Retain a signed and dated approval page from the reviewer, explicitly referencing the full scope covering people, processes, and technologies.
properties.text: Scope covers people, processes, and technologies (not just one dimension — auditor-defensible reviews must touch all three)

guidance: State in the review report whether the review was conducted as part of the regular schedule or triggered by a significant change.
Describe the nature of any significant change that prompted the review, such as mergers, major system redesigns, or regulatory changes.
Record the date the review was initiated and reference any related change management or incident documentation.
Name the person who authorized the review, ensuring this is a specific individual and not a group or generic title.
Attach supporting evidence, such as a change request or incident report, if the review was triggered by a significant event.
properties.rationale: 27002:5.35 — planned intervals or on significant change
properties.text: Significant-change trigger check stated (whether this review was triggered by planned cadence OR by a significant change — M&A, major architectural shift, regulatory upheaval, major breach)

guidance: Document the specific continuous-compliance monitoring tools in use, including their names, scope, and the date they were implemented.
Record the output from these tools showing recent configuration drift, control health checks, or CSPM signals, with timestamps.
Cross-reference each compliance review record with the relevant monitoring tool output to demonstrate that findings were considered during the review.
Name the individual who reviewed the tooling output and made decisions, avoiding generic roles like "the team" or "IT".
Retain evidence of actions taken in response to tool findings, such as remediation tickets or meeting notes, with dates and responsible persons.
properties.text: Continuous-compliance monitoring tooling output considered (where used — config drift, control health checks, CSPM signal)

guidance: Record each nonconformity finding in a dated compliance review log, including a clear description of the issue identified.
Assign a named individual as the owner responsible for addressing each nonconformity, avoiding generic labels like "the team" or "IT."
Document a specific corrective action for each nonconformity, including a realistic target completion date.
Cross-reference each corrective action entry to the corresponding item in the nonconformity register to ensure traceability.
Retain evidence of follow-up, such as status updates or closure confirmation, signed or acknowledged by the assigned owner.
properties.text: Corrective actions opened per nonconformity finding (with owner, target date) — feeds the nonconformity register

guidance: Record the date, scope, and participants for each compliance review in a dedicated log or register.
Document each finding from the review, clearly stating whether it is compliant, a nonconformity, or an opportunity for improvement.
Attach or reference concrete evidence supporting each finding, such as screenshots, policy excerpts, or audit trails.
Assign a severity level to each nonconformity and opportunity for improvement, using defined criteria in your documented review procedure.
Name the reviewer(s) as specific individuals, not as a group or department, and obtain their signature or electronic approval on the review record.
properties.text: Findings recorded per review with severity (compliance vs. nonconformity vs. opportunity-for-improvement; concrete, evidenced)

guidance: List each policy, rule, and standard reviewed, including its unique title and version, in a dated compliance review record.
Record the specific review method used for each item, such as control sampling, formal audit, automated check, attestation, or walkthrough.
State the rationale for choosing the review method for each item, referencing the item’s type, complexity, or risk level.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual, not a group or department, for each entry in the record.
Attach supporting evidence, such as checklists, screenshots, or audit logs, to demonstrate that the stated review method was actually performed.
properties.text: Method used per item (control sampling, formal audit, automated check, attestation, walkthrough); rationale for method choice given the item type

guidance: Record the method used to select samples for each compliance review, including criteria and rationale, in a dated review log.
Retain copies of attestation responses or confirmations from staff, with names and dates, as part of the review documentation.
Store audit working papers, such as checklists, notes, and findings, in a version-controlled folder linked to the specific review event.
Name the reviewer and approver for each compliance review as specific individuals, not generic roles or teams.
Attach all supporting evidence to the compliance review record to allow independent verification of the review process and outcomes.
properties.text: Method evidence retained (sample selection notes, attestation responses, audit working papers) for audit defensibility

guidance: Document the process for generating alerts when a nonconformity remains open past its target closure date in the Compliance Nonconformity Register.
Record the date and recipient of each overdue alert notification sent, keeping a log that shows timely communication of missed deadlines.
Name the responsible individual who monitors the register and triggers overdue notifications, avoiding generic roles like "the team" or "compliance department."
Retain a sample of an actual overdue alert email or system notification, showing the message content and timestamp.
properties.text: Aged-overdue alerting (notification when target date passes without closure)

guidance: Record a unique identifier for each nonconformity in the register to allow clear tracking from discovery to closure.
Attach or link the specific document, ticket, or signed record that proves corrective action was completed for each closed nonconformity.
Enter the closure date and the name of the individual who verified the evidence for each nonconformity entry.
Name the closure evidence reference specifically for each nonconformity — do not use generic phrases like "see attached" or "fixed".
properties.text: Closure evidence reference per closed NC (link to the artefact that proves the NC was addressed)

guidance: Record the corrective action for each nonconformity as a clear, specific commitment such as "update password policy" or "deliver phishing training."
Name the individual responsible for implementing each corrective action, using a full name rather than a role or team.
State the target completion date for each corrective action and update the register when the action is completed, including the actual completion date.
Attach supporting evidence for completed actions, such as a revised policy document, training attendance records, or control implementation screenshots.
Avoid using vague descriptions like "fix issue" or "address gap" as corrective actions; specify the exact change to be made.
properties.text: Corrective action stated per NC (the specific change committed — policy update, control implementation, training delivery)

guidance: Cross-reference each compliance nonconformity entry with the corresponding independent-review finding by including the unique identifier from the A.5.35 register.
State in the register header or introduction that this document combines both compliance nonconformities and independent-review findings, if the artefacts are merged.
Name the owner responsible for maintaining the register as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Record the date when the cross-linking between the two registers was last reviewed and updated.
Attach or link supporting evidence, such as meeting minutes or emails, confirming agreement to maintain a combined artefact if applicable.
properties.text: Cross-link to A.5.35 independent-review finding register where the two are kept as one artefact

guidance: Record each risk-accepted nonconformity in the Compliance Nonconformity Register, including a clear description and the date the acceptance decision was made.
Assign a specific expiry date for every risk-accepted nonconformity, showing when the acceptance must be reviewed or closed.
Name the individual who approved the risk acceptance, ensuring their full name and role are listed, not just a team or department.
Cross-reference each risk-accepted nonconformity to the relevant entry in the Exception Register, linking both records for traceability.
Document the review outcome or closure action by the expiry date, attaching evidence of follow-up or renewed acceptance if applicable.
properties.text: Exception register integration — risk-accepted NCs with expiry date (so 'we accept this' doesn't drift into 'we forgot this')

guidance: Assign a unique identifier to each nonconformity entry in the register that does not repeat or overlap with any other entry.
Cross-reference each nonconformity’s identifier to the specific review record or audit report where it was first identified.
Record the date and name of the reviewer or auditor who documented the nonconformity in the register.
Avoid using generic or sequential numbers without a link to the source review, as auditors will flag untraceable entries.
properties.text: Per-NC unique identifier traceable back to the source review record

guidance: Record each nonconformity with a unique reference number and a clear description in the Compliance Nonconformity Register.
Name a specific individual as the owner for each nonconformity entry, avoiding generic labels like "IT" or "the team".
Enter a target closure date for each nonconformity, ensuring the date is realistic and agreed upon by the named owner.
Review and update the register regularly to reflect progress, documenting any changes to ownership or closure dates with dates and initials.
properties.text: Named owner per NC (named individual, not generic team) with target closure date

guidance: Record the root cause for each nonconformity in the register, using clear language that explains why the issue occurred.
Name the person or team who investigated and determined the root cause for each entry, including the date of determination.
Reference supporting evidence, such as investigation reports or meeting notes, for each root cause entry in the register.
Avoid leaving the root cause field blank or using generic terms like "human error" without further explanation.
properties.text: Root cause noted per NC where determined (drives systemic improvements vs point fixes)

guidance: Record the severity of each nonconformity in the Compliance Nonconformity Register using the same classification terms as your review record.
Cross-reference each nonconformity entry with its corresponding review record to show the severity matches exactly.
Name the person responsible for assigning severity for each nonconformity, ensuring a specific individual is listed rather than a group or department.
Date each severity entry in the register to confirm when the classification was assigned.
properties.text: Severity recorded per NC (matches the review record's severity classification)

guidance: Record the current status of each nonconformity in the register using clear terms such as open, in-progress, closed, aged-overdue, or risk-accepted-with-exception.
Enter the last-updated date for each nonconformity status, ensuring the date field is never left blank or marked as "ongoing."
Name a specific individual responsible for updating each nonconformity entry, avoiding generic roles like "the team" or "compliance department."
Review the register regularly and update statuses to reflect actual progress, not leaving items in "in-progress" indefinitely without review.
Retain a change log or history showing previous statuses and update dates for each nonconformity to demonstrate ongoing management.
properties.text: Current status per NC (open / in-progress / closed / aged-overdue / risk-accepted-with-exception) with last-updated date

guidance: Name the individual responsible for running the compliance review cycle, using their full name and job title in the review record.
Record the date the compliance review was completed in the official review log or tracking document.
