Document the scope and outcome of the review, referencing specific policies, rules, and standards evaluated during the cycle.
Avoid listing the owner as "the team," a department, or a generic role; always identify a single, accountable person.
properties.text: Named owner of this review cycle (the person who ran it — typically compliance lead or designate)

guidance: Cross-reference the list of reviewers for both the compliance review program and the independent review program, and record any individuals serving in both roles.
Document whether findings from both programs are logged in a shared register or separate registers, including the location and access details for each.
State any processes or tools that are shared between the two programs, such as scheduling systems or reporting templates, and provide supporting documentation.
Name the person responsible for coordinating alignment between the two programs, ensuring this is a specific individual rather than a team or department.
Record the date and outcome of the most recent meta-review that checked for alignment between the compliance and independent review programs.
properties.text: Alignment check with A.5.35 independent review program (shared reviewer pool? shared finding register? leverage opportunities)

guidance: List all current information security policies, rules, and standards in a dated catalogue, including their publication or revision dates.
Cross-reference the catalogue against the periodic review schedule to confirm all new and updated items have assigned review dates.
Remove any retired or superseded policies, rules, or standards from the review schedule and document the removal date and reason.
Name the catalogue owner as a specific individual, not a group or department, to avoid ambiguity in responsibility.
Record the date and outcome of each catalogue currency check, including any discrepancies found and actions taken.
properties.rationale: 27002:5.36 — InfoSec policy + topic-specific policies + rules + standards
properties.text: Catalogue currency check — did new policies / rules / standards land without entering the schedule? are retired items still scheduled?

guidance: Record the total number of compliance findings identified during the review period in a dated summary report.
Document the current status of each finding as open, aged (with the date it became overdue), or closed, referencing supporting evidence for closure.
Calculate and state the findings-closure rate by showing counts and percentages for open, aged, and closed findings in the report.
Name the individual responsible for tracking and reporting findings status, avoiding generic labels like "the team" or "compliance department."
Retain evidence of management review and sign-off on the findings-closure rate summary, including the date and names of reviewers.
properties.text: Findings-closure rate across the program (open / aged / closed)

guidance: Document the actual dates each scheduled compliance review took place during the period in a dated review log.
Record which items from the compliance catalogue were reviewed in each session, referencing catalogue identifiers.
Calculate and state the percentage of the total compliance catalogue that was reviewed during the period, showing your working.
Name the person who verified the review coverage calculation as a specific individual, not a group or department.
Attach evidence of any missed or rescheduled reviews, including explanations and approval from a named decision-maker.
properties.text: Coverage check — did the schedule actually run? what fraction of catalogue reviewed in period?

guidance: Record the date of the most recent compliance review meta-review in a dated log or register.
State the planned interval for meta-reviews in a documented schedule or policy, referencing the relevant control.
Compare the actual meta-review date to the planned interval and document the result in the review log.
Name the reviewer who confirmed the timing as a specific individual, not a group or department.
Retain evidence of the meta-review, such as meeting minutes or a signed checklist, showing the date and participants.
properties.text: Meta-review date within the planned interval

guidance: Assign a named individual to conduct the meta-review of the compliance review program, recording their name and date in the review log.
Document the specific methods used to identify nonconformities, referencing actual findings and corrective actions from recent compliance reviews.
Compare the number and severity of nonconformities found over time, noting any patterns that suggest underreporting or superficial reviews.
Record any adjustments made to the review methods as a result of the meta-review, including rationale and approval by a designated authority.
Name the reviewer as a specific person—do not list a team, department, or leave the owner field blank.
properties.text: Method effectiveness review — are the chosen methods surfacing real nonconformities, or is the program rubber-stamping?

guidance: State the next planned date for the meta-review of the compliance review program in the program documentation.
Record the date in a version-controlled document or register that tracks all scheduled meta-reviews.
Name the individual responsible for scheduling and conducting the next meta-review, listing their full name and role.
Avoid leaving the next meta-review date as "TBD" or blank, as auditors will flag missing or unclear scheduling.
properties.text: Next planned meta-review date stated

guidance: Record each decision to change the frequency or method of compliance reviews, including the specific item type affected and the rationale, in a dated log.
Name the individual who approved each adjustment decision, ensuring the owner is a specific person rather than a group or department.
Attach supporting evidence, such as risk assessments or incident trends, that justify the need for each cadence or method adjustment.
Document the date when the adjustment takes effect and schedule the next review to confirm the change was implemented as planned.
properties.text: Cadence-adjustment or method-adjustment decisions (tighten / loosen / change method per item type)

guidance: Name both the compliance program owner and the Information Security lead as joint reviewers in the meta-review documentation.
Record the full names and job titles of both reviewers on the meta-review sign-off page.
Sign and date the meta-review document with both reviewers’ signatures to confirm joint participation.
Avoid listing a group, team, or department as reviewer; specify named individuals only.
properties.text: Reviewer identity (compliance program owner + InfoSec lead jointly)

guidance: Record the exact start and end dates of each compliance review in the review log or register.
Document the period covered by the review, specifying which policies, rules, or standards were assessed.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual, not just a team or department, in the review record.
Attach or reference the signed review report that includes the review date and scope for each completed review cycle.
properties.text: Review date and period covered (start/end of the review activity)

guidance: List each compliance item in the review schedule, specifying the required review frequency for each based on risk and rate of change.
Assign a named individual as the responsible owner for scheduling and tracking each review, avoiding generic roles like "the team."
Record the date when the review frequency was last set or updated for each item, along with who approved it.
Attach supporting risk assessments or rationale justifying any review cadence shorter or longer than annual for specific items.
Review the schedule at least annually to confirm all listed frequencies remain appropriate and update the record with the review date and reviewer’s name.
properties.text: Cadence per item (annual baseline; tighter for high-risk or fast-changing items — e.g. acceptable use, access control)

guidance: List specific ad-hoc triggers such as policy changes, regulatory updates, or incidents in your compliance review schedule with clear, concrete examples.
Document the process for initiating an out-of-cycle review, including who is responsible and how the trigger is recognized and recorded.
Record each ad-hoc review decision with the date, the trigger event, and the named reviewer who authorized the review.
Name the owner of the schedule as a specific individual, not a team or department, to avoid ambiguity in accountability.
Retain evidence of completed ad-hoc reviews, such as meeting minutes or approval emails, linked to the triggering event.
properties.text: Ad-hoc change triggers documented (policy edit, regulator action, incident affecting a policy area) — fires reviews outside the planned cadence

guidance: List all planned compliance review dates for the year in a central schedule, naming the responsible individual for each review.
Record the actual completion date for each scheduled review, updating the schedule promptly after each review occurs.
Track any missed or delayed reviews by highlighting scheduled dates without a matching completion date in the schedule.
Name the owner as a specific individual — not a group or department — to avoid ambiguity in accountability.
Retain both the original schedule and the updated version showing completed and missed reviews for auditor inspection.
properties.text: Scheduled-vs-completed delta tracked (so missed reviews surface)

guidance: List every in-scope information security policy, topic-specific policy, rule, and applicable standard in a single, dated compliance review schedule.
Cross-reference each item in the schedule to its unique document identifier or location, so auditors can trace every entry to a real artefact.
Name the owner for each listed item as a specific individual, not a team or department, to avoid accountability gaps.
Confirm that no required policy, rule, or standard is missing by comparing the schedule against your documented scope and regulatory obligations.
Record the date the schedule was last reviewed and approved by a named, responsible manager.
properties.rationale: 27002:5.36 — InfoSec policy + topic-specific policies + rules + standards
properties.text: Full catalogue of in-scope items enumerated (InfoSec policy + every topic-specific policy + rules + applicable standards — completeness is the integrity check)

guidance: Record the last review date for each compliance item in the schedule, using a clear date format such as YYYY-MM-DD.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual for each item, avoiding generic labels like "Compliance Team" or "IT Department."
Retain evidence of the review, such as meeting minutes or a signed checklist, linked to each item's last review date.
Cross-reference the review schedule with supporting documentation to confirm each listed date matches the actual review activity.
properties.text: Last review date per item

guidance: List each compliance item in the review schedule, specifying the exact control, policy, or process to be reviewed.
State the planned review method for each item, clearly indicating whether you will use sampling, a full audit, or an automated check.
Name the responsible individual for each review method, avoiding generic roles like "the team" or "IT department".
Record the scheduled review date and frequency for each item, ensuring these are explicit and not left as "TBD" or blank.
Attach supporting documentation or tool outputs for automated checks, showing how the method will be applied in practice.
properties.text: Planned method per item (which items use sampling vs audit vs automated check)

guidance: List each compliance item in the review schedule with a unique identifier and a clear description.
Record the next planned review date for every listed item in a dedicated column of the schedule.
Name the responsible reviewer for each item as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Update the schedule immediately after each review to show the new next review date, with a timestamp of the update.
Retain previous review dates and outcomes in an audit log linked to each item for historical reference.
properties.text: Next review date per item

guidance: List each compliance item in the review schedule with a unique identifier and clear description.
Name a specific individual as the owner responsible for each item, avoiding group or team names.
Record the date when each owner was assigned responsibility for their respective item.
Document the next scheduled review date for each item alongside the assigned owner's name.
Retain a signed or acknowledged record from each owner confirming their acceptance of responsibility.
properties.text: Named owner per item (reviewer accountable for the next cycle)

guidance: List each policy, rule, and standard scheduled for review in the current cycle, including the planned review date and responsible reviewer.
Record the actual review date and reviewer name for each item, attaching evidence of the completed review such as meeting notes or sign-off.
Flag any item not reviewed as scheduled by documenting the missed review, reason, and plan for completion in the next cycle.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual for each item, not as a team or department.
properties.text: Schedule honoured for this cycle (each planned policy/rule/standard actually reviewed in the period; gaps flagged for next cycle)

guidance: List each policy, rule, and standard included in the current review cycle by title and unique identifier in a dated review log.
Cross-reference the reviewed items against your full policy catalogue to show which documents were in scope and which were deferred.
Name the specific individual who determined the scope for this cycle, avoiding generic labels like "the team" or "management".
Attach a copy or extract of the policy catalogue as it existed at the start of the review cycle to evidence completeness.
properties.rationale: 27002:5.36 — InfoSec policy + topic-specific policies + rules + standards
properties.text: Scope of this cycle (which policies / rules / standards were reviewed — typically a slice of the full catalogue if rotated across cycles)

guidance: List the intended audience for each operating procedure by naming specific job titles or roles, not generic groups like "staff" or "IT".
Document the rationale for why each listed role requires access to the procedure, referencing relevant job responsibilities or tasks.
Cross-reference each procedure in the register with the corresponding training records for the named roles to show alignment.
Record the date and name of the person who last reviewed and confirmed the accuracy of the intended audience for each procedure.
properties.text: Intended audience per procedure (which personnel 'need' the procedure — drives access permissions and training links)

guidance: State the exact location where each operating procedure is published, such as a specific intranet URL, wiki path, or document repository.
Record the access permissions for each procedure, listing which personnel or roles can view or edit the document.
Name the owner responsible for maintaining the availability of each procedure as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Document the date when each procedure’s availability mechanism was last verified or updated in the register.
properties.text: Availability mechanism stated per procedure (where personnel find them — intranet location, runbook system, wiki path with permissions, code-of-conduct package)

guidance: Add a dedicated "Emergency Use" column to your Operating Procedures Register, allowing each procedure to be clearly flagged as emergency-use or not.
Mark each procedure in the register with a "Yes" or "No" in the "Emergency Use" column, based on documented business impact analysis or risk assessment.
Name the reviewer who approved each emergency-use designation, and record the approval date directly in the register.
Avoid leaving the "Emergency Use" column blank or using vague labels like "maybe" or "as needed"—make each entry specific and unambiguous.
Cross-reference each emergency-use procedure in the register with its latest review date to show it receives more frequent updates.
properties.text: Emergency-use flag per procedure (procedures needed under pressure — DR, incident response — get higher visibility and tighter currency)

guidance: List each operating procedure in a central register, including the full procedure name and a unique identifier for reference.
Name the owner for each procedure as a specific individual or named role who actively performs or oversees the procedure.
Record the date each procedure was last reviewed or updated, along with the name of the person who conducted the review.
Avoid listing generic owners such as "IT" or "the team"; specify a real person or role with clear accountability.
Retain a signed or approved version of the register showing current ownership and review dates.
properties.text: Ownership per procedure (named role or individual responsible for currency — the operator who runs the procedure, not 'IT')

guidance: Document every edit to the procedure in a dedicated change-log, including the date, description of change, and name of the editor.
Retain previous versions of the procedure alongside the current version to allow auditors to trace the full history.
Assign responsibility for maintaining the change-log to a named individual, not a group or department.
Record approvals for each significant change in the change-log, including the approver’s name and approval date.
Cross-reference the change-log in the procedure document so auditors can easily locate and verify the audit trail.
properties.text: Change-log requirement for procedure edits (so the audit trail is preserved across versions)

guidance: Name a specific individual as the maintainer of the operating procedures register, avoiding generic titles like "the team" or "operations."
Document the maintainer’s name and role in the header section of the maintenance procedure, including the date of assignment.
Record the InfoSec partner’s name and their supporting responsibilities in the same section for clear accountability.
Review and update the named maintainer and InfoSec partner details at least annually, keeping a dated change log of updates.
properties.text: Named maintainer of the register (typically operations lead with InfoSec partner) accountable for catalogue currency

guidance: Document the retirement process in your maintenance procedure, specifying that obsolete procedures must be archived and not deleted.
Record the date and reason for each procedure's retirement in a central register, linking to the archived version.
Assign responsibility for archiving retired procedures to a named individual, not a team or department.
Retain archived procedures in a secure, access-controlled location with a clear folder structure and retention period.
properties.text: Retirement path for obsolete procedures (system decommissioned, procedure superseded) — retired procedures are archived, not deleted

guidance: Name the peer reviewer by full name and role in the procedure's review section before publishing the operating procedure.
Record the date and outcome of the peer review in a tracked change log or approval table within the procedure document.
Obtain InfoSec sign-off with a dated signature for any procedure that impacts security controls, attaching the approval to the final document.
Avoid using generic group names like "Operations Team" or "Security Department" as reviewers; always specify individual names.
properties.text: Review path before publication (peer review by other operators, InfoSec sign-off for procedures touching security controls)

guidance: Schedule and document runbook drills for all emergency-use procedures, recording dates, participants, and scenarios exercised in a central log.
Assign a named individual to lead each drill and record their name in the drill log for accountability.
Capture lessons learned and required updates after each drill in a dated after-action report, referencing specific procedures tested.
Name the procedures selected for each drill explicitly—do not use generic terms like "critical processes" or "key runbooks."
properties.text: Runbook-drill cadence — periodic exercise of selected procedures (especially emergency-use ones) so they're verified actionable under pressure

guidance: State the required template sections: purpose, scope, prerequisites, steps, verification, rollback, and contacts in the documented procedure.
Name the person responsible for maintaining and updating the template definition, listing their full name and role.
Record the date when the template definition was last reviewed or updated in the procedure document.
Attach a completed example of an operating procedure using the defined template to demonstrate consistent application.
Specify each template section clearly; avoid using generic placeholders or leaving any section blank.
properties.text: Template definition stated (purpose / scope / prerequisites / steps / verification / rollback / contacts) — drives consistent shape

guidance: List all specific events that require an update to the operating procedure, including system changes, control changes, review findings, exercise outcomes, and operator-reported errors.
Cross-reference each update trigger with its relevant control or process, such as A.8.32 for system changes or A.5.35/A.5.36 for review findings.
Document the date and version number of the procedure each time an update is made in response to a listed trigger.
Name the person responsible for maintaining and updating the procedure as a specific individual, not a generic role or team.
Retain records of the most recent procedure review, showing that all update triggers were considered and the procedure remains current.
properties.text: Update triggers enumerated (system change A.8.32 → procedure update, control change, finding from A.5.35/A.5.36 review, exercise outcome from A.5.24/A.5.29, operator-reported error)

guidance: List all critical operating procedures, specifying which facilities or systems each procedure covers, in a centralized register.
Name the responsible owner for each procedure as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Record the latest review date and version number for each procedure entry in the register.
Cross-reference each procedure in the register to its full documentation, ensuring links or file paths are current and accessible.
Document any gaps or missing procedures in the register, along with assigned action owners and target completion dates.
properties.text: Inventory of operating procedures (which facilities/systems they cover — backup, restore, patching, on-call response, change deployment, monitoring response, capacity, log-handling, etc.)

guidance: Cross-reference each documented operating procedure to all related ISO27001 controls, listing specific control numbers and titles in the register entry.
Record the date each cross-link was last reviewed or updated, and name the individual responsible for maintaining the register.
Attach supporting evidence, such as procedure documents or mapping tables, that clearly show how each procedure aligns with the referenced controls.
Name the owner of each procedure as a specific individual, not a team or department, to avoid ambiguity in responsibility.
Review the register for any procedures missing cross-links to relevant controls, and update entries to ensure no procedure stands alone without references.
properties.text: Cross-link to related controls per procedure (A.5.24/A.5.26 incident, A.5.29 disruption, A.5.30 ICT recovery, A.8.x technical controls)

guidance: Select a random sample of operating procedures and record the procedure names, sample size, and selection date in a review log.
Assign a named operator to walk through each sampled procedure end-to-end, recording their name and the date of the walkthrough.
Capture screenshots or outputs from the current system during the walkthrough to demonstrate that steps, commands, and dependencies are up to date.
Compare each procedure’s documented steps and screenshots to the actual system interface and commands, noting any discrepancies in the review log.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual—do not list a team or department as the reviewer.
properties.text: Accuracy sampling — operator walked through a sample procedure end-to-end? procedure matches current system reality (UI screenshots current, commands work, dependencies still valid)

guidance: List specific ad-hoc review triggers in the operating procedures program documentation, such as major incidents, mergers and acquisitions, and major system migrations.
Record the date and details of the most recent ad-hoc review, including what triggered it and who participated.
Name the responsible individual who determines when an ad-hoc review is required, avoiding generic titles like "the team" or "IT".
Attach supporting evidence, such as incident reports or project plans, that directly led to an ad-hoc review being initiated.
properties.text: Ad-hoc review triggers listed (major incident exposing procedure gap, M&A, major system migration)

guidance: Record the date of the last operating procedures program review in a central log, including the name of the reviewer.
Schedule the next review within 12 months of the previous review date and document this planned interval in the same log.
Attach the signed and dated review summary or meeting minutes as evidence of the most recent review.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual, not a group or department, in all review records.
properties.text: Review date within the planned interval (typically within 12 months of last review)

guidance: List all emergency-use procedures relevant to disaster recovery and incident response, including document names, version numbers, and last review dates.
Assign a named individual with operational responsibility to review each procedure for accuracy and completeness at least annually.
Record the completion of each review with the reviewer's name, date, and a summary of any updates or confirmations of accuracy.
Attach evidence of a recent test or simulation using each procedure to demonstrate that instructions are practical and up to date.
Name the owner as a specific person, not a generic group or department, to avoid ambiguity in responsibility.
properties.text: Emergency-use procedure review — confirmed available and accurate for DR/incident scenarios (these are the procedures where stale = catastrophic)

guidance: State the next planned review date in the operating procedures program document, listing it clearly in a dedicated section.
Record the date of the most recent review alongside the planned next review date for clear tracking of review cycles.
Name the individual responsible for scheduling and conducting the next review, avoiding generic titles like "the team" or "management".
Retain a copy of the approved program document showing the next planned review date and responsible person’s name.
properties.text: Next planned review date stated

guidance: List each operating procedure reviewed, including its unique title and version, in a dated review log for the current review cycle.
Record the outcome for each procedure as verified, amended, retired, or new added, with a brief note explaining any changes or decisions.
Confirm and document that each procedure remains accessible to relevant staff through the intended mechanism, such as an intranet link or shared drive location.
Name the reviewer(s) as specific individuals, not just a team or department, and include their signatures or electronic approval for each procedure reviewed.
Attach supporting evidence for any amendments or retirements, such as updated documents or decommissioning records, to the review log.
properties.text: Per-procedure outcome (verified / amended / retired / new added) with availability-mechanism-still-works confirmation

guidance: Record the date and outcome of the periodic operating procedures review in a dedicated review log, including any required changes identified.
Update the live register of operating procedures to reflect all approved changes, citing the review log entry as the source.
Name the individual responsible for updating the live register, avoiding generic attributions such as "the team" or "operations."
Cross-reference each updated procedure in the register to the specific review date and log entry that triggered the change.
properties.text: Changes propagated back to the live register with reference to this review

guidance: Record the full names and job titles of both the operations lead and the information security lead responsible for each program review.
Document the date each review was completed and ensure both leads are listed as reviewers on the same record.
Obtain signatures or electronic approval from both the operations lead and the information security lead on the review record.
Name the reviewers as specific individuals—do not use generic titles like "the team" or "management" in the reviewer field.
properties.text: Reviewer identity and role recorded (operations lead + InfoSec lead jointly)

guidance: Cross-reference the current list of operating procedures with your up-to-date inventory of systems, SaaS environments, and facility types.
Identify any new or changed systems, SaaS tools, or facility classes that have been added since the last review date.
Name a specific individual responsible for confirming that each new or changed item has appropriate operating procedures in place.
Record the review date, findings, and any required procedure updates in a dated review log signed by the reviewer.
Avoid listing "all sites" or "IT" as owners—assign each procedure to a named person for each facility or system.
properties.text: Cross-check against the applicable-facilities scope — any new system / SaaS environment / facility class that should add procedures

guidance: List each information processing facility in your documented scope, using clear names that match entries in your asset register.
Cross-reference every facility in your scope to its corresponding entry in the A.5.9 asset register, noting register IDs or unique identifiers.
Link each facility to one or more documented operational procedures, citing exact procedure titles or document references for traceability.
Name the owner of each facility as a specific individual, not a team or department, in both the scope and asset register records.
Record the date of your last cross-check between the scope, asset register, and procedures to show the mapping is current.
properties.text: Cross-link to A.5.9 asset register — every information asset that is a facility should map to one or more procedures

guidance: List all triggers that require a review of the information processing facilities scope, such as new systems, SaaS adoption, M&A, or decommissioning.
Document each trigger in a dated register, specifying the event and the individual responsible for initiating the re-scoping process.
Assign a named owner to review and update the facilities scope when any trigger occurs—do not use a team or department as the owner.
Retain evidence of each scope review, including the date, trigger event, and decision, in a version-controlled document.
properties.text: Trigger list for re-scoping (new system entering production, SaaS adoption, M&A bringing new facilities, decommission)

guidance: List every information processing facility in use, including physical, virtual, and cloud-based, with a unique identifier and location for each.
Cross-reference each facility in the register with its corresponding documented operating procedure, noting the procedure's title and last review date.
State the scope coverage clearly at the top of the register, specifying that all information processing facilities are included.
Name a specific individual responsible for maintaining the register, not a team or department.
Highlight any facility without a documented operating procedure as an action item, with a due date and assigned owner for resolution.
properties.text: Scope coverage stated (every information processing facility represented — gaps surface where a facility exists without a documented procedure)

guidance: List all information processing facilities in your environment, including physical sites, cloud services, and critical infrastructure, with responsible owners named for each.
Identify which facilities must remain operational or accessible during emergencies or disaster recovery scenarios, and record these in a dated emergency-use subset register.
Document the criteria used to select facilities for emergency-use, including business impact and recovery objectives, and reference this in your register.
Name the emergency-use subset owner as a specific individual, not a team or department, to avoid ambiguity in accountability.
Review and update the emergency-use subset register at least annually, recording the review date and the reviewer’s name.
properties.text: Emergency-use subset identified (which facilities need procedures available even when normal tooling is down — DR scenarios)

guidance: List all information processing facilities in scope, specifying their class or category such as compute, storage, network, security tooling, identity, or observability.
Document the template variations required for each facility class, including any unique security or operational requirements.
Assign operator personas to each facility class, naming specific individuals or roles responsible for management and oversight.
State the rationale for including each facility class in scope, referencing relevant business or compliance needs.
Name the owner for each facility as a specific individual—do not use generic terms like "the team" or "IT department".
properties.text: Facility classes / categories (compute, storage, network, security tooling, identity, observability) — drives template variations and operator personas

guidance: List all SaaS environments where your organisation manages configuration, such as M365, Salesforce, or ServiceNow, in a dated register.
Name a specific individual as the owner responsible for each SaaS environment — avoid using generic roles or teams.
Document the scope of information processing activities for each listed SaaS environment, including what data is handled and how.
Cross-reference each SaaS environment in your operating procedures to show how configuration and management responsibilities are met.
properties.text: Key SaaS environments where the org operates the configuration (M365, Salesforce, ServiceNow, etc.) — even SaaS-hosted facilities need operating procedures for the org-side operator

guidance: List all production applications, databases, and key infrastructure components in a dated document labeled as the current scope of information processing facilities.
Name the person responsible for maintaining the scope list as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Cross-reference each listed facility with its physical or logical location and relevant owner to enable traceability.
Record the approval of the scope document by a named senior manager, including the date of sign-off.
properties.text: Systems in scope enumerated (production applications, databases, key infrastructure components — drives 'which facilities need a procedure')

guidance: List each operating procedure in the register with a unique title and version number for clear identification.
Attach the completed template for each procedure, showing sections for purpose, scope, prerequisites, steps, verification, and rollback.
Mark a template adherence flag for each procedure, indicating whether all required sections are present and filled out.
Name the reviewer who checked template adherence for each procedure, avoiding anonymous or group attributions.
Record the date of the most recent template adherence check for each procedure in the register.
properties.text: Template adherence flag per procedure (consistent shape across the catalogue — purpose / scope / prerequisites / steps / verification / rollback)

guidance: Record the current version number, last-updated date, and review-due date for each operating procedure in the register.
Name the owner of each procedure as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Cross-reference each procedure entry in the register with its corresponding approved document to confirm version and date alignment.
Retain previous versions and their dates in an accessible archive to demonstrate version history.

guidance: List a named contact person for each threat intelligence feed entry, including their full name and direct contact details.
