Attach supporting documentation showing communication with each contact, such as an email thread or support ticket.
Avoid using generic roles or team names as contacts; specify an individual for each feed entry.
properties.text: Contact per row (vendor support, ISAC liaison)

guidance: Record the cost for each threat intelligence feed in the register, clearly stating if it is a paid or free source.
Name the specific individual responsible for maintaining and updating the feed cost information in the register.
Document the date when each feed's cost was last reviewed or updated in the register.
Attach supporting invoices or contracts for paid feeds to the corresponding register entries as evidence of actual costs.
Avoid listing costs as "varies" or "unknown"; enter a specific amount or state "free" for each feed.
properties.text: Cost per row (paid feeds vs free) — required for value review

guidance: Record each decommissioned threat intelligence feed in the register, including the exact end-date when the feed was removed from use.
State the specific reason for decommissioning each feed, such as redundancy, cost, or reliability issues, in a dedicated column of the register.
Name the individual who approved the decommissioning decision for each feed, avoiding generic entries like "the team" or "IT department."
Retain the full register, including all decommissioned entries, as a dated and version-controlled document for future audit reference.
properties.text: Decommissioned sources retained with end-date and reason (audit trail)

guidance: List each threat intelligence feed in the register, clearly marking whether the source is internal or external for every entry.
Record specific internal sources, such as incident response observations or security interest group outputs, with named contacts and dates.
Cross-reference each internal feed to its originating process or team, not just a generic department or function.
Attach or link supporting evidence for each feed, such as meeting notes, incident summaries, or membership communications, with clear dates.
properties.text: Internal sources captured alongside external (e.g. A.5.6 SIG-membership outputs, internal IR observations)

guidance: Record the exact date and time each threat intelligence feed was last received in a dedicated column for every row in the register.
Assign responsibility for updating the last-received timestamp to a named individual, not a generic team or department.
Review the register monthly to confirm no feed shows a last-received timestamp older than your defined collection cadence.
Retain historical versions of the register to show evidence of regular updates and detection of any stale feeds.
properties.text: Last-received timestamp per row (stale-feed detection)

guidance: List each threat intelligence feed in a dedicated row of the register, using a unique identifier and source name.
Assign the intelligence layer for each feed as "strategic", "tactical", or "operational" in a separate column for every row.
Name the person responsible for classifying each feed’s intelligence layer, using their full name rather than a team or department.
Record the date when each feed’s intelligence layer was last reviewed or updated in the register.
Check that no row is missing an intelligence layer classification, and update any incomplete entries before finalizing the register.
properties.text: Intelligence layer per row (strategic / tactical / operational)

guidance: Name a specific individual as the internal owner for each threat intelligence feed entry, avoiding generic labels like "IT" or "Security Team".
Record the date each owner was assigned to their respective feed entry in the register.
Document the responsibilities of each owner, including renewal, escalation, and value assessment, in a dedicated column for every feed.
Cross-reference each feed entry with supporting evidence of the owner's recent review or action, such as a dated email or meeting note.
properties.text: Internal owner per row accountable for the source (renewal, escalation, value assessment)

guidance: Record a signal/noise rating of high, medium, or low for each threat intelligence feed entry in the register.
Update the signal/noise rating for every feed entry during each scheduled program review, noting the review date.
Name the reviewer responsible for assigning or updating each signal/noise rating in the register.
Avoid leaving any feed entry without a current signal/noise rating or with an outdated rating from a previous review cycle.
properties.text: Signal/noise rating per row (high/medium/low) updated at each program review

guidance: List each active threat intelligence feed in the register, assigning a unique identifier that is not reused for any other source.
Record the name, provider, and activation date for each feed entry to ensure clear traceability.
Cross-reference each identifier with supporting documentation or contracts to confirm the feed’s legitimacy and current status.
Name the register owner as a specific individual, not a team or department, to avoid ambiguity in responsibility.
properties.text: Each active source captured with a unique identifier

guidance: Record all action items from each threat intelligence program review in a dated meeting minutes document or an action tracking log.
Assign each action item to a named individual with a clear due date, avoiding generic owners like "the team" or "security."
Document the rationale for each action item, such as why a new feed is added or a source is retired, in the review record.
Confirm that completed action items are marked as closed with the completion date and the responsible person's name in the tracking log.
properties.text: Action items captured for the program (e.g. add new feed, retire stale source, tune analysis cadence)

guidance: Name specific individuals from each consumer group (security operations, supplier risk, detection, executive team) who provided feedback on the threat intelligence program.
Document the date, method, and summary of feedback collected from each named consumer group in a review log or meeting minutes.
Retain copies of feedback forms, emails, or meeting notes showing direct input from the identified consumers.
Avoid using generic terms like "the team" or "stakeholders"—list actual names and roles for each feedback provider.
properties.text: Consumer feedback collected from named consumers (sec ops, A.5.21 supplier risk, A.5.25 detection, exec briefing)

guidance: Record the most recent threat intelligence program review date in a central log, clearly showing the day, month, and year.
Name the individual responsible for scheduling and conducting each review, listing them by full name rather than a team or department.
Document the planned review interval as 180 days in the program documentation or review schedule.
Retain evidence of the last two completed reviews, such as signed meeting minutes or summary reports, with visible completion dates.
Cross-reference the review log with calendar invites or meeting records to confirm the review was not missed or delayed beyond 180 days.
properties.text: Review date within the planned 180-day interval

guidance: List each threat intelligence feed source in a dated review document, specifying the period covered and the individual conducting the analysis.
Record for each source which indicators or advisories were actionable and used, and which were dropped or found irrelevant.
Document the criteria used to determine feed value, including examples of actionable and non-actionable items for the review period.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual, not a team or department, to avoid ambiguity in accountability.
Retain evidence of any decisions to discontinue or add sources, including the rationale and approval date.
properties.text: Feed-value analysis per source (which feeds delivered actionable IOCs / advisories; which were dropped)

guidance: Document the date and source of at least one external threat report or vendor briefing reviewed during the last program cycle.
Name the individual responsible for collecting and summarizing external threat intelligence, specifying their full name and role.
Attach a summary of key findings from the external source, highlighting relevance to your organization’s threat landscape.
Retain meeting notes or review records showing discussion of the external threat snapshot in your periodic program review.
Avoid referencing only generic or outdated sources—cite current, industry-specific intelligence to demonstrate relevance.
properties.text: External threat-landscape snapshot considered (industry reports, vendor briefings)

guidance: Assign a named individual to lead the missed-event analysis, recording their name and role in the review documentation.
Document each security event surfaced by A.5.25 triage or A.5.27 lessons that was not previously flagged by threat intelligence.
Cross-reference each missed event with the relevant threat intelligence sources and note any gaps or reasons for the oversight.
Record the date and outcome of the review, including any updates made to the threat intelligence program as a result.
State clearly if any events were missed due to lack of timely review, avoiding vague explanations such as “unknown cause” or “oversight.”
properties.text: Missed-event analysis (events surfaced by A.5.25 triage or A.5.27 lessons that intel didn't flag in advance)

guidance: Record the date of the current threat intelligence program review in an official meeting record or review log.
State the next planned review date in the same document, ensuring it is no more than 180 days after the current review.
Name the individual responsible for scheduling and conducting the next review, listing their full name and role.
Avoid leaving the next review date blank or stating "TBD"—auditors will flag missing or vague scheduling details.
properties.text: Next planned review date stated (within 180d of this review)

guidance: Record the number of threat intelligence reports or products delivered during the review period in a dated summary document.
List the recipients or business units that received each threat intelligence product, showing distribution across the organisation.
Attach copies or redacted examples of delivered threat intelligence products to the review record as evidence of actual output.
Name the person responsible for compiling and submitting the periodic review, ensuring a specific individual is identified rather than a team or department.
properties.text: Products delivered count and distribution evidenced (proves the program ran, not just the procedure existed)

guidance: Name both the program owner and the InfoSec lead as individual reviewers in the review record for each periodic threat intelligence program review.
Record the date when the review was completed and ensure both reviewers are listed for that specific review cycle.
Obtain signatures or documented approval from both the program owner and the InfoSec lead on the review outcome.
Avoid listing generic roles or teams as reviewers; specify full names to clearly identify accountability.
properties.text: Reviewer identity (program owner + InfoSec lead jointly)

guidance: Document how threat intelligence findings are reviewed at least quarterly to identify new or changed exposures relevant to your organisation.
Record each instance where threat intelligence leads to an update or new entry in the risk register, including the date and responsible person.
Cross-reference updated risk register entries to the specific threat intelligence source or report that triggered the reassessment.
Name the individual responsible for reviewing threat intelligence and updating the risk register—do not list a team or department.
properties.text: Feedback loop into the risk register / risk assessment (intel that surfaces new exposures triggers reassessment)

guidance: Document the specific process for sharing analysed threat intelligence externally, including which types of information may be shared and with whom.
Name the responsible individual who approves outbound intelligence sharing, ensuring this is not listed as a generic team or department.
Record each instance of outbound intelligence sharing in a dated log, including recipient, content summary, and approval evidence.
Cross-reference your sharing process with any legal or contractual restrictions, attaching relevant guidance or decisions to the procedure.
properties.text: Outbound intelligence sharing path (ISAC contributions, peer briefings)

guidance: List all threat intelligence sources in the procedure, specifying each by name and type, such as open-source, vendor, ISAC, government, or paid service.
Record the date each source was last reviewed or updated to show regular evaluation of relevance and reliability.
Name the individual responsible for maintaining and updating the list of threat intelligence sources, not just a team or department.
Attach supporting documentation, such as subscription confirmations or access agreements, for each paid or restricted intelligence source.
properties.text: Threat intelligence sources enumerated (open-source feeds, vendor feeds, ISACs, government advisories, paid intel services)

guidance: State the specific risk-acceptance thresholds for each project tier in the procedure, including clear criteria for when escalation is required.
Name the individual approver for each risk tier, ensuring each is a specific person and not a generic role or group.
Document the process for recording risk-acceptance decisions, including the date, project name, risk description, and approver’s signature or written confirmation.
Cross-reference the procedure with the organisation’s risk register to show how project risks align with overall risk management practices.
Review the procedure to confirm that no risk-acceptance criteria are left as “to be determined” or copied boilerplate from templates.
properties.text: Risk-acceptance criteria stated (when residual risk forces escalation; named approver per tier)

guidance: Update the procedure to describe how security requirements are reviewed at each sprint or iteration, not just at project start and end.
Assign a named security contact for each project who participates in regular agile ceremonies, such as sprint planning or retrospectives.
Record security-related decisions and actions in sprint or iteration meeting notes, including the date and responsible individual.
Specify in the procedure that security checkpoints are embedded in the agile workflow, replacing any references to one-time "phase gates."
Avoid using generic statements like "security is considered throughout" without naming when and how this happens in the agile process.
properties.text: Adaptation for agile/iterative delivery (continuous security touchpoints rather than waterfall gates only)

guidance: Name a specific individual as the project security assessment owner in the procedure, avoiding generic titles like "the team" or "IT department".
Document the completion date and results of the security assessment, including penetration test findings and control verification, in the project records.
Record formal residual risk acceptance, signed and dated by the designated risk owner, before the project go-live decision.
Cross-reference the security assessment evidence in the project closure or go-live approval documentation.
properties.text: Security assessment before go-live (pen test, control verification, residual-risk acceptance)

guidance: Describe the process for identifying and documenting changes to project scope or security requirements during the project lifecycle in the procedure.
Assign responsibility for change assessment to a named individual, not a generic role or team, in the documented procedure.
Record each change and its security impact assessment in a dated change log or register, referencing who performed the assessment.
Require that any change with potential security impact triggers a formal re-assessment before implementation, with evidence of review and approval.
State that late detection of security-impacting changes after project completion is a non-conformance, and require immediate documentation and escalation if this occurs.
properties.text: In-project change control step (scope/security-impact changes during build trigger re-assessment, not late-detection)

guidance: Document a formal project closure checklist that includes a security sign-off section, with the checklist version and date clearly recorded.
Assign a named individual to complete and sign the security sign-off, confirming all security requirements have been addressed at closure.
Record any outstanding security risks at closure in a risk register, including the date, risk owner, and transfer details to operations.
Attach evidence of the handover to operations, such as a dated email or meeting minutes acknowledging receipt of outstanding risks.
Name the risk owner as a specific person, not a team or department, to avoid ambiguity in responsibility for outstanding risks.
properties.text: Project closure security sign-off step (handover to operations; outstanding-risk transfer documented)

guidance: List all required security artefacts for the project, including threat model, penetration test report, DPIA if applicable, and exception register, in the closure record.
Attach or link each artefact directly within the closure record, ensuring each file is dated and final.
Name the responsible individual who verified the completeness of the artefact archive, not a team or department.
Record the date when the closure record and all artefacts were archived, creating a clear audit trail.
Confirm that no referenced artefact is missing or marked as "to be provided later" before finalising the closure record.
properties.text: Security artefacts archived per record (threat model, pen-test report, DPIA where applicable, exception register)

guidance: Record the exact date the project security closure was completed in the closure record, using a standard date format.
Name the individual who confirmed project security closure, ensuring the person is identified by full name, not just a role or team.
Sign and date the closure record to provide clear evidence of when and by whom the closure was finalized.
Attach supporting documentation, such as final security review results, to the closure record to show all requirements were addressed before closure.
properties.text: Closure date recorded

guidance: List each security gate relevant to the project and record the actual closure date for each in the Security Closure Record.
Document any security gates not closed at project end, clearly stating the reason and referencing an approved risk acceptance or mitigation plan.
Name the individual who reviewed and signed off on the closure record, including their role and the date of sign-off.
Avoid using generic statements like "all gates closed" without specifying which gates and their closure dates.
properties.text: Gates-passed summary per record (which gates closed and when; gaps explicitly noted with risk acceptance)

guidance: Document a summary of security lessons learned for each project where new patterns, issues, or improvements were identified during closure.
Cross-reference each relevant project closure record to the central lessons-learned register maintained under A.5.27, using a unique register entry ID.
Name the individual responsible for submitting the lesson to the A.5.27 register, ensuring this is a specific person, not a team or role.
Record the date the lesson was added to the A.5.27 register in the project closure documentation.
Attach supporting evidence, such as meeting minutes or incident reports, that substantiate the lesson and its relevance to broader organisational learning.
properties.text: Lessons-learned link per record where project surfaced patterns worth feeding into A.5.27 lessons register

guidance: Record the unique project identifier from your project register on each security closure record.
Cross-reference the project identifier in the closure record with the entry in the official project register to confirm accuracy.
Name the project owner as a specific individual, not a team or department, on the closure record.
Date each closure record to show when the security closure was completed for the project.
properties.text: Project identifier per record (links to project register)

guidance: List all outstanding risks for the project in the security closure record, using clear descriptions that match those in the main risk register.
Name the operational owner accepting each outstanding risk as a specific individual, not a role or team.
Record the date each operational owner formally accepts responsibility for their assigned residual risks in the closure record.
Cross-reference each accepted risk to its entry in the organisation’s central risk register for traceability.
Attach evidence of acceptance, such as a signed or digitally approved statement from each named operational owner.
properties.text: Residual-risk register transfer per record (outstanding risks named, accepted by named operational owner with date)

guidance: Name the project sponsor, InfoSec gate-owner, and operational owner as specific individuals on each closure record, avoiding group or team names.
Obtain dated signatures from all three named individuals on the closure record to confirm final project security handover.
Attach supporting evidence of completed handover activities, such as checklists or meeting minutes, to each closure record.
Retain the fully signed and dated closure record in a central repository linked to the project documentation.
properties.text: Final signoff per record (project sponsor + InfoSec gate-owner + operational owner — three-way)

guidance: Identify each project that introduced a new third-party contract and record this in the security closure record with project name and contract date.
Name the operational owner assigned to take over ongoing supplier review duties for each relevant contract, listing them as a specific individual.
Attach a copy of the supplier agreement handover document, signed and dated by both the project lead and the operational owner.
Cross-reference the handover in the supplier management register, noting the date the operational owner assumed responsibility for A.5.22 review.
Avoid leaving the operational owner field blank or listing only a team or department; always specify a named person.
properties.text: Supplier-agreement handover per record where project introduced new third-party contracts (operational owner takes A.5.22 review duty)

guidance: Document a formal project initiation checklist that includes mandatory fields for risk assessment, information classification, and personal data scope.
Assign a named individual as the project security gate reviewer, listing their full name and role on each project record.
Record the date when the security gate review is completed and retain the signed or digitally approved checklist with the project documentation.
State the information classification level and whether personal data is involved in the project initiation artefacts, referencing supporting evidence.
Avoid leaving the project security gate reviewer as "the team" or an unnamed group; always specify a single accountable person.
properties.text: Security gate at project initiation (risk assessment, classification of information, scope of personal data if applicable)

guidance: Add a column in the Project Security Register to record the specific cloud service introduced by each project.
Cross-reference each new cloud service entry with its corresponding record in the Cloud Register, including a direct link or unique identifier.
Record the date when the cloud service was added to both the Project Security Register and the Cloud Register.
Name the project owner as a specific individual responsible for verifying the cloud service link, not as a team or department.
Review the register to confirm that no project introducing a cloud service is missing a cross-reference to the Cloud Register.
properties.text: Cloud-service link per row where project introduces a new cloud service (cross-ref to A.5.23 cloud register)

guidance: Name the information security liaison for each project as a specific individual, not a team or department, in the Project Security Register.
Record the date when the liaison was assigned to each project entry to show when responsibility was established.
Document the liaison’s review of each security gate by capturing their signature or written confirmation for every project milestone.
Cross-reference the liaison’s name with their current contact details to ensure they can be reached for follow-up or clarification.
properties.text: InfoSec liaison per row (named individual reviewing this project's security gates)

guidance: Name the project owner for each project row as a specific individual, including full name and job title.
Record the date each project owner is assigned in the register to show current accountability.
Avoid listing groups, teams, or departments as project owners; use only named individuals to meet accountability requirements.
Cross-reference each project owner with their contact details or personnel record to confirm identity and role.
properties.text: Project owner per row (named individual accountable for delivery + security)

guidance: Enter a planned closure date for each security action or issue listed in the Project Security Register.
Record the name of the person responsible for setting each planned closure date next to the corresponding entry.
Update the planned closure date if project timelines change, and keep a dated record of each revision.
Avoid leaving any row with a blank or placeholder date such as "TBD" or "ongoing"; every entry must have a specific planned closure date.
properties.text: Planned closure date per row (drives the closure-gate trigger)

guidance: List every in-scope project in the Project Security Register, assigning a unique identifier to each entry that does not repeat across projects.
Record the project name, start date, and responsible project manager alongside each unique identifier in the register.
Confirm that no project is described only as "miscellaneous," "various," or with generic terms that could apply to multiple projects.
Date each register entry when it is first created and update the date if project scope or status changes.
properties.text: Each in-scope project captured with a unique identifier

guidance: Cross-reference each project involving software development to its corresponding SDLC documentation, such as design reviews or testing results, in the Project Security Register.
Document the specific outputs from secure development (A.8.25) and secure coding (A.8.26) activities for each relevant project row.
Name the responsible individual for maintaining SDLC links in the register, not just a team or department.
Record the date when each SDLC link was last reviewed or updated in the register.
Attach or hyperlink the actual SDLC artefacts referenced, avoiding placeholder text like "see SDLC" without a working link or file.
properties.text: SDLC link per row where project involves software development (cross-ref to A.8.25 / A.8.26 outputs)

guidance: List each project in the Project Security Register with a unique name and identifier to avoid confusion between similarly named initiatives.
Record the current lifecycle stage for every project row, selecting only from the defined stages: initiation, requirements, build, pre-go-live, live, or closed.
Update the lifecycle stage in the register immediately after each project gate is formally passed, noting the date of the update.
Name the person responsible for updating each project’s stage, avoiding generic entries like "the team" or "IT department".
Retain evidence of formal gate approvals, such as signed meeting minutes or approval emails, and cross-reference these in the register.
properties.text: Current stage per row (initiation / requirements / build / pre-go-live / live / closed) updated as gates are passed

guidance: Cross-reference each project entry that results in a new third-party contract with the relevant supplier agreement, including agreement title and unique identifier.
Record the date when the supplier agreement was signed and the name of the individual who authorized the contract.
Link each project entry to the corresponding supplier risk assessment or due diligence record as required by A.5.20.
Name the responsible project owner as a specific individual for each register entry, not as a team or department.
Attach a copy or direct reference to the signed supplier agreement for every project that triggers a new third-party contract.
properties.text: Supplier-agreement link per row where project triggers new third-party contracts (cross-ref to A.5.20)

guidance: Assign a security tier to each project row in the register, using clear labels such as "full," "lightweight," or "waived-with-justification."
Record the date and name of the person who determined the security tier for each project entry.
Document the justification for any project marked as "waived-with-justification," including a brief risk assessment and approval reference.
Name the owner of the register as a specific individual, not a generic team or department.
Cross-reference each project’s security tier to the documented criteria or policy that defines the tiering process.
properties.text: Security tier per row (drives which gates apply — full / lightweight / waived-with-justification)

guidance: Identify and list all information security requirements, including both functional and non-functional needs, in the project plan or requirements document.
Reference relevant data protection obligations, such as personal data handling or retention, directly within the project documentation.
Assign a named project manager or security lead responsible for reviewing and confirming the inclusion of security requirements, with their name and date recorded.
Attach supporting evidence, such as a signed checklist or approval page, showing that security requirements were reviewed and agreed before project commencement.
Specify security requirements in detail; avoid using vague or generic statements that could apply to any project.
properties.text: Security requirements captured in project plan / requirements document (functional + non-functional, including data protection)

guidance: Record all action items from each project-security program review in a dated log, specifying the issue, required change, and responsible person.
Assign each action item to a named individual, not a group or generic role, to avoid unclear accountability.
Document the completion status and date for each action item, updating the log as progress is made or tasks are finished.
Retain meeting minutes or review summaries that clearly reference the captured action items and their linkage to program adjustments.
properties.text: Action items captured for the program (e.g. update templates, retrain PMs, tighten tiering criteria, add reviewer capacity)

guidance: Name a specific individual responsible for reviewing information security capacity against the project pipeline, avoiding generic titles like "the team" or "IT department".
Document the dates and outcomes of each periodic review in a register, including any identified gaps between capacity and project needs.
Record any instances where security review gates were missed or bypassed due to insufficient reviewer capacity, with explanations.
Assign follow-up actions to address capacity shortfalls, listing the responsible person and target completion date in meeting minutes or action logs.
Retain evidence of management decisions to adjust project timelines or resource allocations in response to review findings, such as signed approvals or updated project plans.
properties.text: InfoSec capacity vs project pipeline reviewed (gates fail silently when reviewer capacity is exhausted)

guidance: Record the date of the most recent project-security program review in a central log, specifying the exact day, month, and year.
Name the individual responsible for scheduling and conducting the review, avoiding generic titles like "the team" or "IT department."
Cross-reference the review date against the planned annual interval to confirm it falls within the required timeframe.
Retain a copy of the signed review report or meeting minutes that clearly show the review date and attendees.
properties.text: Review date within the planned annual interval

guidance: Record each project that bypassed a security gate in a dated log, including project name, gate skipped, and responsible project lead.
Document the root cause for each gate skip, referencing supporting communications or decision records where applicable.
Assign a specific individual to investigate and approve the documented root cause and proposed remediation for each gate skip.
Track completion of remediation actions with a dated entry and evidence of implementation, such as updated process documentation or training records.
Name the reviewer of the gate-skip analysis as a specific person, not a group or department, and capture their sign-off date.
properties.text: Gate-skip rate analysed (projects that bypassed gates; root cause and remediation per skip)

guidance: Document each security issue discovered after project go-live, including the date detected and a brief description of the issue.
Record an analysis for each late-detected issue explaining why it was not identified earlier in the project lifecycle.
Assign responsibility for the analysis to a named individual, not a team or department, to ensure clear accountability.
Review and update the project security program based on findings from late-detection analyses, noting changes and the date of each update.
properties.text: Late-detection analysis (security issues surfaced at or after go-live that should have been caught earlier)

guidance: Document the current project delivery methods in use, listing each as waterfall, agile, or hybrid, with supporting examples and dates.
Name a specific individual responsible for reviewing whether the existing gate model aligns with these delivery methods.
Record the date, participants, and outcome of the most recent methodology fit assessment in a signed meeting summary.
Attach evidence of any updates made to the gate model, such as revised process diagrams or approval emails, following the review.
Avoid using generic statements like "model fits all projects" without documented analysis or examples, as auditors will flag unsupported claims.
properties.text: Methodology check (does the gate model still fit the org's delivery mix — waterfall vs agile vs hybrid)

guidance: State the next planned review date in the project-security program review document, using a clear and specific calendar date.
Record who set the next review date by naming the responsible individual and including their job title.
Sign and date the review document to confirm when the next review date was established.
Name the owner as a specific individual — not a group, team, or department — responsible for scheduling the next review.
properties.text: Next planned review date stated

guidance: Name both the Information Security lead and the head of the PMO or project office as joint reviewers in the review documentation.
Record the full names, job titles, and signatures of both reviewers on each completed project-security program review form.
State the date the joint review was conducted on the review record to provide a clear timeline.
Avoid listing a group or department as reviewer; specify individual names to meet accountability requirements.
properties.text: Reviewer identity (InfoSec lead + PMO/project office head jointly)

guidance: Select a representative sample of current projects and record their names, owners, and assigned security tiers in a dated review log.
Re-assess each sampled project's tier using the documented tiering criteria, and record any changes or confirmations alongside the rationale and date.
Name the reviewer who conducted each re-tiering decision, ensuring the individual is specifically identified and not listed as a group or department.
Document any updates made to the tiering criteria as a result of the review, including the date and the approver’s name.
Retain evidence of the review meeting, such as signed minutes or an attendance record, showing discussion and agreement on tiering calibration.
properties.text: Tiering audit (sample of projects re-tiered to validate the tier criteria are still calibrated to actual risk)

guidance: Name a specific individual as the information security role in each project’s governance documents, avoiding generic titles like "the team" or "IT".
Document the responsibilities of the information security role, including advisory, review, and veto authority, in the project management procedure.
Record the date and version of the procedure where the information security role and responsibilities are defined.
Cross-reference the project governance documents with the procedure to show alignment of assigned information security responsibilities.
properties.text: Information security role defined in the project governance (advisor / reviewer / gate-owner with veto authority where warranted)

guidance: List all standard project templates used, including initiation pack, requirements template, and closure checklist, in the procedure with their current version numbers.
Reference specific security-related sections within each template, stating their section numbers or headings in the documented procedure.
Attach or link the actual templates to the procedure document, ensuring they are accessible and match the referenced versions.
Name the template owner as a specific individual responsible for updates, not a generic team or department.
Record the date the procedure was last reviewed and updated to reflect any changes in the templates.
properties.text: Standard project templates referenced (security sections in initiation pack, requirements template, closure checklist)

guidance: Define clear project tiering criteria based on data sensitivity, regulatory requirements, and third-party involvement in a dated procedure document.
Assign responsibility for project tiering decisions to a named individual, not a group or department.
Record each project’s assigned tier and the rationale in a project register, including the date and the person making the decision.
Review and update tiering criteria at least annually, documenting the review date and the reviewer’s name.
Avoid using generic or boilerplate criteria that do not reflect your organisation’s actual risk environment.
properties.text: Project tiering (which projects need full vs lightweight security review; criteria based on data sensitivity, regulatory scope, third-party exposure)

guidance: List all information assets, software, hardware, services, and cloud resources in a central inventory with unique names and descriptions for each item.
Assign a specific individual as the owner for every asset entry, avoiding generic terms like "IT" or "the team".
Record the date each asset was added or last updated in the inventory to show records are current.
Cross-reference each asset with supporting documentation, such as purchase orders, service agreements, or configuration files, to confirm its existence.
Review the inventory at least annually and keep a signed record of the review, noting any changes or confirmations.
properties.text: Asset records exist (information assets, software, hardware, services, cloud resources)

guidance: List each asset in the inventory with a unique identifier and a clearly assigned asset type: information, software, hardware, service, or facility.
Document the asset type for every entry in a dedicated column or field, ensuring the type is visible and unambiguous.
Name the asset owner as a specific individual, not a team or department, for each asset listed.
Review the inventory to confirm no asset is missing a type tag or has a generic or unclear category.
properties.text: Asset type tag (information / software / hardware / service / facility) so type-specific controls can be applied

guidance: List each information asset and its associated assets in a central inventory, including a unique identifier and asset description.
Assign a classification label to every asset in the inventory, referencing the organisation’s approved classification scheme from control A.5.12.
Record the name of the person responsible for each asset’s classification decision, ensuring it is a specific individual and not a group or department.
Date each classification entry in the inventory to show when the classification was last reviewed or updated.
Cross-reference each asset’s classification entry to the current version of the classification scheme, avoiding use of outdated or generic labels.
properties.text: Classification per asset (links to the A.5.12 classification scheme)

guidance: List each information asset and its associated assets in the inventory, clearly showing how they depend on or relate to each other.
Cross-reference each asset entry with relevant records in your risk register and network topology diagrams, using unique identifiers.
Name the owner of each asset as a specific individual, not a team or department, to avoid ambiguity in responsibility.
Record the date each relationship or dependency was last reviewed and updated in the inventory.
properties.text: Dependency or relationship to other assets (supports A.8.x topology and risk mapping)

guidance: Identify each asset in your information asset inventory that holds personal data, listing them individually with clear asset names.
Cross-reference each relevant asset entry to the corresponding record in your GDPR Article 30 data flow inventory, using a unique identifier or link.
Record the date and name of the person responsible for verifying the cross-link between the asset inventory and the GDPR data flow record.
Name the owner of each asset as a specific individual, not a generic role or team, to avoid ambiguity in accountability.
Document any assets reviewed that do not hold personal data, noting this explicitly to show completeness of the cross-linking process.
properties.text: Cross-link to GDPR Art.30 data flow inventory where the asset holds personal data

guidance: Cross-reference each asset discovery scan in your asset register to the relevant data leakage prevention or network mapping control where the scan serves both purposes.
Document the date and scope of each scan, clearly stating when it also fulfills requirements for A.8.12 or A.8.20.
Name the individual responsible for confirming that cross-links between asset discovery and related controls are kept up to date.
Avoid using generic statements like "see other controls"—specifically list the control numbers and scan dates in your records.
properties.text: Cross-link to A.8.12 (data leakage prevention) or A.8.20 (network mapping) where those scans double as discovery

guidance: Document the discovery frequency for each upstream asset source in a dated register, specifying if it is continuous, daily, or weekly.
Name the person responsible for monitoring each asset source’s discovery cadence, listing their full name and role in the register.
Record the last three completed discovery cycles for each source, including start and end timestamps, in an auditable log.
State the method used to verify that discovery is occurring as scheduled, such as automated reports or manual checks, and attach a sample verification record.
Avoid using generic terms like "as needed" or "periodically" for cadence; specify exact intervals for each source.
properties.text: Discovery cadence per source (continuous / daily / weekly)

guidance: Document a written procedure describing how asset coverage gaps are identified, evaluated, and addressed, including steps for procurement or mandatory registration.
Assign a named individual responsible for reviewing asset inventory reports and initiating gap closure actions, not a generic team or department.
Record each identified coverage gap, the chosen remediation method, and the date of closure in a central, version-controlled register.
Retain evidence of decisions to procure new tools or enforce registration, such as signed approval forms or meeting minutes with named approvers.
Review and update the gap closure process at least annually, noting the date and responsible person for each review cycle.
properties.text: Process for closing coverage gaps (procuring new tools, mandating registration in ungovernable zones)

guidance: Document the reconciliation process in a written procedure that describes how newly discovered assets are compared against the asset register.
Record each instance where an asset is discovered but not found in the register, including the date, asset details, and discovery source.
Assign a named individual to review flagged assets and update the register with owner assignment and classification within a defined timeframe.
Retain evidence of each completed reconciliation, such as a signed or timestamped log entry showing the asset was added and classified.
Name the asset owner as a specific person in the register—do not use generic roles or team names.
properties.text: Reconciliation rule — discovered-but-not-in-register entries are flagged for owner assignment and classification

guidance: List all asset discovery sources and specify which asset categories each one identifies, referencing a dated inventory or mapping document.
Document any asset categories not covered by current discovery sources, such as personal devices or operational technology, in a gap analysis record.
Name the person responsible for maintaining the coverage statement as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Review and update the coverage statement at least annually, recording the review date and the reviewer’s name.
properties.text: Coverage statement — what categories of assets each source covers and where gaps exist (e.g., personal devices, OT)

guidance: List each asset discovery source by name, such as network scan tool, cloud security posture management tool, endpoint inventory, procurement system, and license database.
Document the responsible owner for maintaining each discovery source as a named individual, not a group or department.
Record the date when each discovery source was last reviewed or updated in a central asset management register.
Attach supporting screenshots or export files from each discovery source to the register as evidence of current integration and use.
properties.text: Discovery sources enumerated (network scan tool, CSPM tool, EDR/MDM inventory, procurement system, license database)

guidance: Record a clear "last updated" date for each asset entry in the inventory to show when information was most recently reviewed or changed.
Name the person responsible for updating each asset record, listing a specific individual rather than a team or department.
Document any changes to asset details by updating the "last updated" date immediately after each modification.
Review the inventory regularly and update the "last updated" date for each asset even if no changes are needed, confirming ongoing maintenance.
properties.text: Last-updated date per record (proves the register is actively maintained, not snapshotted)

guidance: List every information asset and its current lifecycle status (such as active, retired, in-procurement, or in-disposal) in the asset inventory spreadsheet.
Assign a named individual as the owner responsible for updating each asset’s lifecycle status, avoiding generic labels like “IT” or “the team.”
Record the date each time an asset’s lifecycle status changes, creating an audit trail in the inventory.
Review the inventory quarterly and document the review date and reviewer’s name to confirm lifecycle statuses remain accurate.
properties.text: Lifecycle status per asset (active, retired, in-procurement, in-disposal)

guidance: Record the physical or virtual location for each asset in the inventory, specifying data centre address, cloud region, or endpoint pool name.
Cross-reference each asset entry with its corresponding hosting system or platform, using unique identifiers or URLs where applicable.
Name the asset owner as a specific individual responsible for the asset’s location details, not as a team or department.
Date each inventory update to show when the location or hosting system information was last verified or changed.
properties.text: Location or hosting system where the asset resides (data centre, cloud region, endpoint pool)

guidance: List each information asset and associated asset in an inventory, assigning a unique entry for every item.
Name the owner for each asset as a specific individual or clearly defined role responsible for protection and risk decisions.
Record the date when each owner assignment was last reviewed or updated in the inventory.
Avoid using vague terms like "the team" or "IT department" as owners; specify a person or formal role title for each asset.
Cross-reference the inventory with supporting documentation, such as job descriptions or appointment letters, to confirm the owner's accountability.
properties.text: Owner named per asset (individual or role accountable for protection and risk decisions)

guidance: Document the process for classifying assets at the point of creation, including who is responsible and how the classification is recorded.
Record each asset’s classification decision with the name of the person assigning the classification and the date it was set.
Update and re-document the asset’s classification whenever there is a material change, capturing the date and the person making the update.
Cross-reference the classification process in your procedure to the requirements set out in your Information Classification Policy under control A.5.12.
Name the asset classification owner as a specific individual, not as a team or department.
properties.text: Classification at creation and on material change (cross-link to A.5.12)

guidance: Document each cloud asset's creation method in the asset register, specifying whether it was provisioned via pipeline or manual process.
Configure infrastructure-as-code pipelines to automatically trigger asset registration, capturing asset owner, creation date, and unique identifier.
Require manual asset creators to submit a completed register entry before provisioning, including asset details and responsible individual.
Name the asset owner as a specific person in the register—do not use generic labels like "IT team" or "Cloud group".
Retain logs showing successful auto-registration events and manual register submissions for all new cloud assets.
properties.text: Cloud-provisioning hooks (IaC pipelines auto-register infra; manual creations require a register entry first)

guidance: Document the intake process by listing each step required to register a new asset before it is used in operations.
Assign a named individual responsible for verifying and recording each new asset in the asset register.
Record the registration date and asset details in the asset register, linking to procurement or build documentation.
Name the asset owner as a specific person, not a team or department, in the asset register entry.
Retain evidence of completed registration, such as a signed or digitally approved intake form for each asset.
properties.text: Intake path — every new asset (procured, built, granted) is registered before going operational

guidance: Name a specific individual as the maintainer of the asset register, listing their full name and job title in the procedure document.
Document the escalation path with named roles and contact details to follow when asset intake requests are not completed as expected.
Record the date the maintainer and escalation path were last reviewed or updated in the procedure.
Avoid listing the owner as "the team" or a department; always specify a single accountable person.
properties.text: Named maintainer of the register and escalation path when intake fails

guidance: Name the asset owner as a specific individual by full name and job title in the asset register, not as a team or department.
Document clear criteria for who can be assigned as an asset owner, including required role, authority, and responsibilities, in the procedure.
State the step-by-step process for transferring asset ownership when someone changes roles or leaves, including required approvals and documentation.
Record the date and details of each ownership transfer in the asset register, including both outgoing and incoming owners.
properties.text: Ownership assignment rules (who can be an owner, transfer process on role change)

guidance: Record the retirement date and reason for each asset in the asset register, marking its status as "retired" with a named individual responsible.
Document the disposal method for each retired asset, referencing compliance with secure disposal procedures outlined in A.7.14 and A.8.10.
Archive the asset’s register row with a timestamp and the name of the person authorizing the retirement and disposal.
Name the asset owner and disposal approver as specific individuals, not generic roles or teams, in the archived record.
properties.text: Retirement and disposal handoff (status set to retired, disposal handled per A.7.14/A.8.10, register row archived)

guidance: Document the process for identifying unregistered assets during regular network or inventory scans, including the tools and scan frequency, in the procedure.
Assign a named individual or role responsible for investigating and deciding the action for each unregistered asset found.
Record each unregistered asset discovery, the action taken (blocked, registered, or removed), and the date in an asset management log.
Name the decision and action taken for each asset with a specific person’s approval, not just a generic team or department.
Retain evidence of asset registration or removal, such as screenshots or system logs, linked to the corresponding asset management log entry.
properties.text: Shadow-IT handling — unregistered assets discovered in scans are blocked, registered, or removed

guidance: Name a responsible individual to conduct the classification sampling check, avoiding generic roles like "IT team" or "Asset Manager."
Document the sample selection method and list of assets reviewed, including asset IDs and last known classification.
Record the actual use of each sampled asset and compare it to the assigned classification under A.5.12.
Note any discrepancies found and log the date, reviewer, and corrective action taken for each mismatch.
Retain evidence of the completed sampling check, such as annotated inventory reports or signed review summaries, for audit reference.
properties.text: Classification sampling check — are A.5.12 classifications still appropriate for the asset's actual use

guidance: Record the date of each asset inventory reconciliation in a central log, showing the interval since the previous reconciliation.
Name the person responsible for performing and signing off each reconciliation, using their full name rather than a generic role or team.
Cross-reference the reconciliation log entry with the corresponding asset inventory report to confirm the review covered all listed assets.
Retain evidence of the planned reconciliation schedule, showing that actual reconciliation dates do not exceed the 90-day interval.
properties.text: Reconciliation date within the planned interval (typically within 90 days of last reconciliation)

guidance: Record the next planned asset inventory reconciliation date in the asset management log, including the day, month, and year.
Name the person responsible for conducting the next reconciliation, listing a specific individual rather than a team or department.
Document the date this next reconciliation schedule was last reviewed or updated, and keep a copy of the review record.
Cross-reference the scheduled reconciliation date with your organisation’s calendar or meeting system to confirm it is booked.
properties.text: Next planned reconciliation date stated

guidance: Record the results of each asset discovery source in a dated log, listing all assets identified during each reconciliation period.
Cross-reference each discovery source's asset list with the current asset register, clearly marking additions, removals, and mismatches.
Document the specific actions taken to resolve each discrepancy, including who resolved it and the completion date.
Name the person responsible for reviewing and approving the reconciliation results — do not use a group or team name.
Retain signed or digitally approved records of each completed reconciliation cycle, including evidence of review and resolution.
properties.text: Per-source delta — what each discovery source surfaced vs what the register held (additions, removals, mismatches)

guidance: Record the date the asset inventory reconciliation was completed in the asset register, referencing the specific review period.
Update the asset register to reflect any additions, removals, or changes identified during the reconciliation, with clear descriptions.
Name the person responsible for updating the register as a specific individual, not a generic role or team.
Attach or link the reconciliation report or summary directly to the updated asset register entry for traceability.
Retain evidence of management review or approval of the updated asset register, such as a signed or timestamped record.
properties.text: Register updated as a result of the reconciliation with reference to this review

guidance: Record the full name of the individual who completed the asset inventory reconciliation in the reconciliation log or report.
Specify the reviewer’s job title or role alongside their name in the same reconciliation documentation.
Capture the date the reconciliation was performed and reviewed to provide a clear audit trail.
Avoid listing a group or department as the reviewer; always identify a single, accountable person.
properties.text: Reviewer identity and role recorded

guidance: Review the asset inventory and identify any assets without a named owner listed in the owner column.
Assign a specific individual as the owner for each unassigned asset, recording their full name and assignment date in the inventory.
Retire or remove any asset entries that cannot be assigned to a responsible owner, documenting the reason and date of removal.
Avoid listing the owner as "the team", "IT", or any non-specific group; use only named individuals for ownership records.
Retain a dated record of each reconciliation activity, including who performed the review and any changes made to asset ownership.
properties.text: Treatment of unassigned-owner rows (owner assignment forced or row retired)

guidance: List each type of background check required for all roles, including identity, employment history, education, criminal record, financial, and sanctions/PEP where relevant.
Specify which roles require each type of check, linking the check type to the job title or function in a documented table.
Reference applicable laws or regulations that limit or require specific checks, and note any exceptions with a dated explanation.
Name the procedure owner as a specific individual, not a team or department, in the procedure document.
Record the approval date and the approver’s name on the latest version of the personnel screening procedure.
properties.text: Types of checks defined (identity, employment history, education, criminal record where lawful, financial where role-relevant, sanctions/PEP for finance-sector roles)

guidance: Name the decision authority for screening outcomes as specific individuals by role, such as Hiring Manager, HR Manager, and Information Security Lead.
Document the acceptance or rejection decision for each candidate in a dated record, signed or acknowledged by the named authority.
State the escalation process for disputed screening outcomes, including who is responsible for final resolution and how this is recorded.
Avoid listing generic groups like "the team" or "HR department" as decision-makers; use named roles or individuals only.
properties.text: Decision authority named (who accepts or rejects screening outcomes — typically Hiring Manager + HR + InfoSec for sensitive roles)

guidance: Identify and list all jurisdictions where personnel screening occurs, including countries of employment and data processing, in a dated procedure document.
Document the specific legal and regulatory requirements for personnel screening in each jurisdiction, citing relevant laws or regulations by name and section.
State the consent and transparency obligations under GDPR or equivalent laws, and attach a copy of the consent form used for EU/UK hires.
Name the procedure owner as a specific individual, not a department or generic title, in the procedure document.
Attach a legal review or sign-off confirming that all screening activities described comply with local laws in each jurisdiction.
properties.text: Legal, regulatory, and ethical constraints applied per jurisdiction (some checks unlawful or restricted in EU/UK; consent + transparency obligations under GDPR)

guidance: Name a specific individual in HR as the operational owner of the personnel screening procedure in the document header.
Name a specific individual in Information Security as the owner responsible for setting and updating risk-tier criteria in the procedure.
Record the date and version number on the procedure to show when ownership was last reviewed or updated.
Avoid listing "HR department" or "InfoSec team" as owners; use named individuals with current job titles.
properties.text: Named owner of the screening procedure (HR + InfoSec jointly; HR runs operationally, InfoSec sets risk-tier criteria)

guidance: State in the procedure how screening requirements differ by job role, information classification accessed, and risk level, with clear examples for each.
Document the criteria and rationale used to determine screening depth for at least three distinct roles, such as junior staff, administrators, and senior management.
Name the person or role responsible for reviewing and updating screening criteria, ensuring it is not listed as "HR" or "the team."
Retain dated records showing when the proportionality criteria were last reviewed and approved by a named decision-maker.
properties.text: Proportionality stated by role, information classification accessed, and perceived risk (junior office role vs admin vs CISO — different check depth)

guidance: Name the authoriser for each candidate screening record as a specific individual, not a group or department.
Record the date the accept or reject decision was made for each candidate entry in the register.
Document the decision outcome (accept or reject) alongside the authoriser's name and date for every candidate.
Retain evidence of the authoriser’s decision, such as a signed or digitally approved record, for each candidate screening entry.
properties.text: Authoriser per record (named individual making the accept/reject decision)

guidance: Assign each candidate a unique, anonymised identifier in the screening record register before hire, avoiding use of names or personal details.
Cross-reference the candidate identifier with the identity register entry under control A.5.16 once the candidate is hired, ensuring traceability.
Document the date each identifier is assigned and linked, creating a clear audit trail for every candidate record.
Avoid using generic or duplicate identifiers; each must be unique to a single candidate and not reused.
properties.text: Per-record candidate identifier (links to identity register A.5.16 once hired; anonymised pre-hire to comply with data minimisation)

guidance: Record the full name of each candidate alongside the job role and date the screening was initiated in the register.
List the specific verification checks completed for each candidate, such as identity, employment history, education, criminal, financial, and sanctions.
Attach or reference dated evidence for each completed check, such as certificates, reports, or confirmation emails, within the register entry.
Name the individual who performed and confirmed each check, avoiding generic entries like "HR team" or "recruitment".
Note any incomplete or failed checks with an explanation and a dated decision on whether to proceed, signed by the hiring manager.
properties.text: Checks performed per record (identity / employment-history / education / criminal / financial / sanctions — actual checks run, not just planned)

guidance: Record the exact date when the screening decision was made for each candidate in the register.
State the name of the individual who approved the screening decision for each candidate.
Cross-reference each candidate’s access start date to confirm it is after the screening decision date.
Avoid leaving the decision date field blank or using placeholders like "TBD" or "upon hire" in the register.
properties.text: Decision date per record (proves the screening completed BEFORE access was granted per A.5.18)

guidance: Record the screening outcome for each candidate as "cleared", "cleared-with-conditions", "blocked", or "superseded by waiver" in the register.
Name the individual who made the screening decision for each candidate, not just a department or team.
Enter the date the screening decision was finalized for each candidate in the register.
Attach or cross-reference any waiver documentation for candidates marked as "superseded by waiver".
properties.text: Outcome per record (cleared / cleared-with-conditions / blocked / superseded by waiver)

guidance: Record the full legal name of the third-party screening provider for each candidate entry where such a provider was used.
Document the date the third-party provider was engaged for each candidate, matching it to the relevant screening record.
Cross-reference each candidate’s screening record with the corresponding contract or agreement with the third-party provider.
Name the third-party provider specifically for each record—do not use generic terms like "external agency" or "screening partner".
properties.text: Third-party provider reference per record where used

guidance: Record the most recent rescreening date for each candidate in the register, using a clear date format such as YYYY-MM-DD.
Name the individual responsible for updating each candidate’s rescreening status, listing their full name rather than a generic title.
Cross-reference each rescreening entry with supporting documentation, such as a signed rescreening confirmation or background check report.
Confirm that all roles requiring ongoing checks have a non-blank, current rescreening date; do not leave fields empty or marked "N/A" for these roles.
properties.text: Last rescreen date per record (for roles with ongoing-check obligations)

guidance: Assign a specific role tier to each candidate record in the register, using clear categories like junior, standard, sensitive, or privileged.
Document the name of the person who determined the role tier and the date the decision was made for each candidate.
Cross-reference the assigned role tier with the documented screening depth applied, showing that proportional checks were performed.
Avoid using vague or generic role tier labels such as "various" or "N/A"; always specify the exact tier for each record.
properties.text: Role tier per record (drives the proportional check-depth applied; junior / standard / sensitive / privileged)

guidance: List all re-screening triggers in the Personnel Screening Procedure, including significant role change, escalated access, and security incidents involving the individual.
Document the date each trigger was last reviewed and updated, showing ongoing attention to changes in risk or organisational context.
Name the person responsible for initiating re-screening, ensuring this is a specific individual rather than a team or department.
Record examples of completed re-screenings, including the trigger event, date, and outcome, in a central log.
properties.text: Re-screening triggers (significant role change, escalated access from A.5.18, security incident involving the individual)

guidance: State the specific retention period for both positive and negative screening results, referencing the relevant law or regulation that applies.
Document the legal or regulatory source that requires longer retention for certain roles, such as financial or regulated positions.
Assign responsibility for reviewing and updating retention rules to a named individual, not a generic team or department.
Record the date when the retention rules were last reviewed and updated, including the reviewer’s name.
Retain evidence that screening results are deleted or anonymized after the retention period expires, such as a log or deletion confirmation.
properties.text: Retention rules for screening results (often short retention for negative results to comply with GDPR; longer where law mandates — financial roles)

guidance: List specific ad-hoc review triggers in the screening program document, including regulator enforcement actions and security incidents involving inadequately-screened personnel.
Document the date and details of the most recent ad-hoc review, including what triggered the review and who conducted it.
Name the responsible individual who approves updates to the screening program after each ad-hoc review, not just a department or team.
Retain evidence of communications or meeting minutes where ad-hoc review triggers and outcomes were discussed and agreed upon.
properties.text: Ad-hoc review triggers listed (regulator enforcement action in sector, security incident involving inadequately-screened personnel)

guidance: Record the most recent review date of the screening program in a dated log or review register.
Document the planned review interval for the screening program, referencing the approved policy or management decision.
Confirm the next scheduled review date is within the documented interval by cross-referencing the last review date and the interval.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual, not a team or department, in the review record.
Retain evidence of management acknowledgment or sign-off on the review schedule, such as a dated email or signed meeting minutes.
properties.text: Review date within the planned interval

guidance: State the next planned review date for the periodic screening program in the official review schedule document.
Record the date in a version-controlled document or register that tracks all review cycles for the screening program.
Name the individual responsible for confirming the next review date, avoiding generic titles like "HR" or "the team".
Retain evidence of the last review meeting where the next date was agreed, such as meeting minutes or an email confirmation.
properties.text: Next planned review date stated

guidance: Document the list of all new hires in the relevant tier for the review period, including their names, start dates, and roles.
Record the specific screening checks completed for each new hire, with check dates and the responsible staff member named.
Identify and log any gaps where required checks were missed or incomplete, including a description and date discovered.
Assign remediation actions for each gap to a named individual, and record the completion date for each action taken.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual who signs and dates the final review outcome—avoid leaving the reviewer field blank or using a generic title.
properties.text: Per-tier outcome (did every new hire in this tier get the right checks? gaps flagged and remediated)

guidance: Record the date and findings of the most recent periodic screening program review in a version-controlled document.
Update the screening procedure or scope to reflect any approved changes, referencing the specific review by date and summary.
Assign a named individual to approve and sign off on all updates made as a result of the review.
Cross-reference the updated procedure or scope with the review record to demonstrate that changes were directly linked to review outcomes.
Name the owner as a specific individual—do not use generic titles like "HR team" or "Compliance department".
properties.text: Changes propagated back to the procedure / scope with reference to this review

guidance: Identify all roles with ongoing background check requirements and list them in a dated register maintained by HR or compliance.
Record the completion date of each periodic screening for individuals in these roles in a centralized tracking log.
Calculate and document the percentage of required screenings completed on schedule versus those overdue, updating this metric at least quarterly.
Name a specific individual responsible for monitoring and reporting screening status—avoid assigning this responsibility to a team or department.
Retain evidence of follow-up actions taken for any overdue screenings, including communications and escalation steps, in an auditable folder.
properties.text: Rescreen status — for roles with ongoing-check obligations, what fraction completed on cadence vs aged-overdue

guidance: Record the full names and job titles of both the HR lead and InfoSec lead who jointly reviewed the screening program in the review log.
Obtain a dated signature or written approval from legal counsel when the review involves material changes to jurisdictional requirements.
Attach the documented review outcomes to the official screening program file, clearly referencing the reviewers and legal counsel sign-off where applicable.
Name each reviewer as a specific individual; do not use group names such as "HR team" or "Security department".
properties.text: Reviewer identity and role recorded (HR lead + InfoSec lead jointly; legal-counsel sign-off where jurisdictional shifts material)

guidance: Cross-reference the list of roles included in the latest screening program review with your current HR role inventory, noting any new or changed roles.
Document any new jurisdictions or sector-specific regulations that have come into scope since the last review, citing the relevant legal or regulatory source.
Record the date and outcome of the most recent screening program review, including who conducted the cross-check and their findings.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual responsible for the cross-check, not a group or generic title.
Attach supporting evidence, such as meeting minutes or annotated role matrices, showing how changes were identified and addressed.
properties.text: Cross-check against the applicable-roles scope — any new role tier, new jurisdiction, new sectoral driver?

guidance: Cross-reference the roles and check-depth scope document to the specific entry in the A.5.31 legal and regulatory obligations register.
State the jurisdictional and sectoral check requirements in the roles and check-depth scope, citing the relevant register entry by name and date.
Name the owner of the roles and check-depth scope as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Record the date when the cross-link to the legal/regulatory register was last reviewed or updated in the roles and check-depth scope document.
properties.text: Cross-link to A.5.31 legal/regulatory register — jurisdictional and sectoral check requirements should be sourced from the single legal-obligations register

guidance: List all events that require a re-scoping review, such as entering a new country, sector, or responding to regulator changes, in a dated document.
Assign a named individual to monitor for these trigger events and record their name and role in the document.
State the review frequency for the trigger list and record the last review date and reviewer’s name.
Name the owner as a specific person, not a team or department, to avoid ambiguity in responsibility.
Retain evidence of communication of the trigger list to all relevant stakeholders, such as an email or meeting minutes.
properties.text: Trigger list for re-scoping (new geography, new sector entry, new regulator action affecting screening)

guidance: Name each role tier and check type in a matrix, using clear and specific titles that match your organisation's terminology.
Document which check types apply to each role tier by marking the corresponding cells in the matrix with a clear indicator, such as a tick or "Yes".
Assign a named individual as the owner of the matrix, listing their full name and job title in the document header.
Record the date the matrix was last reviewed and approved, and include the approver’s name and signature.
Avoid using generic role descriptions like "staff" or "IT team" in the matrix; specify actual role titles to prevent ambiguity.
properties.text: Check matrix — which check types apply to which role tier (matrix is the spec; rows show consistency)

guidance: List all jurisdictions where background checks are conducted, including countries, states, or regions, in a dated register.
Document specific legal or regulatory constraints for each jurisdiction that impact the depth or type of checks performed.
Name the individual responsible for maintaining the jurisdictional register, ensuring they are identified by full name and job title.
Record any jurisdictions where checks are not performed or are limited, along with the reason and relevant legal reference.
Avoid using generic statements like "all applicable laws"—specify the actual laws or regulations for each jurisdiction in the register.
properties.text: Jurisdictions covered (where checks happen — local legal constraints apply; some checks unavailable in some jurisdictions)

guidance: List all roles in your organisation, grouping them into the required tiers: junior office, standard, sensitive, privileged, and executive.
Document the criteria used to assign each role to its tier, including examples of access or responsibilities for each.
Name the owner responsible for maintaining and updating the role tier definitions as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Record the date when the role tier definitions were last reviewed and approved by management.
Cross-reference each role tier to the relevant access controls or systems in your access management register.
properties.text: Role tiers defined (junior office, standard, sensitive [access to special-category PII or financial systems], privileged [admin / production access], executive)

guidance: List all roles with access to sensitive data, specifying the sectoral regulations that apply to each role, such as PCI, HIPAA, or financial sanctions.
Document the legal and regulatory requirements for each role in a table, including the relevant law or standard and the check-depth required.
Name the owner responsible for maintaining this mapping as a specific individual, not a group or department.
Attach dated evidence showing when the sectoral requirements were last reviewed and updated for each role.
Cross-reference each role’s regulatory obligations to supporting policies or procedures, ensuring the links are current and not generic boilerplate.

guidance: Name all groups included in the programme’s audience, listing employees, contractors, and third parties with access in a dated document.
Document the scope of the training programme, specifying which information security topics and activities are covered in a formal statement.
