Assign a specific individual as the owner responsible for maintaining the audience and scope list, avoiding generic titles like "the team" or "HR".
Record the approval of the defined scope and audience by a named senior manager, including the date of approval.
properties.text: Scope and audience defined (all personnel + relevant interested parties such as contractors, third parties with access)

guidance: List all audience segments by specific role or function, such as developers, admins, finance, HR, executives, contractors, and board members, in a dated document.
Name the person responsible for maintaining the audience list as a specific individual, not a group or department.
Cross-reference each audience segment to the relevant training curriculum or materials in a curriculum mapping table.
Record the date when the audience list was last reviewed and updated, and retain the reviewer’s name.
properties.text: Audience segments enumerated (all-staff baseline, role-specific tiers — developers, admins, finance, HR, executives, contractors, board)

guidance: List specific events that require re-scoping of training, such as new roles, new compliance obligations, or adoption of new technologies.
Document the date each trigger was last reviewed or updated, and name the person responsible for maintaining the trigger list.
Name the owner as a specific individual, not a team or department, to avoid ambiguity about accountability.
Cross-reference each trigger to relevant training materials or curriculum updates, showing how changes are incorporated.
Retain a signed record of management approval for the current trigger list and curriculum scope.
properties.text: Trigger list for re-scoping (new role/function, new compliance regime, new technology adoption requiring training)

guidance: List every training module delivered, including baseline awareness, role-specific sessions, and special topics such as data protection, secure coding, fraud, and PII handling.
Document the intended audience for each module, specifying roles or departments rather than using generic terms like "all staff" or "the team."
Record the date each module was last updated and the person responsible for maintaining its content.
Cross-reference each module to its relevant compliance requirement or business need in the catalogue.
Retain a signed approval from a designated authority confirming the accuracy and completeness of the current module catalogue.
properties.text: Module catalogue stated (every training module the org delivers — baseline awareness, role-specific deep dives, special topics — DPbD, secure coding, fraud, PII handling)

guidance: List all job roles or audience segments that require security awareness or training, using specific titles rather than generic groupings.
Map each training module to the relevant job roles in a matrix, showing which roles are assigned which modules.
Document the rationale for each mapping, explaining why each module is required for each role based on job responsibilities.
Record the date the matrix was last updated and the name of the person who approved the current version.
Name the owner of the matrix as a specific individual, not a team or department.
properties.text: Role-to-module matrix (which audience segment receives which modules — drives the completion-register expected-set)

guidance: Identify all staff roles that handle personal data, payment card data, or healthcare data, listing named individuals and their assigned compliance regimes.
Document the curriculum for each special-topic module, clearly linking content to the relevant compliance regime (GDPR, PCI DSS, HIPAA).
Record completion dates and participant names for each special-topic training session, keeping attendance logs for each compliance regime.
Name the training module owner as a specific individual responsible for content accuracy and updates, not as a team or department.
Retain copies of training materials and attendance records for each compliance regime, dated and version-controlled.
properties.text: Special-topic modules tied to specific compliance regimes (GDPR for PII handlers, PCI for payment-card handlers, HIPAA for healthcare)

guidance: Identify all third-party roles, such as contractors and visitors, who require access to your premises or systems, and list them in a dated register.
Document the specific awareness topics or onboarding briefing content provided to each third-party role, referencing the curriculum or summary materials.
Record the date and method of delivery for each third-party awareness session, linking attendance records to named individuals.
Name the responsible staff member who approves third-party access after confirming completion of the required briefing—avoid generic titles like "HR" or "Security Team".
Retain signed or acknowledged records from third parties confirming receipt and understanding of the awareness briefing.
properties.text: Third-party audience handling (where contractors/visitors with access need awareness — typically a lighter onboarding briefing rather than full curriculum)

guidance: Record each employee’s full name, training module completed, and completion date in a central training register.
Retain copies of completion certificates or digital confirmations for each training session, linked to the individual’s training record.
Update the training register immediately after each session; do not rely on memory or informal lists.
Name the training register owner as a specific individual responsible for its accuracy and updates.
properties.text: Training records maintained (who completed what, when) for audit and the completion register leaf

guidance: Cross-reference each disciplinary case in the disciplinary process log with its corresponding entry in the compliance nonconformity register, using a unique case identifier.
Document the date and outcome of each disciplinary case in both the disciplinary log and the nonconformity register to ensure records match.
Name the person responsible for maintaining the cross-link between the disciplinary process log and the nonconformity register, listing a specific individual.
Attach supporting evidence, such as investigation reports or decision letters, to both records for each disciplinary case tracked.
properties.text: Cross-link to A.5.36 compliance nonconformity register — disciplinary cases are a particular type of compliance NC and should be tracked in concert

guidance: List each possible disciplinary action in the written process, including verbal warning, written warning, suspension, termination, legal referral, and regulator notification.
Document the criteria and escalation steps for when each type of disciplinary action may be applied, with clear examples.
Name the person or role responsible for deciding and recording disciplinary actions as a specific individual, not just a department or "the team."
Date and approve the disciplinary process document with a signature from a senior manager or HR lead.
properties.text: Range of actions defined (verbal warning, written warning, suspension, termination, legal referral, regulator notification where mandatory)

guidance: Document a formal appeals or review process in the disciplinary policy, including clear steps for how an employee can challenge a decision.
Name the individual or committee responsible for handling appeals, specifying their role and contact details in the documented process.
Record the date the appeals process was last reviewed and approved by senior management, attaching the signed approval.
State the maximum timeframe within which appeals must be lodged and resolved, and include this in the written process.
Avoid describing the appeals reviewer as "management" or "the team"—identify a specific person or defined panel by name or title.
properties.text: Appeals or review process

guidance: Document the disciplinary process in a formal policy that is version-controlled and includes the approval date and approver’s name.
Publish the disciplinary process in accessible locations, such as the intranet, employee handbook, and onboarding materials, with clear publication dates.
Record evidence that all current personnel have been notified of the disciplinary process, such as signed acknowledgements or digital read receipts.
Name the policy owner as a specific individual, not a department or generic role, to avoid ambiguity in responsibility.
Retain training records or attendance logs showing the disciplinary process was covered in awareness sessions, including session dates and trainer names.
properties.text: Communicated to personnel and interested parties (in employment contract, code of conduct, intranet, awareness training)

guidance: Document each disciplinary case with a written summary that explicitly lists intent, recurrence, impact, and the person’s security training completion status.
Name the individual who assessed contributory factors for each case, avoiding group or department-level attribution.
Record the date and outcome of the awareness training the person received before the incident, attaching relevant training logs.
State in the disciplinary decision file how each contributory factor influenced the chosen action or sanction.
Retain evidence that each case was reviewed for proportionality, such as a signed statement or checklist completed by the decision-maker.
properties.text: Consideration of contributory factors (intent, recurrence, impact, awareness training status — was the person trained on what they breached?)

guidance: Name the decision authority for disciplinary actions as specific individuals from HR, line management, and Legal, not just departments or teams.
Document the escalation process for disciplinary decisions involving senior personnel, specifying which executive roles are responsible for final approval.
Record the date and signatures of all authorities involved in each disciplinary decision to provide a clear audit trail.
Cross-reference the disciplinary process document with your organisational chart to show that named authorities hold appropriate roles.
properties.text: Decision authority named (HR + line management + Legal as appropriate; escalation to executive for senior personnel)

guidance: Document the disciplinary process in a written policy that clearly outlines steps, potential outcomes, and criteria for information security breaches.
Name the policy owner as a specific individual, not a department or team, to ensure clear accountability.
Record the date and names of HR and Legal representatives who reviewed and approved the policy before implementation.
Retain evidence of communication to all staff, such as a dated email or intranet announcement, confirming the policy’s distribution.
Review and update the policy at least annually, recording the review date and approver’s name each time.
properties.text: Formalised in writing with HR + Legal review (drives consistent application; ad-hoc disciplinary action is a fairness / employment-tribunal risk)

guidance: Document the investigation process in a written procedure, including steps for gathering facts and evidence before any disciplinary action is considered.
Name the decision-maker responsible for conducting the investigation as a specific individual, not a group or department.
Record that the individual involved was given an opportunity to explain their actions, with date and summary of their response.
Retain signed and dated records of the investigation outcome and any disciplinary decision, showing the process was followed as documented.
properties.text: Investigation step before action, with right of explanation (procedural fairness — drives employment-tribunal defensibility)

guidance: Name a specific individual in HR as the primary owner of the disciplinary process, listing their full name and job title in the document.
Assign a named partner from the Information Security team, including their full name and job title, as co-owner in the procedure.
Document the date of last review and approval by both the HR owner and InfoSec partner, capturing their signatures or digital approvals.
Avoid listing the owner as "HR department," "the team," or any generic group—use only named individuals to meet accountability requirements.
properties.text: Named owner of the procedure (HR with InfoSec partner)

guidance: Record the specific action taken for each disciplinary case in the register, matching the action to one of the defined action_range categories.
State "no action" as the outcome in the register if the investigation did not substantiate the case, rather than leaving the field blank.
Name the person who approved the action taken for each case, ensuring a specific individual is listed and not a generic role or team.
Date each entry in the register to show when the action was decided and implemented.
Cross-reference each case entry with supporting documentation, such as investigation reports or decision memos, to confirm the action taken.
properties.text: Per-case action taken (matches the action_range categories; 'no action' is a valid outcome where investigation didn't substantiate)

guidance: Record the date each appeal is lodged in the disciplinary case register, along with the name of the person submitting the appeal.
Track and update the status of each appeal in the register, noting key milestones such as review, decision, and closure dates.
Assign a specific individual to oversee and update the appeals log, avoiding generic roles like "HR team" or "management."
Document the final outcome of each appeal, including the decision and the name of the person or panel responsible for the resolution.
properties.text: Per-case appeals log (where appeal was lodged; status tracked)

guidance: Assign a unique case identifier to each disciplinary case in the register, ensuring no two cases share the same identifier.
Record the mapping between each case identifier and the relevant personnel record in a secure, access-controlled location.
Document the process for generating and managing case identifiers, including how external anonymisation is maintained.
Name a specific individual responsible for maintaining the identifier mapping, avoiding generic roles like "HR team" or "management".
Confirm that no personally identifiable information appears alongside case identifiers in any externally shared reports or summaries.
properties.text: Per-case unique identifier (anonymised externally; internal traceability to personnel record preserved)

guidance: Record the closure date for each disciplinary case in the register as soon as the case is formally concluded.
Name the person responsible for entering and verifying the closure date for each case in the register.
Retain supporting documentation that confirms the closure decision and matches the recorded closure date for each case.
Avoid leaving the closure date field blank or using placeholders like "TBD" or "N/A"—enter a specific, actual date for every closed case.
properties.text: Per-case closure date

guidance: Name the decision authority for each disciplinary case as a specific individual, not as a generic role or team.
Record the decision authority’s full name and job title in the register entry for each disciplinary case.
Document the date on which the decision authority was assigned for each case in the register.
Retain evidence of the decision authority’s approval or signature for each disciplinary case outcome in the register.
properties.text: Per-case decision authority (named role)

guidance: Record the investigation outcome for each disciplinary case as "substantiated," "not-substantiated," or "partially-substantiated" in the register, with the case reference number.
Name the individual who determined the investigation outcome, ensuring a specific person is listed rather than a team or department.
Date the entry for each investigation outcome to show when the decision was finalized.
Retain supporting evidence or documentation for each outcome, such as investigation reports or meeting notes, linked to the corresponding case entry.
properties.text: Per-case investigation outcome (substantiated / not-substantiated / partially-substantiated)

guidance: Record each disciplinary case where a control gap was identified, including a brief description of the gap and the date it was discovered.
Name the specific control owner notified about the gap, including the date and method of communication.
Document the lesson learned and any recommended changes or updates to the relevant control or awareness training.
Attach evidence of follow-up actions taken, such as updated procedures, revised training materials, or meeting minutes confirming discussion of the lesson.
Name the individual responsible for reviewing and closing each lesson learned entry—avoid leaving this field blank or assigning it to a generic group.
properties.text: Per-case lessons feed (where the violation surfaced a control gap, feeds back to relevant control owner / awareness curriculum)

guidance: Cross-reference each disciplinary case entry with the violation categories listed in your official disciplinary procedure to ensure alignment.
Record the specific violation type for every case in the register, using the exact wording from your procedure’s violation_scope section.
Document the date and name of the person assigning the violation type for each case entry.
Name the violation type for each case individually—do not use generic terms like "other" or leave the field blank.
properties.text: Per-case violation type (matches the procedure's violation_scope categories)

guidance: Document each ad-hoc review trigger, such as tribunal rulings, regulator actions, or major personnel incidents, in a dated review log.
Name the individual responsible for monitoring and initiating reviews when a trigger event occurs, specifying their full name and job title.
Record the date, reason, and summary of each ad-hoc review decision in meeting minutes or an official change log.
Attach supporting evidence, such as tribunal decisions or regulator notices, to the review documentation for each triggered event.
Avoid listing generic triggers; describe each trigger with enough detail to show it is specific to your organisation’s disciplinary process.
properties.text: Ad-hoc review triggers (employment tribunal ruling affecting the process, regulator enforcement action, major incident with personnel involvement)

guidance: Assign a named individual or committee to conduct the consistency analysis of disciplinary case outcomes, recording their names and roles in a dated document.
Document the review process, including the specific cases and demographic data compared, in a table or report with clear references to each case file.
Record the analysis findings, highlighting any patterns or inconsistencies identified, and include recommendations for addressing any issues found.
Sign and date the final review report, ensuring it is approved by a designated senior manager or compliance officer.
Avoid using generic summaries or omitting demographic data, as auditors will flag missing or vague evidence of consistency checks.
properties.text: Consistency analysis — case outcomes reviewed for consistent application across cases / demographics (avoids discriminatory enforcement patterns)

guidance: Record the most recent review date of the disciplinary process in a central log, showing it falls within the planned review interval.
Name the individual responsible for conducting the review, listing their full name and job title in the review documentation.
Attach a signed or approved summary of the review findings, including any updates or confirmation that no changes were needed.
Specify the next planned review date in the same log, ensuring it aligns with the documented review interval.
Avoid leaving the review owner field blank or listing a group; always identify a single accountable person.
properties.text: Review date within the planned interval

guidance: Assign a named legal counsel to review the disciplinary process for compliance with current employment laws in each relevant jurisdiction.
Document the date, jurisdiction, and summary of legal counsel’s findings in a formal review record.
Record any required updates or changes to the disciplinary process, citing the specific legal advice or law that prompted each change.
Retain written confirmation from legal counsel that the review addressed all applicable jurisdictions, not just the primary business location.
Name the legal counsel as a specific individual in the review record — do not list only a law firm or generic title.
properties.text: Employment-law drift check per jurisdiction (legal counsel input)

guidance: Document each disciplinary case review outcome, including any lessons learned, in a dated record signed by the review lead.
Cross-reference each lesson learned to specific updates in the awareness training curriculum, control procedures, or policy documents, noting the change date.
Assign responsibility for implementing each lesson to a named individual, not a group or department.
Retain evidence of communication, such as emails or meeting minutes, showing that updates were shared with relevant staff.
Record a periodic review meeting, with attendees and date, confirming that all recent lessons have been considered for process or policy improvements.
properties.text: Lessons-propagation check — did case-driven lessons feed back to awareness curriculum (A.6.3), control updates, or policy amendments?

guidance: State the next planned review date for the disciplinary process in the documented review schedule.
Record the date in a version-controlled document, such as the disciplinary process policy or review log.
Name the responsible individual who set the next review date, ensuring a specific person is listed rather than a role or team.
Retain evidence of management approval for the scheduled review date, such as a signed or emailed confirmation.
properties.text: Next planned review date stated

guidance: Record the date and outcome of each disciplinary process review in a dedicated log, including any identified changes or improvements.
Document each specific change made to the disciplinary procedure, referencing the corresponding review entry and date in the procedure’s change history.
Name the individual responsible for approving changes to the procedure, and obtain their dated signature on the updated document.
Attach a copy of the revised disciplinary procedure to the review record, showing the updated version number and effective date.
Avoid using generic statements like “procedure updated as needed”—specify the actual changes and link them to the documented review.
properties.text: Changes propagated to the procedure with reference to this review

guidance: Name the reviewer for each discipline process review as a specific individual from HR, Information Security, and Legal, not just by job title.
Record the date each reviewer completed their part of the process review in a version-controlled document.
Collect signatures or written approvals from all three named reviewers on the final review summary.
Retain the review summary and approvals in a location accessible to auditors and management.
properties.text: Reviewer identity (HR lead + InfoSec lead + Legal counsel)

guidance: List all current jurisdictions and worker categories in a dated scope document, naming the person responsible for maintaining its accuracy.
Document a trigger list that includes new geographies, sectoral regulators, and major employment-law reforms, with clear examples for each.
Assign a specific individual to monitor for changes in jurisdictions or regulations, recording their name and review frequency in the scope document.
Record each re-scoping event with the trigger, date, and decision-maker’s name, attaching supporting evidence such as regulatory notices or legal updates.
Avoid using generic or outdated triggers; update the trigger list regularly and reference the latest version in the scope document.
properties.text: Trigger list for re-scoping (new geography, new sectoral regulator, major employment-law reform)

guidance: List all countries and regions where your workers are employed or contracted, including US states, EU countries, and UK jurisdictions, in a dated document.
Name the employment-law category for each jurisdiction, such as "at-will," "just-cause," or "notice-period," with a brief description for each.
Assign a specific individual responsible for maintaining and updating the jurisdictions and categories list; do not use a team or department name.
Cross-reference each listed jurisdiction to the relevant employment process documents that reflect the local legal requirements.
Retain a record of the last review date and the reviewer’s name on the scope document.
properties.text: Jurisdictions covered (employment-law variants — at-will US states vs just-cause EU vs notice-period UK — drive process step variations)

guidance: Document the specific situations that require local employment counsel involvement, such as all dismissals and suspensions exceeding a set number of days, in a written policy.
Name the decision-maker responsible for determining when legal review is triggered, listing a specific individual rather than a group or department.
Record the date of the most recent legal review of this policy, including the name of the reviewing counsel or firm.
Cross-reference the policy section that outlines the legal review path in your jurisdictions and worker categories scope document.
State the escalation process for exceptions, ensuring it includes a requirement for written approval by a named senior manager.
properties.text: Legal review path stated (when local employment counsel must be engaged before action — typically all dismissal cases + suspension cases over X days)

guidance: List each jurisdiction where your organisation operates, with a named contact responsible for regulatory notifications in that area.
Document the categories of workers whose actions could trigger regulator notification, referencing specific roles and departments.
Record the exact notification triggers for each regulator, such as FSA for financial misconduct or healthcare bodies for professional breaches, with legal references.
Attach a dated summary of regulator notification requirements, reviewed and signed by your compliance lead or legal counsel.
Name the responsible individual for each notification trigger — do not use generic titles like "Compliance Team" or "HR Department".
properties.text: Regulator-notification triggers per jurisdiction (financial-services FSA notification for serious misconduct, healthcare professional body notification)

guidance: List all worker categories relevant to your organisation, including employees, contractors, and secondees, in a dated scope document.
Describe the specific process applied to each worker category, detailing full process for employees, contract-based termination for contractors, and escalation for secondees.
Name the individual responsible for maintaining and updating the scope document, using a specific person rather than a generic role or team.
Attach supporting evidence, such as sample contracts or process flowcharts, that demonstrate the described processes for each worker category.
Review and update the scope document annually, recording the review date and the reviewer’s name.
properties.text: Worker categories addressed (employees → full process; contractors → contract-based termination; secondees → escalation to home employer)

guidance: List each type of violation covered by the disciplinary process, including policy breach, negligence, deliberate misuse, repeated training non-compliance, and circumvention of controls.
Reference the exact section and page in your disciplinary policy where these violation types are defined and described.
Name the person or role responsible for maintaining and updating the list of covered violations in the disciplinary process.
Avoid using vague categories like "misconduct" without examples; specify each violation type clearly in the documented process.
properties.text: Scope of violations covered (policy breach, negligence, deliberate misuse, repeated non-compliance with awareness training, deliberate circumvention of security controls)

guidance: Assign a named individual in HR or Security to deliver the exit briefing to each departing employee and record their name in the leaver-briefing register.
Document the date, time, and method of each exit briefing in the leaver-briefing register, linking to the relevant employee.
Obtain a signed acknowledgment from the departing employee confirming receipt and understanding of their ongoing information security responsibilities.
Cross-reference each signed acknowledgment with the corresponding entry in the leaver-briefing register to ensure completeness.
Name the responsible person for maintaining the leaver-briefing register as a specific individual, not a generic team or department.
properties.text: Communication mechanism to leavers (exit briefing with signed acknowledgment; reminder letter; intranet reference) — drives the leaver-briefing register

guidance: Cross-reference the offboarding clause in your supplier agreement with the employee exit checklist to confirm both cover information security responsibilities.
Document the process for removing access and returning assets for contractors and other third parties in a written procedure.
Name the person responsible for enforcing offboarding steps for contractors and interested parties, listing them as a specific individual.
Retain signed supplier agreements that include the information security offboarding clause, dated and linked to each contractor or third party.
properties.text: Equivalent process for contractors and interested parties (offboarding clause in supplier agreement A.5.20)

guidance: State the duration of each post-employment obligation in the employee exit checklist, specifying "indefinite" for confidentiality and exact dates for other restrictions.
Document any legal or jurisdictional limits that cap the duration of non-compete or similar obligations, referencing the relevant law or regulation.
Name the responsible individual who approves and updates these durations, avoiding generic titles like "HR" or "the team."
Retain a signed acknowledgment from the departing employee confirming their understanding of each obligation's duration.
properties.text: Duration of each obligation (indefinite for confidentiality; time-limited for non-compete; per-jurisdiction limits where law caps duration)

guidance: Document the enforcement actions available for post-employment or role-change breaches, such as legal action, breach of contract claims, and regulatory referrals, in a formal policy.
Name the individual or role responsible for initiating enforcement actions, ensuring this is a specific person and not a generic group or department.
Record examples of recent enforcement actions or referrals taken in the past 12 months, including dates and outcomes, in an incident log.
Cross-reference the enforcement policy with relevant employment contracts and regulatory obligations to show alignment and coverage of sector-specific requirements.
State the process for notifying regulators or sector bodies in cases of serious misconduct, including required timelines and contact details, in a documented procedure.
properties.text: Enforcement approach (legal action for breach, breach of contract claims, regulatory referral where misconduct + sectoral notification obligations apply)

guidance: Document a checklist that includes information security responsibilities for employees exiting or changing roles, with version and approval date clearly shown.
Assign a named individual to conduct and sign off on the checklist for each departing or transferring employee.
Record the completion date and outcome of each checklist in the employee’s personnel file.
State any outstanding information security items or assets not returned, with actions and deadlines, in a dated record.
Name the responsible person for follow-up actions as a specific individual, not a generic team or department.
properties.text: Exit interview / role-change checklist with info-security touchpoints

guidance: State in the exit briefing document that the employee’s confidentiality obligations continue after employment, referencing the relevant NDA clause.
Cross-reference the NDA signed by the employee, ensuring it includes a post-employment confidentiality section with clear survival terms.
Record the date and name of the person who delivered the exit briefing, and have the departing employee sign to acknowledge receipt.
Name the responsible HR or security staff member overseeing the exit process as a specific individual, not as a team or department.
properties.text: NDA continuation note — most NDAs survive employment per A.6.6 templates; the exit briefing reinforces this

guidance: Document the specific information security responsibilities that continue after employment or role change in a signed HR exit or transfer checklist.
Cross-reference the HR checklist with operational offboarding records for asset return, identity, credential, and access revocation, noting completion dates.
Name the responsible HR staff member who verifies that all contractual and operational offboarding steps are completed for each departing or transferring individual.
Record any exceptions or delays in offboarding steps, including the reason and the person authorizing the exception, in the individual's HR file.
Avoid using generic terms like "HR team" or "IT" as responsible parties; specify named individuals for each step.
properties.text: Integration with operational offboarding (A.5.11 asset return, A.5.16 identity revocation, A.5.17 credential revocation, A.5.18 access revocation — A.6.5 is the contractual/HR layer; those are the operational layers)

guidance: Name a specific individual in HR as the documented owner of the post-employment and role-change procedure, not just "HR" or a team.
List named contacts from Information Security and Legal as documented partners in the procedure, including their roles and current titles.
Record the date the ownership and partner roles were last reviewed and updated in the procedure document.
Retain a signed approval page from all listed owners and partners, showing agreement on responsibilities and current procedure version.
properties.text: Named owner of the procedure (HR with InfoSec + Legal partners)

guidance: Cross-reference each leaver entry in the Leaver Briefing Register to the corresponding row in the A.5.11 return-of-assets register using a unique identifier.
Record the date and name of the person who completed the cross-link for each leaver event.
Confirm that every leaver event in the Briefing Register has a matching entry in the return-of-assets register; flag and investigate any missing links.
Name the responsible individual for maintaining the cross-links, avoiding generic roles like "HR team" or "IT department".
properties.text: Per-row cross-link to A.5.11 return-of-assets register (same leaver event)

guidance: Record each leaver’s name, last working date, and the specific briefing materials provided in a dedicated row of the register.
Obtain a digital signature or signed PDF from each leaver confirming receipt and understanding of the briefing.
Store the signed acknowledgment alongside the corresponding register entry, ensuring each row links directly to its evidence.
Name the leaver as an individual in each row—do not use generic terms like "staff" or "employee".
properties.text: Per-row signed acknowledgment evidence (digital signature / signed PDF / recorded receipt of intranet artefact)

guidance: Record the full name of the HR partner who conducted each leaver briefing in a dedicated column for every entry in the register.
Document the line manager’s full name alongside the HR partner for any leaver cases involving a role change.
Enter the date each briefing was completed next to the corresponding briefer identities in the register.
Name the briefer as a specific individual—avoid using group labels like "HR team" or "management".
properties.text: Per-row briefer identity (HR partner; line manager joins for role-change cases)

guidance: Record the exact date each leaver or role-changer received their exit or transition briefing in a dedicated column of the Leaver Briefing Register.
Name the individual who conducted each briefing, listing their full name rather than a team or department.
Cross-reference each briefing entry with supporting documentation, such as a signed briefing acknowledgement or email confirmation, for every leaver or role-changer.
Avoid leaving briefing date fields blank or using placeholders like "TBC"; update the register with the actual date as soon as the briefing occurs.
properties.text: Per-row briefing date (typically last working day or shortly after; for role change, at point of role transition)

guidance: Record each leaver's unique identifier in the Leaver Briefing Register, matching the identifier used in the identity register for A.5.16.
Cross-reference the Leaver Briefing Register entry to the corresponding return-of-assets record required by A.5.11.
Link each register entry to the documented identity revocation record maintained under A.5.16.
Name the leaver using a specific identifier or full name—do not use generic labels like "staff" or "user."
properties.text: Per-row leaver identifier (links to identity register A.5.16; cross-link to A.5.11 return-of-assets record + A.5.16 identity revocation)

guidance: List all post-employment obligations for each leaver in the register, specifying confidentiality, intellectual property, non-poach, and non-compete as applicable.
Reference the relevant contract clause or policy for each obligation listed, ensuring traceability to the original signed document.
Name the jurisdiction or country for each leaver to confirm which obligations apply based on local legal requirements.
Assign a specific individual to review and update the register entry for each leaver, recording their name and the date of review.
Avoid using generic terms like "standard obligations"—detail each obligation explicitly for every leaver row.
properties.text: Per-row covered obligations list (confidentiality + IP + non-poach + non-compete where applicable per jurisdiction)

guidance: Record the date and outcome of each post-briefing check for every leaver, specifying the 30, 90, or 180-day interval based on role seniority.
Assign a named individual to conduct and sign off each check, avoiding generic entries like "HR" or "IT team".
Document any incidents or breaches identified during the check, including details of investigation and resolution, even if none occurred.
Cross-reference each check entry with supporting evidence, such as access logs or incident reports, to confirm no breach has taken place.
Retain all completed check records in the Leaver Briefing Register, ensuring each entry is dated and attributable to a specific person.
properties.text: Per-row post-briefing check (30/90/180-day check that no breach has occurred — proportional to role seniority)

guidance: Record the specific trigger event for each leaver entry, choosing from termination, contract end, role change within organisation, or retirement.
Name the leaver and their unique identifier, such as employee ID or email address, in each row of the register.
Enter the date the trigger event was communicated to HR or management for each leaver entry.
Assign a named individual responsible for processing each leaver’s exit, avoiding generic labels like "HR team" or "Manager".
Retain supporting documentation for each trigger event, such as resignation letters or contract end notices, and reference their location in the register.
properties.text: Per-row trigger (termination / contract end / role change within org / retirement)

guidance: Document each ad-hoc review trigger with a clear description and the date it was identified in a dedicated section of your review log.
Name the individual responsible for initiating ad-hoc reviews, ensuring a specific person is listed rather than a team or department.
Record the decision to conduct an ad-hoc review, including the reason, trigger event, and approval by a named manager, in meeting minutes or an action register.
Attach supporting evidence for each trigger, such as regulator notifications, tribunal rulings, or high-profile resignation letters, to the review documentation.
properties.text: Ad-hoc review triggers (high-profile leaver, regulator action affecting post-employment terms, employment-tribunal ruling)

guidance: Name a specific individual responsible for conducting the post-employment breach history review, avoiding generic titles like "HR team" or "management."
Document all identified post-employment breaches in a dated register, including details of the incident, individuals involved, and discovery date.
Record how each breach was handled, referencing the enforcement approach and attaching supporting evidence such as investigation reports or disciplinary records.
Capture and summarize lessons learned from each breach in a review report, noting any changes made to policies or procedures as a result.
Retain meeting minutes or sign-off from management confirming the review was completed and lessons were formally acknowledged.
properties.text: Breach history review — any post-employment breaches occurred? handled per enforcement approach? lessons captured?

guidance: Cross-reference the leavers register for the review period against the post-employment briefing log to identify all individuals who exited.
Confirm each leaver has a dated record of receiving and acknowledging the post-employment briefing, such as a signed form or email receipt.
Name the reviewer who performed the completeness check as a specific person, not a generic role or team.
Document any missing acknowledgements with an explanation and actions taken, attaching supporting correspondence or escalation records.
Retain the final checklist or summary report showing all leavers, briefing dates, acknowledgements, and reviewer sign-off.
properties.text: Briefing coverage check — every leaver in the period received and acknowledged a briefing (the register's completeness gate)

guidance: Record the date of the most recent post-employment program review in a central log, showing it falls within the planned review interval.
Name the individual responsible for scheduling and conducting the review, listing them by full name and job title.
Document the planned review interval in months or years within the program documentation, referencing the policy or procedure version.
Retain meeting minutes or a signed review summary that confirms the review was completed on the recorded date.
Specify the next scheduled review date in the log, avoiding open-ended or "as needed" intervals.
properties.text: Review date within the planned interval

guidance: Assign a named legal counsel to review post-employment program requirements for each jurisdiction covered by your workforce.
Document the date, jurisdiction, and summary of legal counsel’s input on enforceability or changes in employment law.
Retain written confirmation from legal counsel that all post-employment terms remain compliant or highlight required updates.
Name the legal counsel as a specific individual, not just "legal team" or "HR department", in the review record.
Record any program changes made as a result of legal counsel’s advice, including the date and person responsible for implementation.
properties.text: Employment-law drift check per jurisdiction (legal counsel input on enforceability changes)

guidance: State the next planned review date for the post-employment program in the review documentation, using a clear and specific calendar date.
Record the name of the individual responsible for scheduling and conducting the next review, not just a department or team.
Retain the most recent review record with the stated next review date, signed or acknowledged by the responsible individual.
Cross-reference the stated next review date in the program documentation with the organisation’s compliance calendar or tracking system.
properties.text: Next planned review date stated

guidance: Record the date and outcome of each post-employment program review in a version-controlled document.
Document all changes made to the procedure or scope, clearly referencing the specific review that triggered each change.
Name the individual responsible for approving and updating the procedure following each review.
Attach the updated procedure and scope documents, ensuring each includes the revision date and a summary of changes.
Avoid referencing reviews generically; cross-reference each change to a specific, dated review entry.
properties.text: Changes propagated to the procedure / scope with reference to this review

guidance: Name the HR lead, InfoSec lead, and Legal counsel who reviewed the program in the review meeting minutes, using their full names and job titles.
Record the date of the most recent post-employment program review in a dated document signed by all three required reviewers.
Attach each reviewer’s signature or written approval to the final review summary to confirm their participation and agreement.
Avoid listing a group or department as the reviewer; specify each individual by name to meet accountability requirements.
properties.text: Reviewer identity (HR lead + InfoSec lead + Legal counsel)

guidance: Document specific information security responsibilities for employees changing roles, including access rights, in a signed and dated role change checklist.
Record completion of access reviews and updates for each role change, with evidence of removed or modified permissions in system logs.
Name the individual responsible for authorising security changes during role transitions — avoid listing only departments or generic titles.
Retain a copy of the communication sent to the employee outlining their new or changed security responsibilities, with a timestamp.
Confirm that all handover tasks, including return of assets and transfer of sensitive information, are tracked in a completed checklist signed by both old and new role owners.
properties.text: Coverage of role change within the organisation, not just termination (joiner-mover-leaver — mover is the typically-missed leg)

guidance: List specific triggers for re-scoping, such as entry into a new country, major changes in employment law, or new sectoral regulator requirements.
Document the date each trigger was last reviewed and the person responsible for monitoring changes in legal or regulatory obligations.
Name the owner as a specific individual, not a team or department, who is accountable for initiating re-scoping when a trigger occurs.
Retain evidence of periodic reviews, such as meeting minutes or review logs, showing that the trigger list has been checked and updated as needed.
properties.text: Trigger list for re-scoping (new geography with distinct employment law, major employment-law reform, sectoral regulator action)

guidance: Identify all jurisdictions where your organisation operates and record them in a dated obligations register.
Document the specific legal limits on non-compete enforceability for each jurisdiction, citing the relevant law or regulation.
Name the person responsible for monitoring changes in employment law for each jurisdiction, listing them as a specific individual.
Cross-reference each contractual clause with the corresponding jurisdictional requirement, showing how local law is addressed.
Retain copies of legal reviews or external counsel opinions that confirm your approach complies with each jurisdiction’s enforceability limits.
properties.text: Jurisdictional limits on enforceability (US California voids non-compete; EU restricts duration; UK courts test reasonableness)

guidance: List each surviving obligation individually in your catalogue, specifying confidentiality, intellectual property, non-disparagement, non-poach, non-compete, and cooperation-with-investigations.
Name the owner responsible for maintaining and updating the obligation catalogue as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Record the date when the obligation catalogue was last reviewed and updated.
Cross-reference each obligation in the catalogue to the relevant contract clause or policy document.
properties.text: Obligation catalogue enumerated (confidentiality / IP / non-disparagement / non-poach / non-compete / cooperation-with-investigations)

guidance: List each executive, standard staff member, and sales/CSM role by title in a table alongside their specific post-employment obligations.
Document the exact non-compete, confidentiality, intellectual property, non-poach, and non-solicit clauses that apply to each role, referencing contract sections.
Name the responsible HR or legal manager who maintains and updates the role-to-obligation mapping, not just "HR" or "the team".
Record the date the mapping was last reviewed and updated, attaching a signed approval from an executive or legal counsel.
Cross-reference the mapping to actual signed employment agreements to confirm obligations are consistently applied as documented.
properties.text: Role-to-obligation mapping (executive level may have extended non-compete; standard staff only confidentiality + IP; sales/CSM commonly have non-poach + non-solicit)

guidance: List all worker categories involved with your organisation, such as employees, contractors, and interns, in a dated obligations scope document.
Specify the information security obligations that apply to each worker category, referencing relevant policy sections or contractual clauses.
Name the person responsible for maintaining and updating the obligations scope, ensuring this is a specific individual, not a team or department.
Attach supporting evidence, such as sample contracts or onboarding checklists, that demonstrate the distinct obligations communicated to each worker category.
Review the obligations scope annually and record the review date and reviewer’s name in the document.
properties.text: Worker categories addressed (employees vs contractors vs interns — different obligation scope)

guidance: List all information security responsibilities that continue after employment or role change in a formal document, such as an exit checklist or contract addendum.
Specify confidentiality, intellectual property protection, and any lawful non-compete, non-poach, or non-disparagement obligations with clear, plain-language descriptions.
State the duration of each surviving obligation, noting if any are indefinite, and include relevant jurisdictional limitations where applicable.
Obtain a signed acknowledgment from the departing individual confirming their understanding and acceptance of these ongoing responsibilities.
Name the responsible individual who updates and maintains these records, avoiding generic titles like "HR team" or "management."
properties.text: Surviving duties enumerated (confidentiality — typically indefinite; IP protection; non-disparagement; non-poach where lawful; non-compete where lawful)

guidance: Cross-reference the Confidentiality / Non-Disclosure Agreement template to the specific section in the employment terms that addresses information security obligations.
Document the version number and approval date of both the NDA template and the employment terms in a change log.
Name the owner of the NDA template as a specific individual, not a group or department.
Attach a copy of the current employment terms to the NDA template file or provide a direct link in the template header.
Record a statement in the NDA template that both documents together form the full personnel information security contract package.
properties.text: Cross-link to A.6.2 employment terms — for employees the NDA and employment terms together form the personnel info-security contract package

guidance: State the duration of confidentiality obligations in the agreement, specifying "indefinite" for trade secrets and a fixed period for other confidential information.
Name the type of information covered by each duration, clearly distinguishing between trade secrets and other confidential data in the template.
Reference the section and clause number in the template where the duration is defined, so it is easily located by an auditor.
Name the template owner as a specific individual, not a generic role or team, to avoid ambiguity about responsibility.
properties.text: Duration of confidentiality obligation (indefinite for trade secrets; time-limited for non-trade-secret confidential info — typically 3-5 years post-termination)

guidance: Cross-reference the agreement template to your documented information classification scheme, citing the exact policy or register section covering confidential, restricted, and trade-secret data.
State in the template which information classes are protected, using the same terms and definitions as your classification policy.
Include a section in the template that explicitly addresses protection of personal data if the agreement may cover personally identifiable information.
Name the template owner as a specific individual responsible for updates, not a generic team or department.
Record the template version and last review date in the document footer.
properties.text: Information classes protected (cross-link to A.5.12 classification — confidential / restricted / trade-secret tiers; PII overlay where applicable)

guidance: Insert a governing law clause that clearly states the specific country or state whose laws apply to the agreement.
Include a remedies section that explicitly allows for injunctive relief in the event of a breach of confidentiality.
State any liquidated damages provisions only if they are enforceable under the chosen jurisdiction’s laws, referencing legal review if applicable.
Name the template owner as a specific individual responsible for maintaining legal accuracy, not a generic role or team.
Record the latest legal review date and reviewer’s name on the template to show it reflects current enforceability standards.
properties.text: Jurisdiction and remedies clauses (governing law, injunctive relief, liquidated damages where lawful)

guidance: Display the last-reviewed date clearly on the first page of the Confidentiality / Non-Disclosure Agreement template.
Record the name of the person who conducted the most recent review directly on the template.
Retain a copy of the review log or meeting minutes showing when and by whom the template was last reviewed.
Avoid using undated or generic templates; always update the review date after each formal review.
properties.text: Last-reviewed date on the template (review evidence — drives the freshness check)

guidance: Name the owner of the Confidentiality/Non-Disclosure Agreement template as a specific individual from Legal counsel, not a generic team or department.
Document the InfoSec partner who co-owns or reviews the template by listing their full name and role on the template cover page.
Record the date when ownership was assigned or last reviewed in the template’s version history or change log.
Confirm both owners have signed or formally approved the current version of the template, attaching their signatures or approval emails.
properties.text: Named owner of the template (Legal counsel with InfoSec partner)

guidance: List all categories of parties who may access sensitive information in the agreement template, including employees, contractors, suppliers, visitors, and M&A counterparties.
Specify that each party must be named individually or as a clearly defined entity, avoiding generic terms like "the team" or "all staff."
Record the date of the latest template review and the name of the person who approved the covered parties section.
Attach a cross-reference in the template to the organisation’s information classification policy to show alignment with internal definitions of sensitive information.
properties.text: Parties covered (employees, contractors, suppliers, visitors with access to sensitive info, M&A counterparties)

guidance: Record each suspected breach of NDA terms as a new entry in the NDA Signature Register, including the date the breach was identified.
Document the details of the investigation for each breach, naming the investigator and summarizing findings in the corresponding register row.
State the enforcement decision for each breach, including any disciplinary or remedial actions taken, and record the decision date.
Name the individual who approved the enforcement decision for each breach, avoiding generic titles or group names.
Attach supporting evidence for each breach entry, such as investigation reports or correspondence, and cross-reference these documents in the register row.
properties.text: Per-row breach log (any suspected breach of NDA terms recorded with investigation outcome and enforcement decision)

guidance: Record the status of each NDA in the register as "active," "expired-with-surviving-obligations," or "superseded-by-new-version" for every entry.
State the date when the status was last updated for each NDA row to show current and accurate tracking.
Name the specific individual responsible for updating each NDA status, avoiding generic labels like "Legal" or "HR team."
Cross-reference each "superseded-by-new-version" entry with the new NDA version number or identifier in the register.
Document any surviving obligations for expired NDAs in a dedicated field, not just as a note or in a separate file.
properties.text: Per-row status (active / expired-with-surviving-obligations / superseded-by-new-version)

guidance: Record the full legal name of each NDA signatory in the register, matching the name exactly as it appears in the relevant identity source.
Cross-reference each signatory’s entry with their unique identifier from the employee, supplier, or visitor register, as appropriate.
Document the date and method of signature for each NDA entry, ensuring both are clearly visible and unambiguous.
Avoid using generic labels like "contractor" or "visitor" without a specific linked identifier, as auditors will flag missing traceability.
properties.text: Per-row signatory identifier (links to identity register A.5.16 for employees; supplier register A.5.19 for contractors; visitor-log for visitors)

guidance: Record the full name of each individual who signed an NDA in a dedicated column of the NDA Signature Register.
Enter the exact date each NDA was signed in a separate column, ensuring the date is before any access to confidential information is granted.
Cross-reference each NDA entry with the corresponding access grant record to confirm that signature dates precede access dates.
Name the NDA signatory as a specific individual, not a group or generic title, to avoid ambiguity in the register.
Retain a scanned copy of each signed NDA linked to its register entry for verification of both signature and date.
properties.text: Per-row signature date (proves signing happened BEFORE access granted per A.5.18)

guidance: Record the signature method for each NDA entry, specifying either "wet signature" or the exact e-signature platform used.
Document the date and time each NDA was signed, matching the signature method to the corresponding record.
Name the signatory for each NDA row as a specific individual, not a generic role or group.
Attach or cross-reference the original signed NDA file or e-signature audit trail for each entry in the register.
properties.text: Per-row signature method (wet / e-signature platform reference — ensures non-repudiation)

guidance: Record the exact NDA template version used for each signature entry in the register, using a unique version identifier and approval date.
Cross-reference each NDA template version in the register to its corresponding stored, approved document to confirm authenticity.
Name the NDA template version owner as a specific individual, not a generic role or team, for each version entry.
Flag any register entries missing a template version or using an outdated version for review and potential re-signing.
properties.text: Per-row template version (drives currency check — old-version signers may need re-signing on material template changes)

guidance: Add a column to the NDA Signature Register to record the date and reference of any offboarding event linked to each individual.
Cross-reference each applicable NDA entry with the corresponding offboarding record, including the briefing date and responsible HR staff member.
Name the responsible person who updates the register as a specific individual, not a generic role or team.
Retain evidence of leaver briefings, such as signed acknowledgements, and link these documents to the relevant NDA register entry.
Avoid leaving the cross-link field blank for leavers; explicitly record "not applicable" only for current staff or contractors.
properties.text: Per-row cross-link to the offboarding event where applicable (A.6.5 leaver briefing reinforces surviving NDA obligations)

guidance: Record the NDA variant for each entry in the register, using clear labels such as employee, contractor, supplier-bilateral, M&A, or visitor.
Cross-reference each NDA entry to the specific template or variant_tier used, ensuring the register matches the actual document signed.
Name the NDA signatory and their relationship to your organisation for every row, avoiding generic terms like "external party" or "staff".
Confirm the NDA variant listed aligns with the proportionality principle in ISO 27002:6.6, reflecting the risk and context of the relationship.
Retain a dated copy of the signed NDA linked to each register entry, showing the correct variant was actually executed.
properties.text: Per-row NDA variant (employee / contractor / supplier-bilateral / M&A / visitor — matches the template variant_tiers SHOULD)

guidance: Insert a clause in the template requiring all confidential information to be returned or destroyed at the end of the relationship.
Specify in the template that paper records must be destroyed with a certificate of destruction from a reputable provider.
State in the template that digital records must be securely deleted using methods that prevent recovery, referencing secure deletion standards.
Cross-reference the template’s destruction and deletion requirements to your organisation’s asset disposal policy, as required by control A.8.10.
Name the owner of the template as a specific individual, not a generic title or team.
properties.text: Return or destruction obligation at end of relationship (with certified-destruction option for paper, secure-deletion for digital — links to A.8.10)

guidance: Document each ad-hoc NDA template review trigger, such as material classification changes, legal precedent shifts, or mergers and acquisitions, in a dated log entry.
Name the person responsible for monitoring and identifying events that trigger ad-hoc NDA template reviews, listing them as an individual, not a team.
Record the date and outcome of each ad-hoc NDA template review, including any updates made to the template, in a central register.
Attach supporting evidence, such as legal memos or M&A announcements, to each review entry to show the reason for the ad-hoc review.
properties.text: Ad-hoc review triggers (material classification change, case-law shift, M&A bringing new counterparty types)

guidance: Review the latest approved information classification scheme under A.5.12 and note any changes since the last NDA template review.
Cross-reference each NDA template clause with the current classification scheme to identify misalignments or outdated terminology.
Document the date and outcome of the classification drift check in the NDA review log, including any required template updates.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual responsible for the drift check, not a generic role or team.
Attach evidence of communication to stakeholders if NDA templates were updated due to classification changes.
properties.text: Information-classification drift check — has A.5.12 classification scheme changed in ways affecting NDA info_classes?

guidance: Record the most recent review date for the NDA template in a central register, including the name of the reviewer.
Name the responsible individual for scheduling and conducting NDA template reviews, not just a team or department.
Document the planned review interval for the NDA template and cross-reference it with actual review dates to confirm alignment.
Retain a copy of the reviewed NDA template with tracked changes or a summary of updates, dated and attributed to the reviewer.
properties.text: Review date within the planned interval

guidance: Assign a named legal counsel to review the NDA template for enforceability in each relevant jurisdiction, recording their name and date of review.
Document the specific legal sources or case law referenced during the review, including any recent changes that impact enforceability.
Record legal counsel’s written confirmation that the NDA template addresses cross-border data flow risks, especially in light of recent legal developments.
Retain a signed and dated statement from legal counsel confirming the NDA template’s compliance with current applicable laws in all relevant jurisdictions.
Name the legal counsel as a specific individual, not just “Legal” or “the legal team,” to avoid ambiguity in responsibility.
properties.text: Enforceability check per jurisdiction (legal counsel input — case-law shifts, Schrems-style impacts on cross-border data flows in NDA scope)

guidance: State the next planned review date directly on the NDA template document in a clearly visible location.
Name the responsible individual for the next review, avoiding generic titles like "Legal Team" or "HR Department".
Record the date this review schedule was last updated in a change log or document history section.
Retain evidence of communication to relevant stakeholders about the scheduled review date, such as an email or meeting note.
properties.text: Next planned review date stated

guidance: Document the date and details of each NDA template review in a change log, including who conducted the review and the outcome.
Update the live NDA template immediately after approved changes, and save the new version with a unique version number and date.
Cross-reference the updated template version in the signer re-signing plan, ensuring the plan lists which signers need to re-sign and by when.
Name the person responsible for updating both the live template and the re-signing plan, avoiding generic roles like "Legal Team" or "HR".
properties.text: Changes propagated to the live template and to the signer-re-signing plan

guidance: Name both the Legal Counsel and Information Security Lead as joint reviewers in the NDA template review record for each review cycle.
Document the date each reviewer completes their assessment on the NDA template review checklist or meeting minutes.
Require both reviewers to sign or formally approve the reviewed NDA template, capturing their names and approval dates.
Avoid listing a generic group or department as reviewer; specify named individuals for both required roles.
properties.text: Reviewer identity (Legal counsel + InfoSec lead jointly)

guidance: Document the current NDA template version number and effective date in a central register, listing any material changes from previous versions.
Cross-reference all signed NDAs against the register to identify which version each signer has agreed to, noting any outdated agreements.
Calculate and record the percentage of active signers who are on the current NDA template version, using a dated summary report.
Name a specific individual responsible for tracking NDA template usage and re-signing plans—do not assign this to a generic team or department.
Create a documented plan, with target dates, for re-signing NDAs where material clauses have changed, and attach evidence of communication to affected signers.
properties.text: Signer-currency analysis (% on current template version; plan for re-signing the gap where material clauses changed)

guidance: List all current party categories in scope, including employees, contractors, vendors, and any unique groups such as gig workers or open-source contributors.
Document a trigger list that specifies events requiring re-scoping, such as onboarding a new party type, expanding to a new country, or launching a new partnership model.
Assign a named individual responsible for monitoring business changes and initiating scope review when a trigger event occurs.
Record the date of the most recent scope review and the outcome, including any new party categories added or considered.
Name the owner as a specific person, not a generic group or department, to avoid ambiguity in accountability.
properties.text: Trigger list for re-scoping (new party category — e.g. open-source-contributor NDA, gig workers, new geography)

guidance: List all countries and regions where signatories are based or where data is processed in a dated, version-controlled document.
Name the specific laws or regulations in each jurisdiction that apply to the agreement and information protection.
Assign a responsible individual to review and update the jurisdictions list annually or when business operations change.
Avoid using generic terms like "global" or "all applicable laws"; specify each jurisdiction and law by name.
properties.text: Jurisdictions covered (where signatories sign / where info is protected — drives governing-law clause and enforceability)

guidance: List all categories of parties relevant to your organisation, including employees, contractors, suppliers, visitors, M&A counterparties, and joint-development partners, in a dated document.
Name the person responsible for maintaining and updating the list of party categories, ensuring a specific individual is identified.
Cross-reference each party category to supporting documentation or contracts that define their relationship and access to information.
Avoid using generic terms such as "others" or "external parties" without clear definitions, as auditors will flag vague categories.
properties.text: Party categories enumerated (employees, contractors, suppliers, visitors, M&A counterparties, partners with joint-development)

guidance: Define each information classification category in a written document, including clear examples of what data falls under each class.
State the specific classification level(s) that require a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) before access is granted, referencing the documented categories.
Record the decision and rationale for each trigger threshold in a dated approval document signed by a named responsible individual.
Cross-reference the NDA trigger thresholds in your information classification policy so auditors can verify alignment between documents.
Name the owner of the trigger threshold decision as a specific person, not a group or department.
properties.text: Trigger threshold per category (which info-class triggers NDA — typically access to confidential class and above; some orgs all-access)

guidance: List all relevant party types involved with your organisation, such as employees, contractors, suppliers, and M&A partners, in a dated document.
Map each party type to its specific confidentiality agreement variant, clearly referencing the actual agreement template or document name.
Name the individual responsible for maintaining and updating the party-to-variant mapping, avoiding generic titles like "HR" or "Legal team."
Attach or link the current versions of each agreement variant to the mapping record for direct cross-reference.
Record the date when the mapping was last reviewed and updated, and retain evidence of the reviewer's name.
properties.text: Party-to-variant mapping (employees → light employee NDA; contractors → contractor NDA; suppliers → bilateral; M&A → heavy)

guidance: State in the NDA template that a physical or electronic signature is required from the non-employee before any access is provided.
Record the full name, signature, and date for each non-employee on a dedicated NDA log or register before access is granted.
Cross-reference each signed NDA with the corresponding access request record to confirm no access is enabled prior to signature.
Name the individual responsible for verifying and enforcing the signed NDA requirement, avoiding generic roles such as "HR" or "IT team".
Retain all signed NDAs in a secure, retrievable location for the duration of the individual's access and for any required retention period.
properties.text: Signature requirement enforced before access granted (no access without signed NDA — gates A.5.18 access grant for non-employees)

guidance: List all NDA template variants by type (employee, contractor, supplier, M&A counterparty) in a single document with version numbers and dates.
Document the rationale for each NDA variant, explaining why its terms are lighter or heavier based on the relationship and risk.
Assign a named owner responsible for maintaining and updating each NDA template, not just "Legal" or "HR".
Attach a sample completed NDA for each variant, signed and dated by both parties, to demonstrate actual use.
State the duration and key clauses for each NDA variant in a summary table, avoiding generic or copy-paste language that does not reflect real differences.
properties.text: Tiered NDA variants (employee NDA — lighter; contractor — full; supplier — bilateral; M&A counterparty — heavy with extended duration)

guidance: State the specific access control measures required for remote working, such as multi-factor authentication and device restrictions, in the policy document.
Name the individual responsible for approving and updating remote access permissions, listing their full name and job title.
Document the process for granting, reviewing, and revoking remote access, including required approvals and review frequency, in a dated procedure.
Record the date and version number on the Remote Working Policy to show it reflects current access control requirements.
Specify that generic or shared accounts must not be used for remote access, and include this prohibition explicitly in the policy text.
properties.text: Access control requirements

guidance: List all equipment approved for remote working in the Remote Working Policy, including device types, models, and any required security features.
Name the individual responsible for maintaining the approved equipment list, ensuring this is not a group or department.
Record the date when the approved equipment list was last reviewed and updated in the policy document.
Attach evidence of management approval for the equipment list, such as a signed or digitally authorized policy version.
properties.text: Approved equipment for remote working

guidance: State in the Remote Working Policy that only authorized employees may use work equipment, explicitly prohibiting access by family members or visitors.
Document clear instructions for employees to prevent family or visitors from viewing or handling work devices, including screens and printed materials.
Name a specific individual, such as the Information Security Manager, as the policy owner responsible for updates and enforcement—avoid listing a team or department.
Record the date the policy was last reviewed and approved by management to show it is current and actively maintained.
properties.text: Rules regarding family/visitor access to work equipment

guidance: State in the Remote Working Policy that all remote connections to company systems must use a company-approved VPN or equivalent secure channel.
Name the specific technology or service (e.g., "Acme VPN Client v3.2") required for remote access, including any configuration settings.
Assign a named individual or role responsible for maintaining and updating the list of approved remote access methods.
Record the date of the last policy review and update, ensuring it reflects recent changes in network security requirements.
Specify that generic terms like "secure connection" without naming the actual technology will be flagged as insufficient by auditors.
properties.text: Network security requirements (VPN etc.)

guidance: State in the Remote Working Policy how personal data must be accessed, processed, and stored when working remotely, referencing GDPR requirements.
Name the policy owner as a specific individual responsible for updates and compliance, not a team or department.
Document the approval of the policy by a named senior manager, including the approval date.
Record the date of the last policy review and the reviewer’s name to show regular assessment for GDPR alignment.
Cross-reference the policy to your organisation’s Data Protection Policy to demonstrate consistent personal data handling requirements.
properties.text: Handling of personal data when working remotely

guidance: State in the Remote Working Policy that staff must secure devices and sensitive documents in a locked drawer or room when not in use.
Name the policy owner as a specific individual responsible for updates and enforcement, not a generic team or department.
Document the date of the latest policy review and approval, signed by a senior manager.
Require staff to confirm in writing that they have read and understood the physical security requirements for remote work.
properties.text: Physical security at remote location

guidance: Document each remote worker’s approval using a dated record signed by both their line manager and the designated InfoSec representative.
Record the worker’s written attestation that their remote workspace meets security and privacy requirements before access is granted.
Confirm equipment provisioning by listing all devices issued to the worker in an asset register, with serial numbers and assignment dates.
Verify completion of remote working awareness training by attaching a dated certificate or training log entry to the worker’s approval file.
Name the approvers as specific individuals—avoid using generic titles like “the team” or “management” in approval records.
properties.text: Per-worker approval workflow before remote-working starts (line manager + InfoSec sign-off, suitable-workspace attestation, equipment-provisioning checkpoint, awareness-training completion check)

guidance: Document the process for approving remote work equipment, specifying if only company devices are allowed or if personal devices are permitted with mobile device management.
List any restrictions on peripherals, such as prohibiting external monitors or printers, in the written procedure.
Cross-reference each remote-issued device in the asset register, including serial numbers and assigned user, to show tracking under A.5.9.
Name the equipment approver as a specific individual, not a team or department, in the procedure documentation.
Record the date and method of equipment provisioning for each remote worker in a log that can be produced for audit.
properties.text: Equipment provisioning step (corporate device only / BYOD permitted with MDM / specific peripheral restrictions like external monitors / printers), cross-link to A.5.9 asset register so remote-issued equipment is tracked

guidance: Document the date and time when the worker received a verbal explanation that family members must not use the corporate device.
