State for each entry whether the data can be linked to an identifiable individual, recording the reasoning and evidence for identifiability.
Document the specific processing operation performed (such as collection, storage, or transfer) for each process or system in the register.
Assign a named individual as the owner responsible for confirming the accuracy of each entry — do not use a team or department as owner.
Record the date of the latest review or update for each entry to demonstrate the operational test is current.
properties.text: Operational test for 'involves PII processing' (identifiability + processing operation)

guidance: List all jurisdictions where your organization processes personal data, referencing a dated register or map of processing locations.
Enumerate each permitted lawful basis for processing personal data under GDPR Article 6.1(a-f) and relevant laws for other jurisdictions in a dated procedure document.
Cross-reference each lawful basis in your catalog to the specific law or regulation section it derives from, citing the legal text and date accessed.
Name the person responsible for maintaining and updating the lawful basis catalog, identifying them by full name and job title.
Avoid using generic or boilerplate lists—tailor the catalog to your organization’s actual processing activities and jurisdictions, and document the customization date.
properties.text: Basis catalog — enumerated permitted bases per applicable jurisdiction (GDPR Art.6.1.a-f; other jurisdictions as applicable)

guidance: Document the step-by-step process for reassessing lawful basis whenever the purpose for processing personal data changes or expands.
Name a specific individual responsible for approving any change in lawful basis, avoiding generic titles like "the team" or "management".
Record the date and outcome of each reassessment, including the rationale for the new lawful basis and any supporting evidence.
State in writing when and how affected individuals will be notified of the change in lawful basis, including the method and timing of communication.
Retain copies of all reassessment records and notification materials for each change, ensuring they are dated and easily retrievable.
properties.text: Basis change procedure — changing basis requires re-assessment and often subject notice (§7.3.3)

guidance: Document the specific legitimate interest being pursued, including a clear description and justification, in a dated assessment record.
Record the necessity test by explaining why the processing is needed to achieve the stated interest, with supporting evidence.
Assess and document potential impacts on individuals’ rights and freedoms, listing identified risks and proposed mitigations.
Name the decision-maker who approved the balancing test outcome, ensuring this is a specific individual and not a group or department.
Retain the completed assessment and approval record for each processing activity relying on legitimate interests as a lawful basis.
properties.rationale: GDPR Art.6.1.f — balanced against interests + fundamental rights
properties.text: Legitimate-interests balancing test procedure (necessity + balancing against subject rights)

guidance: Name the Data Protection Officer and legal counsel responsible for signoff in the Lawful Basis Assessment Procedure, listing their full names and roles.
Obtain dated signatures from both the Data Protection Officer and legal counsel on each assessment before the lawful basis is used in production.
Record the final signoff date and attach the signed assessment to the project documentation for each new or updated lawful basis.
Avoid using unsigned or verbally approved assessments—an auditor will flag any basis that lacks clear, written signoff from both required parties.
properties.text: DPO + legal counsel signoff before basis enters production

guidance: Document the selection test for each lawful basis, showing how the chosen basis meets the specific criteria listed in the requirement.
Name the person responsible for conducting and recording the assessment for each processing activity, using their full name and role.
Record the exact law, contract, or public task referenced when relying on legal obligation, contract, or public interest as the lawful basis.
Attach a completed Legitimate Interests Assessment (LIA) with a documented balancing test when using legitimate interests as the lawful basis.
Avoid using generic or boilerplate justifications that could apply to any organisation; tailor each assessment to the specific processing activity.
properties.text: Selection test per basis (consent — freely given + specific + unambiguous; contract — necessity; legal obligation — cited law; vital interests — physical safety; public interest — cited task; legitimate interests — LIA with balancing test)

guidance: Name the specific lawful basis under Article 9 or 10 for each special-category data processing activity in your assessment documentation.
Document the rationale for choosing each Article 9 or 10 basis, referencing the relevant processing purpose and data type.
Assign a named individual responsible for reviewing and updating the lawful basis assessment annually.
Attach supporting evidence, such as policy excerpts or consent forms, that demonstrate compliance with the identified Article 9 or 10 basis.
Avoid using generic justifications or boilerplate text; tailor each assessment to the actual processing activity and data involved.
properties.text: Special-category overlay (Art.9/10 basis required in addition to Art.6 for health, biometric, criminal, etc.)

guidance: Assign a unique identifier to each processing activity row in the Lawful Basis Register, using a sequential number or clear code.
Record the identifier in a dedicated column, ensuring it appears consistently for every processing activity listed.
Cross-reference each identifier with related records or documentation, such as data flow maps or risk assessments, to support traceability.
Name the processing activity clearly and specifically in each row—avoid vague descriptions that could apply to multiple activities.
properties.text: Processing activity identifier per row

guidance: Record the date each lawful basis was first established in the Lawful Basis Register, listing the specific processing activity and legal ground.
Enter the most recent date each lawful basis was re-evaluated, showing a clear timeline of review for every processing activity.
Name the person responsible for each entry’s review, using a specific individual’s name rather than a team or department.
Attach supporting documentation, such as meeting minutes or review sign-offs, that confirm the re-evaluation took place on the recorded date.
properties.text: Date basis established / last re-evaluated

guidance: Record the specific Legitimate Interests Assessment (LIA) reference number next to each processing activity that relies on legitimate interests as the lawful basis.
Cross-reference each LIA entry to a dated and completed balancing test document stored in your records.
Name the individual who approved the LIA and balancing test for each relevant processing activity.
Avoid listing "LIA on file" or generic notes; always provide a unique, traceable LIA reference for each row.
properties.text: LIA reference per row where basis is legitimate interests

guidance: List each processing activity in the Lawful Basis Register with a separate row, ensuring no activities are grouped together.
State the specific lawful basis for each activity by citing the exact article or section, such as "Art.6.1.b" or local equivalent.
Name the owner responsible for each entry as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Record the date each lawful basis was assigned or last reviewed for traceability.
Attach supporting documentation or references that justify the chosen lawful basis for each processing activity.
properties.text: Primary basis cited per row (Art.6.1.a-f or equivalent)

guidance: Cross-reference each lawful basis entry in the register to the specific purpose(s) listed under A.7.2.1 that it authorises.
Record the unique identifier or title of each purpose alongside the lawful basis entry, ensuring the link is clear and unambiguous.
Name the person responsible for maintaining these cross-links, identifying an individual rather than a team or department.
Document the date each cross-link was last reviewed or updated to show ongoing accuracy.
Avoid using generic or catch-all statements like "all purposes"—specify only the relevant purposes for each lawful basis.
properties.text: Purpose link (which A.7.2.1 purpose(s) this basis authorises)

guidance: List each processing activity involving special-category or criminal offence data in the Lawful Basis Register, referencing the relevant GDPR Article 9.2 or 10 basis.
Name the specific lawful basis used for each activity, citing the exact subparagraph (e.g., 9.2(a), 9.2(b)), not just "GDPR Art.9".
Record the decision date and the individual who approved the lawful basis for each special-category processing entry.
Attach supporting documentation or policy references that justify the chosen lawful basis for each processing activity.
Avoid using generic or catch-all justifications; specify the actual condition from Article 9.2 or 10 for every entry.
properties.text: Special-category basis where applicable (Art.9.2.a-j / Art.10 basis)

guidance: List each registered processing activity with its corresponding lawful basis and the date the basis was last reviewed or updated.
Confirm that supporting documentation for each lawful basis, such as consent forms or contractual clauses, is current and accessible.
Assign a named individual responsible for verifying the ongoing validity of each lawful basis, avoiding generic roles like "the team."
Record the outcome of the most recent review for each activity, including the review date and any changes made to the lawful basis.
Cross-reference each activity’s lawful basis with relevant legislation or guidance to demonstrate that the basis remains applicable.
properties.text: Basis currency — every registered activity still has a valid basis in force

guidance: Record the most recent review date of your Lawful Basis Program in a dated document or review log.
State the planned review interval for the Lawful Basis Program in a documented schedule or policy.
Confirm the next scheduled review date is within the documented planned interval and note this in the review log.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual, not a group or department, in the review documentation.
Attach evidence of the completed review, such as meeting minutes or a signed review summary, with a clear review date.
properties.text: Review date within the planned interval

guidance: Identify each legitimate interest activity by name and describe its purpose in a dated review log.
Document the current subject rights context, including any changes in law, guidance, or internal policy since the last review.
Record the outcome of a balancing test for each activity, stating whether the legitimate interest remains valid or requires adjustment.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual and record the date of their assessment for each activity.
Attach supporting evidence for each review, such as meeting minutes or signed decisions, rather than relying on verbal confirmation.
properties.text: LIA reaffirmation — sampled legitimate-interests activities reviewed against current subject-rights context

guidance: State the next planned review date for the Lawful Basis Program in a dedicated section of the review document.
Record the date in a way that is specific and unambiguous, using the full date format (day, month, year).
Name the person responsible for scheduling and carrying out the next review, listing their full name and job title.
Avoid leaving the review date field blank or marked "TBD," as auditors will flag missing or vague dates.
properties.text: Next planned review date stated

guidance: Name the reviewer as a specific individual, listing both the Data Protection Officer and the designated legal counsel by full name and job title.
Record the date each reviewer completed their assessment on the Lawful Basis Program Review document.
Obtain signatures or written confirmation from both the Data Protection Officer and legal counsel to evidence their review and approval.
Attach any correspondence or meeting notes that show both reviewers participated in the review process.
properties.text: Reviewer identity (DPO + legal counsel)

guidance: Identify all processing activities involving special-category or criminal offence data, listing each activity in a dated inventory reviewed within the last 12 months.
Document the lawful basis under GDPR Article 6 and the additional condition under Article 9 or 10 for each processing activity, citing specific legal grounds.
Cross-reference each processing activity to supporting evidence, such as consent records or statutory obligations, ensuring documentation is not generic or boilerplate.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual who confirmed dual-basis coverage, avoiding group or department-level attribution.
Retain a signed and dated record of the latest program review, including any updates or changes to lawful basis decisions.
properties.text: Special-category audit — dual-basis coverage confirmed where Art.9/10 data processed

guidance: List each jurisdiction where personal data is processed or stored in a dated register, naming the country, state, or region specifically.
Document the lawful basis or consent model used for processing personal data in each jurisdiction, referencing the relevant legal article or statute.
Assign a named individual responsible for maintaining and updating the jurisdictional register, avoiding generic titles like "the team" or "compliance department".
Cross-reference each jurisdiction’s entry with supporting evidence, such as privacy notices, consent forms, or contractual clauses, to show alignment with stated legal bases.
Review and update the register at least annually, recording the review date and the name of the reviewer.
properties.text: Per-jurisdiction basis catalog (Art.6.1 GDPR / CCPA opt-out model / LGPD Art.7)

guidance: Name a specific individual responsible for maintaining the list of applicable jurisdictions and legal bases, avoiding generic titles like "the team" or "compliance department".
Document each new jurisdiction or regulation added to your operations with the date of entry and the triggering event.
Record the legal basis for processing personal data in each jurisdiction, referencing the relevant law or regulation by name and section.
Review and update the list whenever a new geography is entered or a new regulation is enacted, and keep a dated change log for each update.
Retain evidence of periodic reviews, such as a signed and dated summary from the responsible individual at least annually.
properties.text: Trigger list (new geo entry, new regulation enacted)

guidance: List all countries or regions where your organisation collects, processes, or stores personal data in a dated document.
State the legal basis for each jurisdiction, specifying whether it is due to establishment, targeting residents, or monitoring behaviour.
Name a specific individual responsible for maintaining and updating the list of applicable jurisdictions.
Attach supporting evidence, such as contracts or business registration documents, to justify inclusion of each jurisdiction.
Avoid using generic terms like "global" or "all markets"—specify each jurisdiction by name.
properties.text: Applicable jurisdictions listed (with basis for each — establishment / target-market / monitoring)

guidance: List all jurisdictions where personal data processing occurs, naming each country or region in a dated register maintained by the privacy team.
Identify and document the legal bases for processing personal data in each jurisdiction, referencing specific laws or regulations for each entry.
Compare requirements across jurisdictions for each processing activity, and record the most restrictive rule that applies in a written summary.
Name the individual responsible for maintaining and updating the overlap rules, avoiding generic titles like "the team" or "Compliance Department."
Approve the documented most-restrictive-basis policy with a dated signature from a designated decision-maker.
properties.text: Overlap rules — where an activity spans jurisdictions, most-restrictive-basis policy documented

guidance: Identify the age of digital consent for each relevant jurisdiction using official government or regulatory sources, and record these thresholds in a dated table.
Document the process for verifying a data subject’s age and obtaining parental consent when required, including responsible roles and step-by-step actions.
Name the owner of the consent determination procedure as a specific individual, not a team or department, in the procedure document.
Attach a sample completed parental consent form, showing the jurisdiction, date, and signatures of both parent and child where applicable.
Review and update the procedure annually, recording the review date and the name of the reviewer in the document revision history.
properties.text: Children-consent overlay — parental consent thresholds per jurisdiction (age of consent varies GDPR Art.8)

guidance: Document each consent collection method by channel, specifying whether it is a web form, mobile app, physical form, or verbal recording, in a dated procedure file.
Name the person responsible for overseeing consent collection for each channel, listing them as a specific individual rather than a team or department.
Attach sample evidence for each channel, such as screenshots of web forms, photos of physical forms, or audio files for verbal consent.
State the date each consent mechanism was last reviewed or updated, and record this in the procedure documentation.
properties.text: Collection mechanism per channel (web form / mobile app / physical form / verbal with recording)

guidance: Document a written procedure that explains how consent requests are separated from service access, except where consent is strictly necessary for delivery.
Name the individual responsible for reviewing and approving all consent language to ensure compliance with the no-bundling rule.
Record examples of consent forms or online flows showing that optional consents are not pre-ticked or required for basic service access.
State in the procedure that any exception to the no-bundling rule must be justified in writing, with a clear explanation of necessity.
Avoid using generic statements like "consent is required for all services" without specific justification, as auditors will flag this as non-compliant.
properties.text: No-bundling rule — consent not conditioned on service delivery except where genuinely necessary

guidance: Name the owner of the Consent Determination Procedure as a specific individual, listing both the Data Protection Officer and a Product or UX lead.
Record the full names, job titles, and contact details of the named owners in the procedure document.
Date the procedure document to show when the ownership was last reviewed or updated.
Obtain a signed confirmation from both the DPO and Product/UX lead acknowledging their responsibility for the procedure.
properties.text: Named owner (DPO + Product / UX)

guidance: Document the consent determination procedure, clearly describing how consent is obtained, recorded, and withdrawn, with version control and approval date.
State the criteria used to judge if consent is freely given, specific, unambiguous, and based on a clear affirmative act, with examples.
Name the individual responsible for reviewing and updating the consent determination procedure—do not list a team or department.
Retain sample consent records demonstrating the procedure in action, showing explicit user action and clear language for each consent type.
Cross-reference the procedure to the relevant privacy notice and data processing activities to show alignment with actual data collection practices.
properties.rationale: §7.2.4 implementation — consent should be freely given, specific, unambiguous, explicit
properties.text: Consent-quality standard (freely given / specific / unambiguous / clear affirmative act)

guidance: Document the procedure for obtaining explicit consent for processing health or biometric data, including the exact wording used to inform individuals.
Record the date, time, and method of each explicit consent obtained, linking it to the relevant data subject and processing activity.
Name the individual responsible for managing and reviewing explicit consent records, ensuring this is a specific person, not a team or department.
Retain copies of all explicit consent forms or digital confirmations, ensuring each is signed or otherwise clearly affirmed by the data subject.
Review all consent records at regular intervals and document the results, noting any withdrawals or updates to consent status.
properties.text: Special-category explicit-consent overlay (Art.9.2.a explicit consent for health/biometric)

guidance: List each processing activity and clearly state if and when consent is required, referencing the relevant legal or contractual basis for each.
Document the specific catalog or regulation (such as GDPR Article 6 or local law) that determines the consent requirement for every activity.
Assign a named individual responsible for reviewing and updating these consent determinations, not a team or department.
Record the date of each determination and any subsequent updates in a version-controlled register.
properties.text: When-consent-required rules per activity (basis catalog references — see A.7.2.2)

guidance: Capture a screenshot of the exact user interface where individuals provide consent, including all visible text and options.
Save the full text presented to users at the time of consent, showing wording, choices, and any linked policies.
Record the version number or date of the consent mechanism displayed, matching it to the screenshot and text.
Name the person responsible for maintaining and updating the consent mechanism artifact register as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Store each consent artifact snapshot with a timestamp and reference to the system or process where it was used.
properties.text: Consent artifact snapshot (text + UI screenshot + version)

guidance: Record the specific channel used to collect consent for each entry, such as "web signup," "iOS app onboarding," or "support-call recording opt-in."
Cross-reference each consent record with a timestamp and user identifier to enable traceability back to the original consent event.
Name the channel clearly for each row—avoid generic labels like "online" or "app" that do not distinguish between different consent mechanisms.
Document the person responsible for maintaining the register, listing their full name and role, not just a department or team.
Retain evidence of any changes to channel identifiers in the register, including the date and person making the update.
properties.text: Channel identifier per row (web signup / iOS app onboarding / support-call recording opt-in)

guidance: Record the effective date for each version of every consent mechanism artifact in the register.
Assign a unique version number to each artifact entry alongside its effective date.
Document the name of the individual who approved the effective date for each artifact version.
Avoid listing artifact versions without a specific effective date—do not use placeholders like "TBD" or leave the field blank.
properties.text: Effective date per artifact version

guidance: Cross-reference each consent entry in the register to the specific, numbered purpose from your A.7.2.1 purposes list that it authorises.
Record the date and method by which each consent was obtained, linking it to the relevant purpose in your documentation.
Name the individual responsible for maintaining the consent register, ensuring this is a specific person rather than a team or department.
Review the register to confirm that no consent entry lacks a clear, direct link to an approved purpose from A.7.2.1.
properties.text: Purpose link (which A.7.2.1 purposes this consent authorises)

guidance: Name the Data Protection Officer and Legal representative who reviewed each consent mechanism artifact version, listing full names and job titles.
Record the date each artifact version was reviewed and approved by both the Data Protection Officer and Legal representative.
Obtain and retain signatures from both the Data Protection Officer and Legal representative on each artifact version approval record.
Avoid using generic titles or group names; specify individual approvers for each artifact version to prevent audit findings of unclear accountability.
properties.text: DPO + Legal signoff per artifact version

guidance: Assign a named individual to conduct a user experience review for each new or updated consent mechanism version.
Document review notes that specifically address the presence or absence of dark patterns in the consent interface.
Record the date of each UX review and the version number of the consent mechanism being assessed.
Attach evidence of any changes made to the consent mechanism in response to UX review findings.
Name the reviewer as a specific person—do not use generic roles like "the team" or "UX department".
properties.text: UX review notes per version (dark-pattern check)

guidance: Select a random sample of completed consent forms from the past year and record their unique identifiers in a review log.
Document the quality standard used for consent forms, including version and approval date, in the review log.
Compare each sampled consent form against the documented quality standard and note any deviations or deficiencies in the review log.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual, not a group or department, and record the review date for each consent form.
Sign and date a summary report of the review findings, including any corrective actions taken or recommended.
properties.text: Artifact audit — sampled consent forms reviewed against quality standard

guidance: Document the process used to determine user age before collecting personal data, including screenshots or workflow diagrams showing age-gate steps.
Record the date and outcome of the most recent test of age-gate functionality, including any issues found and actions taken.
Name the individual responsible for maintaining and monitoring the age-gate mechanism, listing their full name and job title.
Retain evidence of parental consent obtained for users below the age of consent, such as completed consent forms or system logs.
State the specific age threshold used and reference the applicable legal requirement, avoiding generic or missing age values.
properties.text: Children-consent audit — age-gates functioning where age-of-consent applies

guidance: Record the most recent review date of the Consent Determination Program in a dated entry within your compliance tracking system.
State the planned review interval for the program in a documented schedule or policy, referencing the specific time frame (e.g., annually).
Confirm that the actual review date falls within the documented planned interval by cross-referencing the review date and the schedule.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual in the review record, avoiding generic titles like "the team" or "management".
properties.text: Review date within the planned interval

guidance: State the next planned review date for the Consent Determination Program in the review document, using a clear and specific calendar date.
Record the name of the individual responsible for scheduling and conducting the next review, not just a team or department.
Confirm that the stated review date is no more than one year from the current review date, unless justified and documented.
Retain the signed approval of the current review, showing agreement on the next planned review date.
properties.text: Next planned review date stated

guidance: Document each service and its required consents in a dated register, showing that no service access is conditional on unrelated consent.
Cross-reference user journey screens or consent forms to confirm that consent requests are clearly separated and not bundled.
Name the reviewer who performed the regression check, including the review date and any identified issues or exceptions.
Attach screenshots or extracts from live systems demonstrating that users can access services without providing unrelated consents.
Specify any changes made since the last review, avoiding generic statements like "no changes" without supporting evidence.
properties.text: No-bundling regression check — no service gated behind unrelated consent

guidance: Name the reviewer for each Consent Determination Program Review as a specific individual from DPO, UX, and Legal teams.
Record the full names and roles of all reviewers in the review meeting minutes or on the review sign-off sheet.
Confirm the date each reviewer participated in the review by including a dated signature or electronic approval next to their name.
Avoid listing groups or departments as reviewers; always specify named individuals to prevent ambiguity.
properties.text: Reviewer identity (DPO + UX + Legal)

guidance: List all situations where consent is required, such as new marketing programmes or sensitive data collection, in a dated scope document.
Document a trigger list that prompts review of consent needs whenever a new data processing activity is proposed.
Assign a named individual to review and update the trigger list at least annually, recording the review date and outcome.
Name the owner as a specific person, not a generic role or department, to avoid auditor concerns about accountability.
properties.text: Trigger list (new marketing programme, new sensitive data collection)

guidance: Identify each country or jurisdiction where you collect or process children's personal data and record them in a dated scope document.
Research and document the legal age-of-consent threshold for each listed jurisdiction, referencing the specific law or regulation.
Name the individual responsible for maintaining and updating the consent age mapping, ensuring a specific person is listed rather than a team or department.
Cross-reference your documented age-of-consent thresholds with your consent collection process to confirm alignment for each jurisdiction.
Retain evidence of your legal research sources, such as government websites or legal counsel opinions, with access dates clearly noted.
properties.text: Per-jurisdiction age-of-consent thresholds

guidance: List all activities where personal data processing requires consent, such as marketing communications, non-essential cookies, research participation, and processing children’s data.
Document the legal or regulatory basis for requiring consent for each identified activity, referencing relevant laws or standards.
Name the specific individual responsible for maintaining and updating the consent-required activity list, not a team or department.
Record the date of the most recent review or update to the consent-required activity list.
Retain supporting evidence, such as consent forms or system screenshots, showing how consent is collected for each listed activity.
properties.text: Consent-required activity list (marketing / cookies non-essential / research participation / children)

guidance: List all processing activities involving health, biometric, genetic, criminal, or children's data, including a named owner and processing purpose for each.
Document the specific legal basis for each activity, citing GDPR Article 9.2 subsection or explicit consent, with a dated record.
Attach copies of explicit consent forms or records for each activity where consent is the basis, showing date and individual’s signature or digital confirmation.
Name the legal basis owner as a specific individual, not a team or department, to avoid auditor rejection of unclear accountability.
Cross-reference each processing activity to its consent or legal basis evidence in your data processing register.
properties.text: Special-category consent map — health / biometric / genetic / criminal / children require explicit consent unless another Art.9.2 basis applies

guidance: Document the process for handling data subject requests for proof of consent, including required response timelines and responsible roles, in a dated procedure.
Assign a named individual as the consent record custodian, ensuring their name and contact details appear in the procedure documentation.
Record each consent retrieval request and its fulfillment date in a log, cross-referencing the original consent record provided to the requester.
State the service level agreement (SLA) for responding to consent proof requests in the procedure, specifying the maximum allowed response time in days.
Avoid using generic or template procedures; tailor the process to your organisation and include at least one real example of a fulfilled request.
properties.text: Demonstration pathway — subject requests proof of consent, org retrieves record within stated SLA

guidance: Document the process for offering individuals a genuine choice to give or withhold consent, including clear language that refusal will not affect service access.
Record a dated example of a consent request form or screen showing that consent is not bundled with unrelated terms or conditions.
State explicitly in the procedure that declining consent does not result in denial of core services or negative consequences.
Name the owner responsible for reviewing consent mechanisms as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Retain evidence of periodic reviews confirming that consent requests remain separate from other agreements and are not presented as mandatory.
properties.text: Freely-given test — no detriment for refusal, no bundled coercion

guidance: List all types of personal data collected and the purposes for processing in a written notice provided to individuals before requesting their consent.
Document the method and date each individual received the pre-consent information, such as through an email, web page, or printed form.
Name the person or role responsible for maintaining and updating the pre-consent information to ensure it aligns with current processing activities.
Attach a copy of the actual pre-consent information delivered, showing it covers all points required by section 7.3.3, including data subject rights and contact details.
Avoid using generic or template notices that are not tailored to your organisation’s specific data processing activities.
properties.rationale: §7.2.4 — information delivered before consent process should follow guidance in 7.3.3
properties.text: Pre-consent information delivery per §7.3.3 (linked to A.7.3.3)

guidance: Document each consent record with the subject's unique identifier, the exact date and time consent was given, and the specific purposes agreed to.
Record the version number or date of the consent form or privacy notice that was presented at the time of consent.
Specify the exact mechanism used to collect consent, such as web form, paper form, or verbal agreement, in each record.
Name the individual responsible for maintaining consent records, avoiding generic labels like "the team" or "admin staff."
Cross-reference each consent entry with the corresponding data processing activity to confirm alignment with stated purposes.
properties.text: Per-consent record fields (subject identifier + timestamp + purposes consented to + artifact version consented to + collection mechanism)

guidance: Document each consent request with a clear description of the specific purpose for which personal data will be processed.
Present individuals with separate consent options for each distinct processing purpose, allowing granular selection rather than a single blanket agreement.
Record the date, time, and method by which each individual provided consent for each specific purpose in a consent log.
Name the person responsible for maintaining and updating the consent records as a specific individual, not a generic team or department.
Retain evidence of the consent form or interface as presented to the individual, showing the per-purpose selection options.
properties.text: Specific test — one consent per purpose (or granular per-purpose selection)

guidance: Document the consent process showing users must actively select or click to give consent, with no pre-ticked boxes or default acceptance.
Capture and retain a dated record of each user's affirmative consent action, such as a checkbox selection or digital signature.
State in the procedure that silence, inactivity, or use of a service does not count as consent, with clear examples.
Name the procedure owner as a specific individual responsible for maintaining and updating the consent capture process.
properties.text: Unambiguous test — clear affirmative action, no pre-ticked boxes, no consent by silence

guidance: Document the exact location of the withdrawal pathway link within the consent capture process, including a screenshot and URL or interface reference.
Cross-reference the withdrawal pathway link in your consent recording procedure, citing the relevant section of ISO27701:2019 §7.3.4.
Name the person responsible for maintaining the withdrawal pathway link and updating procedures when changes occur.
Confirm that the withdrawal pathway link is active and functional by recording the date and result of the most recent test.
Avoid using generic or placeholder links; provide a working, organisation-specific withdrawal pathway that users can access directly.
properties.text: Withdrawal pathway link (per §7.3.4 modify/withdraw consent)

guidance: Record the exact version number or date of the consent statement each individual agreed to in a dedicated column of the register.
Cross-reference each consent entry to the corresponding row in the A.7.2.3 register, using a unique identifier or direct link.
Name the data subject for each row as a specific individual, not as a group or generic label.
Retain a timestamp for when consent was captured, ensuring it matches the version of the consent statement presented at that time.
Document any updates to the consent statement and verify that new consents reference the updated version in the register.
properties.text: Artifact version consented to per row (link to A.7.2.3 register)

guidance: Record the collection channel for each consent entry in the register, specifying whether it was web, mobile, paper, or verbal.
Name the individual responsible for maintaining the register, ensuring a specific person is listed rather than a team or department.
Date each consent entry to show when the consent was obtained and through which channel.
Cross-reference each consent record with the related data processing activity or system, allowing for clear traceability.
Retain supporting evidence for verbal or paper consents, such as audio files or scanned forms, linked to the corresponding register entry.
properties.text: Collection channel per row (web / mobile / paper / verbal)

guidance: Assign a unique consent event ID to each row in the register, using a sequential or system-generated identifier that cannot be reused.
Record the date and time each consent was captured alongside the unique event ID for clear traceability.
Name the data subject and the specific processing activity linked to each consent event ID in the register.

guidance: Document each system, authorised user group, and third party that receives or processes personal data covered by consent, listing them in a dated register.

properties.text: Downstream propagation — withdrawal cascades to systems + authorised users + third parties (see A.7.3.7)

guidance: Record each consent withdrawal in the register with the specific channel used, such as email, web form, phone call, or in-person request.

guidance: Record the date and time each consent modification or withdrawal is logged in the register.

guidance: Record the unique identifier for each data subject in a dedicated column for every consent modification or withdrawal entry.

guidance: Record the exact date and time for each consent modification or withdrawal entry in the register.

guidance: List each communication channel where individuals can withdraw consent, such as email, web form, or phone, in a dated register.

guidance: Record the date of the most recent Withdrawal Program Review in a central log, clearly showing when the review took place.
