Record the specific updates made to the DLP baseline, ruleset, or procedures, including the date and a brief description of each change.
Publish the updated DLP documentation to all relevant staff and confirm distribution with a dated communication record.
Avoid using generic statements like "procedures updated as needed"—list concrete changes linked to review findings.
properties.text: Baseline / ruleset / procedure updates published from findings

guidance: List all communication channels and platforms currently in use, including any added since the last review, in a dated inventory document.
Cross-reference each channel and platform against your Data Loss Prevention (DLP) coverage matrix to identify any missing coverage.
Record the results of the gap check in a review log, naming the reviewer and date of completion.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual responsible for the gap check, not a group or department.
Document any newly identified channels or platforms lacking DLP measures and assign follow-up actions with deadlines.
properties.text: Channel-coverage gap check (new channel / new platform missing)

guidance: Record the date of each Data Loss Prevention (DLP) program review in a central log, showing the most recent review occurred within the last 180 days.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual responsible for the DLP program review, not a group or department.
Retain the signed or approved review summary document, including the date and any follow-up actions identified.
Cross-reference the review date against your documented review schedule to confirm the interval does not exceed 180 days.
properties.text: Review date within the planned interval (≤180 days)

guidance: List all current data loss prevention (DLP) exceptions in a dated inventory, including the original approval date and reason for each exception.
Assign a named individual to review each exception for continued relevance and risk, recording their name and the review date.
Document a clear decision for each exception—either re-confirmed with justification or marked for retirement—with supporting evidence or rationale.
Update the inventory to show the status of each exception as "active" or "retired," including the date of status change.
Name the reviewer as a specific person—do not use generic roles or teams as the responsible party.
properties.text: Exception inventory re-confirmed / retired

guidance: State the next planned review date for the Data Loss Prevention (DLP) program in the official review schedule document.
Record the date the review schedule was last updated, including the name of the person who made the update.
Name the responsible individual for scheduling and conducting the next DLP program review, not just a team or department.
Retain a copy of the most recent DLP program review meeting minutes that reference the agreed next review date.
properties.text: Next planned review date stated

guidance: Name the DLP program review lead, Data Protection officer, and Information Security manager as specific individuals in the review documentation.
Record the full names and job titles of each reviewer in the DLP program review meeting minutes or summary report.
Confirm each reviewer’s participation by collecting their dated signatures or written acknowledgments on the final review document.
Avoid listing groups or teams as reviewers; always identify individuals responsible for the review.
properties.text: Reviewer identity (DLP lead + Data Protection + InfoSec)

guidance: Document the true-positive rate for each review period in a dated record, showing the number of true positives versus total alerts.
Chart the true-positive rate trend across multiple review periods in a single visual, such as a line graph, with clear date labels.
Name the reviewer who validated the true-positive rate calculations for each period, using their full name and review date.
Attach supporting evidence, such as sample alert logs or case summaries, to demonstrate how true positives were identified and confirmed.
Record any changes made to detection rules or processes between review periods, linking them to observed changes in the true-positive rate.
properties.text: True-positive rate trending (detection effectiveness)

guidance: State in the backup procedure that all backup data must be encrypted both when stored and during transfer.
Name the encryption methods and tools used for backup data, referencing specific technologies and versions in the procedure.
Cross-reference the procedure to the relevant section of your cryptography policy that covers encryption requirements, including A.8.24.
Assign a named individual responsible for verifying encryption is applied to all backups, not just "the team" or "IT".
Record the date of the last review and approval of the backup procedure, signed by the designated owner.
properties.text: Encryption of backups at rest + in transit (cross-link to A.8.24)

guidance: List each asset class in the backup procedure, specifying the required backup frequency for each one.
Document the rationale for each backup frequency, referencing the relevant recovery point objective (RPO) for that asset class.
Record the date and name of the person who approved the backup frequencies for all asset classes.
Name the owner of the backup procedure as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Attach evidence of the most recent review of backup frequencies, showing the review date and reviewer’s name.
properties.text: Frequency per asset class (continuous / hourly / daily / weekly aligned to RPO)

guidance: Name the procedure owner as a specific individual, such as "Jane Smith, Backup Operations Lead," in the header of the Information Backup Procedure document.
Document the Infrastructure partner’s name and contact details alongside the procedure owner within the procedure.
Record the date the procedure owner was assigned responsibility in the document’s revision history table.
Avoid listing the owner as "the team" or "IT department"; use only named individuals to ensure clear accountability.
properties.text: Named procedure owner (Backup Operations lead with Infrastructure partner)

guidance: Record the exact date each restore test is performed in the Restore Test Register.
Name the individual responsible for conducting each restore test alongside the test date.
Attach supporting evidence, such as screenshots or logs, showing the date of each restore test completion.
Avoid using vague timeframes like "monthly" or "recent"—always enter a specific calendar date for each test.
properties.text: Per-test date

guidance: Record the date, scope, and outcome of each restore test in the Restore Test Register, including whether recovery objectives were met.
Document any issues or failures identified during the restore test, describing what went wrong and the impact.
State the corrective actions assigned for each missed target, naming the responsible individual and setting a due date.
Attach evidence of follow-up, such as updated procedures or confirmation of retest, to show corrective actions were completed.
Name the owner of each test and action as a specific individual, not a team or department.
properties.text: Per-test findings + corrective actions where target missed

guidance: Record the date, time, and location of each restore test in the Restore Test Register.
Document the specific integrity verification method used for each restore test, such as checksum, hash comparison, or functional test.
Attach or reference the actual integrity verification artefact (e.g., hash output file, test results) for each restore test entry.
Name the individual who performed and validated the integrity verification for each restore test, ensuring a specific person is listed.
Confirm that each restore test entry is complete and not missing the integrity-verification artefact, as auditors will flag incomplete records.
properties.text: Per-test integrity-verification artefact (checksum / hash / functional test of restored data)

guidance: Record the date, time, and system or data set involved for each restore test in the Restore Test Register.
Document the outcome of each test as "success," "partial," or "failure" with a brief description of any issues encountered.
Name the individual who performed and validated each restore test, ensuring a specific person is listed rather than a team or department.
Retain supporting evidence for each test, such as screenshots or logs, and cross-reference these in the register entry.
properties.text: Per-test outcome (success / partial / failure)

guidance: Record the date and time of each restore test alongside the system or dataset name in the Restore Test Register.
State the Recovery Point Objective (RPO) for each system or dataset tested, matching the value to your documented backup policy.
Confirm and mark in the register whether the data restored during each test met the stated RPO, using a clear "yes" or "no" flag.
Name the individual who verified the RPO was met for each test, avoiding generic entries like "IT team" or "admin".
Retain supporting evidence for each test, such as screenshots or logs, cross-referenced to the corresponding register entry.
properties.text: Per-test RPO-met flag (data-recoverable-to-RPO confirmed; auditor-critical proof parallels A.5.30 rec_success_status)

guidance: Record each backup restore test with the specific system, dataset, or configuration targeted, including test date and responsible person.
Document the outcome of each restore test, noting whether the backup was successfully restored to its intended target.
Name the backup target in clear, specific terms—avoid vague labels like "production" or "main system" that could apply to multiple assets.
Retain evidence of the restore process, such as screenshots, logs, or completion reports, attached to each test entry in the register.
properties.text: Per-test backup target tested (system / dataset / configuration)

guidance: Assign a unique identifier to each restore test entry in the register before conducting the test.
Record the unique identifier alongside the test date, system restored, and responsible person for each entry.
Cross-reference the unique identifier in all related test documentation, such as test results and issue logs.
Avoid reusing or leaving identifiers blank—each test must have its own distinct, non-empty identifier.
properties.text: Per-test unique identifier

guidance: State the restore-test frequency for each asset class in the backup procedure, specifying annual minimum and quarterly for tier-1 assets.
Name the person responsible for scheduling and overseeing restore tests for each asset class within the procedure.
Record the date of the last restore test for each asset class in a table or log included in the procedure.
Avoid using vague terms like "regularly" or "as needed"—clearly define the exact cadence for each asset class.
properties.text: Restore-test cadence stated per asset class (annual minimum; quarterly for tier-1)

guidance: List each information asset class in a table within the backup procedure, including examples such as email, databases, and user files.
State the specific retention period for backups of each asset class, using clear timeframes such as "30 days" or "7 years."
Name the person or role responsible for approving and reviewing retention periods, ensuring it is a named individual, not a generic team or department.
Record the date of the last review and approval of the retention periods in the backup procedure document.
Cross-reference the retention periods in the backup procedure with your organisation’s data retention policy to confirm alignment.
properties.text: Retention period per asset class (drives storage cost + recovery range)

guidance: Record the most recent backup program review date in a log or register, clearly showing when the review took place.
State the planned review interval for the backup program in a documented schedule or policy.
Confirm that the actual review date falls within the documented planned interval, and note any deviations with an explanation.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual, not a group or department, in the review record.
Retain the signed or approved review outcome as evidence of completion.
properties.text: Review date within the planned interval

guidance: State the next planned review date for the backup program in the documented review schedule.
Record the date in a version-controlled document or calendar entry that is accessible to relevant stakeholders.
Name the individual responsible for scheduling and conducting the next review, not just a team or department.
Cross-reference the stated date with meeting minutes or approval records from the most recent backup program review.
properties.text: Next planned review date stated

guidance: Document each backup program review finding in a dated record, clearly describing the issue and recommended change.
Assign responsibility for each finding to a named individual, not a group or department, for follow-up action.
Update relevant backup procedures or scope documents to reflect changes, referencing the specific review finding and date.
Retain evidence of communication showing that updated procedures were shared with all affected staff.
properties.text: Findings propagated to procedure / scope

guidance: Name the reviewer for Backup Operations as a specific individual, not a team or department, in the review record.
Record the full name and job title of the Infrastructure reviewer in the documented backup program review.
Document the InfoSec reviewer's identity, including date of review, in the signed backup program review log.
Cross-reference the review record with supporting evidence, such as meeting minutes or approval emails, showing each named reviewer participated.
properties.text: Reviewer identity (Backup Operations + Infrastructure + InfoSec)

guidance: List all systems currently in scope for backup, including any new systems added since the last review, in a dated inventory document.
Cross-reference each in-scope system against the backup program documentation to confirm inclusion and coverage.
Record the date and outcome of the most recent backup program review, specifically noting any new systems and their backup status.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual responsible for confirming scope completeness, not a team or department.
Retain evidence of any updates made to the backup program as a result of the review, such as revised schedules or procedures.
properties.text: Scope-completeness check (new in-scope system covered)

guidance: Record the dates and results of each restore test for every backup tier, showing that tests were performed according to the defined schedule.
Document the actual restore point achieved in each test and compare it to the required recovery point objective (RPO) for that tier.
Name the individual responsible for overseeing restore tests for each backup tier, rather than listing a team or department.
Retain evidence of any failed restore tests and the corrective actions taken, including dates and responsible persons.
Confirm that restore test records are reviewed and signed off by management after each testing cycle.
properties.text: Restore-test attainment per tier (cadence met, RPO met)

guidance: Assign a named individual to lead the periodic review of backup strategies for ransomware resilience, listing them with contact details in the review record.
Document the date, attendees, and summary of the most recent backup program review, specifically addressing immutability, air-gap, and 3-2-1 adequacy.
State any changes made to backup controls or procedures as a result of the review, including rationale and approval by a named decision-maker.
Record evidence that backup test restores were performed since the last review, noting dates and outcomes for each test.
Name the current backup strategy explicitly; avoid using generic terms like "industry standard" or "best practice" without describing your actual implementation.
properties.text: Threat-posture review (ransomware-resilience: immutability / air-gap / 3-2-1 still adequate)

guidance: Cross-reference each system's Recovery Point Objective (RPO) from the Business Impact Analysis (BIA) with the documented backup schedule in the procedure.
State the backup frequency for each system in the procedure, ensuring it meets or exceeds the RPO identified in the BIA.
Name the individual responsible for reviewing and updating backup schedules when BIA RPOs change, rather than listing a team or department.
Record the date of the most recent alignment check between BIA RPOs and backup frequencies within the procedure document.
Attach or link the relevant BIA summary for each system to the backup procedure as supporting evidence of RPO requirements.
properties.text: RPO alignment with A.5.30 ICT readiness (each system's BIA RPO ≤ backup frequency)

guidance: List all information types, software, and systems included in backup, specifying each by name and location in the backup procedure document.
Assign a backup frequency tier to each class of information, software, and system, recording the schedule in a dated table or matrix.
Name the backup procedure owner as a specific individual, not a team or department, in the procedure document.
Cross-reference each item in the scope to its corresponding backup job or process, including job IDs or automation references where applicable.
Record the date of the last procedure review and the reviewer’s name in the procedure document.
properties.text: Scope — which information, software, systems are backed up (with frequency tier per class)

guidance: List all current systems, applications, and data sources included in your backup scope, with named owners and last review dates.
Document a trigger list that requires immediate backup scope review when adding a new system, changing Recovery Point Objectives, or onboarding a new vendor.
Assign responsibility for monitoring trigger events to a specific individual, not a team or department, and record their name in the backup policy.
Record each backup scope review decision with the date, reason for review, and names of participants in a version-controlled register.
Cross-reference the trigger list and backup scope in your change management records to show prompt action when a trigger event occurs.
properties.text: Trigger list for re-scoping (new system, RPO change, new vendor)

guidance: List all information assets and systems, marking those excluded from backup with a clear identifier in your backup scope document.
State a specific reason for each exclusion, such as "ephemeral data," "reconstructable from source," or "publicly available," in a dated rationale log.
Name the individual who approved each exclusion, avoiding generic titles like "IT team" or "management," and record their approval date.
Attach supporting evidence, such as system architecture diagrams or data flow maps, that demonstrate why excluded data does not require backup.
Review and update the exclusion list at least annually, recording the review date and reviewer’s name in your backup documentation.
properties.text: Exclusion rationale where backup not required (ephemeral / reconstructable / public)

guidance: List all systems and datasets that require backup, referencing the outputs from your A.5.30 Business Impact Analysis.
Assign a Recovery Point Objective (RPO) tier to each system or dataset in a dedicated column, based on business needs.
Cross-reference each entry with the corresponding BIA record or identifier to show alignment between backup scope and impact analysis.
Name the responsible individual for maintaining this backup scope list, not just a team or department.
Date and version the backup scope document to confirm it reflects the most current BIA results.
properties.text: Systems / datasets enumerated with RPO tier per row (drawn from A.5.30 BIA)

guidance: List all systems and data types in your environment, marking which are backed up by your vendors and which are your responsibility.
Document the specific vendor names and contract references for each system or dataset where backup is handled externally.
State in your backup scope record that vendor-managed backups are excluded, with a cross-reference to the relevant supplier obligation controls (A.5.19/A.5.21).
Name the individual responsible for maintaining the backup scope, avoiding generic roles like "IT team" or "Operations".
Attach the latest signed supplier agreements that explicitly mention backup responsibilities and obligations.
properties.text: Vendor-managed backups delegated to A.5.19/A.5.21 supplier obligations

guidance: State in the backup procedure which storage separation method is used, such as offsite, air-gapped, or immutable storage.
Document how the 3-2-1 backup rule is implemented, specifying the number of copies, media types, and offsite location details.
Name the individual responsible for verifying storage separation, avoiding generic roles like "IT team" or "admins".
Record the date of the most recent successful test demonstrating that backups can be restored from the separated storage location.
Attach evidence, such as screenshots or logs, showing that backup copies exist in the designated separated storage.
properties.text: Storage separation (offsite OR air-gapped OR immutable-storage) — 3-2-1 rule applied

guidance: Name a specific individual responsible for planning and overseeing chaos-engineering or fault-injection exercises for high-criticality services.
Document the schedule and scope of each chaos-engineering or fault-injection exercise, including the date, systems tested, and scenarios used.
Record the outcomes, lessons learned, and any follow-up actions from each exercise in a dated report approved by the responsible individual.
Attach evidence of management review or sign-off for each completed exercise, such as a signed meeting note or email confirmation.
Avoid using generic or template exercise reports; tailor documentation to reflect the unique risks and architecture of your actual high-criticality services.
properties.text: Chaos-engineering / fault-injection practice for high-criticality services

guidance: List all critical services in a table, referencing the most recent Business Impact Analysis (BIA) for each entry.
State the specific availability requirement for each critical service, such as uptime percentage or maximum allowable downtime, with supporting BIA data.
Name the owner of each service as a specific individual, not a team or department, in the table.
Record the date when the redundancy baseline was last reviewed and approved by management, attaching the approval record.
Cross-reference each service entry to the relevant BIA section or page number to show the source of the availability requirement.
properties.text: Critical services enumerated with availability requirement per service (drawn from A.5.30 BIA)

guidance: Document the cloud-hosted services that require redundancy, listing each service and its current deployment architecture with date of assessment.
Record the specific regions and availability zones where each service is deployed, including screenshots or configuration exports as evidence.
Name the individual responsible for maintaining and reviewing the redundancy baseline, avoiding generic roles like "IT" or "the team".
Confirm that no critical service is deployed in a single availability zone by cross-referencing deployment records with the redundancy requirement.
Retain approval of the redundancy baseline by a named senior manager, including the date and version of the approved document.
properties.text: Cross-AZ / cross-region distribution for cloud-hosted services (modern baseline; single-AZ insufficient)

guidance: Document the list of all redundant components in your environment, including their locations and the systems they support, in an inventory record.
Assign a named individual responsible for monitoring each redundant component, specifying their name and contact details in the monitoring log.
Record the monitoring method and frequency for each component, including automated alerts or manual checks, in a dated monitoring procedure.
Capture and retain evidence of regular monitoring activity, such as system logs or monitoring reports, showing detection of failures before failover is required.
Name the owner as a specific individual for each redundant component — do not use generic terms like "IT team" or "Operations".
properties.text: Monitoring of redundant components — failures detected before failover need (no silent single-point loss)

guidance: List each critical service and specify its redundancy approach, such as active-active, active-passive, cold-standby, or multi-region, in a dated baseline document.
Name the responsible individual for maintaining and updating the redundancy baseline for each service, not just a team or department.
Record the last test date and outcome for each redundancy approach to demonstrate that the configuration is operational and sufficient.
Cross-reference the redundancy baseline with current architecture diagrams or system inventories to confirm accuracy and completeness.
properties.text: Redundancy approach per service (active-active / active-passive / cold-standby / multi-region)

guidance: Document the specific redundancy level provided for each service, clearly stating whether it is single-instance or has failover capability.
State the exact service level commitments regarding redundancy in the SLA, including any limitations or exclusions.
Cross-reference the SLA text with technical architecture diagrams or system inventories to confirm the described redundancy matches actual deployment.
Name the responsible individual who approved the SLA language, avoiding generic titles like "the team" or "IT department."
Retain a dated record of the final, agreed SLA version that was communicated to tenants.
properties.text: SLA implications documented (what tenants are promised — honest about redundant vs single-instance)

guidance: Reference the broader organisational recovery plan by title and version number within the failover procedure document.
Cross-link the failover procedure to the ICT readiness control (A.5.30) by including a specific section or appendix with relevant references.
Name the individual responsible for maintaining alignment between the failover procedure and the organisational recovery plan.
Avoid using generic statements such as “refer to recovery plan” without specifying the exact document and section referenced.
properties.text: Cross-link to A.5.30 ICT readiness — coordinated with broader recovery plan

guidance: Name a specific individual responsible for stakeholder communications during failover in the procedure, avoiding generic roles like "the team" or "IT department."
Document the exact methods and channels for notifying stakeholders, such as a public status page URL and customer email templates, within the procedure.
Record the timing and triggers for each communication step, including who approves sending notifications and when updates must be posted.
Retain copies of previous stakeholder notifications and status page updates from past failover events as evidence of execution.
properties.text: Stakeholder communications during failover (status page, customer notifications)

guidance: Document a step-by-step failback procedure that details how to safely return operations from the backup site to the primary site, including required checks.
Name the individual responsible for authorizing the failback process, listing their full name and job title in the procedure.
Record the date of the most recent test of the failback procedure, including the test results and any lessons learned.
State specific conditions that must be met before initiating failback, such as system integrity checks and confirmation of primary site readiness.
Avoid using generic statements like "reverse the failover steps"—provide tailored instructions specific to your environment.
properties.text: Failback procedure — return to primary after recovery (often more risky than failover)

guidance: Name the person or role with authority to invoke failover for each service in the procedure, specifying if the process is automated or manual.
Document the escalation path and contact details for on-call authority, including after-hours or emergency contacts, in the procedure.
State the date the failover authority list was last reviewed and updated, and include the reviewer’s name.
Avoid listing authority as "the team" or a department—identify a specific individual or named role for each service.
properties.text: Failover invocation authority per service (automated vs manual; on-call authority)

guidance: Name the Site Reliability lead and the Infrastructure partner as the specific owners at the top of the failover procedure document.
Record the date when the ownership assignment was last reviewed or updated in the document’s version history.
Avoid listing a team or department as the owner; use named individuals to ensure clear accountability.
Sign the procedure document by both named owners to confirm their acceptance of responsibility.
properties.text: Named procedure owner (Site Reliability lead with Infrastructure partner)

guidance: Document a separate failover runbook for each critical service, listing step-by-step actions, validation checks, and clear success criteria.
Assign a named individual as the owner of each runbook, avoiding generic roles like "IT team" or "Operations".
Record the date of the most recent test or walkthrough for each runbook, including the names of participants and test outcomes.
Cross-reference each runbook with the relevant business continuity plan section to show alignment and coverage.
State any known limitations or prerequisites for the failover process directly in the runbook, with version-specific details.
properties.text: Per-service failover runbook (steps, validation checks, success criteria)

guidance: Record the exact date each failover test is performed in the Failover Test Register.
Name the person responsible for entering the test date to allow traceability.
Cross-reference each test entry with supporting evidence, such as test logs or screenshots, that show the test date.
Avoid using vague timeframes like "monthly" or "Q1"—enter a specific calendar date for every test.
properties.text: Per-test date

guidance: Record the date, test scenario, and actual failover results for each test entry in the Failover Test Register.
Document any test where the recovery target was not met, including specific details of the missed objective.
List the corrective actions assigned for each failed test, naming the responsible individual and target completion date.
Attach evidence of corrective action completion, such as updated procedures or test rerun results, to the corresponding test entry.
Name the owner of each test as a specific individual, not a team or department, to avoid ambiguity in accountability.
properties.text: Per-test findings + corrective actions where target missed

guidance: Record each failover test with the test date, system tested, and the individual responsible for overseeing the test.
Document the outcome of each test as "success," "partial," or "failure" in the register, using clear and unambiguous language.
State the actual recovery time achieved for each test and compare it directly against the documented target recovery time.
Name the test owner as a specific individual for each entry—do not use generic roles or team names.
Retain supporting evidence for each test, such as logs or screenshots, alongside the register entry.
properties.text: Per-test outcome (success / partial / failure) + actual recovery time vs target

guidance: Record the name of each service tested in the Failover Test Register for every individual failover test entry.
State the date and time each failover test was performed alongside the corresponding service name in the register.
Name the person responsible for conducting or overseeing each failover test for every service, not just a generic team or department.
Cross-reference each test entry with supporting evidence, such as test logs or screenshots, to confirm the specific service tested.
properties.text: Per-test service tested

guidance: Assign a unique identifier to each failover test entry before the test begins, using a sequential or timestamp-based numbering system.
Record the unique identifier alongside the test date, test scope, and responsible individual in the Failover Test Register.
Cross-reference the unique identifier in all related test documentation, such as test plans, results, and incident logs.
Name the test owner as a specific individual for each entry, avoiding generic labels like "IT team" or "Operations".
properties.text: Per-test unique identifier

guidance: Record the type of each failover event in the register as "planned drill," "unplanned real," or "fault-injection" at the time of entry.
Name the person responsible for classifying the test type for each failover event, using their full name rather than a team or department.
Document the date and time each failover event was initiated, linking this information to the specific test type recorded.
Retain supporting evidence, such as test plans or incident reports, that clearly show the intent and context for each failover event type.
Review the register quarterly to confirm all entries have a clearly stated and accurate test type; flag and correct any missing or ambiguous classifications.
properties.text: Per-test type (planned drill / unplanned real / fault-injection)

guidance: Document the date and results of each redundancy program review in a central log, including any identified gaps or improvement areas.
Assign a named individual to update the baseline or runbook with specific changes resulting from the review findings.
Publish the revised baseline or runbook with a new version number and date, making it accessible to all relevant staff.
Record evidence that the updated baseline or runbook was communicated to all affected teams, such as an email distribution list or meeting minutes.
Name the owner responsible for approving runbook updates as a specific person, not a group or generic title.
properties.text: Baseline / runbook updates published from findings

guidance: Name the person responsible for the redundancy program review as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Cross-reference the most recent Business Impact Analysis (BIA) record, including its date and any documented availability-tier changes.
Document any changes in system or service availability tiers and explicitly state if these triggered a re-evaluation of redundancy measures.
Record the outcome of the redundancy approach re-evaluation, including the date, findings, and any actions taken or decisions made.
Retain meeting minutes or review notes that show the linkage between BIA updates and redundancy program adjustments.
properties.text: Cross-check with A.5.30 BIA (any availability-tier change → redundancy approach re-evaluation)

guidance: Record the most recent review date of the redundancy program in a dated log or register.
State the planned review interval for the redundancy program in a documented schedule or policy.
Confirm the next scheduled review date is within the documented interval by cross-referencing the last review date and the planned interval.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual, not a group or department, in the review documentation.
Retain evidence of the completed review, such as a signed review report or meeting minutes, with the review date clearly visible.
properties.text: Review date within the planned interval

guidance: State the next planned review date for the redundancy program in the most recent review report or meeting minutes.
Record the name of the individual responsible for scheduling the next review alongside the planned date.
Confirm the review date is specific and future-dated, not left as "TBD" or "annually" without a calendar date.
Retain a copy of the dated document where the next review date is clearly stated and approved.
properties.text: Next planned review date stated

guidance: Name each reviewer as a specific individual from Site Reliability, Infrastructure, and the relevant business-service owner in the review record.
Record the date each reviewer completed their review in the periodic redundancy program review log.
Retain evidence of each reviewer's input, such as comments or sign-off, attached to the review documentation.
Avoid listing groups or roles only; specify named persons to clearly show individual accountability.
properties.text: Reviewer identity (Site Reliability + Infrastructure + business-service owners)

guidance: List all current critical services in a dated inventory, including any new services added since the last review.
Remove any services from the inventory that have been retired, and record the date and reason for removal.
Confirm the updated critical-service list is reviewed and signed off by a named responsible manager.
Name the owner as a specific individual responsible for maintaining the critical-service list, not a generic team or department.
Retain the previous and current versions of the critical-service list to show changes made during the review.
properties.text: Critical-service list re-confirmed (new service in scope; retired service removed)

guidance: Document the date, scope, and results of each service failover test in a centralized log, including whether defined recovery targets were met.
Name the individual responsible for scheduling and overseeing each service's failover test, avoiding generic roles like "IT team."
Record evidence that failover tests occurred at the required intervals, such as calendar invites, meeting minutes, or system-generated test reports.
Retain signed management approval of test results and any remediation plans for services that did not meet recovery targets.
Cross-reference each service's test record with the documented test schedule to confirm that all required tests were performed on time.
properties.text: Failover-test attainment per service (cadence met; targets met)

guidance: Cross-reference your logging procedure to the monitoring process described under control A.8.16, showing how log data is actively analysed for security events.
Document the specific tools or methods used to review and analyse log data, including how alerts or anomalies are identified.

properties.text: Exclusion rationale (vendor-shipped code / generated code with documented review path)

guidance: List all programming languages currently used in your codebase, including versions, in a dated document maintained by your development lead.
Record the specific static analysis tools, linters, and formatters applied to each language, including tool versions and configuration files.
Name the individual responsible for maintaining and updating the secure coding tooling list; avoid generic roles like "the team" or "developers".
Cross-reference each language and tool pairing with evidence of recent scan or linting reports, showing active use within the last quarter.
Review and update the documented scope and tooling list at least annually, recording the date and approver of each review.
properties.text: Languages in use with tooling stack per language (SAST tool / linter / formatter)

guidance: Cross-reference each secure coding repository against your A.8.4 repository inventory and record the unique identifier for each in a dated list.
Name the specific individual responsible for maintaining the secure coding scope, avoiding generic roles like "the team" or "IT department".
Document the inclusion or exclusion rationale for each repository, with a brief justification and the date of the decision.
Retain a signed approval from a designated authority confirming the completeness and accuracy of the secure coding scope list.
properties.text: Repositories in scope (drawn from A.8.4 repo inventory)

guidance: Document the approved process for storing secrets in a secure vault, including the vault technology and access controls, in the Secure Coding Procedure.
Name the individual responsible for maintaining the secrets management process, avoiding generic titles like "the team" or "developers".
Record the configuration and usage of automated pre-commit scanning tools that detect secrets in code, including tool names and activation dates.
Retain logs or reports from pre-commit scanning runs that show detection and blocking of secrets before code is committed to repositories.
State in the procedure that secrets must never be hardcoded in source code, referencing specific examples or past incidents if available.
properties.text: Secrets management — no secrets in code; vaulting + pre-commit scanning required

guidance: Document the names of all developers who have completed secure-coding training, including training dates and the specific course or provider.
Cross-reference the secure-coding training records with the staff training register required by control A.6.3.
Retain attendance certificates or completion confirmations for each developer as evidence of training.
Name the training owner as a specific individual responsible for maintaining training records, not as a team or department.
properties.text: Secure-coding training for developers (cross-link to A.6.3)

guidance: Document secure coding procedures that explicitly reference the OWASP Top 10 and CWE Top 25, mapped to relevant programming languages used in your environment.
Name a specific individual as the procedure owner, avoiding generic titles like "the team" or "IT department".
List concrete coding patterns and examples for each vulnerability class, showing how to prevent them in your primary development languages.
Record the date of the last review and update of the secure coding procedure, ensuring it is current within the past 12 months.
Cross-reference your procedure with actual code review checklists or training materials to show practical application of the guidance.
properties.text: Common-vulnerability prevention guidance (OWASP Top 10 / CWE Top 25 mapped to language patterns)

guidance: State the specific severity levels of security findings that will block release in the procedure, using clear language and defined thresholds.
Name the individual or role authorized to approve exceptions to acceptance criteria, avoiding vague terms like "the team" or "management".
Document the process for recording and approving exceptions, including required signatures and dates for each exception granted.
Cross-reference the acceptance criteria in the procedure with recent release records to show they were applied before deployment.
properties.text: Acceptance criteria (severity thresholds that block release; documented exception authority)

guidance: Document the existence of a bug-bounty or responsible-disclosure program in your Security Testing in Development and Acceptance Procedure, including scope and contact details.
Name a specific individual responsible for managing the program, not a generic team or department.
Publish clear instructions for external parties to report security vulnerabilities, including a dedicated email address or online submission form.
Record all received vulnerability reports and your responses in a dated log, including actions taken and resolution dates.
Review and update the procedure annually, noting the review date and reviewer’s name in the document.
properties.text: Bug-bounty / responsible-disclosure programme

guidance: Document the full defect lifecycle in the procedure, including creation, triage, assignment, fixing, retesting, and closure with clear criteria.
Record each defect in a tracking system with a unique ID, date reported, description, and the person responsible for resolution.
Name the defect owner as a specific individual for each defect, not a generic group or department.
Confirm that closure criteria are stated for each defect and that closure is logged with the date and the person authorizing closure.
Retain evidence of retesting for each fixed defect, such as test logs or screenshots, attached to the defect record.
properties.text: Defect handling (creation / triage / fix / retest cycle with closure criteria)

guidance: Document each test gate in the development lifecycle by name, trigger point, and required tests in the Security Testing in Development and Acceptance Procedure.
Assign a specific individual as the owner responsible for approving test results at each gate, listing their name and role.
Record the date and outcome of security tests at each gate in a version-controlled log linked to the relevant code change or release.
Attach evidence of test completion, such as signed reports or automated tool outputs, to each stage’s acceptance checklist.
Specify test gate owners by individual name, not by team or generic role, to avoid auditor concerns about unclear accountability.
properties.text: Test gates in lifecycle (per-commit / pre-merge / pre-release / post-deployment)

guidance: State the required frequency for third-party penetration testing as at least annually and after significant changes to customer-facing applications handling personal data.
Name the specific individual responsible for scheduling and overseeing third-party penetration tests, not a team or generic role.
Document each completed penetration test with the test date, scope, third-party provider, and summary of findings in a central register.
Retain signed engagement agreements and final reports from third-party testers for each annual and post-change test.
Record the decision and rationale for what qualifies as a "significant change" to ensure consistent application of the testing trigger.
properties.text: Third-party penetration-testing cadence (annual + on significant change for customer-facing PII-touching apps; modern baseline)

guidance: Record each security test entry with a unique identifier, test date, and the specific application tested as listed in the application register.
Cross-reference the tested application by linking to its entry in the application register maintained for A.8.26.
Name the responsible tester as a specific individual, not a team or generic role.
Document the test outcome and any follow-up actions, including dates and responsible persons for remediation steps.
Avoid using generic or missing application names; confirm each test is clearly tied to a registered application entry.
properties.text: Per-test application (cross-link to A.8.26 application register)

guidance: Record each security test entry in the register with a unique identifier matching the corresponding test artefact, such as a report or scan output.
Attach or link the actual test artefact—such as a PDF report or scan file—to the register entry, ensuring the file is accessible and unaltered.
State the date the artefact was received or generated, and name the individual or vendor who delivered the test results.
Name the artefact location specifically; avoid vague references like "on file" or "with IT" that do not point to a concrete, retrievable source.
Retain all referenced artefacts for the period required by your retention policy, and confirm their presence during each register review.
properties.text: Per-test artefact reference (report / scan output / pen-test deliverable retained)

guidance: Record for each security test whether it was performed by an independent external party or by internal staff, using a clear yes/no or named provider.
Name the individual or company responsible for each test, avoiding generic entries like "the team" or "IT department".
Date each test entry to show when the test was conducted and by whom.
Cross-reference each test entry with supporting documentation, such as contracts or statements of work for external parties.
properties.text: Per-test external/internal flag (independent vs internal)

guidance: Record the specific lifecycle phase (e.g., design, development, pre-production, production) for each security test entry in the register.
Name the individual responsible for confirming the lifecycle phase for each test, ensuring this is not left blank or listed as a team.
Date each test entry to show when the test was conducted relative to the project timeline.
Cross-reference each test with related project documentation that defines lifecycle phases, such as project plans or development schedules.
properties.text: Per-test lifecycle gate (where in lifecycle this test ran)

guidance: Record the outcome of each security test as "pass", "fail", or "waived-with-exception" in the Security Test Register with the test date.
Document the exact number of findings identified for each test, linking them to the relevant test entry in the register.
Name the person who approved any "waived-with-exception" outcome, ensuring their full name and approval date are included.
Avoid using vague outcome labels such as "OK" or "N/A"—use only "pass", "fail", or "waived-with-exception" for each test entry.
properties.text: Per-test outcome (pass / fail / waived-with-exception) + findings-count

guidance: Assign a unique identifier to each security test entry in the register before recording any test details.
Record the assigned identifier alongside the test date, scope, and responsible person for every new entry.
Cross-reference the unique identifier in related documentation, such as test reports or remediation logs, to maintain traceability.
Avoid using generic or reused identifiers—ensure each identifier is distinct and not repeated across different tests.
properties.text: Per-test unique identifier

guidance: Cross-reference each test entry in the Security Test Register with the corresponding test type listed in the approved security testing procedure.
Record the specific test type for every test entry, using exact wording from the procedure’s test-types list.
Name the individual who verified the match between the register entry and the procedure’s test type, including the date of verification.
Avoid using generic or undefined test type labels such as "other" or "miscellaneous" that do not appear in the procedure’s test-types list.
properties.text: Per-test type (matches procedure's test-types list)

guidance: State in the procedure that all identified security issues must be retested after remediation before release to production.
Document the retesting process with required steps, responsible individual, and evidence to be collected for each remediation.
Record the date, tester’s name, and test results for each retest in a log or defect tracking system.
Name the owner responsible for approving that no fixes are released without successful retest — use a specific individual, not a team.
Attach evidence of retest completion, such as screenshots or reports, to the corresponding remediation ticket or acceptance record.
properties.text: Retesting requirement after remediation (no fix-without-retest)

guidance: List all assets, systems, and processes in the current security testing scope, referencing the latest asset inventory and risk assessment.
Cross-reference each item in the scope against the actual security testing schedule or reports from the last review period.
Identify and document any assets, systems, or processes not covered by recent security tests, noting the specific gaps.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual responsible for confirming the gap analysis, avoiding generic roles like "the team."
Record the review date and maintain the signed summary of findings, including any action plans to address identified gaps.
properties.text: Test-coverage gap check vs applicable scope

guidance: Record the date of each security testing program review in a central log, showing the most recent review occurred within the past 180 days.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual responsible for the periodic review, not a generic role or team.
Retain a signed or approved summary of the review findings, including the date and reviewer’s name.
Cross-reference the review log with your documented testing schedule to confirm the review interval does not exceed 180 days.
properties.text: Review date within the planned interval (≤180 days)

guidance: Document each security testing finding in a dated report, clearly linking it to the relevant procedure, scope, or tool affected.
Assign a named individual to review each finding and determine required updates to procedures, scope, or tooling.
Record the specific changes made to procedures, scope, or tooling in a change log, referencing the original finding.
Attach evidence of updated procedures, scope documents, or tool configurations, showing the date and approver for each change.
Name the person responsible for confirming that all findings have been addressed—do not leave this as "the team" or an unnamed group.
properties.text: Findings propagated to procedure / scope / tooling

guidance: State the next planned review date for the security testing program in the documented review schedule.
Record the name of the individual responsible for scheduling and conducting the next review.
Update the review schedule immediately after each review to reflect the new planned date.
Specify the review date as a calendar date, not just a vague timeframe like "quarterly" or "annually".
properties.text: Next planned review date stated

guidance: Compile a log of security testing findings from the past 12 months, including dates, descriptions, and associated systems or processes.
Analyze the log to identify recurring issues or patterns, documenting any trends that appear across multiple test cycles.
Record any actions taken to address root causes, such as updates to development processes, targeted training, or changes in security tools.
Name a specific individual responsible for reviewing and approving the analysis and resulting action plan, not a group or department.
Retain dated meeting minutes or review records showing discussion of trends and decisions on process, training, or tooling improvements.
properties.text: Finding-pattern trending (recurring patterns → SDLC / training / tooling action)

guidance: Document the date and results of the most recent penetration test in your security testing program review file.
Record any changes made to security procedures, scope, or staff training that directly resulted from penetration test findings, with clear links to the test report.
Name the individual responsible for reviewing penetration test outcomes and updating relevant procedures or training materials.
Attach evidence of communication to staff about updated procedures or training, such as a dated email or training attendance record.
Avoid referencing generic lessons learned; specify how each pen-test outcome led to a concrete update in your documented processes.
properties.text: Pen-test outcomes feeding back into procedure / scope / training

guidance: Name the reviewer by full name and job title, specifying both a Security Engineering lead and an Engineering lead for each review cycle.
Record the date each review was completed and link it to the corresponding periodic security testing program documentation.
Sign the review outcome using a digital or handwritten signature from both designated leads to confirm their participation.
Avoid listing generic roles or teams as reviewers; always identify specific individuals responsible for the review.
properties.text: Reviewer identity (Security Engineering + Engineering leads)

guidance: List all application classes in a dated document, using clear categories relevant to your environment such as web, mobile, or internal tools.
Define and record the specific security testing types required for each application class, such as penetration testing, code review, or vulnerability scanning.
Cross-reference each application class with its required test types in a matrix format, ensuring every class has at least one associated test type.
Name the person responsible for maintaining the application class and test-type matrix, avoiding generic roles like "IT" or "the team".
Review and update the matrix at least annually, recording the date and approver for each update.
properties.text: Application classes enumerated with test-type matrix per class

guidance: List specific triggers that require a review of the security testing scope, such as new application types, testing methods, or regulatory changes.
Document each trigger in a dated register, including a brief description and the person responsible for monitoring changes.
Assign a named individual—not a team or department—to review the scope when a trigger occurs.
Record each instance when a trigger is activated and the resulting decision, including the date and the approver’s name.
Review the trigger list annually and update it as needed, keeping a record of the review date and reviewer’s name.
properties.text: Trigger list for re-scoping (new app class, new test technique, new regulator)

guidance: List all systems, applications, and components considered for security testing, including those proposed for exclusion, in a dated testing scope document.
State the specific rationale for each exclusion, such as "throwaway prototype" or "internal-only micro-service with low blast radius," next to each item.
Name the individual who approved each exclusion decision, ensuring it is not left as a group or department.
Attach supporting evidence, such as architecture diagrams or risk assessments, that justify why each excluded item poses minimal risk.
Sign and date the final scope document, confirming all exclusions and rationales are complete and accurate.
properties.text: Exclusion rationale (e.g. throwaway prototypes; internal-tooling micro-services with low blast radius)

guidance: List all application classes in scope for annual third-party penetration testing, including web, mobile, and APIs, in a dated inventory document.
Name the specific individual responsible for defining and updating the penetration testing scope, not a team or department.
Document the rationale for including or excluding each application class from annual third-party testing in a written, dated record.
Reference the approved penetration testing scope in the annual security testing plan and cross-check against actual testing engagements.
properties.text: Pen-test scope (which application classes require annual third-party testing)

guidance: List each security test type (such as SAST, DAST, IAST, SCA, fuzzing, manual review, penetration testing) in the procedure with a clear definition.
State the specific development or acceptance scenarios where each test type must be applied, referencing project types or risk levels.
Assign a named individual or role responsible for deciding which test types apply to each project, and record this in the procedure.
Document the date and version of the procedure to show it reflects current practices and has not been copied from generic templates.
Cross-reference each test type’s applicability rule to supporting policy or risk assessment records to show alignment with organisational requirements.
properties.text: Test types (SAST / DAST / IAST / SCA / fuzzing / manual review / penetration testing) with applicability rules

guidance: List all system-administration tools in a dated inventory, including the tool name, version, and the systems they manage.
Document each privileged role with access to these tools, naming specific individuals and their job titles.
Record the access approval for each privileged user, including the approver’s name, approval date, and justification.
State in the baseline that non-privileged users are explicitly denied access to system-administration tools.
Name the owner of the privileged access baseline as a specific individual, not a group or department.
properties.text: Access to system-administration tools restricted to privileged roles only

guidance: Document the technical method used to grant privileged access only for a limited time, such as just-in-time elevation or time-bound roles.
Record each privileged access elevation event with the user’s name, start and end time, and the approving authority in an access log.
Name the owner responsible for managing and reviewing privileged access as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Retain evidence showing that standing, permanent privileged accounts have been removed or converted to time-bound elevation, such as deprovisioning records or configuration screenshots.
properties.text: Just-in-time / time-bound elevation capability available — eliminates standing privilege

guidance: Name the specific PAM tool in use and record its configuration version and deployment date in your privileged access baseline document.
Document the enabled features for vaulting, session recording, and command brokering, including screenshots or export files from the PAM tool’s configuration interface.
Assign a named individual responsible for maintaining and updating the PAM configuration, avoiding generic roles like "IT" or "security team".
Confirm that session recording and command brokering are actively enforced by generating and saving a recent audit log showing these controls in action.
Retain evidence of periodic reviews of the PAM configuration, including reviewer names, dates, and any changes made.
properties.text: PAM tooling configured (vaulting, session recording, command brokering)

guidance: List all privileged roles for each system in a central register, including the exact permissions each role grants.
Describe the business purpose for each privileged role, linking it to specific system functions or administrative tasks.
Name the owner of each privileged role as a specific individual, not a group or generic title.
Date and version-control the privileged role catalogue to show when it was last reviewed or updated.
Cross-reference each privileged role to the documented access request and approval process for that system.
properties.text: Privileged role catalogue per system (which roles exist, what they grant)

guidance: Document the list of high-risk privileged actions that require session recording, including clear descriptions and examples for each action.
Name the system or tool used to record sessions, specifying its configuration settings and the date these were last updated.
Assign responsibility for monitoring and maintaining session recording to a specific named individual, not a generic team or department.
Record a sample session log showing a high-risk privileged action, including the date, time, and user involved.
Retain evidence of regular reviews of session recordings, such as a dated log or meeting minutes confirming checks were performed.
properties.text: Session recording active for high-risk privileged actions

guidance: Document the baseline requirement that all privileged accounts must use multi-factor authentication, including the date and the policy owner’s name.
List all privileged accounts in a register and indicate the MFA status for each, with the date of last verification.
Capture a screenshot or system log entry showing MFA enforcement is enabled on privileged access systems, including the timestamp.
Name the owner responsible for MFA enforcement as a specific individual, not a group or department.
Retain evidence of periodic checks confirming MFA remains active on all privileged accounts, with reviewer name and review date.
properties.text: Strong authentication required for all privileged access (MFA enforced)

guidance: List all systems and processes that require privileged access in a dated inventory, referencing unique system or process names.
Assign a named individual as the owner for each system or process, avoiding group or team designations.
Document the criteria used to determine which systems and processes are in scope, including the rationale and approval date.
Cross-reference each system or process in the inventory with supporting access control documentation, such as access logs or privilege assignment records.
properties.text: Systems and processes in scope for privileged access governance

guidance: Document the specific alert rules configured for unusual hours, unusual scope, and unusual commands in the privileged activity log system, including rule descriptions and thresholds.
Record the date and outcome of the most recent test or simulation showing that anomaly alerts trigger as expected and are received by the responsible team.
Name the individual responsible for reviewing and responding to privileged activity anomaly alerts, listing their full name and job title.
Attach a screenshot or export of the current alert configuration settings from the privileged activity log tool, showing each rule is active.
Avoid using generic or default alert rules; customize each rule to your organisation’s environment and document the rationale for any thresholds set.
properties.rationale: Modern baseline — passive logging without alerting fails detect-respond intent (Style v2 promotion)
properties.text: Anomaly alerting configured (unusual hours, unusual scope, unusual command)

guidance: State the exact retention period for privileged activity logs in a documented policy, referencing the relevant ISO27001:2022 control.
Name the person responsible for enforcing the log retention period, listing their full name and job title in the policy or procedure.
Record the current log retention settings from the logging system, including screenshots or configuration exports with visible dates.
Document the process for securely deleting logs after the retention period, including the date and method used for the most recent deletion.
Specify the retention period as a concrete timeframe—avoid vague terms like "as needed" or "until no longer required".
properties.text: Log retention period defined and enforced

guidance: Document the specific SIEM correlation rules in use that are designed to detect misuse of privileged access, including rule names and descriptions.
Record the date each correlation rule was last reviewed and tuned, along with the name of the individual who performed the tuning.
Attach evidence of test results or alert samples showing the rules have triggered on simulated or real privileged-access misuse scenarios.
Name the person responsible for ongoing rule maintenance as a specific individual, not a group or generic role.
Retain a change log showing all updates to privileged-access misuse detection rules, including dates and approvers.
properties.text: SIEM correlation rules tuned for privileged-access misuse patterns

guidance: Document the technical controls in place that prevent log entries from being altered or deleted after creation, such as write-once storage or append-only configurations.
Record the system or process that automatically forwards privileged activity logs to an off-host location, such as a Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) system.
Name the individual responsible for regularly verifying that log forwarding and integrity protections are functioning as intended, including their job title and contact details.
Retain a sample privileged activity log file showing timestamps, event details, and evidence of successful off-host transfer.
Avoid using generic descriptions like "logs are protected" without specifying the exact technology or process used for integrity protection.
properties.text: Log integrity protection (write-once / SIEM forwarding off-host)

guidance: Record each privileged action in the log, including the exact command run, system change made, or data accessed, with a timestamp.
Name the individual user account responsible for each privileged activity, avoiding shared or generic account names.
Document the purpose or reason for each privileged action, referencing a related ticket or change request where applicable.
Retain the original, unaltered activity log entries for a defined period, with the retention timeframe documented and approved by management.
properties.text: Action performed captured (command / change / access)

guidance: Record the exact date and time for each privileged activity in the log, using a synchronized system clock.
Confirm that each log entry includes both the action performed and its corresponding timestamp, with no missing or blank timestamp fields.
Name the system or tool responsible for generating and storing the timestamps, and document its time synchronization method.
Review a sample of recent privileged activity logs to verify that all actions are timestamped and that no entries use generic or default dates.
properties.text: Timestamp captured per action

guidance: Configure the privileged activity logging system to record the unique username or ID of each user performing privileged actions.
Review a recent sample of privileged activity logs and confirm each entry shows the specific individual responsible for the action.
Name the owner of the logging process as a specific person, not a team or department, in documentation or system configuration records.
Document the date and method used to test that the log cannot be edited to obscure or remove the user identity.
properties.text: Identity of the privileged user captured per action

guidance: Name each user with privileged access in a register, including full name, job title, and unique identifier.
Document each user's signed acknowledgement of the privileged access procedure, capturing the date and method of acknowledgement.
Store all signed acknowledgements in a central, access-controlled location, referencing each record to the corresponding user in the register.
Confirm that acknowledgements are renewed and re-signed whenever the privileged access procedure is updated.
Specify the owner responsible for collecting and maintaining acknowledgements as a named individual, not a generic team or department.
properties.text: Users acknowledge accountability for their privileged access (e.g. signed acceptable-use)

guidance: Document a step-by-step process for requesting, reviewing, and approving privileged access, including required forms and approval authority.
Name the approver for privileged access as a specific individual with job title, not a generic group or department.
Record each privileged access grant or change with the requestor, approver, date, and justification in an access log.
Retain copies of completed and signed authorisation forms for all privileged access requests and changes.
properties.text: Formal authorisation process before privileged access is granted or changed

guidance: Document the location and method of sealing break-glass account credentials, including physical or digital controls, in a dated procedure record.
Name a specific individual responsible for authorizing and monitoring all break-glass account usage, avoiding generic titles like "IT" or "the team."
Record each instance of break-glass account use, including date, time, purpose, and the person accessing, in an access log.
Review and sign off on each break-glass account usage after the event, confirming appropriateness and resetting credentials if required.
Retain evidence of periodic audits of sealed credential integrity and access logs, including auditor name and audit date.
properties.rationale: Emergency access without weak ongoing exposure
properties.text: Break-glass account governance (sealed credentials, post-use review)

guidance: State the maximum duration for privileged access rights in the procedure, specifying exact time limits for each type of privileged role.
Document the process for automatically removing or reviewing privileged access when the defined expiry period is reached, including responsible individuals.
Name the person or role responsible for monitoring and enforcing expiry rules, avoiding vague assignments like "the team" or "IT."
Record the date of the most recent review or update of expiry rules within the procedure, showing that the rules are current.
properties.text: Expiry rules defined for privileged access rights

guidance: Document each privileged access request with requester name, reason for access, and specific time period in a dated access log.
Approve privileged access individually for each event, with the approver’s name and approval date recorded alongside the request.
State the exact start and end time for privileged access in the access log; avoid granting open-ended or indefinite access periods.
Name the owner of the privileged access management procedure as a specific individual, not a team or department.
Retain records of privileged access revocation, showing access was removed immediately after the stated period ended.
properties.text: Privileged access granted on need-to-use, event-by-event basis (less than or equal to the period needed)

guidance: Document a step-by-step process for removing privileged access when an employee changes roles or leaves the organization, including responsible parties and timelines.
Name the person or role responsible for initiating and confirming access revocation, ensuring this is a specific individual and not a generic team.
Cross-reference each revocation action to a dated record in your access revocation log, clearly linking it to the relevant personnel change.
State how and where revocation records are stored, ensuring they are easily retrievable for future audits and linked to A.5.18 requirements.
properties.text: Revocation path on role change / termination (links to A.5.18 revocation records)

guidance: State in the procedure that privileged accounts must not be used for routine, non-privileged tasks such as email or web browsing.
Name the owner of the procedure as a specific individual, not a team or department, in the document header.
Document an approval record showing the procedure was reviewed and signed by a manager responsible for access control.
Record the date of the most recent procedure review to confirm it is current and actively maintained.
properties.text: Procedure prohibits routine non-privileged tasks under a privileged account

guidance: State in the Privileged Access Management Procedure that all administrative actions must be performed using dedicated admin accounts, not daily-use accounts.
List the specific systems and applications where separate admin accounts are required, referencing their unique account naming conventions.
Name the individual responsible for approving and monitoring the creation of admin accounts, using their full name and job title.
Attach a sample access request and approval record showing a named user receiving a separate admin account, with dates and signatures.
Specify that no admin account owner is listed as "IT" or "the team"—use only named individuals in all documentation.
properties.text: Separate accounts mandated for administrative actions (admin account distinct from daily-use)

guidance: Cross-reference each privileged user's entry in the privileged access recertification list with their corresponding row in the general access review register.
Record the date and name of the person who verified that every privileged user is also listed under general access.
Document any privileged account found without a matching general access entry and assign a specific individual to resolve the discrepancy.
Name the owner of the cross-linking process as a specific individual, not a team or department.
properties.text: Cross-link to A.5.18 general access review — every privileged subject also appears under their general access row (no orphan privileged paths)

guidance: Record each privileged account that was not reconfirmed during recertification in a dated access review log.
Document the specific revocation or modification action taken for each non-reconfirmed account, including the date and the person who completed the action.
Name the individual who approved the revocation or modification, ensuring the approver is identified by full name, not just a role or team.
Retain evidence of system changes, such as screenshots or audit logs, showing the access was actually removed or changed.
properties.text: Revocation/modification actions completed for non-reconfirmed access

guidance: Record the most recent privileged access recertification date for each user in an access review log, including the reviewer's name.
Confirm that the interval between the last two recertification dates for each user does not exceed 180 days.
Document any overdue recertifications with a reason and corrective action, signed and dated by the responsible manager.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual for each recertification event—do not use group names or roles only.
properties.text: Recertification date within the planned interval (≤180 days since last)

guidance: Record the next planned recertification date for each privileged access account in your access management register.
Name the person responsible for scheduling and overseeing the next recertification, listing them as a specific individual.
Document the method and frequency for recertification reviews in a dated procedure or policy.
Avoid leaving the next recertification date blank or marked as "TBD"—enter a concrete, calendar date for each account.
properties.text: Next planned recertification date stated

guidance: List each privileged account in a register, including the account name, assigned user, and current access level.
Record the outcome of the recertification for each account as "re-confirmed," "amended," or "revoked," with the date of review.
Name the reviewer as a specific individual who made the recertification decision for each account, not a generic team or department.
Retain evidence of any changes made, such as screenshots or system logs, showing access amendments or revocations.
Sign off the completed register with the reviewer’s name and date to confirm all accounts were individually assessed.
properties.text: Per-privileged-account outcome (re-confirmed / amended / revoked)

guidance: Name the reviewer as a specific individual, such as the asset owner or their formally delegated authority, in the recertification record.

guidance: State the specific legitimate interest you rely upon in your privacy notice, using plain language tailored to your organisation’s actual processing purpose.
Name the individual or role responsible for determining and reviewing the legitimate interest, not just a department or generic title.
Document the date when the legitimate interest assessment was last reviewed, and retain a copy of the assessment for reference.
Cross-reference the section of your privacy notice where the legitimate interest is described, ensuring it matches your internal records.
properties.text: Legitimate interests if relied upon

guidance: Write the privacy notice using short sentences and everyday words that a typical user can understand without legal or technical knowledge.
Test the notice’s readability by having at least two non-expert staff or users read it and confirm in writing that they understood the content.
Document the date and names of individuals who reviewed the notice for clarity and readability, keeping their feedback on file.
Name the author or editor responsible for the final wording as a specific person, not just a team or department.
properties.text: Written in plain, clear language

guidance: State the specific purposes for which you collect and use personal data in your published privacy notice, using clear and plain language.
Identify and document the legal basis for each processing purpose, referencing the relevant GDPR article in the privacy notice.
Name the version and publication date of the privacy notice to show when the stated purposes and legal bases were last reviewed.
