properties.title: Transparent information, communication and modalities for the exercise of the rights of the data subject

properties.business_description: This requirement is activated when an organization, acting as a data controller, needs to provide information to data subjects about their personal data processing activities. It mandates that the information be delivered in a manner that is easy to understand and access, using simple language, especially when communicating with children. The goal is to ensure transparency and clarity in how personal data is handled. Organizations often mistakenly believe that complex legal jargon is necessary, but the emphasis here is on clarity and accessibility for the average person.
properties.obligation_text: The controller shall take appropriate measures to provide any information referred to in Articles 13 and 14 and any communication under Articles 15 to 22 and 34 relating to processing to the data subject in a concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible form, using clear and plain language, in particular for any information addressed specifically to a child.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Transparent information, communication and modalities for the exercise of the rights of the data subject — paragraph 1

properties.business_description: This requirement is triggered when a data subject makes a request regarding their rights under Articles 15 to 22 of the GDPR, such as accessing their data or requesting its deletion. The organization, acting as the data controller, must respond to the request promptly, and no later than one month from receiving it. This means acknowledging the request and providing information on any actions taken in response. A common misconception is that the one-month period starts when the request is fully understood, but it actually begins upon receipt of the request. Extensions are possible, but only under specific circumstances.
properties.obligation_text: The controller shall provide information on action taken on a request under Articles 15 to 22 to the data subject without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt of the request.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Transparent information, communication and modalities for the exercise of the rights of the data subject — paragraph 3

properties.business_description: This provision applies when a data controller receives a request from an individual to exercise their data protection rights, but the controller is unsure about the identity of the requester. In such cases, the controller is allowed to ask for additional information to verify the individual's identity. This step is crucial to ensure that personal data is not disclosed to unauthorized individuals. It is important to note that this does not mean the controller can ask for excessive information; only what is necessary to confirm identity. A common misconception is that controllers can ignore requests if identity is uncertain, but they must first attempt to verify identity.
properties.obligation_text: Where the controller has reasonable doubts concerning the identity of the natural person making the request, the controller may request the provision of additional information necessary to confirm the identity of the data subject.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Transparent information, communication and modalities for the exercise of the rights of the data subject — paragraph 6

properties.business_description: When collecting personal data directly from individuals, the controller must provide a defined set of information at the point of collection - not later. The mandatory categories from Art.13.1 are: identity and contact details of the controller; contact details of the Data Protection Officer (DPO) if designated; purposes and legal basis for processing; legitimate interests pursued (if Art.6.1.f applies); and any recipients or categories of recipients. Art.13.2 adds: retention periods; rights of the data subject including withdrawal of consent; the right to complain to a supervisory authority; and whether provision of data is a statutory or contractual requirement. This is the legal basis for the privacy notice or layered privacy information shown at data collection points.

subject: privacy
properties.title: Information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject

properties.business_description: When an organization collects personal data directly from individuals, it must inform them about certain key details at the time of collection. This includes the identity and contact information of the organization, the contact details of the data protection officer if there is one, the reasons for processing the data, and the legal basis for doing so. If the processing is based on legitimate interests, these interests must be specified. Additionally, the organization must disclose who will receive the data and if the data will be transferred to another country. This ensures transparency and builds trust with data subjects.
properties.obligation_text: Where personal data relating to a data subject are collected from the data subject, the controller shall, at the time when personal data are obtained, provide the data subject with all of the following information: (a) the identity and the contact details of the controller; (b) the contact details of the data protection officer, where applicable; (c) the purposes of the processing and the legal basis; (d) where processing is based on Art.6(1)(f), the legitimate interests pursued; (e) the recipients or categories of recipients; (f) where applicable, that the controller intends to transfer personal data to a third country.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject — paragraph 1

properties.business_description: When an organization collects personal data directly from individuals, it must inform them about who is responsible for handling their data. This means providing the identity and contact details of the data controller. This requirement is triggered at the point of data collection, ensuring transparency and accountability. A common misconception is that this information can be omitted if the data is collected indirectly, but this obligation specifically applies to direct collection scenarios. Organizations must ensure that this information is clear and easily accessible to data subjects at the time of collection.
properties.obligation_text: the identity and the contact details of the controller;
subject: privacy
properties.title: Information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject — 1(a)

properties.business_description: When an organization collects personal data directly from individuals, it must provide them with certain information, including the contact details of the Data Protection Officer (DPO), if one is appointed. This requirement is triggered whenever personal data is collected, such as during account creation or survey participation. The purpose is to ensure transparency and provide data subjects with a point of contact for privacy-related inquiries. A common misconception is that all organizations must appoint a DPO; however, this is only necessary under certain conditions, such as when processing large-scale sensitive data.
properties.obligation_text: the contact details of the data protection officer, where applicable;
subject: privacy
properties.title: Information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject — 1(b)

properties.business_description: When an organization collects personal data directly from individuals, it must clearly inform them about why their data is being collected and the legal justification for doing so. This requirement is triggered at the point of data collection, ensuring transparency and enabling individuals to understand the purpose behind the processing of their data. Organizations often mistakenly believe that a general privacy policy suffices, but they must provide specific information relevant to each data collection instance. This helps build trust and ensures compliance with data protection regulations.
properties.obligation_text: the purposes of the processing and the legal basis;
subject: privacy
properties.title: Information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject — 1(c)

properties.business_description: When an organization collects personal data directly from individuals and relies on legitimate interests as the legal basis for processing, it must inform the data subjects about these interests. This requirement is triggered during the data collection process and ensures transparency, allowing individuals to understand why their data is being processed. Organizations must clearly communicate the specific interests they are pursuing, which can include business or commercial objectives. A common misconception is that simply stating 'legitimate interests' is sufficient, but the specific interests must be detailed to comply with this obligation.
properties.obligation_text: where processing is based on Art.6(1)(f), the legitimate interests pursued;

properties.title: Information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject — 1(d)

properties.business_description: When an organization collects personal data directly from individuals, it must inform them about who will receive their data. This means specifying either the actual recipients or the types of recipients. This requirement is triggered during the data collection process, such as when a customer fills out a form or signs up for a service. Organizations must clearly communicate this information to ensure transparency. A common misconception is that organizations only need to disclose this information if they share data externally, but it also applies to internal data sharing within different departments.
properties.obligation_text: the recipients or categories of recipients;

properties.title: Information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject — 1(e)

properties.business_description: This requirement is triggered when an organization collects personal data directly from individuals and plans to transfer that data to a country outside the European Economic Area (EEA). The organization must inform the data subjects about this intention. This means clearly communicating to individuals that their data may be sent to a third country, which could have different data protection laws. A common misconception is that this disclosure is only necessary if the transfer is imminent, but it must be made as soon as the intention exists, regardless of timing. This ensures transparency and allows individuals to understand how their data will be handled.
properties.obligation_text: where applicable, that the controller intends to transfer personal data to a third country.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject — 1(f)

properties.business_description: When an organization collects personal data directly from individuals, it must provide additional information beyond basic details. This includes how long the data will be stored, the individual's right to withdraw consent if consent is the basis for processing, the right to file a complaint with a supervisory authority, whether providing data is legally or contractually required, and if automated decision-making or profiling is involved. This requirement is triggered during the initial data collection phase and aims to ensure transparency and empower data subjects with knowledge about their data rights and processing activities.
properties.obligation_text: In addition to the information in paragraph 1, the controller shall provide the following further information: (a) the period for which personal data will be stored; (b) where processing is based on consent, the right to withdraw consent at any time; (c) the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority; (d) whether the provision of personal data is a statutory or contractual requirement; (e) the existence of automated decision-making including profiling.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject — paragraph 2

properties.business_description: This requirement is triggered when an organization collects personal data directly from individuals. It mandates that the organization must inform the individuals about how long their personal data will be stored. This means the organization needs to clearly communicate the data retention period or the criteria used to determine it. A common misconception is that organizations can provide vague or indefinite timeframes, but the regulation expects specific and understandable information. This helps ensure transparency and allows individuals to understand how long their data will be kept before it is deleted or anonymized.
properties.obligation_text: In addition to the information in paragraph 1, the controller shall provide the following further information: (a) the period for which personal data will be stored;
subject: privacy
properties.title: Information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject — 2(a)

properties.business_description: When an organization collects personal data directly from individuals and relies on their consent to process this data, it must inform them that they have the right to withdraw their consent at any time. This requirement is triggered during the data collection process and ensures transparency, allowing individuals to understand their rights and exercise control over their personal data. A common misconception is that once consent is given, it cannot be revoked, but this is not the case. Organizations must clearly communicate this right and provide an easy way for individuals to withdraw consent if they choose to do so.
properties.obligation_text: In addition to the information in paragraph 1, the controller shall provide the following further information: (b) where processing is based on consent, the right to withdraw consent at any time;
subject: privacy
properties.title: Information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject — 2(b)

properties.business_description: When an organization collects personal data directly from individuals, it must inform them of their right to file a complaint with a supervisory authority. This requirement is triggered during the data collection process and is part of the broader obligation to provide transparency to data subjects. Organizations must clearly communicate this right, ensuring individuals know they can seek recourse if they believe their data is being mishandled. A common misconception is that this information only needs to be provided upon request, but it must be proactively disclosed at the time of data collection.
properties.obligation_text: In addition to the information in paragraph 1, the controller shall provide the following further information: (c) the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority;
subject: privacy
properties.title: Information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject — 2(c)

properties.business_description: When collecting personal data directly from individuals, organizations must inform them if providing this data is required by law or part of a contract. This requirement is triggered whenever data is collected from the data subject. It ensures transparency about why the data is needed and the consequences of not providing it. Organizations often misunderstand this as needing to state all possible legal bases for processing, but it specifically pertains to whether the data provision itself is mandatory under law or contract.
properties.obligation_text: In addition to the information in paragraph 1, the controller shall provide the following further information: (d) whether the provision of personal data is a statutory or contractual requirement;
subject: privacy
properties.title: Information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject — 2(d)

properties.business_description: This requirement is triggered when an organization collects personal data directly from individuals. It mandates that the organization must inform individuals if their data will be subject to automated decision-making processes, including profiling. This means any decision made solely by automated means without human intervention, which could significantly affect the individual, must be disclosed. Organizations often misunderstand this as only relevant to complex AI systems, but it applies to any automated decision-making. The aim is to ensure transparency and allow individuals to understand how their data might influence decisions about them.
properties.obligation_text: In addition to the information in paragraph 1, the controller shall provide the following further information: (e) the existence of automated decision-making including profiling.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject — 2(e)

properties.obligation_text: the existence of automated decision-making, including profiling, referred to in Article 22(1) and (4) and, at least in those cases, meaningful information about the logic involved, as well as the significance and the envisaged consequences of such processing for the data subject.
properties.title: Information to be provided where personal data collected from the data subject — 2(f)

properties.obligation_text: Where the controller intends to further process the personal data for a purpose other than that for which the personal data were collected, the controller shall provide the data subject prior to that further processing with information on that other purpose and with any relevant further information as referred to in paragraph 2.
properties.title: Information to be provided where personal data collected from the data subject — paragraph 3

properties.business_description: Article 14 of the GDPR requires organizations to inform individuals when their personal data is collected from other sources, not directly from them. This obligation is triggered when a controller obtains personal data indirectly. The organization must provide specific information, such as its identity, the data protection officer's contact details, the purpose and legal basis for processing, the types of data collected, and any data sharing intentions. This information must be communicated within one month of acquiring the data. A common misconception is that this requirement only applies to data collected directly from individuals, but it also applies to data obtained from third parties.

This requirement is triggered whenever data is obtained indirectly, and organizations often overlook the need to provide this information promptly and comprehensively.

This obligation is triggered when the data is obtained, and the company has up to one month to provide the necessary information. This includes details like the purpose of processing and the data categories involved. A common misconception is that this requirement only applies if the data is used for marketing, but it applies to all processing activities. Companies must ensure they have processes in place to meet this deadline and provide clear communication to the data subjects.

properties.business_description: Under GDPR Article 15, individuals have the right to know if their personal data is being processed by an organization. If processing occurs, the organization must provide access to the data and explain why it is being processed and what types of data are involved. This right is triggered when an individual requests information about their data. Organizations must respond by confirming whether data processing is happening and, if so, provide the requested details. A common misconception is that organizations must provide all data immediately, but they are only required to confirm processing and provide specific information as outlined.

If processing is occurring, the organization must provide access to the data and additional information such as the purpose of processing, data categories, recipients, storage duration, and rights related to data correction or deletion. Organizations must ensure that this information is clearly communicated, typically in privacy notices or responses to access requests. A common misconception is that this right automatically grants the changes requested, but it only ensures the data subject is informed about their rights to request such changes.

A common misconception is that informing individuals of this right is optional, but it is a mandatory part of the access request process. Organizations should ensure that their privacy notices and responses to data access requests include this information to comply with GDPR requirements.

This requirement ensures transparency and helps individuals understand how their data was obtained. It is important for organizations to maintain records of data sources to comply with this obligation. Organizations must disclose whether any decisions affecting the individual are made solely by automated means, without human intervention. A common misconception is that all automated processing must be disclosed, but this obligation specifically pertains to decisions that significantly affect individuals, such as those impacting legal rights or similar consequences.

properties.business_description: When an individual requests access to their personal data, the organization must provide them with a copy of the data that is currently being processed. This requirement is triggered by a data subject access request (DSAR). The organization must ensure that the data is provided in a clear and understandable format. A common misconception is that organizations can charge a fee for this service; however, the first copy must be provided free of charge. Organizations should be prepared to respond promptly and ensure that the data provided is accurate and complete.
properties.obligation_text: The controller shall provide a copy of the personal data undergoing processing.

properties.business_description: The right to rectification allows individuals to request corrections to their personal data if it is inaccurate or incomplete. This obligation is triggered when a data subject identifies errors or omissions in their data held by an organization. Controllers must act promptly to rectify the data, ensuring it accurately reflects the individual's information. Organizations should have processes in place to handle such requests efficiently. A common misconception is that rectification only applies to factual errors, but it also includes completing incomplete data. Controllers are not required to verify the accuracy of data unless a rectification request is made.

It is triggered when a data subject requests a correction, highlighting inaccuracies or incompleteness in their personal data. Organizations must also allow individuals to provide additional information to complete any incomplete data. A common misconception is that organizations can delay rectification until it is convenient, but the requirement is to act without undue delay. This means promptly updating records to ensure data accuracy and completeness, considering the purpose for which the data is processed.

properties.business_description: The right to erasure, also known as the 'right to be forgotten', allows individuals to request the deletion of their personal data by an organization. This right is triggered when the data is no longer necessary for its original purpose or when the individual withdraws consent and no other legal basis for processing exists. Organizations must act promptly to erase the data upon receiving a valid request. A common misconception is that this right is absolute; however, it only applies under specific conditions outlined in the regulation. Organizations should have processes in place to assess and respond to such requests efficiently.

properties.business_description: The right to erasure, also known as the 'right to be forgotten', requires organizations to delete personal data without undue delay when certain conditions are met. This is triggered when the data is no longer necessary, consent is withdrawn without another legal basis, the data subject objects and there are no overriding reasons to retain the data, the data was unlawfully processed, or erasure is needed to comply with legal obligations. Organizations must have processes to assess and act on these requests promptly. A common misconception is that this right is absolute, but it is subject to specific conditions and exceptions.

A common misconception is that data must be deleted immediately upon request, but the obligation only arises when the data is truly unnecessary. Organizations must ensure they have processes in place to identify and act on such withdrawal requests promptly. properties.business_description: This provision is activated when a data subject objects to the processing of their personal data under Article 21(1) of the GDPR. If the data subject's objection is valid and there are no compelling legitimate grounds for the processing that override the interests, rights, and freedoms of the data subject, the organization must erase the data. In practice, this means that organizations need to assess each objection carefully and determine whether their reasons for processing the data are strong enough to outweigh the individual's rights. A common misconception is that any objection automatically requires data deletion, but the organization can retain the data if they have overriding legitimate grounds.

Organizations must assess whether the processing lacked a legal basis, such as consent or legitimate interest, and if so, they are required to erase the data without undue delay. A common misconception is that any dissatisfaction from a data subject triggers this right, but it specifically applies to unlawful processing. Organizations should have procedures to evaluate and respond to such requests promptly.

This obligation is triggered when a specific legal requirement dictates that data cannot be retained. Organizations should be aware of relevant laws that might necessitate data deletion, such as tax regulations or court orders. A common misconception is that this requirement applies only when a data subject requests erasure, but it can also be triggered independently by legal obligations.

properties.business_description: The right to restriction of processing allows individuals to request that an organization temporarily limit the use of their personal data. This right is triggered when there is a dispute about the accuracy of the data or if the data processing is unlawful and the individual prefers restriction over deletion. properties.business_description: Article 23 allows EU or Member State laws to limit certain GDPR rights and obligations if necessary for reasons like national security or crime prevention. These restrictions must be essential and balanced, ensuring they don't undermine fundamental rights. Organizations should be aware that such restrictions are not arbitrary and must be grounded in law. A common misconception is that any business need can justify these restrictions, which is not the case.

properties.business_description: When two or more organizations jointly decide why and how personal data is processed, they become joint controllers. This requires them to clearly outline their respective responsibilities for GDPR compliance, especially regarding data subject rights. They must create an arrangement that reflects their roles and relationships, and the key aspects of this arrangement should be accessible to the data subjects. A common misconception is that processors have some leeway in decision-making, but they must strictly adhere to the controller's directives. This means businesses must comply with GDPR if they target EU residents, even if they are based elsewhere. properties.business_description: Under GDPR, organizations acting as data controllers must keep a detailed record of their data processing activities. This requirement is triggered when an organization processes personal data. The record must include the names and contact details of the data controller, any joint controllers, their representative, and the Data Protection Officer (DPO). This ensures accountability and transparency in data processing operations. A common misconception is that only large organizations need to maintain these records, but it applies to all controllers unless exempted under specific conditions, such as having fewer than 250 employees and meeting certain criteria.

This requirement is triggered whenever a controller processes personal data, and it mandates that they clearly articulate why each processing activity is necessary. This helps ensure transparency and accountability in data handling practices. A common misconception is that this record only needs to be maintained for high-risk processing activities, but it actually applies to all processing activities under the controller's responsibility.

Specifically, they need to document the types of individuals whose data they process (e.g., customers, employees) and the types of personal data they handle (e.g., names, email addresses). This requirement is triggered whenever an organization processes personal data, and it helps ensure transparency and accountability. A common misconception is that this obligation only applies to large companies, but it actually applies to most organizations, with some exceptions for small businesses. Proper documentation is crucial for compliance and for responding to data subject requests or regulatory inquiries.

Organizations must ensure that their records are up-to-date and accessible so they can comply promptly with such requests. Organizations must be prepared to provide necessary information and support promptly. properties.business_description: This article requires organizations to evaluate the level of security needed for processing personal data by considering the risks involved. It is triggered when an organization processes personal data and must assess potential threats such as accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, or unauthorized access. Organizations should focus on understanding the specific risks associated with their data processing activities and implement appropriate security measures to mitigate these risks. A common misconception is that a one-size-fits-all security solution is sufficient, but the security measures must be tailored to the specific risks identified in the assessment.

properties.obligation_text: In assessing the appropriate level of security account shall be taken in particular of the risks that are presented by processing, in particular from accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to personal data.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Security of processing — paragraph 2

properties.business_description: For controllers and processors, this provision means that they can demonstrate compliance with GDPR by adhering to an approved code of conduct or certification mechanism. This is triggered when an organization seeks to prove its data protection measures are adequate. It requires organizations to align their practices with these approved standards, which can serve as evidence of compliance. A common misconception is that adherence to these codes or certifications alone guarantees full compliance with GDPR, but they are only part of a broader compliance strategy.
properties.obligation_text: Adherence to an approved code of conduct as referred to in Article 40 or an approved certification mechanism as referred to in Article 42 may be used as an element by which to demonstrate compliance.
subject: privacy

properties.obligation_text: In the case of a personal data breach, the controller shall without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it, notify the personal data breach to the supervisory authority, unless the personal data breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. The processor shall notify the controller without undue delay after becoming aware of a personal data breach. The notification referred to in paragraph 1 shall at least: (a) describe the nature of the breach including categories and approximate number of data subjects concerned; (b) communicate the name and contact details of the DPO; (c) describe the likely consequences; (d) describe the measures taken or proposed to address the breach.

properties.business_description: When a personal data breach occurs, organizations must promptly assess and describe the breach's nature to the relevant supervisory authority. This involves identifying the types of data affected and estimating the number of individuals impacted. This requirement is triggered when a breach is detected, and it ensures that the supervisory authority understands the breach's scope and potential impact. A common misconception is that only large breaches need reporting, but any breach that risks individuals' rights and freedoms must be reported. Organizations should focus on providing clear, concise information without unnecessary details.
properties.obligation_text: describe the nature of the personal data breach including where possible, the categories and approximate number of data subjects concerned;
subject: privacy
properties.title: Notification of a personal data breach to the supervisory authority — 3(a)

properties.business_description: When a personal data breach occurs, organizations must notify the relevant supervisory authority. Part of this notification involves providing the name and contact details of the Data Protection Officer (DPO) or another designated contact point. This requirement is triggered when a breach is likely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals. The purpose is to ensure that the supervisory authority can easily communicate with the organization for further information or clarification. A common misconception is that only the DPO's details can be provided, but the regulation allows for any appropriate contact point to be designated.
properties.obligation_text: communicate the name and contact details of the DPO or other contact point;

properties.title: Notification of a personal data breach to the supervisory authority — 3(b)

properties.business_description: This requirement is triggered when a personal data breach occurs. Organizations must assess and describe the potential impacts of the breach on individuals whose data has been compromised. This involves evaluating how the breach could affect individuals' privacy, security, and rights. The description should be detailed enough to inform the supervisory authority about the severity and potential harm of the breach. A common misconception is that this step is optional, but it is a mandatory part of breach notification to the authority.
properties.obligation_text: describe the likely consequences of the personal data breach;

properties.business_description: When a personal data breach occurs, organizations must inform the supervisory authority about the measures they have taken or plan to take to handle the breach. This includes actions to mitigate any potential negative impacts on individuals. This requirement is triggered when a breach is detected and reported. Organizations need to clearly outline their response strategy, including any immediate steps taken to contain the breach and longer-term measures to prevent recurrence. A common misconception is that this only involves technical fixes, but it also includes procedural and organizational measures.

properties.obligation_text: The controller shall document any personal data breaches, comprising the facts relating to the personal data breach, its effects and the remedial action taken.

properties.business_description: When a personal data breach occurs, organizations must promptly inform the affected individuals. This communication should be clear and easy to understand, detailing the breach's nature, potential impacts, and actions taken or planned to mitigate harm. It must also include contact information for the Data Protection Officer (DPO). This requirement is triggered when a breach is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals. A common misconception is that all breaches require notification, but only those posing significant risk do. Organizations must ensure the message is accessible and comprehensible to the average person.

properties.obligation_text: Where a type of processing in particular using new technologies is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller shall, prior to the processing, carry out an assessment of the impact of the envisaged processing operations on the protection of personal data. A data protection impact assessment shall in particular be required in the case of: (a) a systematic and extensive evaluation based on automated processing, including profiling; (b) processing on a large scale of special categories of data; or (c) a systematic monitoring of a publicly accessible area on a large scale. The assessment shall contain at least: (a) a systematic description of the envisaged processing operations and the purposes; (b) an assessment of the necessity and proportionality; (c) an assessment of the risks; and (d) the measures envisaged to address the risks.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Data protection impact assessment

properties.title: Data protection impact assessment — paragraph 1

properties.business_description: A data protection impact assessment (DPIA) is necessary when certain high-risk processing activities are planned. This includes when an organization conducts systematic and extensive evaluations using automated processing, processes large volumes of sensitive data, or monitors public areas on a large scale. The DPIA helps identify and mitigate risks to individuals' privacy. Organizations often misunderstand DPIAs as optional, but they are mandatory in these scenarios. Conducting a DPIA involves assessing the necessity and proportionality of the processing, identifying risks, and implementing measures to address them. It is a proactive step to ensure compliance with data protection laws.
properties.obligation_text: A data protection impact assessment shall in particular be required in the case of: (a) a systematic and extensive evaluation based on automated processing, including profiling; (b) processing on a large scale of special categories of data; or (c) a systematic monitoring of a publicly accessible area on a large scale.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Data protection impact assessment — paragraph 3

properties.business_description: A Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) is a process that organizations must conduct when planning new data processing activities that could pose high risks to individuals' privacy. It requires a detailed analysis of the proposed data processing operations, including their purpose, necessity, and proportionality. Organizations must also evaluate potential risks to data subjects and outline measures to mitigate these risks. This assessment helps ensure that data protection is integrated into the project from the start. A common misconception is that DPIAs are only necessary for large-scale processing, but they are required whenever there is a potential high risk to individuals' rights and freedoms.
properties.obligation_text: The assessment shall contain at least: (a) a systematic description of the envisaged processing operations and the purposes; (b) an assessment of the necessity and proportionality; (c) an assessment of the risks; and (d) the measures envisaged to address the risks.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Data protection impact assessment — paragraph 7

properties.business_description: Article 36 requires organizations to consult with their supervisory authority before processing personal data if a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) reveals a high residual risk that cannot be mitigated. This is triggered when the DPIA, conducted under Article 35, identifies significant risks to data subjects that remain even after implementing risk-reduction measures. Organizations must seek guidance from the authority to ensure compliance and protect data subjects' rights. A common misconception is that this consultation is optional; however, it is mandatory when high risks are identified and unmitigated.
properties.obligation_text: The controller shall consult the supervisory authority prior to processing where a DPIA under Article 35 indicates that the processing would result in a high residual risk in the absence of measures taken by the controller to mitigate the risk.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Prior consultation

properties.business_description: In practice, this requirement means that if your Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) reveals that your planned data processing could lead to significant risks that you cannot adequately mitigate, you must consult with your supervisory authority before proceeding. This step is crucial to ensure that the risks are properly managed and that the rights of data subjects are protected. It is triggered when a DPIA identifies high residual risks despite mitigation efforts. A common misconception is that any high-risk processing requires consultation, but it is specifically when those risks remain unmitigated that consultation is necessary.
properties.obligation_text: The controller shall consult the supervisory authority prior to processing where a DPIA under Article 35 indicates that the processing would result in a high residual risk in the absence of measures taken by the controller to mitigate the risk.

This requirement is triggered when an organization is legally obligated to appoint a DPO, such as when it processes large amounts of sensitive data. The organization must assess the candidate's knowledge and experience in data protection to ensure compliance. A common misconception is that any IT professional can serve as a DPO, but the role requires specific legal and regulatory expertise.

A common misconception is that only large organizations need to comply, but this applies to any controller or processor that appoints a DPO, regardless of size. The DPO should report directly to the highest level of management. A common misconception is that the DPO can be directed by management on how to perform their tasks, which is not allowed. Additionally, DPOs should not face dismissal or penalties for fulfilling their responsibilities. They must report directly to the highest level of management, ensuring their concerns and recommendations are heard at the top. A common misconception is that DPOs can be directed by management on how to perform their tasks, which is not allowed under this regulation.

properties.business_description: The role of the Data Protection Officer (DPO) is crucial for ensuring that an organization complies with GDPR. When an organization processes personal data, the DPO must inform and advise the company and its staff about their GDPR obligations. The DPO also monitors compliance, advises on Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs), and ensures these assessments are carried out properly. Additionally, the DPO acts as a liaison with the supervisory authority, facilitating communication and cooperation. Organizations often misunderstand the DPO's role as purely advisory, but it also includes active monitoring and engagement with regulatory bodies.
properties.obligation_text: The data protection officer shall have at least the following tasks: (a) to inform and advise the controller or the processor and the employees of their obligations pursuant to this Regulation; (b) to monitor compliance with this Regulation; (c) to provide advice where requested as regards the DPIA and monitor its performance; (d) to cooperate with the supervisory authority; (e) to act as the contact point for the supervisory authority on issues relating to processing.

properties.business_description: This article defines key terms used in the GDPR, which are crucial for understanding compliance obligations. For controllers and processors, it clarifies who is responsible for deciding how and why personal data is processed (the controller) and who processes data on their behalf (the processor). It also defines what constitutes personal data and processing activities. A personal data breach is any security incident leading to unauthorized access or loss of personal data. Organizations must identify their role as either controller or processor and ensure they handle personal data securely to prevent breaches. Misunderstandings often arise around the roles and responsibilities of controllers and processors.
properties.obligation_text: For the purposes of this Regulation: 'personal data' means any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person; 'processing' means any operation performed on personal data; 'controller' means the natural or legal person which determines the purposes and means of the processing; 'processor' means a natural or legal person which processes personal data on behalf of the controller; 'personal data breach' means a breach of security leading to accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to, personal data.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Definitions

properties.business_description: Personal data means any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person. The scope is deliberately broad - name, email, phone number, IP address, location data, cookie identifiers, and even combinations of information that together identify someone all qualify. The key test is identifiability: if the data can be linked back to a living individual, directly or indirectly, it is personal data. Information about companies or deceased persons is not personal data. A common misconception is that only obviously identifying data like names applies - pseudonymised data where the key is held separately still counts as personal data under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).
properties.obligation_text: For the purposes of this Regulation: 'personal data' means any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person; 'processing' means any operation performed on personal data; 'controller' means the natural or legal person which determines the purposes and means of the processing; 'processor' means a natural or legal person which processes personal data on behalf of the controller; 'personal data breach' means a breach of security leading to accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to, personal data.

properties.business_description: Article 40 of the GDPR encourages the creation of codes of conduct to help ensure the regulation is applied correctly across different sectors. This is particularly relevant for industries with unique processing activities or for micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises that may have specific needs. Organizations are encouraged to collaborate with supervisory authorities and other stakeholders to develop these codes. The goal is to provide practical guidance tailored to specific industry contexts, helping organizations comply with GDPR requirements more effectively. A common misconception is that these codes are mandatory, but they are actually voluntary and meant to aid compliance efforts.
properties.obligation_text: The Member States, the supervisory authorities, the Board and the Commission shall encourage the drawing up of codes of conduct intended to contribute to the proper application of this Regulation, taking account of the specific features of the various processing sectors and the specific needs of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Codes of conduct

properties.business_description: Article 40.1 of the GDPR encourages the development of codes of conduct to help organizations apply the regulation effectively. This is particularly relevant for different processing sectors and smaller businesses like micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises. In practice, this means that controllers and processors should consider participating in or developing sector-specific codes of conduct that align with GDPR requirements. These codes can provide tailored guidance and best practices, making compliance more manageable. It is important to note that while these codes are encouraged, they are not mandatory. A common misconception is that adhering to a code of conduct is equivalent to full compliance with the GDPR, which is not the case.
properties.obligation_text: The Member States, the supervisory authorities, the Board and the Commission shall encourage the drawing up of codes of conduct intended to contribute to the proper application of this Regulation, taking account of the specific features of the various processing sectors and the specific needs of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises.

properties.title: Codes of conduct — paragraph 1

properties.business_description: Article 41 of the GDPR outlines the process for monitoring compliance with approved codes of conduct. This is relevant for organizations that have adopted such codes to demonstrate their commitment to data protection standards. The monitoring must be conducted by a body with the necessary expertise and accreditation from the relevant supervisory authority. This means that organizations need to ensure that any monitoring body they engage is properly accredited and knowledgeable about the specific code of conduct. A common misconception is that any third-party can monitor compliance, but only accredited bodies are authorized to do so.
properties.obligation_text: Monitoring of compliance with a code of conduct pursuant to Article 40 may be carried out by a body which has an appropriate level of expertise in relation to the subject-matter of the code and is accredited for that purpose by the competent supervisory authority.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Monitoring of approved codes of conduct

properties.business_description: For organizations that adhere to a code of conduct under GDPR, compliance must be monitored by a specialized body. This body should have the necessary expertise related to the code's subject matter and must be accredited by the relevant supervisory authority. This requirement is triggered when an organization chooses to follow an approved code of conduct. It ensures that adherence to the code is independently verified, providing assurance of compliance. A common misconception is that any organization can self-monitor; however, only accredited bodies can perform this role.
properties.obligation_text: Monitoring of compliance with a code of conduct pursuant to Article 40 may be carried out by a body which has an appropriate level of expertise in relation to the subject-matter of the code and is accredited for that purpose by the competent supervisory authority.

properties.title: Monitoring of approved codes of conduct — paragraph 1

properties.business_description: Article 42 of the GDPR encourages the creation of certification mechanisms and data protection seals to help organizations demonstrate compliance with data protection regulations. This is relevant for both data controllers and processors who want to show that their data processing activities meet GDPR standards. While not mandatory, obtaining such certifications can enhance trust with customers and partners by providing independent validation of compliance. Organizations should consider pursuing these certifications when they want to publicly affirm their commitment to data protection. A common misconception is that certification is required for compliance, but it is actually a voluntary process.
properties.obligation_text: The Member States, the supervisory authorities, the Board and the Commission shall encourage the establishment of data protection certification mechanisms and of data protection seals and marks, for the purpose of demonstrating compliance with this Regulation of processing operations by controllers and processors.

properties.title: Certification

properties.business_description: Article 42.1 of the GDPR encourages the creation of certification mechanisms to help demonstrate compliance with data protection regulations. For controllers and processors, this means they can voluntarily seek certifications or seals that show their data processing activities meet GDPR standards. This is particularly useful for building trust with customers and partners. It is triggered when organizations want to prove their compliance in a structured way. However, it's important to note that obtaining a certification is not mandatory under the GDPR, and it does not replace other compliance obligations.
properties.obligation_text: The Member States, the supervisory authorities, the Board and the Commission shall encourage the establishment of data protection certification mechanisms and of data protection seals and marks, for the purpose of demonstrating compliance with this Regulation of processing operations by controllers and processors.

properties.business_description: Article 43 of the GDPR allows certification bodies with the necessary data protection expertise to issue and renew certifications for organizations. This process is voluntary and must be transparent. For controllers and processors, this means that if they choose to pursue certification, they must engage with a recognized certification body. The certification can demonstrate compliance with certain data protection standards, potentially enhancing trust with customers and partners. However, organizations should be aware that certification is not mandatory and does not replace other GDPR compliance obligations.
properties.obligation_text: Without prejudice to the tasks and powers of the competent supervisory authority, certification bodies which have an appropriate level of expertise in relation to data protection shall issue and renew certification. Certification shall be voluntary and available via a process that is transparent.

properties.title: Certification bodies

properties.business_description: This article outlines the role of certification bodies in the GDPR framework. Certification bodies with the necessary data protection expertise can issue and renew certifications for organizations. This process is voluntary, meaning that organizations are not required to obtain certification, but it can be beneficial for demonstrating compliance. The process must be transparent, ensuring that organizations understand how to achieve and maintain certification. This is triggered when an organization seeks to demonstrate compliance with GDPR through certification. A common misconception is that certification is mandatory, but it is actually an optional tool for compliance assurance.
properties.obligation_text: Without prejudice to the tasks and powers of the competent supervisory authority, certification bodies which have an appropriate level of expertise in relation to data protection shall issue and renew certification. Certification shall be voluntary and available via a process that is transparent.

properties.business_description: Article 44 of the GDPR requires that any transfer of personal data to a third country or international organization must comply with specific conditions. This is triggered whenever personal data is moved outside the European Economic Area (EEA). Organizations must ensure that the data protection level is not undermined during such transfers. This means assessing the adequacy of data protection in the destination country and implementing appropriate safeguards. A common misconception is that any transfer outside the EEA is prohibited, but it is allowed if compliance with the GDPR's requirements is ensured.

In such cases, the company must implement appropriate safeguards to ensure data protection. These safeguards can include legally binding agreements between public authorities, binding corporate rules, or standard data protection clauses approved by the EU Commission. The goal is to ensure that data subjects' rights are enforceable and that they have access to legal remedies. A common misconception is that supervisory authority approval is always needed, which is not the case if these safeguards are in place.

properties.business_description: This article applies when a company wants to transfer personal data to a country outside the EU that hasn't been deemed to provide adequate data protection. In such cases, the company must implement appropriate safeguards to ensure the data is protected. This means setting up legal agreements or mechanisms that guarantee data subjects' rights and provide them with effective legal remedies. Common misconceptions include thinking that any contract suffices or that this only applies to large-scale transfers. It's crucial to ensure that the safeguards are robust and enforceable, aligning with GDPR standards.
properties.obligation_text: In the absence of a decision pursuant to Article 45(3), a controller or processor may transfer personal data to a third country or an international organisation only if the controller or processor has provided appropriate safeguards, and on condition that enforceable data subject rights and effective legal remedies for data subjects are available.

properties.title: Transfers subject to appropriate safeguards — paragraph 1

properties.business_description: This article outlines the mechanisms organizations can use to transfer personal data internationally while ensuring compliance with GDPR. It is triggered when a data controller or processor needs to transfer data outside the EU. Organizations must implement appropriate safeguards, such as legally binding agreements between public authorities, binding corporate rules, or standard data protection clauses approved by the Commission or a supervisory authority. A common misconception is that supervisory authority approval is always required, but these safeguards can be implemented without such authorization.
properties.obligation_text: The appropriate safeguards referred to in paragraph 1 may be provided for without requiring any specific authorisation from a supervisory authority, by: (a) a legally binding instrument between public authorities; (b) binding corporate rules; (c) standard data protection clauses adopted by the Commission; (d) standard data protection clauses adopted by a supervisory authority and approved by the Commission.

properties.title: Transfers subject to appropriate safeguards — paragraph 2

properties.business_description: Binding corporate rules (BCRs) are internal policies adopted by multinational companies to allow the transfer of personal data across borders within the same corporate group. They are triggered when a company wants to transfer data internationally and must be approved by a supervisory authority. BCRs must be legally binding, enforceable, and grant rights to data subjects. Companies often misunderstand BCRs as optional or think they apply to external partners, but they are specifically for intra-group transfers. Organizations must ensure BCRs are comprehensive and meet specific legal requirements to gain approval.
properties.obligation_text: The competent supervisory authority shall approve binding corporate rules provided that they: (a) are legally binding and apply to and are enforced by every member of the group; (b) expressly confer enforceable rights on data subjects; and (c) fulfil the requirements laid down in paragraph 2.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Binding corporate rules

properties.business_description: Binding corporate rules (BCRs) are internal policies adopted by multinational companies to allow the transfer of personal data across borders within the same corporate group. This article is triggered when a company seeks to transfer personal data internationally within its group. The rules must be legally binding, applicable to all group members, and enforceable. They must also grant enforceable rights to individuals whose data is being transferred. Approval from the relevant supervisory authority is required, ensuring the BCRs meet specific criteria. A common misconception is that BCRs are optional; however, they are essential for lawful data transfers within a corporate group.
properties.obligation_text: The competent supervisory authority shall approve binding corporate rules provided that they: (a) are legally binding and apply to and are enforced by every member of the group; (b) expressly confer enforceable rights on data subjects; and (c) fulfil the requirements laid down in paragraph 2.

properties.title: Binding corporate rules — paragraph 1

properties.business_description: This article applies when a court or administrative authority from outside the EU requests a company to transfer or disclose personal data. It requires that such requests can only be fulfilled if there is an existing international agreement between the EU (or an EU Member State) and the requesting country. This means that companies cannot comply with these requests based solely on the foreign authority's order. A common misconception is that any foreign legal request must be complied with, but without an international agreement, such requests are not enforceable under GDPR.
properties.obligation_text: Any judgment of a court or tribunal and any decision of an administrative authority of a third country requiring a controller or processor to transfer or disclose personal data may only be recognised or enforceable in any manner if based on an international agreement in force between the requesting third country and the Union or a Member State.

properties.title: Transfers or disclosures not authorised by Union law

properties.business_description: This article means that if a court or administrative authority from a non-EU country orders your organization to transfer or disclose personal data, you can only comply if there is an international agreement in place between that country and the EU or a Member State. This is triggered when you receive such a request from a third country. Organizations must verify the existence of such an agreement before proceeding. A common misconception is that any foreign legal order must be followed, but without the proper international agreement, compliance is not allowed under GDPR.
properties.obligation_text: Any judgment of a court or tribunal and any decision of an administrative authority of a third country requiring a controller or processor to transfer or disclose personal data may only be recognised or enforceable in any manner if based on an international agreement in force between the requesting third country and the Union or a Member State.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Transfers or disclosures not authorised by Union law — paragraph 1

properties.business_description: Article 49 of the GDPR allows for the transfer of personal data to countries without adequate data protection if specific conditions are met. This is relevant when there is no adequacy decision or appropriate safeguards in place. Organizations can transfer data if the individual has given explicit consent, if it's necessary for a contract, for public interest reasons, or for legal claims. It's crucial for controllers and processors to document the justification for such transfers and ensure they meet one of these conditions. A common misconception is that these derogations can be used freely without careful consideration of the specific circumstances.
properties.obligation_text: In the absence of an adequacy decision or appropriate safeguards, a transfer of personal data to a third country shall take place only on one of the following conditions: (a) the data subject has explicitly consented to the proposed transfer; (b) the transfer is necessary for the performance of a contract; (c) the transfer is necessary for important reasons of public interest; (d) the transfer is necessary for the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims.

properties.title: Derogations for specific situations

properties.business_description: Article 49.1 of the GDPR outlines specific situations where personal data can be transferred to a third country without an adequacy decision or appropriate safeguards. This is triggered when a company needs to transfer data internationally but lacks the usual legal frameworks. Organizations must ensure that one of the following conditions is met: obtaining explicit consent from the data subject, necessity for contract performance, public interest reasons, or legal claims. A common misconception is that these derogations can be used freely; however, they are exceptions and should be applied narrowly and with caution.
properties.obligation_text: In the absence of an adequacy decision or appropriate safeguards, a transfer of personal data to a third country shall take place only on one of the following conditions: (a) the data subject has explicitly consented to the proposed transfer; (b) the transfer is necessary for the performance of a contract; (c) the transfer is necessary for important reasons of public interest; (d) the transfer is necessary for the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Derogations for specific situations — paragraph 1
