properties.business_description: Article 50 of the GDPR focuses on fostering international cooperation to ensure the effective enforcement of data protection laws. This is relevant when personal data is transferred across borders, requiring organizations to collaborate with international authorities. It mandates that the European Commission and supervisory authorities work together to create mechanisms for mutual assistance in enforcing data protection laws globally. Organizations should be aware that this article does not impose direct obligations on them but highlights the importance of international collaboration in data protection enforcement. A common misconception is that this article requires organizations to establish their own international agreements, which it does not.
properties.obligation_text: The Commission and supervisory authorities shall take appropriate steps to develop international cooperation mechanisms to facilitate the effective enforcement of legislation for the protection of personal data and to provide international mutual assistance in the enforcement of legislation for the protection of personal data.
subject: privacy
properties.title: International cooperation for the protection of personal data

properties.business_description: Article 50.1 of the GDPR requires the European Commission and supervisory authorities to establish mechanisms for international cooperation. This is important for ensuring that data protection laws are effectively enforced across borders. For controllers and processors, this means that they may be subject to international cooperation efforts if their data processing activities involve multiple jurisdictions. Organizations should be aware that their compliance obligations might extend beyond local laws and involve coordination with foreign authorities. A common misconception is that this article imposes direct obligations on businesses, but it primarily focuses on the roles of the Commission and supervisory authorities.
properties.obligation_text: The Commission and supervisory authorities shall take appropriate steps to develop international cooperation mechanisms to facilitate the effective enforcement of legislation for the protection of personal data and to provide international mutual assistance in the enforcement of legislation for the protection of personal data.
subject: privacy
properties.title: International cooperation for the protection of personal data — paragraph 1

properties.business_description: Article 51 of the GDPR requires each EU Member State to establish one or more independent public authorities, known as supervisory authorities, to oversee the application of the GDPR. This means that organizations processing personal data must be aware of and cooperate with these authorities to ensure compliance. The supervisory authorities are responsible for protecting individuals' data rights and ensuring the free flow of personal data within the EU. Organizations should be prepared to engage with these authorities, especially if they process data across borders. A common misconception is that these authorities only act in a punitive capacity, but they also provide guidance and support for compliance.
properties.obligation_text: Each Member State shall provide for one or more independent public authorities to be responsible for monitoring the application of this Regulation, in order to protect the fundamental rights and freedoms of natural persons in relation to processing and to facilitate the free flow of personal data within the Union.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Supervisory authority

properties.business_description: This article mandates that each EU Member State must establish one or more independent public authorities, known as supervisory authorities, to oversee the application of GDPR. For organizations, this means that there is a designated body responsible for ensuring compliance with data protection laws. This requirement is triggered when personal data is processed within the EU. Organizations must be aware of the supervisory authority in their jurisdiction and understand that this body can investigate complaints, conduct audits, and enforce GDPR compliance. A common misconception is that these authorities only act as advisors, but they have significant enforcement powers.
properties.obligation_text: Each Member State shall provide for one or more independent public authorities to be responsible for monitoring the application of this Regulation, in order to protect the fundamental rights and freedoms of natural persons in relation to processing and to facilitate the free flow of personal data within the Union.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Supervisory authority — paragraph 1

properties.business_description: Article 52 of the GDPR mandates that supervisory authorities operate independently, without any external influence, when carrying out their duties. For organizations, this means that they cannot attempt to influence or direct the actions of these authorities. This requirement is triggered whenever a supervisory authority is engaged in oversight or enforcement activities related to data protection. Organizations must respect the autonomy of these authorities and refrain from any actions that could be perceived as attempting to sway their decisions. A common misconception is that organizations can negotiate or influence decisions, but this is not allowed under GDPR.
properties.obligation_text: Each supervisory authority shall act with complete independence in performing its tasks and exercising its powers. The member or members of each supervisory authority shall remain free from external influence, whether direct or indirect, and shall neither seek nor take instructions from anybody.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Independence

properties.business_description: This article ensures that supervisory authorities, which oversee data protection compliance, operate without any external pressure or influence. For controllers and processors, this means that when interacting with these authorities, they must respect their independence and not attempt to sway their decisions or actions. This requirement is triggered whenever a supervisory authority is performing its duties, such as during audits or investigations. Organizations must understand that these authorities are not to be influenced by external parties, ensuring unbiased enforcement of data protection laws.
properties.obligation_text: Each supervisory authority shall act with complete independence in performing its tasks and exercising its powers. The member or members of each supervisory authority shall remain free from external influence, whether direct or indirect, and shall neither seek nor take instructions from anybody.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Independence — paragraph 1

properties.business_description: This article requires that each member of a country's data protection supervisory authority is appointed through a transparent process. This means that the appointment must be clear and open, typically involving the parliament, government, head of State, or an independent body. For controllers and processors, this ensures that the supervisory authority overseeing their compliance with data protection laws is composed of members appointed in a fair and open manner. This article is relevant when understanding the legitimacy and authority of the supervisory body that may audit or investigate your organization’s data practices.
properties.obligation_text: Member States shall provide for each member of their supervisory authorities to be appointed by means of a transparent procedure by their parliament, government, head of State or an independent body entrusted with the appointment under Member State law.
subject: privacy
properties.title: General conditions for the members of the supervisory authority

properties.business_description: This article requires that the appointment of members to supervisory authorities in each EU Member State be conducted through a transparent process. This means that organizations, particularly controllers and processors, should be aware that the supervisory authorities overseeing their data protection practices are appointed in a manner that ensures independence and accountability. This is triggered when a Member State appoints new members to its supervisory authority. Organizations do not have direct obligations under this article, but understanding the appointment process can help them appreciate the impartiality and reliability of the supervisory authority. A common misconception is that organizations have a role in this appointment process, which they do not.
properties.obligation_text: Member States shall provide for each member of their supervisory authorities to be appointed by means of a transparent procedure by their parliament, government, head of State or an independent body entrusted with the appointment under Member State law.
subject: privacy
properties.title: General conditions for the members of the supervisory authority — paragraph 1

properties.business_description: Article 54 of the GDPR requires each EU Member State to establish a supervisory authority that complies with the GDPR's requirements. For controllers and processors, this means that they must be aware of and interact with the supervisory authority in the Member State where they operate. This is triggered when an organization processes personal data within the EU. Organizations must ensure they understand the role and powers of their local supervisory authority, as it is responsible for monitoring compliance with data protection laws. A common misconception is that organizations can choose any supervisory authority to report to, but they must engage with the one in their Member State.
properties.obligation_text: Each Member State shall provide by law that its supervisory authority is established in accordance with the requirements of this Regulation.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Rules on the establishment of the supervisory authority

properties.business_description: Article 54.1 of the GDPR requires each EU Member State to establish a supervisory authority by law, ensuring it meets the regulation's standards. For controllers and processors, this means understanding that their activities will be overseen by a national authority designed to enforce GDPR compliance. This is triggered when a Member State sets up or modifies its supervisory authority. Organizations must be aware of the authority's role in monitoring compliance, handling complaints, and imposing penalties. A common misconception is that organizations themselves must establish such authorities, but this is a state responsibility.
properties.obligation_text: Each Member State shall provide by law that its supervisory authority is established in accordance with the requirements of this Regulation.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Rules on the establishment of the supervisory authority — paragraph 1

properties.business_description: Article 55 of the GDPR specifies that each supervisory authority is responsible for overseeing GDPR compliance within its own Member State. This means that if your organization operates in multiple EU countries, you will need to interact with the supervisory authority of each country where you process personal data. Organizations must ensure they understand which supervisory authority they are accountable to and comply with any local variations in enforcement. A common misconception is that there is a single EU-wide authority, but in reality, each Member State has its own, and they coordinate through the European Data Protection Board.
properties.obligation_text: Each supervisory authority shall be competent for the performance of the tasks assigned to and the exercise of the powers conferred on it in accordance with this Regulation on the territory of its own Member State.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Competence

properties.business_description: This article means that each country's data protection authority (DPA) is responsible for overseeing compliance with the GDPR within its own borders. For organizations, this means that they must engage with the DPA of the country where they are established or where their data processing activities take place. This is triggered when an organization operates in or targets individuals in a specific EU Member State. Organizations should ensure they understand which DPA they need to interact with, as this can affect how they handle data protection issues. A common misconception is that a single DPA can oversee activities across multiple countries, which is not the case.
properties.obligation_text: Each supervisory authority shall be competent for the performance of the tasks assigned to and the exercise of the powers conferred on it in accordance with this Regulation on the territory of its own Member State.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Competence — paragraph 1

properties.business_description: Article 56 of the GDPR determines which supervisory authority is responsible for overseeing cross-border data processing activities. This is relevant when a company operates in multiple EU countries. The lead supervisory authority is the one in the country where the company has its main or single establishment. This means that for cross-border data processing, the company will primarily interact with this authority for compliance matters. A common misconception is that companies must deal with multiple authorities for cross-border processing, but Article 56 centralizes this to one lead authority, simplifying compliance efforts.
properties.obligation_text: Without prejudice to Article 55, the supervisory authority of the main establishment or of the single establishment of the controller or processor shall be competent to act as lead supervisory authority for the cross-border processing carried out by that controller or processor.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Competence of the lead supervisory authority

properties.business_description: Article 56.1 of the GDPR determines which supervisory authority is responsible for overseeing cross-border data processing activities. This is relevant when a company operates in multiple EU countries. The supervisory authority of the country where the company's main establishment is located will act as the lead authority. This means that if your company processes data across borders, you need to identify your main establishment to know which authority to engage with. A common misconception is that any supervisory authority can take the lead, but it must be the one where the main establishment is based.
properties.obligation_text: Without prejudice to Article 55, the supervisory authority of the main establishment or of the single establishment of the controller or processor shall be competent to act as lead supervisory authority for the cross-border processing carried out by that controller or processor.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Competence of the lead supervisory authority — paragraph 1

properties.business_description: Article 57 outlines the responsibilities of supervisory authorities, which are organizations tasked with ensuring GDPR compliance within their jurisdiction. For controllers and processors, this means they must be prepared for oversight and enforcement actions by these authorities. This article is triggered when personal data processing activities occur, requiring organizations to adhere to GDPR standards. Organizations should be aware that supervisory authorities also work to educate the public and advise government bodies on data protection matters. A common misconception is that supervisory authorities only enforce penalties, but they also play a key role in promoting awareness and understanding of data protection rights and responsibilities.
properties.obligation_text: Without prejudice to other tasks set out under this Regulation, each supervisory authority shall on its territory monitor and enforce the application of this Regulation; promote public awareness and understanding of the risks, rules, safeguards and rights in relation to processing; advise the national parliament, government and other institutions on legislative and administrative measures.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Tasks

properties.business_description: This article outlines the responsibilities of supervisory authorities in each EU member state. For controllers and processors, this means that these authorities will oversee compliance with GDPR within their jurisdiction. Organizations should be aware that supervisory authorities will not only enforce GDPR but also work to educate the public about data protection. This can involve providing guidance to national legislative bodies. Organizations should ensure they are prepared for potential audits or inquiries from these authorities. A common misconception is that supervisory authorities only enforce penalties, but they also play a significant role in public education and legislative advice.
properties.obligation_text: Without prejudice to other tasks set out under this Regulation, each supervisory authority shall on its territory monitor and enforce the application of this Regulation; promote public awareness and understanding of the risks, rules, safeguards and rights in relation to processing; advise the national parliament, government and other institutions on legislative and administrative measures.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Tasks — paragraph 1

properties.business_description: Article 58 of the GDPR outlines the powers of supervisory authorities, which include the ability to investigate, correct, authorize, and advise on data protection matters. For organizations, this means that if a supervisory authority believes there is a potential infringement of GDPR, they can conduct investigations and impose corrective measures, such as fines. Organizations must cooperate with these authorities and ensure compliance to avoid penalties. A common misconception is that supervisory authorities only have the power to impose fines, but they also provide guidance and support to help organizations comply with GDPR requirements.
properties.obligation_text: Each supervisory authority shall have investigative powers, corrective powers, authorisation and advisory powers and the power to bring infringements of this Regulation to the attention of judicial authorities, including the power to impose administrative fines pursuant to Article 83.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Powers

properties.business_description: Article 58.1 of the GDPR outlines the powers granted to supervisory authorities. These authorities can investigate compliance with GDPR, correct non-compliance, authorize certain data processing activities, and provide advice. They can also alert judicial authorities about breaches and impose fines. For organizations, this means that if a supervisory authority initiates an investigation, they must cooperate fully, provide necessary information, and comply with any corrective measures imposed. A common misconception is that supervisory authorities only have the power to impose fines, but they also play a significant advisory and corrective role.
properties.obligation_text: Each supervisory authority shall have investigative powers, corrective powers, authorisation and advisory powers and the power to bring infringements of this Regulation to the attention of judicial authorities, including the power to impose administrative fines pursuant to Article 83.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Powers — paragraph 1

properties.business_description: Article 59 requires each supervisory authority to create an annual report detailing their activities over the year. This report may include information about the types of data protection infringements they have been notified of and the measures they have taken in response. For controllers and processors, this means that supervisory authorities are actively monitoring compliance and publicly reporting on enforcement actions. Organizations should be aware that their interactions with supervisory authorities could be reflected in these reports. properties.business_description: This provision requires that personal data processing is lawful only if the data subject has given clear consent for their data to be used for specific purposes. Organizations must ensure they obtain explicit permission from individuals before processing their personal data. This is triggered when an organization intends to use personal data and must be able to demonstrate that consent was freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous. A common misconception is that consent can be implied or bundled with other terms, but it must be a separate, clear action by the data subject.
properties.obligation_text: Processing shall be lawful only if and to the extent that at least one of the following applies: (a) the data subject has given consent to the processing of his or her personal data for one or more specific purposes;

properties.business_description: This provision allows organizations to process personal data when it is necessary to fulfill a contract with the data subject. It is triggered when a data subject is party to a contract, and the processing is essential to deliver the contracted services or goods. Organizations must ensure that the data processing is directly related to the contract's execution. A common misconception is that any processing related to a contract is permissible, but it must be strictly necessary for the contract's performance. This basis cannot be used for processing that is merely convenient or beneficial but not essential to the contract.
properties.obligation_text: Processing shall be lawful only if and to the extent that at least one of the following applies: (b) processing is necessary for the performance of a contract to which the data subject is party;

properties.business_description: This provision allows organizations to process personal data when it is necessary to comply with a legal obligation. It is triggered when a law or regulation requires the organization to process certain data. For example, financial institutions may need to process data to comply with anti-money laundering laws. Organizations must ensure that the processing is strictly necessary for compliance and not for other purposes. A common misconception is that any legal requirement justifies processing, but it must be a specific obligation applicable to the controller.
properties.obligation_text: Processing shall be lawful only if and to the extent that at least one of the following applies: (c) processing is necessary for compliance with a legal obligation to which the controller is subject;

properties.business_description: This provision allows for the lawful processing of personal data when it is necessary to protect someone's vital interests, such as life or physical safety. It is typically triggered in emergency situations where obtaining consent is impractical or impossible, like during medical emergencies or natural disasters. Organizations must ensure that the processing is genuinely necessary for protecting vital interests and not used as a blanket justification for other purposes. A common misconception is that this basis can be used for any important interest, but it is strictly limited to vital interests, meaning those essential for survival or safety.

properties.business_description: This provision allows organizations to process personal data when it is necessary to perform a task in the public interest. Organizations must ensure that the processing is genuinely necessary for the task and not just convenient. A common misconception is that any activity with a public benefit qualifies, but the task must be clearly defined and legally recognized as serving the public interest.
properties.obligation_text: Processing shall be lawful only if and to the extent that at least one of the following applies: (e) processing is necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest;

A common misconception is that any business interest qualifies, but it must be legitimate and balanced against the data subject's rights.

properties.business_description: Article 60 of the GDPR requires the lead supervisory authority to work collaboratively with other relevant supervisory authorities to reach a consensus on decisions related to data protection matters. This process is triggered when a cross-border data processing activity involves multiple EU member states. The lead authority must share relevant information and draft decisions with the other authorities involved. Organizations should understand that this cooperation is about ensuring consistent application of GDPR across borders, not about bypassing local laws. A common misconception is that the lead authority can make unilateral decisions without consulting others, which is not the case.
properties.obligation_text: The lead supervisory authority shall cooperate with the other supervisory authorities concerned in an endeavour to reach consensus. This involves sharing necessary information and proposing a draft decision for review. Organizations should be prepared to engage with multiple authorities and provide comprehensive information to facilitate this process. A common misconception is that only the lead authority's opinion matters, but consensus with other authorities is crucial.

properties.business_description: Article 61 requires supervisory authorities across different jurisdictions to share relevant information and assist each other to ensure the GDPR is applied consistently. For controllers and processors, this means that if they operate in multiple EU countries, they may be subject to coordinated investigations or enforcement actions by these authorities. This provision is triggered when cross-border data processing activities are involved. Organizations should be prepared for potential inquiries from multiple supervisory bodies and ensure they have clear communication channels and documentation ready. A common misconception is that this only applies to large companies, but it can affect any organization with cross-border data activities.
properties.obligation_text: Supervisory authorities shall provide each other with relevant information and mutual assistance in order to implement and apply this Regulation in a consistent manner, and shall put in place measures for effective cooperation with one another.

properties.business_description: Article 72 outlines how the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) makes decisions. For most decisions, a simple majority of the Board members is needed. However, when it comes to adopting its own rules of procedure, a two-thirds majority is required. This means that controllers and processors should be aware that the Board's decisions are made collectively and that the rules governing these decisions are established with a higher level of consensus. This article is relevant when understanding how the EDPB's decisions, which can impact data protection practices, are formulated and agreed upon.
properties.obligation_text: The Board shall take decisions by a simple majority of its members, unless otherwise provided for in this Regulation. The Board shall adopt its own rules of procedure by a two-thirds majority of its members.

properties.title: Procedure

properties.business_description: This article outlines how the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) makes decisions. For controllers and processors, this means understanding that the EDPB's decisions are typically made by a simple majority vote among its members. However, when it comes to adopting its own rules of procedure, a two-thirds majority is required. This is relevant when the EDPB issues guidelines or decisions that may impact your data processing activities. Organizations should be aware that these decisions can influence compliance requirements and should monitor EDPB outputs for any changes that may affect their operations.
properties.obligation_text: The Board shall take decisions by a simple majority of its members, unless otherwise provided for in this Regulation. The Board shall adopt its own rules of procedure by a two-thirds majority of its members.

properties.business_description: This article outlines the process for electing leadership within the European Data Protection Board (EDPB). The Board is responsible for electing a chair and two deputy chairs from its members through a simple majority vote. Each elected position has a term of five years, with the possibility of one renewal. This process is primarily internal to the EDPB and does not directly impose obligations on controllers or processors. However, understanding the leadership structure can help organizations anticipate how decisions and guidance from the EDPB might be influenced. A common misconception is that this election process affects the roles within individual organizations, which it does not.
properties.obligation_text: The Board shall elect a chair and two deputy chairs from amongst its members by simple majority. The term of office shall be five years and shall be renewable once.

properties.title: Chair

properties.business_description: This article outlines the process for selecting leadership within the European Data Protection Board (EDPB). It requires the Board to elect a chair and two deputy chairs from its members through a simple majority vote. This leadership structure is essential for guiding the Board's activities and ensuring effective decision-making. The election occurs every five years, with the possibility of re-election for one additional term. This process is internal to the Board and does not directly impose obligations on data controllers or processors, but understanding the Board's leadership can help organizations anticipate regulatory priorities and actions.
properties.obligation_text: The Board shall elect a chair and two deputy chairs from amongst its members by simple majority. The term of office shall be five years and shall be renewable once.

properties.business_description: Article 74 outlines the responsibilities of the Chair of the European Data Protection Board (EDPB). In practice, this means that the Chair is responsible for organizing and leading the Board's meetings, setting the agenda, and ensuring that decisions made by the Board are communicated to the relevant supervisory authorities. This article is triggered when the Board needs to convene to discuss data protection matters. Organizations should be aware that the Chair plays a crucial role in coordinating the Board's activities, but this does not impose direct obligations on controllers or processors.
properties.obligation_text: The Chair shall convene the meetings of the Board and prepare its agenda; notify decisions adopted by the Board to the lead supervisory authority and supervisory authorities concerned; ensure the timely performance of the tasks of the Board.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Tasks of the Chair

properties.business_description: This article outlines the responsibilities of the Chair of the European Data Protection Board (EDPB). In practice, it means that the Chair is responsible for organizing and setting the agenda for Board meetings. The Chair must also communicate decisions made by the Board to the relevant supervisory authorities, ensuring that these decisions are implemented effectively. This process is triggered when the Board needs to meet to discuss data protection issues or make decisions. Organizations should be aware that the Chair's role is crucial for the smooth operation of the Board, but they are not directly responsible for these tasks themselves.
properties.obligation_text: The Chair shall convene the meetings of the Board and prepare its agenda; notify decisions adopted by the Board to the lead supervisory authority and supervisory authorities concerned; ensure the timely performance of the tasks of the Board.

properties.business_description: Article 75 of the GDPR establishes that the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) will have a secretariat provided by the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS). This secretariat operates solely under the direction of the Chair of the Board. For controllers and processors, this means that the EDPB's administrative and logistical support is centralized and managed by the EDPS, ensuring consistency in the Board's operations. Organizations are not directly affected by this article in terms of compliance actions, but understanding the structure can help in navigating interactions with the EDPB.
properties.obligation_text: The Board shall have a secretariat, which shall be provided by the European Data Protection Supervisor. The secretariat shall perform its tasks exclusively under the instructions of the Chair of the Board.

properties.business_description: Article 75.1 outlines that the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) must have a secretariat, which is provided by the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS). properties.obligation_text: The Board shall have a secretariat, which shall be provided by the European Data Protection Supervisor. The secretariat shall perform its tasks exclusively under the instructions of the Chair of the Board.

properties.business_description: Article 76 of the GDPR requires that discussions within the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) remain confidential when deemed necessary by the Board itself. This means that any sensitive deliberations or decisions made by the Board are not to be disclosed publicly unless specified otherwise. For organizations, this means that any documents submitted to the Board are subject to confidentiality rules and are accessed according to specific regulations. This is triggered when an organization is involved in proceedings or consultations with the Board. A common misconception is that all Board discussions are public, but confidentiality is maintained as needed.
properties.obligation_text: The discussions of the Board shall be confidential where the Board deems it necessary, as provided for in its rules of procedure. Access to documents submitted to the Board shall be governed by Regulation (EC) No 1049/2001.

properties.title: Confidentiality

properties.business_description: This article means that when the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) holds discussions, these discussions are kept confidential if the Board decides it's necessary. This confidentiality is based on the Board's internal rules. For organizations, this means that any documents they submit to the Board are subject to access rules under a separate regulation, specifically Regulation (EC) No 1049/2001. This is triggered when an organization is involved in proceedings with the Board. Organizations should ensure that they understand when their submissions might be accessed by others and under what conditions confidentiality applies.
properties.obligation_text: The discussions of the Board shall be confidential where the Board deems it necessary, as provided for in its rules of procedure. Access to documents submitted to the Board shall be governed by Regulation (EC) No 1049/2001.

properties.title: Confidentiality — paragraph 1

properties.business_description: Article 77 of the GDPR allows individuals, known as data subjects, to file a complaint with a supervisory authority if they believe their personal data is being processed in violation of GDPR. This right is activated when a data subject feels their data rights have been infringed, and it requires organizations to be prepared for potential investigations by these authorities. Organizations should ensure they have processes to handle such complaints efficiently and transparently. A common misconception is that this right only applies in the country where the organization is based, but it actually applies in the data subject's country of residence, work, or where the infringement occurred.
properties.obligation_text: Without prejudice to any other administrative or judicial remedy, every data subject shall have the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority, in particular in the Member State of his or her habitual residence, place of work or place of the alleged infringement if the data subject considers that the processing of personal data relating to him or her infringes this Regulation.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority

properties.business_description: This article grants individuals the right to file a complaint with a data protection authority if they believe their personal data is being mishandled in violation of GDPR. This right is activated when a data subject feels their data is being processed unlawfully. Organizations must be prepared to respond to inquiries from supervisory authorities and facilitate the complaint process. A common misconception is that complaints can only be lodged in the country where the organization is based, but they can also be filed in the individual's country of residence or where the alleged infringement occurred.
properties.obligation_text: Without prejudice to any other administrative or judicial remedy, every data subject shall have the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority, in particular in the Member State of his or her habitual residence, place of work or place of the alleged infringement if the data subject considers that the processing of personal data relating to him or her infringes this Regulation.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority — paragraph 1

properties.business_description: Article 78 of the GDPR ensures that individuals or organizations can challenge decisions made by data protection authorities in court. This right is triggered when a supervisory authority issues a legally binding decision that affects a person or entity. Organizations must be prepared to respond to such decisions and understand that they have the option to seek judicial review if they disagree with the authority's ruling. A common misconception is that this right only applies to individuals, but it also extends to legal entities. Organizations should be aware of this right and consider it as part of their compliance strategy.
properties.obligation_text: Without prejudice to any other administrative or non-judicial remedy, each natural or legal person shall have the right to an effective judicial remedy against a legally binding decision of a supervisory authority concerning them.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Right to an effective judicial remedy against a supervisory authority

properties.business_description: This article ensures that individuals or organizations have the right to challenge a decision made by a data protection supervisory authority if it legally affects them. It is triggered when a supervisory authority issues a binding decision that impacts a natural or legal person. Organizations must be prepared to facilitate this process by understanding the decisions that can be contested and ensuring they have mechanisms in place to respond to any legal challenges. A common misconception is that this right only applies to individuals, but it also extends to legal entities such as companies.
properties.obligation_text: Without prejudice to any other administrative or non-judicial remedy, each natural or legal person shall have the right to an effective judicial remedy against a legally binding decision of a supervisory authority concerning them.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Right to an effective judicial remedy against a supervisory authority — paragraph 1

properties.business_description: Article 79 of the GDPR provides data subjects with the right to seek a judicial remedy if they believe their rights under the GDPR have been violated due to the processing of their personal data. This means that if an individual feels that a company has mishandled their data, they can take the matter to court. Organizations must be prepared to respond to such legal actions and ensure their data processing activities comply with GDPR standards to avoid litigation. A common misconception is that this right can be bypassed by resolving issues through a supervisory authority, but judicial remedies are always available to data subjects.
properties.obligation_text: Without prejudice to any available administrative or non-judicial remedy, including the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority pursuant to Article 77, each data subject shall have the right to an effective judicial remedy where he or she considers that his or her rights under this Regulation have been infringed as a result of the processing of his or her personal data.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Right to an effective judicial remedy against a controller or processor

properties.business_description: Article 79.1 of the GDPR gives individuals the right to seek a judicial remedy if they believe their data protection rights have been violated by a data controller or processor. This is triggered when a data subject feels their personal data has been mishandled or their rights under the GDPR have been infringed. Organizations must be prepared to address such claims and potentially defend their data processing activities in court. A common misconception is that this right replaces administrative remedies, but it actually complements them, allowing individuals to pursue both avenues if necessary.
properties.obligation_text: Without prejudice to any available administrative or non-judicial remedy, including the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority pursuant to Article 77, each data subject shall have the right to an effective judicial remedy where he or she considers that his or her rights under this Regulation have been infringed as a result of the processing of his or her personal data.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Right to an effective judicial remedy against a controller or processor — paragraph 1

properties.business_description: This article applies when an organization offers online services directly to children and processes their personal data. If the child is 16 or older, they can consent to data processing themselves. For children under 16, consent must be obtained from a parent or guardian. Organizations must make reasonable efforts to verify that parental consent is genuine, considering the technology available. A common misconception is that any form of consent is sufficient, but the law requires specific verification of parental consent for those under 16.
properties.obligation_text: Where point (a) of Article 6(1) applies, in relation to the offer of information society services directly to a child, the processing of the personal data of a child shall be lawful where the child is at least 16 years old. Where the child is below the age of 16 years, such processing shall be lawful only if and to the extent that consent is given or authorised by the holder of parental responsibility over the child. The controller shall make reasonable efforts to verify in such cases that consent is given or authorised by the holder of parental responsibility over the child, taking into consideration available technology.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Conditions applicable to child's consent in relation to information society services

properties.business_description: This article applies when an organization offers online services directly to children and processes their personal data. If the child is 16 or older, their consent is sufficient for lawful data processing. However, if the child is under 16, the organization must obtain consent from a parent or guardian. This means businesses need to implement age verification mechanisms and ensure they have a process for obtaining and verifying parental consent for users under 16. A common misconception is that the age threshold is the same across all EU countries, but some countries may set a lower age limit, not below 13 years.
properties.obligation_text: Where point (a) of Article 6(1) applies, in relation to the offer of information society services directly to a child, the processing of the personal data of a child shall be lawful where the child is at least 16 years old. Where the child is below the age of 16 years, such processing shall be lawful only if and to the extent that consent is given or authorised by the holder of parental responsibility over the child.

The organization must make reasonable efforts to ensure that the consent is genuinely given or authorized by a parent or guardian. This involves using available technology to verify the identity of the person providing consent. It is important to balance the verification process with the need to avoid excessive data collection. A common misconception is that any form of parental consent is sufficient, but the regulation requires verification of the consent's authenticity.
properties.obligation_text: The controller shall make reasonable efforts to verify in such cases that consent is given or authorised by the holder of parental responsibility over the child, taking into consideration available technology.

properties.business_description: Article 80 of the GDPR allows individuals to authorize a non-profit organization to file a data protection complaint on their behalf. This is relevant for controllers and processors when they receive a complaint from such an organization. It requires them to treat the complaint as if it were directly from the data subject. This provision is triggered when a data subject chooses to exercise their rights through a third-party organization. A common misconception is that this allows any organization to represent data subjects, but it must be a non-profit active in data protection and properly constituted under national law.
properties.obligation_text: The data subject shall have the right to mandate a not-for-profit body, organisation or association which has been properly constituted in accordance with the law of a Member State and is active in the field of the protection of data subjects' rights to lodge the complaint on his or her behalf.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Representation of data subjects

properties.business_description: Article 80.1 of the GDPR allows data subjects to appoint a not-for-profit organization to act on their behalf in lodging complaints about data protection violations. This means that if an individual believes their data rights have been infringed, they can authorize a qualified organization to represent them. For controllers and processors, this implies that they may receive complaints not only directly from individuals but also from these organizations. Organizations must be prepared to handle such representations and ensure they have processes in place to respond appropriately. A common misconception is that only individuals can lodge complaints, but this article clarifies that authorized bodies can do so as well.
properties.obligation_text: The data subject shall have the right to mandate a not-for-profit body, organisation or association which has been properly constituted in accordance with the law of a Member State and is active in the field of the protection of data subjects' rights to lodge the complaint on his or her behalf.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Representation of data subjects — paragraph 1

properties.business_description: Article 81 of the GDPR is relevant when a court in one EU Member State becomes aware of ongoing legal proceedings in another Member State concerning the same data processing issue by the same controller or processor. In such cases, the court must reach out to the court in the other Member State to verify the existence of these proceedings. This ensures that there is coordination and awareness between courts handling similar cases, preventing conflicting judgments. Organizations should be aware that this article is triggered when there are parallel legal proceedings in different Member States concerning the same data processing activities.
properties.obligation_text: Where a competent court of a Member State has information on proceedings, concerning the same subject matter as regards processing by the same controller or processor, that are pending in a court in another Member State, it shall contact that court in the other Member State to confirm the existence of such proceedings.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Suspension of proceedings

properties.business_description: This article applies when a court in one EU Member State becomes aware of legal proceedings related to data processing by the same entity that are already underway in another Member State. In such cases, the court must reach out to the court in the other Member State to verify the existence of these proceedings. This ensures coordination and avoids conflicting judgments. Organizations should be aware that if they are involved in cross-border data processing litigation, courts may communicate with each other to confirm parallel cases. This does not impose direct obligations on controllers or processors but affects how their cases might be handled by the courts.
properties.obligation_text: Where a competent court of a Member State has information on proceedings, concerning the same subject matter as regards processing by the same controller or processor, that are pending in a court in another Member State, it shall contact that court in the other Member State to confirm the existence of such proceedings.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Suspension of proceedings — paragraph 1

properties.business_description: Article 82 of the GDPR establishes that individuals who suffer harm due to a breach of the regulation are entitled to compensation from the responsible data controller or processor. This is triggered when a data breach or non-compliance with GDPR obligations results in material or non-material damage to an individual. Organizations must be prepared to address claims and potentially compensate affected individuals. A common misconception is that only controllers are liable, but processors can also be held accountable if they fail to meet their specific obligations under the GDPR.
properties.obligation_text: Any person who has suffered material or non-material damage as a result of an infringement of this Regulation shall have the right to receive compensation from the controller or processor for the damage suffered. Any controller involved in processing shall be liable for the damage caused by processing which infringes this Regulation. A processor shall be liable for the damage caused by processing only where it has not complied with obligations of this Regulation specifically directed to processors.

properties.title: Right to compensation and liability

properties.business_description: Under GDPR Article 82.1, if an individual suffers harm due to a breach of the regulation, they can claim compensation from the organization responsible. This applies to both material and non-material damages. Organizations must be prepared to address claims and potentially compensate affected individuals. This obligation is triggered when a breach occurs that causes harm, requiring organizations to assess and respond to claims appropriately. A common misconception is that only financial losses are compensable, but non-material damages like distress are also covered.
properties.obligation_text: Any person who has suffered material or non-material damage as a result of an infringement of this Regulation shall have the right to receive compensation from the controller or processor for the damage suffered.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Right to compensation and liability — paragraph 1

properties.business_description: This article outlines the liability of controllers and processors when data processing activities violate GDPR and cause harm. Controllers are always liable for damages resulting from their processing activities. Processors, however, are only liable if they fail to meet specific GDPR obligations applicable to them. This means that if a processor follows all their specific obligations, they may not be held liable for damages. Organizations must ensure they understand their role as either a controller or processor and comply with relevant GDPR requirements to avoid liability. A common misconception is that processors are always liable for any data breach, which is not the case if they have complied with their obligations.
properties.obligation_text: Any controller involved in processing shall be liable for the damage caused by processing which infringes this Regulation. A processor shall be liable for the damage caused by processing only where it has not complied with obligations of this Regulation specifically directed to processors.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Right to compensation and liability — paragraph 2

properties.obligation_text: A controller or processor shall be exempt from liability under paragraph 2 if it proves that it is not in any way responsible for the event giving rise to the damage.
properties.title: Right to compensation and liability — paragraph 3

properties.business_description: Article 83 of the GDPR outlines the financial penalties for non-compliance with specific provisions. Organizations, whether controllers or processors, can face fines up to 10 million EUR or 2% of their global turnover for breaches related to operational obligations, such as data protection by design and default, and security measures. More severe breaches, like violating basic data processing principles or data subject rights, can lead to fines up to 20 million EUR or 4% of turnover. This article is triggered when an organization fails to comply with GDPR requirements, emphasizing the importance of adhering to data protection principles and respecting data subjects' rights.

properties.business_description: Article 84 requires EU Member States to establish rules for penalties related to GDPR violations that do not involve administrative fines under Article 83. Organizations must be aware that even if an infringement doesn't lead to an administrative fine, other penalties may still apply. These penalties must be effective, proportionate, and dissuasive. This means that businesses should ensure compliance with all aspects of the GDPR, not just those that carry fines, as other penalties can still have significant impacts. A common misconception is that only administrative fines are enforceable, but this article clarifies that other penalties can also be imposed.
properties.obligation_text: Member States shall lay down the rules on other penalties applicable to infringements of this Regulation in particular for infringements which are not subject to administrative fines pursuant to Article 83, and shall take all measures necessary to ensure that they are implemented. Such penalties shall be effective, proportionate and dissuasive.

properties.business_description: Article 84.1 requires EU Member States to establish rules for penalties related to GDPR violations that do not fall under administrative fines outlined in Article 83. This means that if an organization breaches the GDPR in a way that isn't covered by the standard fines, the Member State must have other penalties in place. These penalties should be effective, proportionate, and dissuasive. Organizations need to be aware that non-compliance can lead to various penalties, not just fines, and should ensure they understand the specific rules in each Member State where they operate.

This is particularly relevant for activities like journalism, academia, art, and literature. When these activities involve processing personal data, Member States may allow exemptions from certain GDPR provisions to ensure freedom of expression is not unduly restricted. Organizations involved in these fields should be aware of national laws that might provide such exemptions and ensure they comply with them. A common misconception is that all GDPR obligations are waived for journalistic purposes, but exemptions are only applicable when necessary to balance these rights.

properties.business_description: Article 86 of the GDPR allows public authorities or bodies to disclose personal data contained in official documents if such disclosure is permitted by Union or Member State law. This provision is triggered when there is a need to balance public access to official documents with the protection of personal data. Organizations must ensure that any disclosure complies with applicable laws and does not infringe on individuals' data protection rights. properties.obligation_text: Processing of personal data revealing racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, or trade union membership, and the processing of genetic data, biometric data for the purpose of uniquely identifying a natural person, data concerning health or data concerning a natural person's sex life or sexual orientation shall be prohibited. properties.business_description: This article prohibits the processing of certain sensitive personal data categories, such as racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious beliefs, and health data. Organizations must avoid handling this data unless specific exceptions apply, such as explicit consent from the data subject or processing necessary for employment law obligations. This rule is triggered when an organization collects or uses data that falls into these special categories. A common misconception is that all personal data is treated equally under GDPR, but this article highlights that some data types require stricter handling due to their sensitive nature.
properties.obligation_text: Processing of personal data revealing racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, or trade union membership, and the processing of genetic data, biometric data for the purpose of uniquely identifying a natural person, data concerning health or data concerning a natural person's sex life or sexual orientation shall be prohibited.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Processing of special categories of personal data — paragraph 1

properties.business_description: This article outlines exceptions where the prohibition on processing special categories of personal data does not apply. Organizations can process such data if they have explicit consent from the data subject, or if it is necessary for fulfilling legal obligations related to employment or social security. It also allows processing to protect someone's vital interests, for medical or occupational health purposes, or for archiving, research, or statistical purposes. Organizations must ensure they meet one of these specific conditions before processing sensitive data. A common misconception is that any consent is sufficient, but it must be explicit.
properties.obligation_text: Paragraph 1 shall not apply if one of the following applies: (a) the data subject has given explicit consent; (b) processing is necessary for employment or social security law obligations; (c) processing is necessary to protect vital interests; (h) processing is necessary for medical or occupational health purposes; (j) processing is necessary for archiving, research or statistical purposes.
subject: privacy
properties.title: Processing of special categories of personal data — paragraph 2

properties.business_description: This provision allows organizations to process special categories of personal data if they have obtained explicit consent from the data subject. In practice, this means that before processing sensitive data such as health information, racial or ethnic origin, or political opinions, the organization must ensure that the individual has clearly agreed to this processing. This consent must be informed, specific, and unambiguous. A common misconception is that any form of consent suffices; however, it must be explicit, meaning it cannot be implied or assumed. Organizations should document this consent to demonstrate compliance if needed.
properties.obligation_text: Paragraph 1 shall not apply if one of the following applies: (a) the data subject has given explicit consent;

properties.title: Processing of special categories of personal data — 2(a)

properties.business_description: This provision allows organizations to process special categories of personal data if it is necessary to fulfill obligations related to employment or social security laws. This means that if an organization needs to handle sensitive data to comply with legal requirements in these areas, such as ensuring workplace safety or administering employee benefits, they are permitted to do so. Organizations must ensure that the processing is strictly necessary for compliance with these legal obligations and not for other purposes. A common misconception is that any employment-related processing is covered, but it must be legally mandated.
properties.obligation_text: Paragraph 1 shall not apply if one of the following applies: (b) processing is necessary for employment or social security law obligations;
subject: privacy
properties.title: Processing of special categories of personal data — 2(b)

properties.business_description: This provision allows for the processing of special categories of personal data when it is necessary to protect someone's vital interests. This typically applies in emergency situations where an individual's life or health is at risk, and obtaining consent is not feasible. Organizations must ensure that the processing is strictly necessary and proportionate to the threat to the individual's vital interests. A common misconception is that this provision can be used for any health-related processing, but it is strictly limited to situations where there is an immediate threat to life or health.
properties.obligation_text: Paragraph 1 shall not apply if one of the following applies: (c) processing is necessary to protect vital interests;
subject: privacy
properties.title: Processing of special categories of personal data — 2(c)

properties.business_description: This provision allows organizations to process special categories of personal data, such as health information, when it is necessary for medical or occupational health purposes. This means that if you are handling data for reasons like providing healthcare services or ensuring workplace safety, you may be exempt from the general prohibition on processing sensitive data. However, the processing must be strictly necessary for these purposes. Organizations should ensure they have clear documentation justifying the necessity of processing and should not assume that any health-related processing automatically qualifies under this exemption.
properties.obligation_text: Paragraph 1 shall not apply if one of the following applies: (h) processing is necessary for medical or occupational health purposes;

properties.title: Processing of special categories of personal data — 2(h)

properties.business_description: This provision allows organizations to process special categories of personal data if it is necessary for archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or historical research purposes, or statistical purposes. Organizations must ensure that the processing is genuinely necessary for these purposes and that appropriate safeguards are in place to protect the data. A common misconception is that any research or statistical activity automatically qualifies, but it must be in the public interest and meet the necessity requirement.
properties.obligation_text: Paragraph 1 shall not apply if one of the following applies: (j) processing is necessary for archiving, research or statistical purposes.

properties.business_description: Article 90 allows EU Member States to create specific rules for how data protection authorities can interact with organizations bound by professional secrecy, like lawyers or doctors. This is triggered when a controller or processor is subject to confidentiality obligations. Organizations must balance data protection rights with these secrecy obligations, ensuring that they comply with both. A common misconception is that data protection laws override all secrecy obligations, but this article clarifies that both must be reconciled. Organizations should be aware of their national laws that may impose additional requirements in these situations.
properties.obligation_text: Member States may adopt specific rules to set out the powers of the supervisory authorities in relation to controllers or processors that are subject to an obligation of professional secrecy or other equivalent obligations of secrecy where this is necessary and proportionate to reconcile the right of the protection of personal data with the obligation of secrecy.

properties.business_description: This provision allows EU Member States to create specific rules regarding how data protection authorities can interact with organizations bound by professional secrecy, such as lawyers or doctors. It is triggered when a supervisory authority needs to investigate or enforce data protection laws but must also respect the confidentiality obligations of the organization. Organizations must understand that while they have obligations to protect personal data, they also need to maintain confidentiality as required by their professional standards. A common misconception is that data protection laws override all confidentiality obligations, but this provision ensures a balance between the two.
properties.obligation_text: Member States may adopt specific rules to set out the powers of the supervisory authorities in relation to controllers or processors that are subject to an obligation of professional secrecy or other equivalent obligations of secrecy where this is necessary and proportionate to reconcile the right of the protection of personal data with the obligation of secrecy.

properties.business_description: Article 91 of the GDPR allows churches and religious associations in EU Member States to continue using their existing data protection rules, as long as these rules are aligned with the GDPR. This means that if a church or religious community already has comprehensive data protection measures, they can keep using them, but they must ensure these measures meet GDPR standards. This provision is triggered when such organizations are processing personal data and already have established data protection frameworks. It requires them to review and update their rules to ensure compliance with the GDPR, without needing to discard their existing systems entirely.

This means reviewing and updating their policies to meet GDPR standards. It is triggered when such entities are processing personal data under their own frameworks. properties.obligation_text: Where in a Member State, churches and religious associations or communities apply comprehensive rules relating to the protection of natural persons with regard to processing, such rules may continue to apply, provided that they are brought into line with this Regulation.

properties.business_description: Article 92 of the GDPR allows the European Commission to create delegated acts, which are legal acts that supplement or amend non-essential parts of the legislation. This power is granted indefinitely from May 24, 2016. For organizations, this means that the Commission can make certain changes to the GDPR without needing to go through the full legislative process. This is typically triggered when there is a need to update or clarify specific aspects of the regulation. Organizations should stay informed about any new delegated acts as they may impact compliance requirements. A common misconception is that these acts can change core principles of the GDPR, but they only address non-essential elements.

For controllers and processors, this indicates that certain regulatory decisions are made with the input of a specialized committee, ensuring that diverse perspectives are considered. This process is triggered when the Commission needs to adopt specific measures under the GDPR framework. Organizations should be aware that this committee's role is procedural and does not impose direct obligations on them. A common misconception is that this committee directly regulates data processing activities, but its role is advisory to the Commission.

This transition requires organizations to ensure that their compliance frameworks are aligned with the GDPR's requirements, rather than those of the repealed directive. A common misconception is that some parts of the old directive might still apply, but in reality, the GDPR fully supersedes it.

For organizations, this means that all data protection practices must align with the GDPR's requirements instead of the old Directive. This transition is crucial for compliance, as it ensures that data processing activities are up to date with the current legal framework. A common misconception is that some parts of the old Directive might still apply, but this is not the case; the GDPR fully replaces it.

properties.business_description: Article 95 of the GDPR clarifies that it does not add extra obligations for organizations already governed by Directive 2002/58/EC, which deals with electronic communications services. This means if your organization provides publicly available electronic communications services, you should primarily comply with the specific rules in Directive 2002/58/EC for those services. This article is triggered when your processing activities fall under the scope of both the GDPR and the ePrivacy Directive. A common misconception is that GDPR always adds new requirements, but in this case, it defers to the existing ePrivacy rules.
properties.obligation_text: This Regulation shall not impose additional obligations on natural or legal persons in relation to processing in connection with the provision of publicly available electronic communications services in public communications networks in the Union in relation to matters for which they are subject to specific obligations set out in Directive 2002/58/EC.

properties.business_description: This provision applies to international agreements made by EU Member States before May 24, 2016, that involve transferring personal data to third countries or international organizations. These agreements can continue to be used as long as they were compliant with EU laws at the time they were made. Organizations should review such agreements to ensure they remain valid and compliant with current data protection standards. This is particularly relevant when considering amendments or replacements to these agreements. A common misconception is that all pre-existing agreements are automatically invalid under GDPR, which is not the case if they meet the specified criteria.
properties.obligation_text: International agreements involving the transfer of personal data to third countries or international organisations which were concluded by Member States prior to 24 May 2016, and which comply with Union law as applicable prior to that date, shall remain in force until amended, replaced or revoked.

properties.business_description: This article addresses international agreements made by EU Member States before May 24, 2016, that involve transferring personal data to countries outside the EU or to international organizations. These agreements can continue to be valid as long as they complied with EU law at the time they were made. Organizations should review such agreements to ensure they still align with current data protection standards and be prepared to update or replace them if necessary. This provision is triggered when dealing with legacy agreements, and it requires organizations to assess their compliance status without assuming they automatically meet current GDPR requirements.

properties.business_description: Article 97 requires the European Commission to evaluate and review the GDPR and report its findings to the European Parliament and the Council every four years, starting from May 25, 2020. This means that organizations should be aware that the GDPR is subject to periodic review, which may lead to changes or updates in the regulation. However, this article does not impose any direct obligations on controllers or processors. Instead, it ensures that the GDPR remains effective and relevant over time. Organizations should stay informed about these reports as they may influence future compliance requirements.
properties.obligation_text: By 25 May 2020 and every four years thereafter, the Commission shall submit a report on the evaluation and review of this Regulation to the European Parliament and to the Council. The reports shall be made public.

properties.business_description: This article mandates that the European Commission must evaluate and review the GDPR every four years, starting from 25 May 2020. While the article itself does not impose direct actions on controllers or processors, it highlights the importance of monitoring regulatory updates and being prepared to adapt to any changes that may arise from these evaluations.
properties.obligation_text: By 25 May 2020 and every four years thereafter, the Commission shall submit a report on the evaluation and review of this Regulation to the European Parliament and to the Council. The reports shall be made public.

properties.business_description: Article 98 of the GDPR allows the European Commission to propose changes to other EU laws related to data protection. This article is triggered when inconsistencies in data protection laws are identified, prompting the Commission to consider amendments. properties.obligation_text: The Commission shall, if appropriate, submit legislative proposals with a view to amending other Union legal acts on the protection of personal data, in order to ensure uniform and consistent protection of natural persons with regard to processing.

properties.obligation_text: The Commission shall, if appropriate, submit legislative proposals with a view to amending other Union legal acts on the protection of personal data, in order to ensure uniform and consistent protection of natural persons with regard to processing.

This means they must ensure compliance with its provisions by this time. Per ISO 27003:2017 §10.2 (renumbered to §10.1 in ISO 27001:2022): the ISMS is evaluated for continual improvement across suitability (do external/internal issues, interested-parties requirements, objectives, and risks remain properly addressed?), adequacy (are ISMS processes and controls compatible with organizational purposes and activities?), and effectiveness (are intended outcomes achieved, risks managed to meet objectives, and resources commensurate with results?). Improvement opportunities can also emerge from managing nonconformities. Actions to address improvement opportunities should be treated as a subset of §6.1.1 risk-and-opportunity actions.
properties.obligation_text: The organization shall continually improve the suitability, adequacy and effectiveness of the information security management system.
subject: information_security
properties.title: Continual improvement

properties.business_description:
When a nonconformity occurs, the organization shall: a) react to the nonconformity, and as applicable: 1) take action to control and correct it; 2) deal with the consequences; b) evaluate the need for action to eliminate the causes of nonconformity, in order that it does not recur or occur elsewhere, by: 1) reviewing the nonconformity; 2) determining the causes of the nonconformity; and 3) determi

[Related guidance: ISO 27003:2017]

Per ISO 27003:2017 §10.1 (renumbered to §10.2 in ISO 27001:2022): a nonconformity is a non-fulfilment of an ISMS requirement. Corrections address the nonconformity immediately; corrective actions eliminate the cause to prevent recurrence. The handling process should identify extent and impact, decide on corrections, analyse root cause, determine corrective action, plan and implement, verify effectiveness. Sources of nonconformities include audits, complaints, incidents, monitoring results, unmet objectives. Documented information on nonconformities and actions must be retained.
properties.obligation_text: When a nonconformity occurs, the organization shall: a) react to the nonconformity, and as applicable: 1) take action to control and correct it; 2) deal with the consequences; b) evaluate the need for action to eliminate the causes of nonconformity, in order that it does not recur or occur elsewhere, by: 1) reviewing the nonconformity; 2) determining the causes of the nonconformity; and 3) determining if similar nonconformities exist, or could potentially occur; c) implement any action needed; d) review the effectiveness of any corrective action taken; and e) make changes to the information security management system, if necessary. Corrective actions shall be appropriate to the effects of the nonconformities encountered. Documented information shall be available as evidence of the nature of the nonconformities and any subsequent actions taken, and the results of any corrective action.
subject: information_security
properties.title: Nonconformity and corrective action

properties.business_description:
The organization shall determine external and internal issues that are relevant to its purpose and that affect its ability to achieve the intended outcome(s) of its information security management system.

[Related guidance: ISO 27003:2017]

Per ISO 27003:2017 §4.1: understanding the organization's context is a continuous ISMS function. External issues include social, cultural, political, legal, financial, technological, natural, and competitive aspects; internal issues span culture, policy, governance, contractual relationships, capabilities, physical infrastructure, information systems, and prior audit results. Analysis serves three purposes — scoping the ISMS, determining risks and opportunities, and ensuring the ISMS adapts to change. Reviews should be regular; outputs feed §4.3 (scope), §6.1 (risk actions), and §9.3 (management review).

properties.obligation_text: The organization shall determine external and internal issues that are relevant to its purpose and that affect its ability to achieve the intended outcome(s) of its information security management system.
